وَنَعْتَقِدُ الْمَسْحَ عَلَى الْخُفَّيْنِ:
 ثَلَاثًا لِلْمُسَافِرِ وَيَوْمًا وَلَيْلَةً لِلْمُقِيمِ وَنَعْتَقِدُ الصَّبْرَ عَلَى السُّلْطَانِ مِنْ قُرَيْشٍ؛ مَا كَانَ مِنْ جَوْرٍ أَوْ عَدْلٍ. مَا أَقَامَ الصَّلَاةَ مِنْ الْجُمَعِ وَالْأَعْيَادِ. وَالْجِهَادُ مَعَهُمْ مَاضٍ إلَى يَوْمِ الْقِيَامَةِ. وَالصَّلَاةُ فِي الْجَمَاعَةِ حَيْثُ يُنَادَى لَهَا وَاجِبٌ؛ إذَا لَمْ يَكُنْ عُذْرٌ أَوْ مَانِعٌ وَالتَّرَاوِيحُ سُنَّةٌ؛ وَنَشْهَدُ أَنَّ مَنْ تَرَكَ الصَّلَاةَ عَمْدًا فَهُوَ كَافِرٌ وَالشَّهَادَةُ وَالْبَرَاءَةُ بِدْعَةٌ وَالصَّلَاةُ عَلَى مَنْ مَاتَ مَنْ أَهْلِ الْقِبْلَةِ سُنَّةٌ؛ وَلَا نُنَزِّلُ أَحَدًا جَنَّةً وَلَا نَارًا حَتَّى يَكُونَ اللَّهُ يُنَزِّلُهُمْ؛ وَالْمِرَاءُ وَالْجِدَالُ فِي الدِّينِ بِدْعَةٌ. وَنَعْتَقِدُ أَنَّ مَا شَجَرَ بَيْنَ أَصْحَابِ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ أَمْرُهُمْ إلَى اللَّهِ وَنَتَرَحَّمُ عَلَى عَائِشَةَ ونترضى عَنْهَا؛ وَالْقَوْلُ فِي اللَّفْظِ وَالْمَلْفُوظِ؛ وَكَذَلِكَ فِي الِاسْمِ وَالْمُسَمَّى بِدْعَةٌ؛ وَالْقَوْلُ فِي الْإِيمَانِ مَخْلُوقٌ أَوْ غَيْرُ مَخْلُوقٍ بِدْعَةٌ. وَاعْلَمْ أَنِّي ذَكَرْت اعْتِقَادَ أَهْلِ السُّنَّةِ عَلَى ظَاهِرِ مَا وَرَدَ عَنْ الصَّحَابَةِ وَالتَّابِعِينَ مُجْمَلًا مِنْ غَيْرِ اسْتِقْصَاءٍ؛ إذْ تَقَدَّمَ الْقَوْلُ مِنْ مَشَايِخِنَا الْمَعْرُوفِينَ مَنْ أَهْلِ الْإِبَانَةِ وَالدِّيَانَةِ إلَّا أَنِّي أَحْبَبْت أَنْ أَذْكُرَ 
" عُقُودَ أَصْحَابِنَا الْمُتَصَوِّفَةِ "
 فِيمَا أَحْدَثَتْهُ طَائِفَةٌ نُسِبُوا إلَيْهِمْ مَا قَدْ تخرصوا مِنْ الْقَوْلِ بِمَا نَزَّهَ اللَّهَ تَعَالَى الْمَذْهَبُ وَأَهْلُهُ مِنْ ذَلِكَ.
 إلَى أَنْ قَالَ:
 وَقَرَأْت لِمُحَمَّدِ بْنِ جَرِيرٍ الطبري فِي كِتَابٍ سَمَّاهُ 
" التَّبْصِيرَ "
 كَتَبَ بِذَلِكَ إلَى أَهْلِ طبرستان فِي اخْتِلَافٍ عِنْدَهُمْ؛ وَسَأَلُوهُ أَنْ يُصَنِّفَ لَهُمْ
translated_text:
And we believe in wiping over leather socks: for three days for a traveller, and for a day and a night for a resident. We believe in patiently bearing with a ruler from Quraysh, whether he is unjust or just, so long as he maintains the Friday and Eid prayers. Jihad under their leadership continues until the Day of Resurrection. Congregational prayer wherever the call to it is made is obligatory, unless there is an excuse or impediment, and the Tarāwīh prayers are a sunnah.

We testify that whoever deliberately abandons prayer is a disbeliever. Testifying to individuals’ ultimate fate and disavowing them are innovations. Offering the funeral prayer for deceased Muslims is a sunnah. We assign no one to Paradise or Hell until Allah assigns them there. Quarrelling and disputation over religion are innovations.

We believe that the disputes that arose among the Companions of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, are for Allah to judge. We pray for mercy upon ʿĀ’ishah and ask Allah to be pleased with her. Theological pronouncements concerning the utterance and what is uttered, and likewise concerning the name and the named, are innovations. Declaring faith to be created or uncreated is an innovation.

Know that I have briefly set out the beliefs of Ahl al-Sunnah according to the apparent meaning of what has been transmitted from the Companions and their successors, without attempting an exhaustive account. Our shaykhs, known for their clear exposition and religious devotion, have already addressed this. However, I wished to mention ‘the creedal tenets of our Sufi companions’ in response to the innovations introduced by a group affiliated with them: fabricated claims from which Allah Most High has kept this school and its adherents free.”

He went on to say:

“I read a book by Muhammad ibn Jarīr al-Tabarī entitled al-Tabsīr (Clarification), which he wrote to the people of Tabaristān concerning a disagreement among them. They had asked him to compose for them

original_text:
مَا يَعْتَقِدُهُ وَيَذْهَبُ إلَيْهِ؛ فَذَكَرَ فِي كِتَابِهِ اخْتِلَافَ الْقَائِلِينَ بِرُؤْيَةِ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى؛ فَذَكَرَ عَنْ طَائِفَةٍ إثْبَاتَ الرُّؤْيَةِ فِي الدُّنْيَا وَالْآخِرَةِ. وَنَسَبَ هَذِهِ الْمَقَالَةَ إلَى 
" الصُّوفِيَّةِ "
 قَاطِبَةً لَمْ يَخُصَّ طَائِفَةً. فَبَيَّنَ أَنَّ ذَلِكَ عَلَى جَهَالَةٍ مِنْهُ بِأَقْوَالِ الْمُخْلَصِينَ مِنْهُمْ؛ وَكَانَ مَنْ نُسِبَ إلَيْهِ ذَلِكَ الْقَوْلُ - بَعْدَ أَنْ ادَّعَى عَلَى الطَّائِفَةِ - ابْنِ أُخْتِ عَبْدِ الْوَاحِدِ بْنِ زَيْدٍ؛ وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ بِمَحِلِّهِ عِنْدَ الْمُخْلَصِينَ؛ فَكَيْفَ بِابْنِ أُخْتِهِ. وَلَيْسَ إذَا أَحْدَثَ الزَّائِغُ فِي نِحْلَتِهِ قَوْلًا نُسِبَ إلَى الْجُمْلَةِ؛ كَذَلِكَ فِي الْفُقَهَاءِ وَالْمُحَدِّثِينَ لَيْسَ مَنْ أَحْدَثَ قَوْلًا فِي الْفِقْهِ؛ وَلَيْسَ فِيهِ حَدِيثٌ يُنَاسِبُ ذَلِكَ؛ يُنْسَبُ ذَلِكَ إلَى جُمْلَةِ الْفُقَهَاءِ وَالْمُحَدِّثِينَ. وَاعْلَمْ أَنَّ لَفْظَ 
" الصُّوفِيَّةِ "
 وَعُلُومَهُمْ تَخْتَلِفُ فَيُطْلِقُونَ أَلْفَاظَهُمْ عَلَى مَوْضُوعَاتٍ لَهُمْ وَمَرْمُوزَاتٍ وَإِشَارَاتٍ تَجْرِي فِيمَا بَيْنَهُمْ فَمَنْ لَمْ يُدَاخِلْهُمْ عَلَى التَّحْقِيقِ وَنَازَلَ مَا هُمْ عَلَيْهِ رَجَعَ عَنْهُمْ وَهُوَ خَاسِئٌ وَحَسِيرٌ. ثُمَّ ذَكَرَ إطْلَاقَهُمْ لَفْظَ 
" الرُّؤْيَةِ "
 بِالتَّقْيِيدِ.
 فَقَالَ:
 كَثِيرًا مَا يَقُولُونَ رَأَيْت اللَّهَ يَقُولُ.
 وَذَكَرَ عَنْ جَعْفَرِ بْنِ مُحَمَّدٍ قَوْلُهُ لَمَّا سُئِلَ:
 هَلْ رَأَيْت اللَّهَ حِينَ عَبَدْته؟ قَالَ رَأَيْت اللَّهَ ثُمَّ عَبَدْته. فَقَالَ السَّائِلُ كَيْفَ رَأَيْته؟
 فَقَالَ:
 لَمْ تَرَهُ الْأَبْصَارُ بِتَحْدِيدِ الْأَعْيَانِ؛
 وَلَكِنْ رُؤْيَةُ الْقُلُوبِ بِتَحْقِيقِ الْإِيقَانِ ثُمَّ قَالَ:
 " وَإِنَّهُ تَعَالَى يُرَى فِي الْآخِرَةِ كَمَا أَخْبَرَ فِي كِتَابِهِ وَذَكَرَهُ رَسُولُهُ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ. هَذَا قَوْلُنَا وَقَوْلُ أَئِمَّتِنَا دُونَ الْجُهَّالِ مِنْ أَهْلِ الْغَبَاوَةِ فِينَا.
translated_text:
an account of his beliefs and views. In his book, he described the differences among those who affirm seeing Allah Most High, mentioning a group who affirm seeing Him both in this world and in the Hereafter. He attributed this position to the “Sufis” as a whole, without singling out any particular group.”

He explained that this reflected al-Tabarī’s ignorance of the views of the sincere among them. After attributing this position to the entire group, the individual he named as holding it was the nephew of ‘Abd al-Wāhid ibn Zayd. Allah knows best ‘Abd al-Wāhid’s standing among the sincere—so what, then, of his nephew? When someone who has gone astray introduces an opinion into his own school, it should not be attributed to the whole group. The same applies to jurists and hadith scholars: if someone introduces an opinion in jurisprudence for which there is no corresponding hadith, it should not be attributed to all jurists and hadith scholars.

Know that the Sufis’ terminology and disciplines vary. They apply their expressions to meanings particular to them, and to symbols and allusions current among themselves. Anyone who has not truly associated with them and engaged with their way will leave them humbled and exhausted.

He then discussed their qualified use of the word “seeing,” saying: “They often say, ‘I saw Allah.’” He goes on to relate that Ja‘far ibn Muhammad was asked, “Did you see Allah when you worshipped Him?” He replied, “I saw Allah, then worshipped Him.” The questioner asked, “How did you see Him?”

He replied: “The eyes have not seen Him by discerning a bounded entity; rather, hearts see Him through firmly established certainty.”

He then said: “Allah Most High will indeed be seen in the Hereafter, as He has stated in His Book and as His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, has related. This is our position and that of our imams, not that of the ignorant and foolish among us.

original_text:
وَإِنَّ مِمَّا نَعْتَقِدُهُ أَنَّ اللَّهَ حَرَّمَ عَلَى الْمُؤْمِنِينَ دِمَاءَهُمْ وَأَمْوَالَهُمْ وَأَعْرَاضَهُمْ وَذَكَرَ ذَلِكَ فِي حَجَّةِ الْوَدَاعِ فَمَنْ زَعَمَ أَنَّهُ يَبْلُغُ مَعَ اللَّهِ إلَى دَرَجَةٍ يُبِيحُ الْحَقَّ لَهُ مَا حُظِرَ عَلَى الْمُؤْمِنِينَ - إلَّا الْمُضْطَرَّ عَلَى حَالٍ يَلْزَمُهُ إحْيَاءٌ لِلنَّفْسِ لَوْ بَلَغَ الْعَبْدُ مَا بَلَغَ مِنْ الْعِلْمِ وَالْعِبَادَاتِ - فَذَلِكَ كُفْرٌ بِاَللَّهِ وَقَائِلٌ ذَلِكَ قَائِلٌ بِالْإِبَاحَةِ وَهُمْ المنسلخون مِنْ الدِّيَانَةِ. وَإِنَّ مِمَّا نَعْتَقِدُهُ تَرْكُ إطْلَاقِ تَسْمِيَةِ 
" الْعِشْقِ "
 عَلَى اللَّهِ تَعَالَى وَبَيَّنَ أَنَّ ذَلِكَ لَا يَجُوزُ لِاشْتِقَاقِهِ وَلِعَدَمِ وُرُودِ الشَّرْعِ بِهِ.
 وَقَالَ:
 أَدْنَى مَا فِيهِ إنَّهُ بِدْعَةٌ وَضَلَالَةٌ وَفِيمَا نَصَّ اللَّهُ مِنْ ذِكْرِ الْمَحَبَّةِ كِفَايَةٌ.
وَإِنَّ مِمَّا نَعْتَقِدُهُ:
 أَنَّ اللَّهَ لَا يَحِلُّ فِي الْمَرْئِيَّاتِ وَأَنَّهُ الْمُتَفَرِّدُ بِكَمَالِ أَسْمَائِهِ وَصِفَاتِهِ بَائِنٌ مِنْ خَلْقِهِ مُسْتَوٍ عَلَى عَرْشِهِ وَأَنَّ الْقُرْآنَ كَلَامُهُ غَيْرَ مَخْلُوقٍ - حَيْثُ مَا تُلِيَ وَدُرِّسَ وَحُفِظَ -
 وَنَعْتَقِدُ أَنَّ اللَّهَ تَعَالَى اتَّخَذَ إبْرَاهِيمَ خَلِيلًا وَاِتَّخَذَ نَبِيَّنَا مُحَمَّدًا صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ خَلِيلًا وَحَبِيبًا وَالْخُلَّةُ لَهُمَا مِنْهُ عَلَى خِلَافِ مَا قَالَهُ الْمُعْتَزِلَةُ:
 إنَّ الْخُلَّةَ الْفَقْرُ وَالْحَاجَةُ.
 إلَى أَنْ قَالَ:
 " وَالْخُلَّةُ وَالْمَحَبَّةُ صِفَتَانِ لِلَّهِ هُوَ مَوْصُوفٌ بِهِمَا وَلَا تَدْخُلُ أَوْصَافُهُ تَحْتَ التَّكْيِيفِ وَالتَّشْبِيهِ وَصِفَاتُ الْخَلْقِ مِنْ الْمَحَبَّةِ وَالْخُلَّةِ جَائِزٌ عَلَيْهَا الْكَيْفُ؛ فَأَمَّا صِفَاتُهُ تَعَالَى فَمَعْلُومَةٌ فِي الْعِلْمِ وَمَوْجُودَةٌ فِي التَّعْرِيفِ قَدْ انْتَفَى عَنْهُمَا التَّشْبِيهُ فَالْإِيمَانُ بِهِ وَاجِبٌ وَاسْمُ الْكَيْفِيَّةِ عَنْ ذَلِكَ سَاقِطٌ.
translated_text:
We also believe that Allah has made the lives, property, and honour of believers inviolable to one another, as was declared at the Farewell Pilgrimage. Whoever claims that he can attain a station with Allah at which the True One permits him what is forbidden to believers—except for someone compelled by necessity in circumstances requiring him to preserve life—such a claim is disbelief in Allah, however far a servant may have advanced in knowledge and acts of worship. Whoever says this advocates freedom from religious prohibitions; such people have cast off religion.

We also believe that the term ‘ʿishq’ (passionate love) should not be applied to Allah Most High.” He explained that this is impermissible because of the term’s derivation and because it has no basis in the revealed law. He said: “At the very least, it is an innovation and a departure from right guidance. What Allah has explicitly stated concerning love is sufficient.

We also believe that Allah does not indwell visible things; that He alone possesses perfection in His names and attributes, is separate from His creation, and is established above His Throne; and that the Quran is His uncreated speech—wherever it is recited, studied, or memorized.

We believe that Allah Most High took Abraham as an intimate friend, and took our Prophet Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, as an intimate friend and a beloved one. This intimate friendship is bestowed upon them both by Him, contrary to the Muʿtazilah’s assertion that intimate friendship means poverty and need.”

He went on to say: “Intimate friendship and love are two attributes of Allah with which He is described. His attributes are not subject to specifying their manner or likening them to those of creation. The love and intimate friendship of created beings, by contrast, may be described in terms of their manner. As for His attributes, Most High, they are known as matters of knowledge and are set forth in the descriptions through which He is made known. Any likeness to creation is excluded from these two attributes. Belief in this is obligatory, while assigning a manner to it is excluded.

وَمِمَّا نَعْتَقِدُهُ أَنَّ اللَّهَ أَبَاحَ الْمَكَاسِبَ وَالتِّجَارَاتِ وَالصِّنَاعَاتِ وَإِنَّمَا حَرَّمَ اللَّهُ الْغِشَّ وَالظُّلْمَ وَأَمَّا مَنْ قَالَ بِتَحْرِيمِ تِلْكَ الْمَكَاسِبِ فَهُوَ ضَالٌّ مُضِلٌّ مُبْتَدِعٌ؛ إذْ لَيْسَ الْفَسَادُ وَالظُّلْمُ وَالْغِشُّ مِنْ التِّجَارَاتِ وَالصِّنَاعَاتِ فِي شَيْءٍ إنَّمَا حَرَّمَ اللَّهُ وَرَسُولُهُ الْفَسَادَ؛ لَا الْكَسْبَ وَالتِّجَارَاتِ؛ فَإِنَّ ذَلِكَ عَلَى أَصْلِ الْكِتَابِ وَالسُّنَّةِ جَائِزٌ إلَى يَوْمِ الْقِيَامَةِ وَإِنَّ مِمَّا نَعْتَقِدُ أَنَّ اللَّهَ لَا يَأْمُرُ بِأَكْلِ الْحَلَالِ ثُمَّ يُعْدِمُهُمْ الْوُصُولَ إلَيْهِ مِنْ جَمِيعِ الْجِهَاتِ؛ لِأَنَّ مَا طَالَبَهُمْ بِهِ مَوْجُودٌ إلَى يَوْمِ الْقِيَامَةِ؛ وَالْمُعْتَقَدُ أَنَّ الْأَرْضَ تَخْلُو مِنْ الْحَلَالِ وَالنَّاسَ يَتَقَلَّبُونَ فِي الْحَرَامِ؛ فَهُوَ مُبْتَدِعٌ ضَالٌّ إلَّا أَنَّهُ يَقِلُّ فِي مَوْضِعٍ وَيَكْثُرُ فِي مَوْضِعٍ؛ لَا أَنَّهُ مَفْقُودٌ مِنْ الْأَرْضِ.
وَمِمَّا نَعْتَقِدُهُ أَنَّا إذَا رَأَيْنَا مَنْ ظَاهِرُهُ جَمِيلٌ لَا نَتَّهِمُهُ فِي مَكْسَبِهِ وَمَالِهِ وَطَعَامِهِ؛ جَائِزٌ أَنْ يُؤْكَلَ طَعَامُهُ وَالْمُعَامَلَةَ فِي تِجَارَتِهِ؛ فَلَيْسَ عَلَيْنَا الْكَشْفُ عَمَّا قَالَهُ. فَإِنْ سَأَلَ سَائِلٌ عَلَى سَبِيلِ الِاحْتِيَاطِ؛ جَازَ إلَّا مِنْ دَاخِلِ الظُّلْمَةِ.

 فَالسُّؤَالُ وَالتَّوَقِّي؛ كَمَا سَأَلَ الصِّدِّيقُ غُلَامَهُ؛ فَإِنْ كَانَ مَعَهُ مِنْ الْمَالِ سِوَى ذَلِكَ مِمَّا هُوَ خَارِجٌ عَنْ تِلْكَ الْأَمْوَالِ فَاخْتَلَطَا فَلَا يُطْلَقُ عَلَيْهِ الْحَلَالُ وَلَا الْحَرَامُ إلَّا أَنَّهُ مُشْتَبَهٌ؛ فَمَنْ سَأَلَ اسْتَبْرَأَ لِدِينِهِ كَمَا فَعَلَ الصِّدِّيقُ. وَأَجَازَ ابْنُ مَسْعُودٍ وَسَلْمَانُ الْأَكْلَ مِنْهُ وَعَلَيْهِ التَّبِعَةُ وَالنَّاسُ طَبَقَاتٌ وَالدِّينُ الْحَنِيفِيَّةُ السَّمْحَةُ.
وَإِنَّ مِمَّا نَعْتَقِدُ أَنَّ الْعَبْدَ مَا دَامَ أَحْكَامُ الدَّارِ جَارِيَةٌ عَلَيْهِ فَلَا يَسْقُطُ عَنْهُ
translated_text:
We also believe that Allah has permitted earning a livelihood, commerce, and crafts, and has forbidden only fraud and injustice. Whoever declares these means of livelihood forbidden is a misguided innovator who leads others astray. Corruption, injustice, and fraud are not intrinsic to commerce or crafts. Allah and His Messenger have forbidden corruption, not earning a livelihood or commerce; these remain permissible until the Day of Resurrection on the basis of the Quran and Sunnah.

We also believe that Allah does not command people to consume what is lawful and then deny them every means of obtaining it. What He requires of them remains available until the Day of Resurrection. Whoever believes that the earth is devoid of lawful provision and that people conduct all their affairs through what is forbidden is a misguided innovator. Lawful provision may be scarce in one place and abundant in another, but it is not absent from the earth.

We also believe that, when we see someone whose outward conduct is good, we do not suspect his earnings, wealth, or food. It is permissible to eat his food and conduct business with him, and we are not required to investigate what he says. If someone makes inquiries as a precaution, this is permissible—except in the case of someone who associates with oppressors.

As for someone who withdraws from injustice, has acquired wealth wrongfully, and also possesses other wealth, inquiry and caution are called for, just as al-Siddīq questioned his servant. If he possesses other wealth apart from those funds and the two become mixed, the mixture cannot be described categorically as lawful or forbidden; rather, it is doubtful. Whoever makes inquiries safeguards his religion, as al-Siddīq did. Ibn Masʿūd and Salmān permitted eating from it, with responsibility resting upon its owner. People are of differing ranks, and the religion is the upright, tolerant faith.

fear and hope. Whoever claims “security” is ignorant of Allah and of what He has declared concerning Himself:

“None feel secure from Allah’s plan except the losers.”

I have devoted a separate work to exposing the failings of those who hold this view.

We believe that servitude to Allah remains binding upon a person so long as he retains his reason and understands his rights and duties. He remains subject to the rulings appropriate to his strength and ability, for Allah did not exempt the prophets, the steadfastly truthful, the martyrs, or the righteous from this servitude. Whoever claims to have passed from the bondage of servitude into the open expanse of freedom by casting off servitude and entering into the ordinances of oneness, interwoven with the bonds of otherness, is unquestionably an unbeliever—except someone afflicted by an illness or tenderness of feeling, who consequently becomes mentally impaired, insane, or delirious, with his reason disordered, or is overcome by a swoon that suspends the rulings dependent upon reason and deprives him of discernment and understanding. Such a person is outside the faith and has departed from the Sharia.

Whoever claims insight into people, knowing their stations and their standing before Allah without revelation conveyed through the words of a Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is outside the faith. Whoever claims to know people’s ultimate fate and destination, the state in which they will die, and how their lives will end—without revelation from the words of Allah and His Messenger—has incurred Allah’s wrath. “Intuitive discernment” is real, according to the principles we have mentioned; it has nothing to do with the claims we have described.

Whoever claims that His attributes, exalted is He, are bound up with his own attributes—not referring merely to a sign of greatness, divine enabling, and guidance, but meaning His eternal attributes, Mighty and Majestic is He—is an adherent of indwelling who professes divinity and fusion. This is unquestionably unbelief.

{الَّذِينَ يَسْتَمِعُونَ الْقَوْلَ فَيَتَّبِعُونَ أَحْسَنَهُ}
 الْآيَةَ.
translated_text:
We believe that all souls are created. Whoever says that they are uncreated has echoed the Nestorian Christians’ belief concerning the Messiah. This is unbelief in Allah, the Most Great.

Whoever says that any of Allah’s attributes indwells a servant, or maintains that Allah is divisible, has disbelieved. The Quran is Allah’s speech: it is neither created nor indwelling in anything created. However it is recited, read, or memorized, it remains an attribute of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. The act of reading is distinct from what is read, and recitation is distinct from what is recited, for He, Mighty and Majestic, together with all His attributes and names, is uncreated. Whoever says otherwise is an unbeliever.

We believe that recitation “set to song-like melodies” is an innovation and a deviation, and that “poems” are an innovation. These fall into two categories. The good among them mention Allah’s blessings and favours and describe the righteous and the God-fearing. This is permissible, although it is preferable to leave it aside and occupy oneself with remembering Allah, the Quran, and religious knowledge.

As for poetry describing visible things and created beings, listening to it while applying those descriptions to Allah is unbelief. Listening to songs and quatrains while applying their words to Allah is unbelief. Dancing to a beat and attributing religious merit to dancers constitute wickedness; as practices of induced ecstasy and singing, they are idle amusement and play.

It is forbidden for anyone to listen to poems and quatrains set to melodies—as encountered among people of such inclinations—as a form of remembrance, except someone who already understands the principles of monotheism, knows Allah’s names and attributes, and understands which expressions may be applied to Allah Most High and which are unbefitting His majesty and things He transcends. Such a person’s listening should accord with His words:

“Those who listen to what is said and follow the best of it”—to the end of the verse.

 وَبَلَغَنِي أَنَّهُ قِيلَ لِبِشْرِ بْنِ الْحَارِثِ:
 إنَّ أَصْحَابَك قَدْ أَحْدَثُوا شَيْئًا يُقَالُ لَهُ الْقَصَائِدُ. قَالَ مِثْلُ أيش؟
 قَالَ مِثْلُ قَوْلِهِ:
 اصْبِرِي يَا نَفْسُ حَتَّى تَسْكُنِي دَارَ الْجَلِيلِ فَقَالَ: حَسَنٌ وَأَيْنَ يَكُونُ هَؤُلَاءِ الَّذِينَ يَسْتَمِعُونَ ذَلِكَ؟ قَالَ قُلْت بِبَغْدَادَ فَقَالَ كَذَبُوا - وَاَللَّهِ الَّذِي لَا إلَهَ غَيْرُهُ - لَا يَسْكُنُ بِبَغْدَادَ مَنْ يَسْتَمِعُ ذَلِكَ.
 قَالَ أَبُو عَبْدِ اللَّهِ:
 وَمِمَّا نَقُولُ - وَهُوَ قَوْلُ أَئِمَّتِنَا - إنَّ الْفَقِيرَ إذَا احْتَاجَ وَصَبَرَ وَلَمْ يَتَكَفَّفْ إلَى وَقْتٍ يَفْتَحُ اللَّهُ لَهُ كَانَ أَعْلَى فَمَنْ عَجَزَ عَنْ الصَّبْرِ كَانَ السُّؤَالُ أَوْلَى بِهِ عَلَى قَوْلِهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ 
{لَأَنْ يَأْخُذُ أَحَدُكُمْ حَبْلَهُ}
 الْحَدِيثَ وَنَقُولُ: إنَّ تَرْكَ الْمَكَاسِبِ غَيْرُ جَائِزٍ إلَّا بِشَرَائِطَ مَوْسُومَةٍ مِنْ التَّعَفُّفِ وَالِاسْتِغْنَاءِ
translated_text:
Anyone who is ignorant of these matters and deliberately listens to such words as referring to Allah, without making these distinctions, undoubtedly commits unbelief. Thus, gathering such words and listening to them as referring to Allah is impermissible, except for someone familiar with what I have described concerning the remembrance of Allah, His blessings, and His attributes, Mighty and Majestic, in which created beings share no quality or description. Even then, refraining from this is preferable and more prudent. Fundamentally, it is an innovation, and listening to singing carries a risk of temptation. “Quatrains,” too, are an innovation. This was condemned by al-Muttalibī, Mālik, al-Thawrī, Yazīd ibn Hārūn, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and Ishāq. Following their example is preferable to following people who are unknown in religion and have no standing among the elect.

I have heard that Bishr ibn al-Hārith was told, “Your companions have introduced something called poems.”

He asked, “Such as what?”

The reply was, “Such as these words:

Be patient, O my soul, until you dwell
In the abode of the Majestic One.”

He said, “Good. And where are these people who listen to this?”

The narrator said, “I replied, ‘In Baghdad.’”

He said, “They have lied! By Allah, besides whom there is no god, no one who listens to this lives in Baghdad.”

Abū ‘Abd Allāh said:

Among our teachings—which are also the teachings of our imams—is that a poor person who suffers need, remains patient, and does not beg until Allah grants him relief holds a higher rank. For someone unable to endure patiently, asking is more appropriate, in accordance with the Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“For one of you to take his rope”—to the end of the hadith.

We also maintain that abandoning the pursuit of a livelihood is impermissible except under specified conditions involving abstaining from begging and being independent

translated_text:
of what others possess; anyone who makes begging his profession while able-bodied is truly blameworthy and has overstepped the bounds.

We also maintain that, regarding one who listens to singing and musical entertainments, the matter is as he, peace be upon him, said:

“Singing causes hypocrisy to grow in the heart.”

Even if it does not render one an unbeliever, it is unquestionably sinful.

The position we adopt is that of our imams: to refrain from disputation in religion and from debating whether faith is created or uncreated. Whoever claims that the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is an intermediary conveying the message, and that those to whom he was sent are superior to him, is an unbeliever in Allah. Whoever advocates dispensing with intermediaries altogether has disbelieved. End of quotation.

Among their later scholars was the shaykh and imam Abū Muhammad ‘Abd al-Qādir ibn Abī Sālih al-Jīlānī. He said in his book al-Ghunya:

“As for knowing the Creator through signs and proofs, stated briefly, it means knowing with certainty that Allah is One, Unique.”

Later he said:

“He is in the direction of elevation, established over the Throne, encompassing all dominion; His knowledge encompasses all things:

‘To Him ascends good speech, and righteous deeds raise it.’

‘He directs the affairs from heaven to earth; then they ascend to Him in a Day whose measure is a thousand years by your reckoning.’

It is impermissible to describe Him as being everywhere. Rather, it should be said that He is above the heavens, over the Throne, as He said:

‘The Most Merciful established Himself over the Throne.’

He then cited verses and hadiths, until he said:

“The attribute of establishment over the Throne should be affirmed without reinterpretation; it is His Essence that is established over the Throne.”

He said: “His being over the Throne is mentioned in every Book revealed to every prophet sent, without specifying how.”

He discussed this at length, beyond what can be accommodated here, and made similar statements concerning the other attributes. Were I to mention everything the scholars have said on this subject, the book would become exceedingly long.

Abū ‘Umar ibn ‘Abd al-Barr said:

“We have transmitted from Mālik ibn Anas, Sufyān al-Thawrī, Sufyān ibn ‘Uyayna, al-Awzā‘ī, and Ma‘mar ibn Rāshid, concerning the hadiths on the divine attributes, that they all said: ‘Let them stand as they have been transmitted.’”

Abū ‘Umar said:

“Whatever has come from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, through reliable transmitters, or from his Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, is knowledge upon which religious practice is based. Whatever was introduced after them, without any foundation in what was transmitted from them, is innovation and misguidance.”

In his Commentary on al-Muwatta’, when discussing the hadith of the descent, he said:

“This hadith is firmly established in transmission and authentic in its chain of transmission. Hadith scholars do not differ concerning its authenticity. It has also been transmitted through routes other than this one, through reports of upright transmitters from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. It provides evidence that Allah is above the heavens, established over the Throne, above the seven heavens, as the community has affirmed. It is among their proofs against the Mu‘tazila, who claim that Allah Most High is everywhere in His holy Essence.”

He said:

“The evidence supporting the correctness of what the people of truth have said is Allah’s saying”—and he cited some verses—

until he said:

“This is so well known among ordinary people and scholars alike that it needs no more than to be stated, for it is self-evident knowledge that no one taught them and that no Muslim has disputed with them.”

Abū ‘Umar ibn ‘Abd al-Barr also said:

“The scholars among the Companions and their successors from whom interpretations have been transmitted unanimously agreed, in explaining His saying:

‘There is no private conversation among three but He is their fourth,’

that He is over the Throne and His knowledge is everywhere. No one whose opinion carries evidentiary weight disagreed with them on this.”

Abū ‘Umar also said:

“Ahl al-Sunnah unanimously agree on acknowledging all the attributes mentioned in the Quran and Sunnah, believing in them, and understanding them in their real, not figurative, sense. However, they do not specify how any of them are, nor do they set a limited definition for any of them.

“As for the people of innovation—the Jahmiyya, all the Mu‘tazila, and the Khawārij—they all deny these attributes and do not understand any of them in their real sense. They claim that whoever affirms them likens Allah to His creation, whereas those who affirm them regard these deniers as denying the One who is worshipped. The truth lies with those who uphold what the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, declare. They are the leading scholars of the Muslim community.”

These are the words of Ibn ‘Abd al-Barr, the leading scholar of the Maghrib.

His contemporary, the hadith master “Abū Bakr al-Bayhaqī,” despite his allegiance to the speculative theologians among the followers of Abū al-Hasan al-Ash‘arī and his defence of them, said in his book “The Names and Attributes”:

“Chapter on the reports affirming the two Hands as two attributes—not as bodily limbs—in view of the transmitted report of

the truthful one to that effect.” Allah Most High said:

“O Iblīs, what prevented you from prostrating to what I created with My two Hands?”

And He said:

“Rather, both His Hands are outstretched.”

He cited the authentic hadiths on this subject, including the words found in more than one report of the hadith of intercession:

“O Adam, you are the father of mankind; Allah created you with His Hand.”

And the words in the agreed-upon hadith:

“You are Moses; Allah chose you by speaking to you and inscribed the Tablets for you with His Hand.”

In another wording:

“And He wrote the Torah for you with His Hand.”

And the report in Sahīh Muslim:

“He, glorified be He, planted with His Hand, in the Garden of Eden, the honour reserved for His friends.”

And the saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“On the Day of Resurrection, the earth will become a single loaf of bread, which the Compeller will turn over with His Hand as one of you turns over his loaf while travelling, as a welcoming provision for the people of Paradise.”

He also cited hadiths containing such sayings as:

“The command is in My Hand.”

“And all good is in Your Hands.”

“By Him in whose Hand is Muhammad’s soul.”

And:

“Allah extends His Hand at night so that those who sinned during the day may repent, and He extends His Hand during the day so that those who sinned during the night may repent.”

And his saying:

“Those who act justly will be with Allah on pulpits of light, to the right of the Most Merciful—and both His Hands are right Hands.”

Abū al-Hasan al-Ash‘arī also said in his book entitled al-Ibānah fī Usūl al-Diyānah (An Exposition of the Foundations of Religion)—which his followers have stated was the last book he authored and upon which they rely when defending him against his critics:

“Chapter: An Exposition of the Position of the People of Truth and the Sunnah

If someone says, ‘You have rejected the positions of the Mu‘tazilah, the Qadariyyah, the Jahmiyyah, the Harūriyyah, the Rāfidah and the Murji’ah. Tell us, then, the position you hold and the religious beliefs you profess,’ he should be told:

‘The position we hold and the religious beliefs we profess consist in adhering to the words of our Lord, the Sunnah of our Prophet, and what has been transmitted from the Companions, the Successors and the imams of hadith. To these we hold fast. We affirm the positions held by Abū ‘Abd Allāh Ahmad ibn Hanbal—may Allah make his face radiant, raise his rank and grant him abundant reward—and oppose whatever contradicts his position. For he is the eminent imam and consummate leader through whom Allah made the truth manifest, repelled error, clarified the path, and suppressed the innovations of the innovators, the deviations of those who stray, and the doubts of the doubters. May Allah have mercy on him: a foremost imam, a revered man of high standing, and a great teacher who imparted understanding.’

Our position, in brief, is that we affirm belief in Allah, His angels, His Books, His messengers, what they brought from Allah, and what trustworthy transmitters have related from the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. We reject none of this;

His rising over the Throne to mean power. If it were as they claim, there would be no distinction between the Throne and the seventh earth, for Allah has power over everything. As for the earth, Allah has power over it, over latrines, and over everything in the world. If Allah’s rising over the Throne meant exercising dominion—and He, mighty and majestic, exercises dominion over all things—then He would have risen over the Throne, the earth, the heavens, latrines, and filth, since He has power and dominion over all these things.

Since He has power over everything, yet no Muslim considers it permissible to say that Allah has risen over latrines and privies, rising over the Throne cannot mean exercising the dominion that encompasses all things. Rather, its meaning must pertain specifically to the Throne, to the exclusion of everything else.

He also cited evidence from the Quran, hadith, scholarly consensus, and reason.

Then he said:

(Chapter on the Face, the Two Eyes, Sight, and the Two Hands, and the Verses Concerning Them.

He extensively refuted those who interpret these attributes figuratively, in a discussion too long to reproduce here. Among his statements is the following:

“If we are asked, ‘Do you say that Allah has two Hands?’

We reply: We do affirm this, as indicated by His words, exalted is He:

‘The Hand of Allah is above their hands.’

And His words, exalted is He:

‘What I created with My two Hands.’

It is narrated that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

‘Allah stroked Adam’s back with His Hand and brought forth his descendants from him. He created the Garden of Eden with His Hand and wrote the Torah with His Hand.’

The aforementioned report from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, also states:

‘Allah created Adam with His Hand, created the Garden of Eden with His Hand, wrote the Torah with His Hand, and planted the Tūbā tree with His Hand.’

translated_text:
Nor is it permissible, either in the Arabic language or in customary speech, for someone to say, ‘I did such and such with my hand,’ intending by ‘hand’ a favor. Since Allah addressed the Arabs in their own language, using what was understood in their speech and intelligible in their discourse, and since eloquent speakers cannot say, ‘I did such and such with my hand,’ intending thereby a favor, it is untenable to interpret His words, exalted is He, ‘with My two Hands,’ as meaning a favor.” He discussed this and similar points at length.

The judge Abū Bakr Muhammad ibn al-Tayyib al-Bāqillānī, the theologian—who was the most accomplished of the theologians affiliated with al-Ashʿarī, with none equal to him either before or after him—said in his own work, Kitāb al-Ibānah (The Book of Clarification):

“If someone asks, ‘What is the evidence that Allah has a Face and a Hand?’ he is answered with His words:

‘And there will remain the Face of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Honor.’

And His words, exalted is He:

‘What prevented you from prostrating to that which I created with My two Hands?’

Thus, He affirmed for Himself a Face and a Hand.

If he asks, ‘Why, then, do you deny that His Face and Hand are bodily organs, when you cannot conceive of a face or a hand except as a bodily organ?’ we reply: This does not necessarily follow. Likewise, even if we cannot conceive of a living, knowing, powerful being except as a body, neither we nor you must therefore judge Allah, glorified and exalted is He, to be a body. Nor must everything that subsists in itself be a substance merely because neither we nor you have encountered anything self-subsisting in our observable experience except as such;

translated_text:
and the same answer applies if they say, ‘His knowledge, life, speech, hearing, sight, and all His other essential attributes must be accidents,’ appealing to what is found in experience as their justification.”

He also said:

“If someone asks, ‘Do you then say that He is everywhere?’ he is answered: Allah forbid! Rather, He is established above His Throne, as He stated in His Book:

‘The Most Merciful rose over the Throne.’

And Allah, exalted is He, said:

‘To Him ascends good speech, and righteous deeds raise it.’

And He said:

‘Do you feel secure that He who is above the heaven will not cause the earth to swallow you as it suddenly shakes?’”

He said:

“If He were everywhere, He would be inside a person’s belly and mouth, in latrines, and in places one prefers not to mention. He would necessarily increase as places increased, whenever He created places that had not existed, and decrease as they decreased, whenever places that had existed ceased to exist. It would also be proper to turn to Him in supplication toward the earth, behind us, to our right, or to our left. Yet the Muslims have unanimously agreed to the contrary and have deemed anyone who says this mistaken.”

He also said in this book:

“His essential attributes, which He has always possessed and will always possess, are life, knowledge, power, hearing, sight, speech, will, everlastingness, the Face, the two Eyes, the two Hands, anger, and pleasure.”

He said more than this in Kitāb al-Tamhīd (The Book of Introduction), but I do not have a copy at hand. His statements and those of other theologians on matters of this kind are plentiful for anyone who seeks them, although the Book, the Sunnah, and the reports from the early generations suffice us without recourse to any other discourse.

وَكَذَلِكَ قَالَ أَبُو الْمَعَالِي الجُوَيْنِي فِي كِتَابِهِ 
" الرِّسَالَةِ النِّظَامِيَّةِ "
 اخْتَلَفَ مَسَالِكُ الْعُلَمَاءِ فِي هَذِهِ الظَّوَاهِرِ؛ فَرَأَى بَعْضُهُمْ تَأْوِيلَهَا وَالْتَزَمَ ذَلِكَ فِي آي
translated_text:
“The crux of the matter” is that Allah grants His servant wisdom and faith, giving him the intellect and religious commitment to understand and follow the faith. Then the light of the Book and the Sunnah suffices him without need of anything else. Yet many people have affiliated themselves with particular groups of theologians, thinking well of them to the exclusion of others and imagining that they have established truths in this field that no one else has established. Even if every sign were brought to such a person, he would not follow it until something from their statements was presented to him. Yet, despite this, they oppose their own predecessors rather than follow them.

If they embraced the guidance they find in their predecessors’ statements, one could hope that, with sincerity in seeking the truth, they would increase in guidance. Whoever accepts the truth only from a particular group, but then fails to adhere to the truth that this group has brought, bears some resemblance to the Jews of whom Allah said:

“And when it is said to them, ‘Believe in what Allah has revealed,’ they say, ‘We believe in what was revealed to us,’ and they disbelieve in what came after it, although it is the truth confirming what they have. Say, ‘Why, then, did you kill the prophets of Allah before, if you were believers?’”

For the Jews said, “We believe only in what was revealed to us.” Allah, exalted is He, said to them:

“Why, then, did you kill the prophets of Allah before, if you were believers?”

That is, if you believed in what was revealed to you. He, glorified and exalted is He, is saying: You follow neither what your own prophets brought you nor what the other prophets brought you; rather, you follow only your desires. Such is the condition of someone who accepts the truth neither from his own group nor from any other, while remaining partisan toward his group without any proof or clear evidence from Allah.

Likewise, Abū al-Ma‘ālī al-Juwaynī said in his book al-Risāla al-Nizāmiyya (The Nizāmiyya Epistle):

“Scholars have taken different approaches to these apparent meanings. Some favored interpreting them beyond their apparent meanings and adopted this approach to the verses of

" مِنْ هَذَا الْجَوَابِ "

translated_text:
the Book and the authentic reports of the Sunnah. The leading scholars of the early generations, however, refrained from interpreting these expressions beyond their apparent meanings, left them as they occur in the texts, and entrusted their meanings to the Lord.”

He then said:

“The position we approve and hold as our belief before Allah is to follow the early generations of the Muslim community. The decisive evidence from revelation for this is the community’s consensus, which is binding proof and the foundation of most of the Sharia. The Companions of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, consistently refrained from addressing their meanings or seeking to fathom their contents. They were the finest of the Muslims and bore the responsibilities of the Sharia, sparing no effort to establish the principles of the faith accurately, exhort one another to preserve them, and teach people what they needed to know of them.

“If interpreting these expressions beyond their apparent meanings had been permissible or obligatory, their concern for them would very likely have exceeded their concern for the subsidiary rulings of the Sharia. If their age and that of the Successors passed without their engaging in such interpretation, then that is the course to follow. A religious person must therefore believe that the Creator is exalted above the attributes of created beings, refrain from delving into the interpretation of difficult passages, and entrust their meaning to the Lord Most High. He should accordingly treat the verse concerning Allah’s rising over the Throne and His coming, and His words:

‘what I created with My two hands,’

‘And there will remain the Face of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Honor,’

and His words:

‘Sailing under Our eyes,’

as well as the authentic reports from the Messenger, such as the report concerning Allah’s descent and others, in the manner we have described.”

I say:

The questioner should understand that the purpose “of this answer” is to cite the words of some of the leading scholars who transmitted the position of the early generations on this subject. Not everyone whose words we have quoted—whether among the theologians or others—agrees with everything we say on this subject or on other subjects. Nevertheless, the truth is accepted from whoever speaks it. Mu‘ādh ibn Jabal used to say in his remarks

الْمَشْهُورِ عَنْهُ؛
 الَّذِي رَوَاهُ أَبُو دَاوُد فِي سُنَنِهِ:

 وَجِمَاعُ الْأَمْرِ فِي ذَلِكَ:
 أَنَّ الْكِتَابَ وَالسُّنَّةَ يَحْصُلُ مِنْهُمَا كَمَالُ الْهُدَى وَالنُّورِ لِمَنْ تَدَبَّرَ كِتَابَ اللَّهِ وَسُنَّةَ نَبِيِّهِ وَقَصَدَ اتِّبَاعِ الْحَقِّ وَأَعْرَضَ عَنْ تَحْرِيفِ الْكَلِمِ عَنْ مَوَاضِعِهِ وَالْإِلْحَادِ فِي أَسْمَاءِ اللَّهِ وَآيَاتِهِ. وَلَا يَحْسَبُ الْحَاسِبُ أَنَّ شَيْئًا مِنْ ذَلِكَ يُنَاقِضُ بَعْضَهُ بَعْضًا أَلْبَتَّةَ؛

{إذْ قَامَ أَحَدُكُمْ إلَى الصَّلَاةِ فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ قِبَلَ وَجْهِهِ}
 وَنَحْوُ ذَلِكَ فَإِنَّ هَذَا غَلَطٌ.
translated_text:
which are well known and were recorded by Abū Dāwūd in his Sunan:

“Accept the truth from whoever brings it, even if he is a disbeliever—or he said, ‘a wicked man’—and beware the lapse of a wise man.”

They asked, “How can we know when a disbeliever speaks a word of truth?”

He replied, “Truth has a light”—or words to that effect.

As for establishing this with evidence, dispelling the doubts that arise, and examining the matter thoroughly so that certainty reaches the heart and brings it peace, and one understands where people’s views stand in these wildernesses—this fatwa does not allow sufficient scope for that. I have previously written something on this subject and discussed some of it with certain people who attend our gatherings. Perhaps, Allah willing, I shall write something that achieves the intended purpose.

The essence of the matter is this: the Book and the Sunnah provide complete guidance and light to anyone who reflects upon Allah’s Book and His Prophet’s Sunnah, seeks to follow the truth, and shuns distorting words from their proper meanings and deviating concerning Allah’s names and signs. No one should imagine that any of these texts contradict one another in any way.

For example, someone might say that what the Book and the Sunnah state about Allah being above the Throne is contradicted by the apparent meaning of His words:

“And He is with you wherever you are,”

and the words of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“When one of you stands to pray, Allah is before his face,”

and other such texts. This is a mistake.

translated_text:
This is because Allah is truly with us and is truly above the Throne, as Allah, glorified and exalted be He, brings both together in His words:

“He is the One who created the heavens and the earth in six days, then rose over the Throne. He knows what enters the earth and what comes out of it, what descends from heaven and what ascends into it. And He is with you wherever you are. And Allah sees all that you do.”

Thus, He states that He is above the Throne, knows everything, and is with us wherever we are. Likewise, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in the hadith of the mountain goats:

“Allah is above the Throne, and He knows your circumstances.”

This is because, when used without qualification, the word “with” signifies in its apparent linguistic sense only association in general, without necessarily implying contact or being alongside something to its right or left. When qualified by a particular meaning, it signifies association in that respect.

For example, one says, “We continued travelling, with the moon with us,” or “with the star with us.” One also says, “This baggage is with me,” because it accompanies you, even if it is above your head. Thus, Allah is truly with His creation and is truly above His Throne.

What this “being with” entails varies according to the context. When He says:

“He knows what enters the earth and what comes out of it,”

and continues to:

“And He is with you wherever you are,”

the apparent meaning of the passage indicates that what this being with entails and implies is that He observes you, bears witness over you, watches over you, and knows you. This is what the early generations meant when they said, “He is with them through His knowledge.” This is the apparent and actual meaning of the passage.

The same applies to His words:

“There is no private conversation among three but He is their fourth,”

through to His words:

“He is with them wherever they may be,”

and the rest of the verse.

When the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to his companion in the cave:

“Do not grieve; indeed, Allah is with us,”

this too was true according to its apparent meaning. The circumstances indicated that this being with them entailed awareness, help, and support. The same applies to His words, exalted be He:

“Indeed, Allah is with those who fear Him and those who do good,”

and likewise to His words to Moses and Aaron:

“Indeed, I am with you both; I hear and see.”

Here, being with them retains its apparent meaning, and in these instances it entails help and support.

Someone who frightens a child may enter, causing him to cry. His father then looks down upon him from the roof and says, “Do not be afraid; I am with you,” or “I am here,” or “I am present,” and similar expressions. He draws the child’s attention to his being with him, which, in those circumstances, entails warding off harm. There is thus a distinction between the meaning of being with someone and what it entails. What it entails may sometimes become part of its meaning, and thus vary according to the context.

The expression “being with” is used in the Quran and Sunnah in contexts where it entails things that it does not entail elsewhere. Either its meaning varies according to the context, or it conveys a meaning common to all its occurrences—even though each context has its own distinctive feature. On either understanding, it does not entail that the essence of the Lord, mighty and majestic, is intermixed with creation, such that one could claim that the expression has been interpreted away from its apparent meaning.

Analogous to this in certain respects are “lordship and servitude.” Although their various instances share the basic meanings of lordship and servitude, when He says:

“in the Lord of all worlds,”

“the Lord of Moses and Aaron,”

His lordship over Moses and Aaron has a particular distinction beyond His general lordship over creation. For whoever Allah has granted greater perfection than others, He has governed and nurtured more perfectly than others.

Likewise are His words:

“A spring from which Allah’s servants drink, making it flow abundantly,”

and:

“Glory be to Him who took His servant by night.”

For “servant” sometimes means one held in subjection, and thus includes all creation, as in His words:

“There is none in the heavens and the earth but will come to the Most Merciful as a servant.”

At other times it means a worshipper, and thus has a restricted scope. These worshippers themselves differ: whoever is more devoted in knowledge and spiritual condition has more perfect servitude. Accordingly, the attribution to Allah is more perfect in his case, although it is literal in every instance.

Some people call expressions of this kind “graded terms,” because the hearer is uncertain whether they are univocal terms or terms that share only their wording. Those who have examined the matter rigorously know that they do not fall outside the category of univocal terms, since whoever established the language assigned the expression to the shared meaning. Even if they constitute a distinct subclass of univocal terms, there is no harm in giving them a separate designation.

Furthermore, whoever imagines that Allah’s being in heaven means that heaven surrounds and contains Him is lying—if he attributes this understanding to someone else—and is astray—if he believes this about his Lord. We have never heard anyone understand this from the wording, nor have we seen anyone attribute it to anyone. If all Muslims were asked, “Do you understand from the statement of Allah and His Messenger, ‘Allah is in heaven,’ that heaven contains Him?” every one of them would immediately reply, “That is something that has perhaps never crossed our minds.”

Since this is so, it is contrived to assign the wording an impossible apparent meaning that people do not understand from it, and then seek to reinterpret it. Rather, people understand “Allah is in heaven” and “He is upon the Throne” as having the same meaning, since “heaven” here means the heights. The meaning, then, is that Allah is on high, not below. Muslims know that His Kursī (Seat), glorified and exalted is He, encompasses the heavens and the earth; that the Kursī, in relation to the Throne, is like a ring cast into an open wilderness; and that the Throne is one of Allah’s creations, bearing no comparison to Allah’s power and greatness. How, after this, could anyone imagine that something created confines and contains Him?

He, glorified is He, has said:

“I will surely crucify you on the trunks of palm trees.”

And He has said:

“So travel through the land.”

Here, fī (“in”) means “on,” and the like. This is literal Arabic usage, not figurative. This is understood by anyone who knows the actual meanings of particles and knows that they are generally univocal rather than equivocal.

Likewise, the following saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace—and the remainder of the hadith—is true in its apparent meaning:

“When one of you stands to pray, Allah is before his face, so he must not spit before his face.”

He, glorified is He, is above the Throne and before the face of the person praying. Indeed, even created things can be described in this way. If someone were to address the sky, or the sun and moon, the sky, sun and moon would be above him and also before his face.

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, gave an analogy of this kind—to Allah belongs the highest description, but the purpose of the analogy is to demonstrate that this is possible, not to liken the Creator to His creation. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“‘There is not one of you who will not see his Lord, alone with Him.’ Abū Razīn al-‘Uqaylī asked him, ‘How, O Messenger of Allah, when He is One and we are so many?’ The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, replied, ‘I will tell you of something comparable among Allah’s blessings: this moon—each of you sees it on his own, yet it is only one of Allah’s signs. Allah is greater.’”

Or words to that effect, as spoken by the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

He also said:

“You will see your Lord just as you see the sun and moon.”

Thus, he compared the act of seeing with the act of seeing, although what is seen is not like what is seen. When the believers see their Lord on the Day of Resurrection and speak intimately with Him, each will see Him above him and before his face, just as he sees the sun and moon. There is no contradiction whatsoever.

The more a person knows Allah and is firmly grounded in knowledge of Him, the more firmly he affirms the Quran and Sunnah as they stand.

translated_text:
Know, moreover, that some among later generations say:

“The way of the early generations is to affirm these texts as they have been transmitted, while believing that their apparent meaning is not intended.”

This wording is “ambiguous.” By saying that their apparent meaning is not intended, a person may mean by “apparent meaning” the characteristics of created beings and the attributes of things brought into existence. For example, he may understand “Allah is before the face of the person praying” to mean that He is settled within the wall toward which that person prays, or understand the apparent meaning of “Allah is with us” to be that He is beside us, and so forth. There is no doubt that this is not intended.

Whoever says that the early generations held that this meaning is not intended is correct in substance, but mistaken in stating without qualification that this is the apparent meaning of the verses and hadiths. This impossible meaning is not their apparent meaning, as we have explained elsewhere. Unless, of course, this impossible meaning has come to appear evident to some people; in that case, the person making this statement would be correct in that respect and excused for using such wording. For what is apparent or obscure may differ according to people’s circumstances; it is a relative matter. It would have been better to explain to anyone who believes this to be the apparent meaning that it is not, thereby doing justice to the words of Allah and the words of His Messenger, both in wording and in meaning.

But if the person reporting the position of the early generations means, by saying that “the apparent meaning is not intended according to them,” that the meanings apparent from these verses and hadiths—meanings befitting Allah’s majesty and greatness, not peculiar to the attributes of created beings, but rather necessary for Allah or possible with respect to Him, whether as a possibility in thought or as a possibility in reality—

No one could ever cite anything from any member of the early generations indicating—either explicitly or by its apparent meaning—that they believed Allah is not above the Throne, or that Allah does not truly possess hearing, sight, or a hand.

I have seen some who attribute this view to the early generations adopt it themselves. They say that the approach of those who advocate nonliteral interpretation is, in fact, the approach of the early generations—meaning that both groups agreed that these verses and hadiths did not indicate the attributes of Allah, glorified and exalted be He. The early generations, however, refrained from interpreting them nonliterally, whereas later generations considered such interpretation beneficial because of the pressing need for it. They say:

“The difference between the two approaches is that the latter may specify the intended meaning through nonliteral interpretation, whereas the former do not specify it, since another meaning may be intended.”

This unqualified claim is an outright lie about the early generations. This is indisputably so with regard to many attributes, such as Allah Most High being above the Throne. Anyone who carefully considers the transmitted statements of the early generations—not even a tenth of which has been cited here—will know beyond doubt that they explicitly affirmed that Allah is truly above the Throne, and that they never believed otherwise. Many of them made similarly explicit statements concerning numerous attributes.

Allah knows that, after thorough research and reading as much of the statements of the early generations as I could, I have not seen any statement from any of them indicating—whether explicitly, by its apparent meaning, or through contextual indications—the negation of the attributes known through transmitted revelation

in reality; rather, what I have found is that many of their statements indicate—either explicitly or by their apparent meaning—that they affirmed this category of attributes. I do not report that every one of them affirmed every attribute; rather, what I have found is that they affirmed this category in general, and I have not seen any of them negate it. They only rejected likening Allah to His creation and condemned those who did so, while also condemning those who negated His attributes.

For example, Nuʿaym ibn Hammād al-Khuzāʿī, al-Bukhārī’s teacher, said:

“Whoever likens Allah to His creation has disbelieved, and whoever denies what Allah has described Himself with has disbelieved. Neither Allah’s descriptions of Himself nor His Messenger’s descriptions of Him amount to likening Him to creation.”

Whenever they saw a man go to extremes in rejecting any likeness between Allah and His creation without affirming His attributes, they would say:

“This is a Jahmī who negates the divine attributes.”

Such statements are exceedingly common in their words. Indeed, to this day, the Jahmiyyah and the Muʿtazilah accuse anyone who affirms any of the attributes of likening Allah to His creation—falsely and slanderously. Some of them have even gone to such extremes as to level this accusation against the prophets, may Allah’s blessings and peace be upon them. Thus, Thumāmah ibn al-Ashras, one of the leaders of the Jahmiyyah, said:

“Three of the prophets liken Allah to His creation: Moses, when he said:

‘This is nothing but Your trial’;

Jesus, when he said:

‘You know what is within myself, and I do not know what is within Yourself’;

and Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, when he said:

‘Our Lord descends.’”

Indeed, most of the Muʿtazilah classify the great majority of the imams—such as Mālik and his followers, al-Thawrī and his followers, al-Awzāʿī and his followers, al-Shāfiʿī and his followers, Ahmad and his followers, Ishāq ibn Rāhawayh, Abū ʿUbayd, and others—as people who liken Allah to His creation.

translated_text:
Abū Ishāq Ibrāhīm ibn ‘Uthmān ibn Dirbās al-Shāfi‘ī also wrote a short treatise entitled “Vindicating the Imams of the Sacred Law against Vile Epithets.” In it, he cited statements of the early generations and others concerning these matters. He explained that every group among the people of innovation applies a fabricated label to “the people of the Sunnah”—claiming, according to its corrupt views, that the label is accurate—just as the polytheists used to apply fabricated labels to the Prophet.

Thus, the Rāfidah call them Nawāsib; the Qadariyyah call them determinists; the Murji’ah call them doubters; the Jahmiyyah call them people who liken Allah to His creation; and the speculative theologians call them Hashwiyyah, Nawābit, scum, rabble, and similar names. Likewise, Quraysh would sometimes call the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, a madman, sometimes a poet, sometimes a soothsayer, and sometimes a fabricator.

They said: This is a sign of truly inheriting his legacy and following him fully. For the Sunnah is the way followed by the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his Companions in belief, moderation, speech, and action. Just as those who deviate from him apply reprehensible, fabricated names to them—even if they believe those names to be accurate on the basis of their corrupt beliefs—so too do they treat those who follow him with clear insight, who are the people closest to him in life and death, inwardly and outwardly.

As for those who conform to him inwardly but are unable to uphold the outward practices, those who conform to him outwardly but are unable to fully realize the inward realities, and those who conform to him both outwardly and inwardly to the extent of their ability: those who deviate from his Sunnah inevitably believe that these followers have some deficiency for which they censure them

Likewise, a member of the Jahmiyyah says: “Whoever says that Allah is above the Throne has thereby claimed that He is confined, that He is a composite, bounded body, and that He resembles His creation.”

Likewise, the Jahmiyyah–Mu‘tazilah say: “Whoever says that Allah possesses knowledge and power has thereby claimed that He is a composite body and is guilty of likening Him to His creation. For these attributes are accidents, and an accident can subsist only in a substance occupying space. Everything occupying space is either a composite body or an indivisible atom. Whoever affirms this likens Allah to His creation, because all bodies are alike.”

Whoever reports people’s “doctrinal positions” and applies these fabricated names to them—on the basis of his own belief, in which they disagree with him—must answer to his Lord. Allah lies in wait for him, and evil plotting engulfs none but those who devise it.

In sum, the possible approaches to the Quranic verses and hadiths concerning the divine attributes fall into “six categories,” each followed by a group among the people of the qiblah. “Two categories” hold that these texts are to be understood according to their apparent meanings; “two categories” hold that their intended meanings differ from their apparent meanings; and “two categories” remain silent.

The first two categories are as follows:

The first consists of those who understand these texts according to their apparent meanings, while taking those meanings to describe attributes of the same kind as those of created beings. These are the proponents of likening Allah to His creation. Their position is false and was condemned by the early generations; it is against them that refutation is rightly directed.

The second consists of those who understand these texts according to their apparent meanings in a manner befitting Allah’s majesty, just as they understand the apparent meanings of the names “the All-Knowing,” “the All-Powerful,” “the Lord,” “God,” “the Existent,” “the Essence,” and the like in a manner befitting Allah’s majesty. For the apparent meanings of these attributes, when applied to a created being, denote either a created substance or an accident subsisting in it.

Indeed, even regarding the “created things in Paradise,” it is authentically reported that Ibn ‘Abbās said: “Nothing in this world resembles what is in Paradise except in name.” Allah Most High has told us that no soul knows what joys have been kept hidden for them. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, also told us that Paradise contains what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has ever conceived. If this is true of the delights of Paradise, which are among Allah’s creations, then what must be true of the Creator, glorified and exalted is He?

As for this “soul” within human beings, any rational person knows how greatly people have differed about it and that the revealed texts refrain from explaining its exact nature. Should a rational person not take this as a lesson and refrain from speaking about the manner of Allah’s being?

Yet we know with certainty that the soul is in the body, that it leaves it and ascends to heaven, and that it is drawn out of it at the moment of death, as the authentic texts state. We do not go to the extremes of the philosophizers and those who agree with them in stripping it of these attributes. They deny that it ascends or descends, is joined to the body or separates from it. They have become confused about it because they regard it as different in kind from the body and its attributes. But its lack of resemblance to the body does not preclude its possessing these attributes in a manner appropriate to it—unless they explain their words in a way consistent with the revealed texts, in which case their error would be one of wording. But how could they do so?

 لَيْسَ لَهَا فِي الْبَاطِنِ مَدْلُولٌ هُوَ صِفَةُ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى قَطُّ وَأَنَّ اللَّهَ لَا صِفَةَ لَهُ ثُبُوتِيَّةً؛ بَلْ صِفَاتُهُ إمَّا سَلْبِيَّةٌ وَإِمَّا إضَافِيَّةٌ وَإِمَّا مُرَكَّبَةٌ مِنْهُمَا أَوْ يُثْبِتُونَ بَعْضَ الصِّفَاتِ - وَهِيَ الصِّفَاتُ السَّبْعَةُ أَوْ الثَّمَانِيَةُ أَوْ الْخَمْسَةَ عَشَرَ - أَوْ يُثْبِتُونَ الْأَحْوَالَ دُونَ الصِّفَاتِ وَيُقِرُّونَ مِنْ الصِّفَاتِ الْخَبَرِيَّةِ بِمَا فِي الْقُرْآنِ دُونَ الْحَدِيثِ عَلَى مَا قَدْ عُرِفَ مِنْ مَذَاهِبِ الْمُتَكَلِّمِينَ.
 فَهَؤُلَاءِ قِسْمَانِ:
 قِسْمٌ يَتَأَوَّلُونَهَا وَيُعَيِّنُونَ الْمُرَادَ مِثْلُ قَوْلِهِمْ: اسْتَوَى بِمَعْنَى اسْتَوْلَى؛ أَوْ بِمَعْنَى عُلُوِّ الْمَكَانَةِ وَالْقَدْرِ أَوْ بِمَعْنَى ظُهُورِ نُورِهِ لِلْعَرْشِ؛ أَوْ بِمَعْنَى انْتِهَاءِ الْخَلْقِ إلَيْهِ؛ إلَى غَيْرِ ذَلِكَ مِنْ مَعَانِي الْمُتَكَلِّمِينَ.
 وَقِسْمٌ يَقُولُونَ:
 اللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ بِمَا أَرَادَ بِهَا؛
 لَكِنَّا نَعْلَمُ أَنَّهُ لَمْ يُرِدْ إثْبَاتَ صِفَةٍ خَارِجِيَّةٍ عَمَّا عَلِمْنَاهُ:
وَأَمَّا الْقِسْمَانِ الْوَاقِفَانِ:
translated_text:
the body and life, or that it varies from body to body and is equal to all other bodies in definition and reality, as certain groups of speculative theologians maintain. Rather, we know with certainty that the soul is a real entity distinct from the body and does not resemble it. It truly possesses the attributes stated in the revealed texts, not merely metaphorically. If our position concerning the reality of the “soul” and its attributes lies between denying its attributes and likening it to the body, what, then, should our position be concerning the attributes of the Lord of all worlds?

As for the two groups who deny their apparent meaning, I mean those who say that these expressions do not, in reality, signify any attribute of Allah Most High whatsoever, and that Allah has no affirmative attributes: His attributes are only negative, relational, or a combination of the two. Others affirm some attributes—the seven, eight, or fifteen attributes—or affirm states rather than attributes. Of the attributes known through revelation, they acknowledge those mentioned in the Quran but not those mentioned in hadith, in accordance with the known positions of the speculative theologians.

These people fall into two groups. One group reinterprets these expressions and specifies their intended meaning. For example, they say that istawā (“rose over”) means istawlā (“took control”), or refers to exalted status and rank, the manifestation of His light to the Throne, or creation reaching its endpoint there, among the other meanings proposed by the speculative theologians.

The other group says: “Allah knows best what He intended by them. But we know that He did not intend to affirm an attribute beyond those we already know.”

As for the two groups who suspend judgment:

translated_text:
one group says: “Their apparent meaning, befitting Allah’s majesty, may be intended; or what is intended may not be an attribute of Allah,” and so forth. This is the approach of many jurists and others. Another group refrains from all of this and does no more than recite the Quran and read hadith, turning their hearts and tongues away from these suppositions. No one can fall outside these “six categories.”

The correct position regarding many verses and hadiths concerning the divine attributes is to adhere with certainty to the established approach, as with the verses and hadiths indicating that Allah—glorified and exalted is He—is above His Throne. The correct approach in this and similar matters is known through the evidence of the Quran, the Sunnah, and scholarly consensus—evidence that admits no contrary conclusion. With some of these texts, however, this may be judged more likely, while the contrary remains possible. A believer’s uncertainty in such matters depends on the knowledge and faith he has been granted. Whoever Allah does not grant light has no light.

Anyone who is uncertain about this or anything else should offer the supplication narrated by Muslim in his Sahīh from ‘Ā’ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, who said:

“When the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, rose to pray at night, he would say: ‘O Allah, Lord of Gabriel, Michael, and Isrāfīl, Originator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the seen! You judge between Your servants concerning that over which they differ. Guide me, by Your permission, to the truth concerning which they have differed. Indeed, You guide whom You will to a straight path.’”

A version narrated by Abū Dāwūd states: “He would say ‘Allah is greatest’ in his prayer, then recite this supplication.”

translated_text:
Thus, when a servant acknowledges his need for Allah, calls upon Him, and persistently studies the words of Allah, His Messenger, the Companions, the Successors, and the leading scholars of the Muslims, the path of guidance opens before him.

If he has also learned the ultimate limits reached by the philosophers and speculative theologians in this matter, recognizes that most of what they claim to be demonstrative proof is merely a specious argument, and sees that most of what they rely upon amounts to an unfounded claim, a specious argument constructed from an invalid inference, a universal proposition that holds only in particular cases, an unfounded claim of consensus, or reliance on terms with multiple meanings in both their positions and their proofs—then his faith in, and knowledge of, what the Quran and Sunnah have brought will increase. When these arguments are dressed up in lengthy, elaborate wording unfamiliar to anyone who does not know their terminology, they deceive the inexperienced just as a mirage deceives the thirsty. For:

“The beauty of a thing is revealed by its opposite.”

The better someone knows falsehood, the more deeply he reveres the truth and appreciates its worth, once he is guided to it.

As for those who have progressed only partway in speculative theology, there is reason to fear for them what need not be feared for those who have never entered it or those who have pursued it to its ultimate conclusion. Those who have never entered it remain unharmed, while those who have pursued it to the end know where it leads and no longer fear that something else remains beyond it. When the truth becomes clear to such a person, he accepts it, thirsting as he does for it. Someone who has progressed only partway, however, is misled by the doctrines he receives through uncritical imitation of those who venerate these thinkers.

Someone once said:

“What does the most harm to the world is a half-trained speculative theologian and a half-trained

jurist, a half-trained physician, and a half-trained grammarian. The first corrupts religions, the second corrupts countries, the third corrupts bodies, and the fourth corrupts language.”

Anyone who knows that speculative theologians, whether philosophers or others, are generally “of conflicting views”—“turned away from it is whoever is turned away”—also knows that the intelligent and sensible among them recognize that they have no clear insight into what they say and that their arguments are not clear proofs. Rather, their arguments are as the poet described them:

“Arguments that shatter like glass—you think them true,
Yet every breaker is itself broken.”

Anyone with a thorough and discerning knowledge of them knows that, from one perspective, they deserve what al-Shāfiʿī, may Allah be pleased with him, prescribed when he said:

“My judgment concerning the practitioners of speculative theology is that they should be beaten with palm branches and sandals, paraded among the tribes and clans, and it should be proclaimed: ‘This is the recompense of anyone who turns away from the Book and Sunnah and turns to speculative theology.’”

From another perspective, however, if you view them in light of divine decree—with bewilderment overwhelming them and Satan holding sway over them—you would pity them and treat them gently. They were given intelligence, yet were not given intelligence; they were given understanding, yet were not given knowledge. They were given hearing, sight, and hearts:

“Yet their hearing, sight, and hearts availed them nothing, since they denied Allah’s signs; and what they used to mock engulfed them.”

For anyone well acquainted with these matters, this makes clear the early Muslim generations’ expertise, knowledge, and experience

in warning against speculative theology, forbidding it, and censuring and reproaching its practitioners. He also recognizes that whoever seeks guidance outside the Book and Sunnah only grows further from Allah.

We therefore ask Allah, the Magnificent, to guide us to His straight path—the path of those He has blessed, not of those who have incurred His anger, nor of those who have gone astray. Āmīn.

All praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds. May His blessings and peace be upon Muhammad, the Seal of the Prophets, and upon all his family and Companions.

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah sanctify his soul—(*) was asked about “Allah’s highness and His being established over His Throne.”

He replied:

Allah, Exalted is He, has described Himself in His Book and through His Messenger as “being on high, being established over the Throne, and being above,” in many verses of His Book. Indeed, some leading scholars among al-Shāfiʿī’s followers said: “The Quran contains a thousand proofs, or more, indicating that Allah, Exalted is He, is high above creation and above His servants.” Another said that it contains “three hundred” proofs indicating this, such as His statements:

“Indeed, those who are with your Lord”

“To Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth, and those who are with Him.”

If “with Him” meant “under His power,” as the Jahmite says, then all creation would be with Him, for they are all subject to His power and will. There would then be no distinction between those in the heavens, those on earth, and those with Him. Likewise, if being established over the Throne meant having dominion over it, He would be established over all created things, and He would always have been established over the Throne, even before creating it; and being established
translated_footnote:
(*) Shaykh Nāsir ibn Hamad al-Fahd stated (pp. 44–46):
This fatwa is an abridgment of his treatise on “Reconciling Highness and Nearness” (5:226–255). Someone other than the Shaykh—may Allah have mercy on him—abridged it, as certain clear indications show. For example:
1. On p. 123, “There is nothing before You, etc.” abridges a passage found on p. 228.
2. On p. 134, “Then, after a lengthy discussion, he said: This shows that everyone who acknowledges Allah…” For the omitted discussion, see pp. 249–245. The words “he said” refer to Shaykh al-Islām, mentioned earlier.

Comparison of the two texts yields the following observations:
1. The original, p. 226, reads: “If ‘with Him’ meant ‘under His power,’ as the Jahmiyya claim, then all creation would be [with Him, for they are] under His power and will.” I say: The words in square brackets were omitted from the original through a copying error caused by the eye skipping ahead. They have been restored from the abridgment, p. 121.
2. The abridgment, p. 123, reads: “This is the more balanced of the two positions transmitted from Ahmad.” The original, p. 258, reads: “This is one of the two positions,” which appears more likely to be correct.
3. The abridgment, p. 123, reads: “Their texts contain statements showing the opposite of their claim.” The original, p. 228, reads: “The texts contain statements showing their inconsistency,” which appears more likely to be correct.
4. The abridgment, p. 124, reads: “Thus, what are called originated things are the exalted; they are so in themselves.” The second hiya (“they are”) does not occur in the original, p. 229, and its omission is correct.
5. The abridgment, p. 124, reads: “Thus Abū ‘Alī al-Ahwāzī—who compiled an account of Ibn Abī Bishr’s faults and refuted Abū al-Qāsim ibn ‘Asākir—was one of the Sālimiyya.” The original, p. 229, has the same wording. This is a textual corruption; the correct reading is: “and Abū al-Qāsim ibn ‘Asākir refuted him.” Ibn ‘Asākir wrote Tabyīn kadhib al-muftarī (Exposing the Slanderer’s Lies) in refutation of this Abū ‘Alī al-Ahwāzī, as the Shaykh—may Allah have mercy on him—mentions at 5:484.
6. The abridgment, p. 127, reads: “Likewise, much of what the Lord says in describing Himself as knowing His servants’ deeds serves to warn and frighten, and as raghba (desire) for good in souls.” The original, p. 232, reads: “Likewise, the Lord frequently describes Himself in terms of knowledge, and of deeds: to warn, frighten, and encourage souls to do good.”
The correct wording appears to be: “Likewise, the Lord frequently describes Himself as knowing His servants’ deeds, to warn, frighten, and encourage souls to do good.”
7. The abridgment, p. 128, reads: “As a king says: ‘We conquered this town, and this army is from us,’ and similar expressions.” The original, p. 233, reads: “and we defeated the army,” which is correct.
8. The abridgment, p. 135, reads: “He has acquired faith through which he worships Allah.” The original, p. 255, reads: “faith through which he knows Allah,” which appears more likely to be correct and suits the context.
9. The abridgment, p. 135, reads: “This is a major principle in teaching people and addressing them, and in general discourse using texts they have all heard.” The original, p. 255, reads: “This is a major principle in teaching people and addressing them through general discourse using texts,” which appears more likely to be correct.

is specific to the Throne after the creation of the heavens and the earth, as He has stated in His Book. This indicates that there was a time when He was established over it and a time when He was not. Thus, according to the leading scholars who affirm the divine attributes, highness is among the attributes known through transmitted revelation, together with reason and religious law. Being established over the Throne, however, is among the attributes known through transmitted revelation alone, not through reason.

The point is that He, Exalted is He, has described Himself as being with His creation and as being near. His “being with” is of two kinds: general and particular. The first is expressed in His statement:

“He is with you wherever you are.”

The second is expressed in His statement:

“Indeed, Allah is with those who fear Him and those who do good.”

There are other verses to this effect. As for “nearness,” it is expressed in such statements as:

“Indeed, I am near.”

And:

“We are nearer to him than you.”

On this matter, people have divided into (four groups:

The “Jahmiyyah” who deny the divine attributes say that He is neither within the world nor outside it, neither above nor below. They affirm neither His highness nor His being above; rather, in their view, all of this is either reinterpreted or its meaning left to Allah. All the adherents of innovation may appeal to scriptural texts—the Khawārij, the Shīʿah, the Qadariyyah, the Murjiʾah, and others—except the Jahmiyyah, for they have not a single statement from the prophets that agrees with the negations they assert.
