The deniers do not say that He will be seen as the sun and the moon are seen. Rather, their actual position is that He cannot be seen at all. Those among them who say that He will be seen, outwardly agreeing with those who uphold affirmation while concealing their disagreement, interpret seeing as an increase in knowledge; it would therefore not be like seeing the sun and the moon.

The point here is that they would inevitably ask him about their Lord whom they worshipped, and, if they asked him, he would necessarily answer them. It is known beyond doubt that what the Jahmī deniers say has not been transmitted by anyone who conveyed his teachings. Rather, they transmitted from him what accords with the position of those who uphold affirmation.

And (the point is that if Allah loves for us to believe this negation, then the Companions and the Successors, who were better than us, would have believed it, and the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would have believed it too. If Allah and His Messenger approve it for us, and it is either obligatory or recommended for us, then the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, must command us to do what is obligatory and encourage us to do what is recommended. Moreover, statements affirming what Allah loves and approves, and what brings one nearer to Him, must necessarily be evident in his teachings and those of the believers—especially given His words, mighty and majestic is He:

“Today I have perfected for you your religion and completed My favor upon you.”

This is all the more so since the Jahmiyyah make this the foundation of religion. To them, it is “monotheism,” which only a wretched person would oppose. How, then, could the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, fail to teach his community monotheism? And how could “monotheism” have been unknown to the Companions and the Successors? and their followers call the doctrine of those who negate the divine attributes “monotheism.” The author of al-Murshidah called his followers the monotheists, since, in their view, the doctrine of negation is “monotheism.” If that were so, it would necessarily follow that the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, must explain it. Yet it is known beyond doubt that the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his Companions did not teach the doctrine of negation. Thus, it is known that this doctrine is neither obligatory nor recommended; indeed, it is known that it is not part of the “monotheism” that Allah Most High prescribed for His servants. If, on the other hand, He loves for us to follow the doctrine of affirmation—which is what we have been commanded to do—then this too must be explained to us.

It is well known that the Quran and Sunnah affirm “Allah’s being above His creation and His attributes” far more extensively than they establish ablution, dry ablution, fasting, the prohibition of marriage to women within the forbidden degrees, the prohibition of unclean foods, and other such “religious ordinances.” Thus, according to those who affirm the divine attributes, the religion is complete; the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, conveyed and explained it; and monotheism is well known and widely transmitted from the early generations. The Quran and Sunnah corroborate one another; the early generations are the best of this community, and their path is the best of paths. The Quran is entirely true: it contains nothing misleading, nor does it point to unbelief or anything impossible. Rather, it is healing, guidance, and light. All these are implications they accept and conclusions they endorse. Their position is therefore consistent, not contradictory, and acceptable, not to be rejected.

But if what Allah loves from us is that we neither affirm nor deny, but remain in mere ignorance and in layers of darkness, unable to distinguish truth from falsehood, guidance from misguidance, or truthfulness from lies; rather, that we stand between those who affirm and those who negate, doubtful and bewildered—“Wavering between the two, belonging neither to these nor to those”—neither believing nor disbelieving, then it necessarily follows that Allah loves for us to have no knowledge of what the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, brought, no knowledge of the perfect attributes that befit Allah, Glorified and Exalted is He, and no knowledge by which to distinguish truth from falsehood; and that He loves bewilderment and doubt from us.

Yet it is well known that Allah does not love ignorance, doubt, bewilderment, or misguidance. Rather, He loves religion, knowledge, and certainty. He has condemned “bewilderment” in His words, Exalted is He:

“Say: Shall we invoke besides Allah that which neither benefits us nor harms us, and be turned back on our heels after Allah has guided us, like someone whom the devils have lured away in the land, bewildered, while he has companions calling him to guidance, ‘Come to us’? Say: Indeed, Allah’s guidance is the true guidance, and we have been commanded to submit to the Lord of all worlds.”

“And to establish prayer and fear Him. It is to Him that you will be gathered.”

Allah Most High has commanded us to say:

“Guide us to the straight path,”

“The path of those You have blessed, not of those who have incurred Your anger, nor of those who have gone astray.”

Thus he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, asks his Lord to guide him to the truth concerning which people have differed. How, then, could Allah love the absence of guidance in disputed matters?

Allah Most High said to him:

“And say: My Lord, increase me in knowledge.”

As for the saying some people attribute to him:

“Increase me in bewilderment concerning You,”

it is a fabrication, according to the unanimous agreement of those versed in his hadith, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Rather, this is the request of someone who is bewildered and has asked for still greater bewilderment. No one who is bewildered may ask and pray for greater bewilderment; rather, he should ask for guidance and knowledge. How much more so in the case of the one who guides creation out of misguidance? Such words are only reported from certain shaykhs who are not to be followed in such matters—if the report from such a person is authentic.

people who suspend judgment inwardly agree with those who negate, or acquiesce in their position, while opposing only those who affirm. Thus, it is clear that they have acquiesced in the position of the people of innovation and opposed the people of the Sunnah.

Second: Not knowing the meanings of the Quran and hadith is not something Allah and His Messenger love. This position is therefore false.

Third: Muslims agree that doubt and bewilderment are not praiseworthy in themselves. At most, someone who has no knowledge warranting either negation or affirmation should remain silent. But when someone knows the truth through evidence consistent with the explanation of His Messenger, may Allah Most High bless him and grant him peace, the doubting, bewildered person who suspends judgment has no right to object to this knowledgeable person, who possesses certainty and insight, follows the Messenger, and understands both transmitted evidence and rational arguments.

Fourth: All the early generations denounced the negating Jahmiyyah, upheld affirmation, and stated it explicitly. Their statements affirming and denouncing those who negate are too numerous to record here. The statements of renowned imams—such as Mālik, al-Thawrī, al-Awzā‘ī, Abū Hanīfah, Hammād ibn Zayd, Hammād ibn Salamah, ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn Mahdī, Wakī‘ ibn al-Jarrāh, al-Shāfi‘ī, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Ishāq ibn Rāhawayh, Abū ‘Ubayd, and the leading scholars among the followers of Mālik, Abū Hanīfah, al-Shāfi‘ī, and Ahmad—are extant in such abundance that no one can enumerate them.

He thus stated, may Allah be pleased with him, that rising over the Throne itself is known, while its manner is unknown. This is precisely the position of those who affirm. As for “those who negate,” they affirm no rising over the Throne whose manner could be unknown. Rather, this doubting speaker and others like him hold that rising over the Throne is unknown, not known. If rising over the Throne were unknown, there would be no need to say that its manner is unknown—especially if rising over the Throne were denied altogether, since what is denied and nonexistent has no manner that could be described as known or unknown. Mālik’s words explicitly affirm rising over the Throne, that it is known, and that it has a manner. That manner, however, is unknown to us; we do not know it.

For this reason, he declared the questioner who asked him about this manner an innovator. For a question can only concern something known to us, whereas we do not know the manner of His rising over the Throne. Not everything that is known and has a manner necessarily has a manner known to us.

This is further clarified by the fact that Mālikī scholars and others transmitted that Mālik said: “Allah is in heaven, and His knowledge is everywhere.” Indeed, Makkī, the preacher of Cordoba, included this in the Book of Quranic Commentary that he compiled from Mālik’s statements. It was also transmitted by Abū ‘Amr al-Talamankī, Abū ‘Umar ibn ‘Abd al-Barr, Ibn Abī Zayd in The Abridgment, and several others. of other writers on the Sunnah. Had Mālik been among those who withhold judgment or those who negate, this affirmation would not have been transmitted from him.

The statement made by Mālik had already been made by his teacher, Rabī‘ah ibn Abī ‘Abd al-Rahmān, as transmitted from him by Sufyān ibn ‘Uyaynah. ‘Abd al-‘Azīz ibn ‘Abd Allāh ibn Abī Salamah al-Mājishūn also made a lengthy statement establishing the position of affirmation and refuting those who negate. We have cited it elsewhere.

The Mālikīs’ statements condemning the Jahmiyyah who negate the divine attributes are well known in their books. The statements of the Mālikī imams and their early scholars affirming the divine attributes are likewise numerous and well known. Their scholars even reported the consensus of Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamā‘ah that Allah Himself is above His Throne. Ibn Abī Zayd merely stated what the other imams of the early generations had stated, and none of the Mālikī imams disagreed with him on this point. He included this in the introduction to al-Risālah so that it would be taught to all Muslims, since the imams of the Sunnah regarded it as one of the beliefs that everyone should be taught.

Only followers of the Jahmiyyah who negate the divine attributes objected to “Ibn Abī Zayd” on this point. Those who opposed him did not base their opposition on its being an innovation or contrary to the Quran and Sunnah. Rather, those who opposed Ibn Abī Zayd and others like him claimed that what he said was contrary to reason. They said: “Ibn Abī Zayd was not proficient in the discipline of speculative theology, through which one knows what is and is not possible with respect to Allah, Mighty and Majestic.”

 وَقَالَ عَبْدُ اللَّهِ بْنُ نَافِعٍ كَانَ مَالِكُ بْنُ أَنَسٍ يَقُولُ:
 اللَّهُ فِي السَّمَاءِ وَعِلْمُهُ فِي كُلِّ مَكَانٍ.
 وَقَالَ معدان:
 سَأَلْت سُفْيَانَ الثَّوْرِيَّ عَنْ قَوْله تَعَالَى 
{وَهُوَ مَعَكُمْ أَيْنَ مَا كُنْتُمْ}
 قَالَ عِلْمُهُ. وَقَالَ حَمَّادُ بْنُ زَيْدٍ فِيمَا ثَبَتَ عَنْهُ مِنْ غَيْرِ وَجْهٍ رَوَاهُ ابْنُ أَبِي حَاتِمٍ وَالْبُخَارِيُّ
translated_text:
The later scholars who objected to Ibn Abī Zayd and others like him took this objection from the later Ash‘arīs, such as Abū al-Ma‘ālī and his followers. These, in turn, derived it from the principles they shared with the Mu‘tazilah and other Jahmiyyah. Thus, the Jahmiyyah—whether Mu‘tazilah or others—are the source of this objection.

The early generations of the Muslim community and its imams agreed on affirming the divine attributes and refuted those who withheld judgment and those who negated them. For example, al-Bayhaqī and others narrated that al-Awzā‘ī said: “While the Successors were still numerous, we used to say: ‘Allah is above His Throne, and we believe in His attributes as reported in the Sunnah.’”

Abū Mutī‘ al-Balkhī said in the well-known book al-Fiqh al-Akbar (The Greater Understanding): “I asked Abū Hanīfah about someone who says, ‘I do not know whether my Lord is in heaven or on earth.’ He replied, ‘He has disbelieved, because Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: “The Most Merciful rose over the Throne.” His Throne is above His seven heavens.’ I said, ‘He says, “He rose over the Throne,” but does not know whether the Throne is in heaven or on earth.’ He replied, ‘If he denies that He is in heaven, he has disbelieved, for He, exalted is He, is in the highest heights, and He is invoked from above, not from below.’”

‘Abd Allāh ibn Nāfi‘ said: “Mālik ibn Anas used to say: ‘Allah is in heaven, and His knowledge is everywhere.’”

Ma‘dān said: “I asked Sufyān al-Thawrī about the words of the Exalted, ‘And He is with you wherever you are.’ He replied, ‘His knowledge.’”

Hammād ibn Zayd said, in a report reliably transmitted from him through several chains and related by Ibn Abī Hātim and al-Bukhārī

وَعَبْدُ اللَّهِ بْنُ أَحْمَد وَغَيْرُهُمْ:
 إنَّمَا يَدُورُ كَلَامُ الْجَهْمِيَّة عَلَى أَنْ يَقُولُوا لَيْسَ فِي السَّمَاءِ شَيْءٌ وَقَالَ عَلِيُّ بْنُ الْحَسَنِ بْنِ شَقِيقٍ قُلْت لِعَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ الْمُبَارَكِ: بِمَاذَا نَعْرِفُ رَبَّنَا؟ قَالَ؛ بِأَنَّهُ فَوْقَ سَمَوَاتِهِ عَلَى عَرْشِهِ بَائِنٌ مِنْ خَلْقِهِ. قُلْت بِحَدِّ؟
 قَالَ:
 بِحَدِّ لَا يَعْلَمُهُ غَيْرُهُ وَهَذَا مَشْهُورٌ عَنْ ابْنِ الْمُبَارَكِ ثَابِتٌ عَنْهُ مِنْ غَيْرِ وَجْهٍ؛ وَهُوَ أَيْضًا صَحِيحٌ ثَابِتٌ عَنْ أَحْمَد بْنِ حَنْبَلٍ وَإِسْحَاقَ بْنِ رَاهَوَيْه وَغَيْرِ وَاحِدٍ مِنْ الْأَئِمَّةِ.
 وَقَالَ رَجُلٌ لِعَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ الْمُبَارَكِ:
 يَا أَبَا عَبْدِ الرَّحْمَنِ قَدْ خِفْت اللَّهَ مِنْ كَثْرَةِ مَا أَدْعُو عَلَى الْجَهْمِيَّة.
 قَالَ:
 لَا تَخَفْ فَإِنَّهُمْ يَزْعُمُونَ أَنَّ إلَهَك الَّذِي فِي السَّمَاءِ لَيْسَ بِشَيْءِ. وَقَالَ جَرِيرُ بْنُ عَبْدِ الْحَمِيدِ؛ كَلَامُ الْجَهْمِيَّة أَوَّلُهُ شَهْدٌ وَآخِرُهُ سُمٌّ وَإِنَّمَا يُحَاوِلُونَ أَنْ يَقُولُوا لَيْسَ فِي السَّمَاءِ إلَهٌ رَوَاهُ ابْنُ أَبِي حَاتِمٍ.
 وَرَوَاهُ هُوَ وَغَيْرُهُ بِأَسَانِيدَ ثَابِتَةٍ عَنْ عَبْدِ الرَّحْمَنِ بْنِ مَهْدِيٍّ قَالَ:
 إنَّ الْجَهْمِيَّة أَرَادُوا أَنْ يَنْفُوا أَنْ يَكُونَ اللَّهُ عَزَّ وَجَلَّ كَلَّمَ مُوسَى بْنَ عِمْرَانَ وَأَنْ يَكُونَ عَلَى الْعَرْشِ أَرَى أَنْ يُسْتَتَابُوا فَإِنْ تَابُوا وَإِلَّا ضُرِبَتْ أَعْنَاقُهُمْ.
 وَقَالَ يَزِيدُ بْنُ هَارُونَ:
 مَنْ زَعَمَ أَنَّ اللَّهَ عَلَى الْعَرْشِ اسْتَوَى عَلَى خِلَافِ مَا يَقِرُّ فِي قُلُوبِ الْعَامَّةِ فَهُوَ جهمي. وَقَالَ سَعِيدُ بْنُ عَامِرٍ الضبعي - وَذَكَرَ عِنْدَهُ الْجَهْمِيَّة فَقَالَ - هُمْ أَشَرُّ قَوْلًا مِنْ الْيَهُودِ وَالنَّصَارَى قَدْ أَجْمَعَ أَهْلُ الْأَدْيَانِ مَعَ الْمُسْلِمِينَ عَلَى أَنَّ اللَّهَ عَلَى الْعَرْشِ وَقَالُوا هُمْ لَيْسَ عَلَيْهِ شَيْءٌ.
translated_text:
and ‘Abd Allāh ibn Ahmad and others: “The discourse of the Jahmiyyah revolves entirely around saying that there is nothing in heaven.”

‘Alī ibn al-Hasan ibn Shaqīq said: “I asked ‘Abd Allāh ibn al-Mubārak, ‘How do we know our Lord?’ He replied, ‘By knowing that He is above His heavens, upon His Throne, distinct from His creation.’ I asked, ‘With a limit?’ He replied, ‘With a limit known to none but Him.’” This is well known from Ibn al-Mubārak and reliably transmitted from him through several chains. It is also authentically and reliably reported from Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Ishāq ibn Rāhawayh, and several other imams.

A man said to ‘Abd Allāh ibn al-Mubārak: “Abū ‘Abd al-Rahmān, I have come to fear Allah because of how often I supplicate against the Jahmiyyah.” He replied: “Do not be afraid, for they claim that your God, who is in heaven, is nothing.”

Jarīr ibn ‘Abd al-Hamīd said: “The discourse of the Jahmiyyah begins as honey and ends as poison. All they are trying to say is that there is no God in heaven.” This was narrated by Ibn Abī Hātim.

He and others also narrated through reliable chains that ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn Mahdī said: “The Jahmiyyah sought to deny that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, spoke to Moses son of ‘Imrān and that He is upon the Throne. In my view, they should be called upon to repent. If they repent, so be it; otherwise, they should be beheaded.”

Yazīd ibn Hārūn said: “Whoever claims that Allah rose over the Throne in a sense contrary to what is settled in the hearts of ordinary people is a Jahmī.”

When the Jahmiyyah were mentioned in his presence, Sa‘īd ibn ‘Āmir al-Duba‘ī said: “What they say is worse than what the Jews and Christians say. The followers of other religions agree with the Muslims that Allah is upon the Throne, whereas these people say that there is nothing upon it.”

translated_text:
‘Abbād ibn al-‘Awwām al-Wāsitī said:

“I spoke with Bishr al-Marīsī and his companions and found that their discourse ultimately led them to say that there is nothing in heaven. By Allah, I hold that there should be neither intermarriage nor mutual inheritance with them.”

Such statements are frequent in their discourse. The speculative theologians who record people’s doctrines likewise described “the doctrine of the people of the Sunnah and the people of hadith” in this way. Among them was Abū al-Hasan al-Ash‘arī, in the book he composed on Differences among Those Who Pray and the Doctrines of the Muslims. In it, he discussed the views of the Khawārij, the Rāfidah, the Mu‘tazilah, the Murji’ah, and others.

He then said:

“An Account of the Doctrine of the People of the Sunnah and the People of Hadith

“Their position, in summary, is to affirm Allah, Mighty and Majestic, His angels, His Books, His messengers, what has come from Allah, and what trustworthy narrators have transmitted from the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. They reject none of this.”

He went on to say:

“And that Allah is upon His Throne, as He said:

‘The Most Merciful rose over the Throne.’

“And that He has two Hands, without specifying how, as He, the Exalted, said:

‘What I created with My two Hands.’

“They affirmed that Allah has knowledge, as He said:

‘He sent it down with His knowledge.’

‘No female conceives or gives birth except with His knowledge.’

“They affirmed hearing and sight and did not deny these of Allah as the Mu‘tazilah did. They said that no good or evil occurs on earth except what Allah wills, and that things come to pass by Allah’s will, as He said:

‘You do not will unless Allah wills.’”

He went on to say: “They say that the Quran is the speech of Allah, uncreated, and they believe the hadiths transmitted from the Messenger of Allah

may Allah bless him and grant him peace, such as:

‘Allah descends to the lowest heaven and says: “Is there anyone seeking forgiveness, that I may forgive him?”’

as related in the hadith. They affirm that Allah will come on the Day of Resurrection, as He said:

‘And your Lord comes, and the angels, rank upon rank.’

“And that Allah draws near to His creation however He wills, as He said:

‘We are nearer to him than his jugular vein.’”

He mentioned many other things before saying: “This, then, is a summary of what they enjoin, practise, and believe. We affirm all that we have mentioned of their teachings, and this is the position we adopt.”

Al-Ash‘arī also said, on the question of rising over the Throne:

“The people of the Sunnah and the scholars of hadith said: ‘He is not a body and does not resemble things, and He is upon His Throne, as He said:

“The Most Merciful rose over the Throne.”

‘We do not presume to speak ahead of Allah and His Messenger. Rather, we say that He rose over the Throne, without specifying how, and that He has two Hands, without specifying how, as He, the Exalted, said:

“What I created with My two Hands.”

‘And that Allah descends to the lowest heaven, as related in the hadith.’”

He said: “The Mu‘tazilah said that His rising over His Throne means that He gained dominion over it.”

Al-Ash‘arī also said in his book al-Ibānah fī Usūl al-Diyānah (The Elucidation of the Foundations of Religion), in the chapter on rising over the Throne:

“If someone asks, ‘What do you say about rising over the Throne?’ the answer is: We say to him that Allah is established over His Throne, as He said:

‘The Most Merciful rose over the Throne.’

“And He said:

‘To Him ascends good speech.’

“And He said:

‘Rather, Allah raised him to Himself.’

“And He said, recounting Pharaoh’s words:

‘O Hāmān, build me a lofty tower, so that I may reach the pathways—the pathways of the heavens—and look upon the God of Moses, though I certainly think he is a liar.’

“Pharaoh accused Moses of lying in his statement:

إنَّ اللَّهَ فَوْقَ السَّمَوَاتِ.
 وَقَالَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى:
 
{أَأَمِنْتُمْ مَنْ فِي السَّمَاءِ أَنْ يَخْسِفَ بِكُمُ الْأَرْضَ فَإِذَا هِيَ تَمُورُ}
 فَالسَّمَوَاتُ فَوْقَهَا الْعَرْشُ وَكُلُّ مَا عَلَا فَهُوَ سَمَاءٌ وَلَيْسَ إذَا قَالَ: 
{أَأَمِنْتُمْ مَنْ فِي السَّمَاءِ}
 يَعْنِي جَمِيعَ السَّمَوَاتِ وَإِنَّمَا أَرَادَ الْعَرْشَ الَّذِي هُوَ أَعْلَى السَّمَوَاتِ أَلَا تَرَى أَنَّهُ ذَكَرَ السَّمَوَاتِ فَقَالَ: 
{وَجَعَلَ الْقَمَرَ فِيهِنَّ نُورًا}
 وَلَمْ يُرِدْ أَنَّهُ يَمْلَأُ السَّمَوَاتِ جَمِيعًا؟ وَرَأَيْنَا الْمُسْلِمِينَ جَمِيعًا يَرْفَعُونَ أَيْدِيَهُمْ إذَا دَعَوْا نَحْوَ السَّمَاءِ؛ لِأَنَّ اللَّهَ مُسْتَوٍ عَلَى الْعَرْشِ الَّذِي هُوَ فَوْقَ السَّمَوَاتِ فَلَوْلَا أَنَّ اللَّهَ عَلَى الْعَرْشِ لَمْ يَرْفَعُوا أَيْدِيَهُمْ نَحْوَ الْعَرْشِ.
وَقَدْ قَالَ قَائِلُونَ مِنْ الْمُعْتَزِلَةِ وَالْجَهْمِيَّة والحرورية:

He has power over the earth, and over latrines and privies. If His being established over the Throne meant gaining dominion, it would be permissible to say that He is established over all things. Some proponents of falsehood have reinterpreted the statement of Shaykh Muhammad ibn Abī Zayd—“He, in His very Being, is above His glorious Throne, and He is everywhere through His knowledge”—by reading al-Majīd (“the Glorious”) in the nominative case. The intended meaning is then that Allah is the Glorious in His very Being. Besides displaying obvious ignorance, this amounts to saying: “The Most Compassionate in His very Being, the Most Merciful in His very Being, and the Almighty in His very Being.”

Ibn Abī Zayd also said in the introduction to al-Risālah (The Epistle): “He rose over the Throne and holds dominion over the kingdom.” He thus distinguished rising over from exercising dominion, in accordance with the principle upheld by the imams whose teachings are followed. Moreover, Ibn Abī Zayd explicitly stated in al-Mukhtasar (The Abridgment) that “Allah is in His heaven, not on His earth.” These are his exact words. What Ibn Abī Zayd stated has consistently been affirmed by the imams of Ahl al-Sunnah across all their groups.

The imam Abū ‘Amr al-Talamankī mentioned in his book, which he entitled al-Wusūl ilā Ma‘rifat al-Usūl (Attaining Knowledge of the Foundations), that Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamā‘ah agree that Allah, in His very Being, rose over His Throne. Muhammad ibn ‘Uthmān ibn Abī Shaybah, the hadith master of Kufa, who belonged to the generation of al-Bukhārī and his peers, likewise related this position from Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamā‘ah. The imam Yahyā ibn ‘Ammār al-Sijistānī also stated it in his well-known epistle on the Sunnah, which he wrote to the king of his land.

The hadith master Abū Nasr al-Sijzī likewise stated this in his book al-Ibānah (The Elucidation). He said: “Our imams, such as al-Thawrī, Mālik, Ibn ‘Uyaynah, Hammād ibn Salamah, Hammād ibn Zayd, Ibn al-Mubārak, Fudayl ibn ‘Iyād, Ahmad, and Ishāq, agree that Allah, in His very Being, is above the Throne, and that His knowledge encompasses every place.” Shaykh al-Islām al-Ansārī, Abū al-‘Abbās al-Tarqī, Shaykh ‘Abd al-Qādir al-Jīlī, and countless imams and shaykhs of Islam, whose number only Allah knows, likewise affirmed this.

The hadith master Abū Nu‘aym al-Asbahānī—the author of Hilyat al-Awliyā’ (The Adornment of the Saints) and other well-known works—said in the creed he compiled: “Our path is the path of the early generations who followed the Book, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the Muslim community.”

He said: “Among their beliefs is that Allah has always been perfect in all His eternal attributes; He neither ceases to be nor changes. He has always known with knowledge, seen with sight, heard with hearing, and spoken with speech. He brought things into existence out of nothing. The Quran is Allah’s speech, as are all His other revealed Books: His speech is uncreated. In every respect—whether read, recited, memorized, heard, written, or uttered—the Quran is truly Allah’s speech, not a representation or a translation of it. As pronounced by us, it is Allah’s uncreated speech. The Wāqifah and the Lafziyyah belong to the Jahmiyyah. Whoever refers to the Quran in any manner, intending thereby to assert that Allah’s speech is created, is, in their view, one of the Jahmiyyah; and in their view, a Jahmī is a disbeliever.”

He mentioned further points before saying:

original_text:
وَأَنَّ الْأَحَادِيثَ الَّتِي ثَبَتَتْ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ فِي 
" الْعَرْشِ وَاسْتِوَاءِ اللَّهِ عَلَيْهِ "
 يَقُولُونَ بِهَا وَيُثْبِتُونَهَا مِنْ غَيْرِ تَكْيِيفٍ وَلَا تَمْثِيلٍ وَأَنَّ اللَّهَ بَائِنٌ مِنْ خَلْقِهِ وَالْخَلْقَ بَائِنُونَ مِنْهُ؛ لَا يَحِلُّ فِيهِمْ وَلَا يَمْتَزِجُ بِهِمْ وَهُوَ مُسْتَوٍ عَلَى عَرْشِهِ فِي سَمَائِهِ دُونَ أَرْضِهِ. وَذَكَرَ سَائِرَ اعْتِقَادِ السَّلَفِ وَإِجْمَاعَهُمْ عَلَى ذَلِكَ. وَقَالَ يَحْيَى بْنُ عُثْمَانَ فِي 
" رِسَالَتِهِ "
: لَا نَقُولُ كَمَا قَالَتْ الْجَهْمِيَّة إنَّهُ بِدَاخِلِ الْأَمْكِنَةِ وَمُمَازِجٌ كُلَّ شَيْءٍ وَلَا نَعْلَمُ أَيْنَ هُوَ؛
 بَلْ نَقُولُ هُوَ بِذَاتِهِ عَلَى عَرْشِهِ وَعِلْمُهُ مُحِيطٌ بِكُلِّ شَيْءٍ وَسَمْعُهُ وَبَصَرُهُ وَقُدْرَتُهُ مُدْرِكَةٌ لِكُلِّ شَيْءٍ وَهُوَ مَعْنَى قَوْلِهِ:
 
{وَهُوَ مَعَكُمْ أَيْنَ مَا كُنْتُمْ}
 .
 وَقَالَ الشَّيْخُ الْعَارِفُ مَعْمَرُ بْنُ أَحْمَد " شَيْخُ الصُّوفِيَّةِ:
 فِي هَذَا الْعَصْرِ أَحْبَبْت أَنْ أُوصِيَ أَصْحَابِي بِوَصِيَّةٍ مِنْ السُّنَّةِ وَأَجْمَعَ مَا كَانَ عَلَيْهِ أَهْلُ الْحَدِيثِ وَأَهْلُ الْمَعْرِفَةِ وَالتَّصَوُّفِ مِنْ الْمُتَقَدِّمِينَ والمتأخرين؛
 فَذَكَرَ أَشْيَاءَ مِنْ الْوَصِيَّةِ إلَى أَنْ قَالَ فِيهَا:
 وَإِنَّ اللَّهَ اسْتَوَى عَلَى عَرْشِهِ بِلَا كَيْفٍ وَلَا تَأْوِيلٍ وَالِاسْتِوَاءُ مَعْلُومٌ وَالْكَيْفُ مَجْهُولٌ؛ وَإِنَّهُ مُسْتَوٍ عَلَى عَرْشِهِ بَائِنٌ مِنْ خَلْقِهِ وَالْخَلْقُ بَائِنُونَ مِنْهُ بِلَا حُلُولٍ وَلَا مُمَازَجَةٍ وَلَا مُلَاصَقَةٍ وَإِنَّهُ عَزَّ وَجَلَّ سَمِيعٌ بَصِيرٌ عَلِيمٌ خَبِيرٌ يَتَكَلَّمُ وَيَرْضَى وَيَسْخَطُ وَيَضْحَكُ وَيَعْجَبُ وَيَتَجَلَّى لِعِبَادِهِ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ ضَاحِكًا وَيَنْزِلُ كُلَّ لَيْلَةٍ إلَى سَمَاءِ الدُّنْيَا كَيْفَ شَاءَ بِلَا كَيْفٍ وَلَا تَأْوِيلٍ وَمَنْ أَنْكَرَ النُّزُولَ أَوْ تَأَوَّلَ فَهُوَ مُبْتَدِعٌ ضَالٌّ.
translated_text:
“And they accept and affirm the hadiths authentically reported from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, concerning ‘the Throne and Allah’s rising over it,’ without specifying how or likening Him to His creation. Allah is distinct from His creation, and His creation is distinct from Him. He neither dwells within them nor intermingles with them. He is above His Throne, in His heaven, not on His earth.” He went on to mention the remaining beliefs of the early generations and their consensus on these matters.

Yahyā ibn ‘Uthmān said in his epistle: “We do not say, as the Jahmiyyah do, ‘He is within places and intermingled with everything, and we do not know where He is.’ Rather, we say that He, in His very Being, is above His Throne; His knowledge encompasses everything, and His hearing, sight, and power extend to everything. This is the meaning of His statement:

‘And He is with you wherever you are.’”

The spiritually learned shaykh Ma‘mar ibn Ahmad, the shaykh of the Sufis, said: “In this age, I wished to leave my companions a testament drawn from the Sunnah and to bring together the beliefs followed by the scholars of hadith and the people of spiritual knowledge and Sufism, both earlier and later.” He mentioned several points in this testament before saying:

“Allah rose over His Throne, without specifying how or reinterpreting it. His rising over the Throne is known, but how is unknown. He is above His Throne, distinct from His creation, and His creation is distinct from Him, without indwelling, intermingling, or contact. He, mighty and majestic, is All-Hearing, All-Seeing, All-Knowing, All-Aware. He speaks, is pleased, is displeased, laughs, and marvels. He will manifest Himself to His servants on the Day of Resurrection, laughing. Every night He descends to the lowest heaven as He wills, without specifying how or reinterpreting it. Whoever denies the descent or reinterprets it is a misguided innovator.”

Imam Abū ‘Uthmān Ismā‘īl ibn ‘Abd al-Rahmān al-Sābūnī al-Naysābūrī said in his book al-Risālah fī al-Sunnah (The Epistle on the Sunnah):

“The scholars of hadith believe and testify that Allah is above His seven heavens, upon His Throne, as His Book declares. The scholars of the Muslim community and the leading figures of its early generations have not differed over Allah Most High being upon His Throne and His Throne being above His heavens.”

He said:

“Our imam, Abū ‘Abd Allāh al-Shāfi‘ī, cited in his book al-Mabsūt, when discussing the freeing of a believing slave as expiation and the invalidity of fulfilling an expiation by freeing an unbelieving slave, the report that ‘Mu‘āwiyah ibn al-Hakam wished to free a black slave woman as expiation. He asked the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, about freeing her. The Prophet tested her to determine whether she was a believer, asking her: “Where is your Lord?” She pointed towards heaven, and he said: “Free her, for she is a believer.”’ Thus, he judged her to be a believer when she acknowledged that her Lord was in heaven and recognized her Lord by His attribute of being high and above.”

The hadith master Abū Bakr al-Bayhaqī said:

“Chapter on Rising over the Throne”

Allah Most High said:

“The Most Merciful rose over the Throne.”

“Then He rose over the Throne.”

“He is the Subduer, above His servants.”

“They fear their Lord above them.”

“To Him good words ascend, and righteous deeds raise them.”

“Do you feel secure from Him who is in heaven?”

What is meant is He who is above heaven, just as He said:

“I will surely crucify you on the trunks of palm trees.”

Here, fī (“in”) means “on the trunks of palm trees.” He also said:

“Travel freely throughout the land.”

That is, upon the land. Everything that is above is termed samā’ (heaven), and the Throne is the highest of the heavens. Thus, the verse means: “Do you feel secure from Him who is upon the Throne?”—as He explicitly stated in the other verses.

He said:

original_text:
وَفِيمَا كَتَبْنَا مِنْ الْآيَاتِ دَلَالَةٌ عَلَى إبْطَالِ قَوْلِ مَنْ زَعَمَ مِنْ الْجَهْمِيَّة:
 أَنَّ اللَّهَ بِذَاتِهِ فِي كُلِّ مَكَانٍ وَقَوْلُهُ: 
{وَهُوَ مَعَكُمْ أَيْنَ مَا كُنْتُمْ}
 إنَّمَا أَرَادَ بِعِلْمِهِ لَا بِذَاتِهِ. وَقَالَ أَبُو عُمَرَ بْنُ عَبْدِ الْبَرِّ فِي 
" شَرْحِ الْمُوَطَّأِ "
 لَمَّا تَكَلَّمَ عَلَى حَدِيثِ النُّزُولِ قَالَ: هَذَا حَدِيثٌ لَمْ يَخْتَلِفْ أَهْلُ الْحَدِيثِ فِي صِحَّتِهِ وَفِيهِ دَلِيلٌ أَنَّ اللَّهَ فِي السَّمَاءِ عَلَى الْعَرْشِ مِنْ فَوْقِ سَبْعِ سَمَوَات؛ كَمَا قَالَتْ الْجَمَاعَةُ؛
 وَهُوَ مِنْ حُجَّتِهِمْ عَلَى الْمُعْتَزِلَةِ قَالَ:
 وَهَذَا أَشْهَرُ عِنْدَ الْخَاصَّةِ وَالْعَامَّةِ وَأَعْرَفُ مِنْ أَنْ يُحْتَاجَ إلَى أَكْثَرَ مِنْ حِكَايَتِهِ؛ لِأَنَّهُ اضْطِرَارٌ لَمْ يُوقِفْهُمْ عَلَيْهِ أَحَدٌ؛ وَلَا أَنْكَرَهُ عَلَيْهِمْ مُسْلِمٌ.
 وَقَالَ أَبُو عُمَرَ أَيْضًا:
 أَجْمَعَ عُلَمَاءُ الصَّحَابَةِ وَالتَّابِعِينَ الَّذِينَ حُمِلَ عَنْهُمْ التَّأْوِيلُ قَالُوا فِي تَأْوِيلِ قَوْلِهِ: 
{مَا يَكُونُ مِنْ نَجْوَى ثَلَاثَةٍ إلَّا هُوَ رَابِعُهُمْ}
 هُوَ عَلَى الْعَرْشِ وَعِلْمُهُ فِي كُلِّ مَكَانٍ؛ وَمَا خَالَفَهُمْ فِي ذَلِكَ أَحَدٌ يُحْتَجُّ بِقَوْلِهِ. فَهَذَا مَا تَلَقَّاهُ الْخَلَفُ عَنْ السَّلَفِ؛ إذْ لَمْ يُنْقَلْ عَنْهُمْ غَيْرُ ذَلِكَ؛ إذْ هُوَ الْحَقُّ الظَّاهِرُ الَّذِي دَلَّتْ عَلَيْهِ الْآيَاتُ الْقُرْآنِيَّةُ وَالْأَحَادِيثُ النَّبَوِيَّةُ؛ فَنَسْأَلُ اللَّهَ الْعَظِيمَ أَنْ يَخْتِمَ لَنَا بِخَيْرِ وَلِسَائِرِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ وَأَنْ لَا يَزِيغَ قُلُوبَنَا بَعْدَ إذْ هَدَانَا؛ بِمَنِّهِ وَكَرَمِهِ إنَّهُ أَرْحَمُ الرَّاحِمِينَ وَالْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ وَحْدَهُ.
translated_text:
“The verses we have cited demonstrate the falsity of the claim made by some of the Jahmiyyah that Allah, in His Essence, is everywhere. As for His words, ‘He is with you wherever you are,’ He meant that He is with them by His knowledge, not in His Essence.”

Abū ‘Umar ibn ‘Abd al-Barr, commenting on the hadith of the Descent in his Sharh al-Muwatta’ (Commentary on al-Muwatta’), said:

“The scholars of hadith have not differed over the authenticity of this hadith. It contains evidence that Allah is in heaven, upon the Throne, above the seven heavens, as the community has affirmed. It is among their proofs against the Mu‘tazilah.”

He said:

“This is so widely known and familiar among the learned and the general public that it needs no more than to be stated. They know it intuitively, without anyone having instructed them in it, and no Muslim has disputed it with them.”

Abū ‘Umar also said:

“The scholars among the Companions and Successors from whom explanations of the Quran have been transmitted unanimously agreed in their explanation of His words, ‘There is no private conversation among three but that He is their fourth,’ saying: ‘He is upon the Throne, and His knowledge is everywhere.’ No one whose opinion carries authority disagreed with them on this.”

This, then, is what the later generations received from the early generations, for nothing else has been transmitted from them. It is the manifest truth indicated by the Quranic verses and the Prophetic hadiths. We therefore ask Allah the Magnificent to grant us and all other Muslims a good end, and, by His grace and generosity, not to let our hearts deviate after He has guided us. Indeed, He is the Most Merciful of those who show mercy. All praise belongs to Allah alone.

Shaykh al-Islām, the pillar of the Sharia, Abū al-‘Abbās Ahmad ibn ‘Abd al-Halīm ibn ‘Abd al-Salām ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah sanctify his soul and illuminate his grave—was asked about the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic:

“The Most Merciful rose over the Throne,”

and the words of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Our Lord descends every night to the lowest heaven.”

Are the rising over the Throne and the descent to be understood literally or not? What does it mean to understand them literally? Does literal usage mean using a word in the sense for which it was originally assigned, as scholars of legal theory say, or not? What follows from understanding the verses concerning the divine attributes literally?

He answered:

All praise belongs to Allah, Lord of all worlds. What is said concerning the rising over the Throne and the descent is like what is said concerning all the other attributes with which Allah has described Himself in His Book and through His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Allah Most High “has given Himself names and described Himself with attributes.” He has named Himself the Ever-Living, the All-Knowing, the All-Wise, the All-Powerful, the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing, the All-Forgiving, the Most Merciful, along with His other most beautiful names.

Allah Most High says:

“And if you speak aloud, He surely knows the secret and what is even more hidden.”

And He says:

“They encompass nothing of His knowledge except what He wills. His Kursī extends over the heavens and the earth.”

And He says:

“Indeed, Allah is the Provider, the Possessor of power, the All-Strong.”

And He says:

“And the heaven We built with might,”

meaning, with strength. And He says:

“My mercy encompasses all things.”

And He relates the words of His angels:

“Our Lord, You encompass all things in mercy and knowledge.”

And He says:

“Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him.”

And He says:

“And the pleasure of Allah is greater.”

And He says:

“Allah is angry with them and has cursed them.”

And He says:

“Anger from their Lord and humiliation in the life of this world will befall them.”

And He, Most High, says:

“And Allah spoke to Moses directly.”

And He says:

“Among them were those to whom Allah spoke.”

And He says:

“The word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice.”

And He says:

“Indeed, I am with you both, hearing and seeing.”

And He says:

“And Allah is ever All-Hearing, All-Seeing.”

And He says:

“What prevented you from prostrating to what I created with My two hands?”

And He, Most High, says:

“He loves them, and they love Him.”

And He, Most High, says:

“Are they waiting for anything but that Allah should come to them in canopies of clouds, along with the angels?”

And He, Most High, says:

“And your Lord comes, with the angels, rank upon rank.”

There are many similar passages. What is said concerning some of these attributes applies equally to the others. The way of the early generations of this community and its leading scholars is to describe Allah as He has described Himself and as His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, has described Him, without distortion or negation, and without describing how His attributes are or likening them to those of created beings.

It is therefore impermissible to deny the attributes with which Allah Most High has described Himself, just as it is impermissible to liken them to the attributes of created beings. Rather, He—glorified be He—is as He says:

“There is nothing like Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing.”

There is nothing like Him in His essence, His attributes, or His actions.

original_text:
وَقَالَ نُعَيْمُ بْنُ حَمَّادٍ الخزاعي:
 مَنْ شَبَّهَ اللَّهَ بِخَلْقِهِ فَقَدْ كَفَرَ وَمَنْ جَحَدَ مَا وَصَفَ اللَّهُ بِهِ نَفْسَهُ فَقَدْ كَفَرَ وَلَيْسَ مَا وَصَفَ اللَّهُ بِهِ نَفْسَهُ وَرَسُولُهُ تَشْبِيهًا.
 وَمَذْهَبُ السَّلَفِ بَيْنَ مَذْهَبَيْنِ وَهُدًى بَيْنَ ضلالتين:
 إثْبَاتُ الصِّفَاتِ وَنَفْيُ مُمَاثَلَةِ الْمَخْلُوقَاتِ؛

{لَيْسَ كَمِثْلِهِ شَيْءٌ}

 وَقَوْلُهُ:
 
{وَهُوَ السَّمِيعُ الْبَصِيرُ}
 -
 رَدٌّ عَلَى أَهْلِ النَّفْيِ وَالتَّعْطِيلِ فَالْمُمَثِّلُ أَعْشَى وَالْمُعَطِّلُ أَعْمَى:
 الْمُمَثِّلُ يَعْبُدُ صَنَمًا وَالْمُعَطِّلُ يَعْبُدُ عَدَمًا. وَقَدْ اتَّفَقَ جَمِيعُ أَهْلِ الْإِثْبَاتِ عَلَى أَنَّ اللَّهَ حَيٌّ حَقِيقَةً عَلِيمٌ حَقِيقَةً قَدِيرٌ حَقِيقَةً سَمِيعٌ حَقِيقَةً بَصِيرٌ حَقِيقَةً مُرِيدٌ حَقِيقَةً مُتَكَلِّمٌ حَقِيقَةً؛
 حَتَّى الْمُعْتَزِلَةُ الْنُّفَاةِ لِلصِّفَاتِ قَالُوا:

 فَإِنَّهُمْ يَقُولُونَ:
 إنَّ هَذِهِ الْأَسْمَاءَ حَقِيقَةٌ لِلْخَالِقِ سُبْحَانَهُ وَتَعَالَى؛ وَإِنْ كَانَتْ تُطْلَقُ عَلَى خَلْقِهِ حَقِيقَةً أَيْضًا.

 إنَّ لَهُ عِلْمًا حَقِيقَةً وَقُدْرَةً حَقِيقَةً وَسَمْعًا حَقِيقَةً وَبَصَرًا حَقِيقَةً.
translated_text:
Nu'aym ibn Hammād al-Khuzā'ī said:

“Whoever likens Allah to His creation has disbelieved, and whoever denies what Allah has described Himself with has disbelieved. What Allah and His Messenger have described Him with does not constitute likening Him to creation.”

The way of the early generations stands between two doctrines, offering guidance between two errors: affirming the attributes while denying any likeness to created beings. Thus, His saying, Most High:

“There is nothing like Him,”

refutes those who liken Allah to creation and assert resemblance between them. His saying:

“And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing,”

refutes those who deny and negate His attributes. The one who likens Him to creation is dim-sighted, while the one who negates His attributes is blind: the former worships an idol, and the latter worships nothingness.

All those who affirm the attributes agree that Allah truly lives, truly knows, truly has power, truly hears, truly sees, truly wills, and truly speaks. Even the Mu'tazilīs, who deny the attributes, say that Allah truly speaks, just as they say—along with all other Muslims—that Allah truly knows and truly has power. Indeed, some of them, such as Abū al-'Abbās al-Nāshi', held that these names apply literally to Allah and figuratively to creation.

The majority of the Mu'tazilīs, however, together with the scholastic theologians who affirm the attributes—the Ash'arī-Kullābīs, Karrāmīs, Sālimīs, the followers of the four imams among the Hanafīs, Mālikīs, Shāfi'īs, and Hanbalīs, the people of hadith, and the Sufis—say that these names apply literally to the Creator, glorified and exalted be He, even though they also apply literally to His creation. They also say that He possesses real knowledge, real power, real hearing, and real sight.

Only the negators among the Qarmatian Ismā‘īlī esotericists and like-minded philosophers deny that these names apply literally. They deny Allah’s most beautiful names and say:

“He is neither living, nor knowing, nor ignorant, nor powerful, nor powerless, nor existent, nor nonexistent.”

These people and those who resemble them deny that these names apply literally to Him. Some of them then say that these names belong to certain created beings and do not apply to Him either literally or figuratively. These are the people whom Muslims call heretics, because they have deviated concerning Allah’s names and signs. Allah Most High has said:

“To Allah belong the most beautiful names, so call upon Him by them, and leave those who deviate concerning His names. They will be recompensed for what they used to do.”

He Most High also said:

“Indeed, those who deviate concerning Our signs are not hidden from Us.”

These people are worse than the polytheists of whom Allah said:

“When it is said to them, ‘Prostrate to the Most Merciful,’ they say, ‘And what is the Most Merciful? Should we prostrate to whatever you command us?’ And it increases them in aversion.”

He Most High also said:

“Thus We have sent you to a community before which other communities have passed away, so that you may recite to them what We have revealed to you; yet they disbelieve in the Most Merciful. Say, ‘He is my Lord; there is no deity but Him. In Him I put my trust, and to Him I turn in repentance.’”

Those polytheists denied only the name ‘the Most Merciful’; they did not deny Allah’s names and attributes. For this reason, Muslims regarded them as greater disbelievers than the Jews and Christians.

If Allah’s names and attributes were figurative, such that they could validly be denied without qualification, it would be permissible to say that Allah is not living, knowing, powerful, hearing, or seeing; that He does not love them, nor do they love Him; that He has not risen over the Throne; and other such things. What Ibn ‘Abd al-Barr reports here concerning the Mu‘tazilah and others like them applies to some of the attributes they deny. As for the names and attributes they affirm, such as the Ever-Living, the All-Knowing, the All-Powerful, and the One who speaks, they say that these apply literally.

Whoever denies that any of these names and attributes applies literally does so only because he does not understand what “literal” means, or because of his disbelief and denial of what rightfully belongs to the Lord of all worlds. Section

As for the questioner’s words, “What does it mean to say that this is literal?”: a literal expression is a word used in the sense for which it was coined. The term may also refer to the meaning assigned to a word and in which that word is used. In the terminology of scholars of legal theory, being literal or figurative is a property of expressions. They sometimes treat it as a property of meanings, but the former usage is more common.

These names and attributes were not coined to denote characteristics peculiar to created beings, whether used without qualification or ascribed to Allah Most High. They denote such characteristics only when ascribed to created beings.

Thus, the word “knowledge” is used without qualification, and it is also ascribed to the servant, as in His words:

“Allah bears witness that there is no deity except Him, as do the angels and those endowed with knowledge. He upholds justice.”

It is also ascribed to Allah, as in His words:

“They encompass nothing of His knowledge except what He wills.”

When knowledge is ascribed to a created being, it cannot include the knowledge of the Creator, glory be to Him, nor is the created being’s knowledge like the Creator’s knowledge. When it is ascribed to the Creator, as in His words:

“He sent it down with His knowledge,”

it cannot include the knowledge of created beings, nor is His knowledge like theirs.

When “knowledge” is mentioned without qualification, it can be divided into categories: knowledge is divided into eternal knowledge and knowledge that has come into being. The word “knowledge” is general, encompassing both in its literal sense. Likewise, when

translated_text:
it is said that existence is divided into eternal existence and existence that has come into being, and into necessary and contingent existence. Likewise, istiwā is divided into the istiwā of the Creator and the istiwā of a created being. Likewise, will, mercy, and giving are divided into Allah’s will, love, and mercy, and the servant’s will, love, and mercy.

Whoever supposes that the “literal sense” encompasses only the servant’s created attributes, which have come into being, and not the Creator’s attributes, is profoundly ignorant. Allah’s attributes are more perfect and complete, and more deserving of these beautiful names. The servant’s attributes bear no comparison to the Lord’s attributes, just as the servant’s essence bears no comparison to His essence. How, then, could the servant truly deserve these beautiful names—deserving to be called knowing, powerful, hearing, and seeing—while the Lord deserves them only figuratively?

It is well known that every perfection possessed by a created being comes from the Lord, glorified and exalted is He, and to Him belongs the highest description. Whatever perfection a created being possesses, the Creator is more entitled to it; and whatever imperfection a created being is free from, the Creator is more entitled to be declared free from it. Thus Allah is “the supreme exemplar”: He cannot be compared to His creation, likened to them, or represented by examples. He and a created being cannot therefore be brought together in an analogical inference based on likeness, nor in a categorical inference whose members stand on an equal footing. Rather:

“To Him belongs the highest description in the heavens and the earth.”

Some people call these names “graded terms,” because the meaning is more fully realized in one subject than in the other. Existence is more properly attributed to the Necessary Existent than to a contingent being, and whiteness more properly to snow than to ivory. His names and attributes belong to this category, for Allah Most High is described by them in

translated_text:
a manner in which He resembles none of His creatures, even though each pair of categories shares a common element. That common element is what the unqualified term denotes; when the term is qualified by reference to either subject, its meaning becomes specific to that subject.

Thus, when one speaks of “existence,” “quiddity,” or “essence,” the term encompasses both the Creator and the created being, although the Creator is more entitled to it than the created being. It is used literally of both.

When one speaks of “Allah’s existence, quiddity, and essence,” this applies specifically to Allah. No created being remains included in what these expressions denote, and they apply literally to Allah alone. Likewise, when one speaks of “the created being’s existence and essence,” this applies specifically to the created being, and the expressions are used literally of it.

When one speaks of “the servant’s existence, quiddity, and true nature,” the Creator is not included in what these expressions denote; they apply literally to the created being alone. The ignorant person supposes that literal usage applies only to created beings. This is an error whose falsity is self-evident according to “reason,” “revealed laws,” and “languages.” For it is self-evident that any two existing things have something in common and something that distinguishes them. An expression indicating only what they have in common does not entail what distinguishes them.

It is also necessarily known in the religion of the Muslims that Allah is entitled to the most beautiful names, and that He has called some of His servants by some of those names. Thus, He has called a servant “hearing,” “seeing,” “living,” “knowing,” “wise,” “compassionate,” “merciful,” “a king,” “mighty,” “a believer,” “generous,” and so forth. Yet it is known that sharing a name does not entail that the Creator resembles the created being. It indicates only that the two named subjects have something in common, while what distinguishes and differentiates them is greater than what they share in common.

translated_text:
rather, their position is that the term “existence” is predicated univocally and that existence is divided into eternal and originated, even while they affirm that the Lord’s existence is identical with His quiddity. For them, the term “existence” is like the term “quiddity.” Just as quiddity and essence are divided into eternal and originated, and the Lord’s quiddity is identical with His essence, so too existence is divided into eternal and originated: the Lord’s existence is identical with His essence, and the servant’s existence is identical with his essence. A thing’s essence is its quiddity.

Thus, “existence” is a univocal term, but when ascribed to either of the two subjects, it becomes specific to that subject. Although the two subjects share the meanings designated by “existence,” “essence,” and “quiddity,” there is nothing common to them in external reality over and above what is particular to each, as Aristotle, Ibn Sīnā, al-Rāzī, and their like suppose. Rather, no unqualified existence, unqualified quiddity, or unqualified essence exists in external reality.

As for the unqualified considered on condition of its being unqualified, these thinkers and others agree that it does not exist in external reality, and that—even assuming this view is authentically attributed to Plato and his followers—it is self-evidently false. As for the unqualified considered without any condition, it may be supposed that it exists in external reality and forms part of a particular entity. This is mistaken. Nothing exists in external reality except particular entities; no unqualified thing exists there as part of a particular entity. translated_text:
the thing described is composed of those attributes which they call essential parts.

For example, they say that a human being is composed of animal and rational, or of animality and rationality. This composition is mental: the composite quiddity in the mind is composed of these elements, which are its parts. As for the reality existing externally, it is characterized by these attributes. Many of these thinkers, however, have confused mental existence with external existence. This error has frequently occurred in the statements of the philosophers. Their early representatives, such as the followers of Pythagoras, maintained that numbers abstracted from numbered things exist in external reality.

The followers of Plato maintain the existence of Platonic Forms: realities abstracted from particular entities in external reality. These realities accompany particular entities in external reality. They likewise affirmed intelligible substances—that is, abstract entities—such as matter and hyle, and, according to some of them, intellects and souls.

Another instance of this is their distinction between essential attributes, which are prior to the quiddity and from which species are composed, and which they call genera and differentiae; and accidental attributes inseparable from the quiddity, which they call properties and common accidents. These five are the universals: genus, differentia, species, common accident, and property.

This has given rise to errors in their “logic” and “metaphysics” through which many people have gone astray. Elsewhere we have drawn attention to this in greater detail than there is room for here. For this reason, the term “composite”

translated_text:
is used by them in five senses: something composed of existence and quiddity; something composed of essence and attributes; something composed of the particular and the universal; something composed of matter and form; and, among those who affirm indivisible atoms, something composed of such atoms. Discerning scholars know that calling such things “composition” is a matter of terminology. Such composition is either a mental construct with no existence in external reality, or it amounts to multiple attributes subsisting in the entity described—and this is true.

The position of Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamā‘ah is to affirm Allah’s attributes. Indeed, the attributes of perfection are inseparable from His essence: His essence cannot exist without the attributes of perfection inseparable from Him. In fact, no essence whatsoever can exist entirely devoid of attributes. All this has been discussed at length elsewhere.

The point here is that, when one says, “This is a human being,” the entity indicated by “this” is what is called a human being. The human being in the abstract is not a part of this individual. Here, a human being exists only as a particular individual; it exists in the abstract only in the mind, not in external reality. When this is said concerning humanity, it means that the two resemble one another in that respect, not that there is something existing in external reality in which they both share. Let the discerning reader reflect on this, for it resolves many specious arguments.  وُجُودُ الْعَبْدِ وَذَاتُهُ وَمَاهِيَّتُهُ وَعِلْمُهُ وَقُدْرَتُهُ وَسَمْعُهُ وَبَصَرُهُ وَكَلَامُهُ وَاسْتِوَاؤُهُ؛
 وَنُزُولُهُ:
 كَانَ هَذَا حَقِيقَةٌ لِلْعَبْدِ مُخْتَصَّةٌ بِهِ مِنْ غَيْرِ أَنْ تُمَاثِلَ صِفَاتِ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى. بَلْ أَبْلَغُ مِنْ ذَلِكَ أَنَّ اللَّهَ أَخْبَرَ أَنَّ فِي الْجَنَّةِ مِنْ الْمَطَاعِمِ وَالْمُشَارِبِ وَالْمَلَابِسِ والمناكح مَا ذَكَرَهُ فِي كِتَابِهِ كَمَا أَخْبَرَ أَنَّ فِيهَا لَبَنًا؛ وَعَسَلًا وَخَمْرًا وَلَحْمًا؛
 وَحَرِيرًا وَذَهَبًا وَفِضَّةً وَحُورًا وَقُصُورًا وَنَحْوَ ذَلِكَ وَقَدْ قَالَ ابْنُ عَبَّاسٍ:
 لَيْسَ فِي الدُّنْيَا مِمَّا فِي الْجَنَّةِ إلَّا الْأَسْمَاءُ.
translated_text:
absolute realities shared by individual entities; and he will know that no other shares in any way in what is proper to the Lord Himself, and that no created thing resembles Him in any attribute. As for a created being, another may resemble it in its attributes, but shares with it only those attributes that properly belong to it. Univocal terms applied to both are used literally of each. When these terms are general, they encompass both; when they are unrestricted, conceiving of the two does not preclude their sharing in them; and when they are qualified, they apply specifically to their respective subjects.

Thus, when one says, “Allah’s existence, Allah’s essence, Allah’s knowledge, Allah’s power, Allah’s hearing, Allah’s sight, Allah’s will, Allah’s speech, Allah’s mercy, Allah’s anger, Allah’s rising above, Allah’s descent, Allah’s love, Allah’s will,” and the like, all these terms apply literally to Allah Most High, without including any created thing and without any created thing resembling Him in them.

When one says, “The servant’s existence, his essence, his quiddity, his knowledge, his power, his hearing, his sight, his speech, his rising above, and his descent,” these terms apply literally to the servant and specifically to him, without his attributes resembling those of Allah Most High.

More striking still, Allah has told us that Paradise contains the foods, drinks, garments, and spouses He has mentioned in His Book. He has told us that it contains milk, honey, wine, meat, silk, gold, silver, houris, palaces, and the like. Yet Ibn ‘Abbās said:

“Nothing of what is in Paradise is found in this world except the names.”

original_text:
فَتِلْكَ الْحَقَائِقُ الَّتِي فِي الْآخِرَةِ لَيْسَتْ مُمَاثِلَةً لِهَذِهِ الْحَقَائِقِ الَّتِي فِي الدُّنْيَا وَإِنْ كَانَتْ مُشَابِهَةً لَهَا مِنْ بَعْضِ الْوُجُوهِ وَالِاسْمِ يَتَنَاوَلُهَا حَقِيقَةً. وَمَعْلُومٌ أَنَّ الْخَالِقَ أَبْعَدُ عَنْ مُشَابَهَةِ الْمَخْلُوقِ فَكَيْفَ يَجُوزُ أَنْ يَظُنَّ أَنَّ فِيمَا أَثْبَتَهُ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى مِنْ أَسْمَائِهِ وَصِفَاتِهِ مُمَاثِلًا لِمَخْلُوقَاتِهِ؟
 وَأَنْ يُقَالَ:
 لَيْسَ ذَلِكَ بِحَقِيقَةِ وَهَلْ يَكُونُ أَحَقُّ بِهَذِهِ الْأَسْمَاءِ الْحُسْنَى وَالصِّفَاتِ الْعُلْيَا مِنْ رَبِّ السَّمَوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ مَعَ أَنَّ مُبَايَنَتَهُ لِلْمَخْلُوقَاتِ أَعْظَمُ مِنْ مُبَايَنَةِ كُلِّ مَخْلُوقٍ.
 وَالْجَاهِلُ يَضِلُّ بِقَوْلِ الْمُتَكَلِّمِينَ:
 إنَّ الْعَرَبَ وَضَعُوا لَفْظَ الِاسْتِوَاءِ لِاسْتِوَاءِ الْإِنْسَانِ عَلَى الْمَنْزِلِ أَوْ الْفُلْكِ أَوْ اسْتِوَاءِ السَّفِينَةِ عَلَى الْجُودِيِّ وَنَحْوِ ذَلِكَ مِنْ اسْتِوَاءِ بَعْضِ الْمَخْلُوقَاتِ فَهَذَا كَمَا يَقُولُ الْقَائِلُ: إنَّمَا وَضَعُوا لَفْظَ السَّمْعِ وَالْبَصَرِ وَالْكَلَامِ لِمَا يَكُونُ مَحَلُّهُ حَدَقَةً وَأَجْفَانًا وَأَصْمِخَةً وَأُذُنًا وَشَفَتَيْنِ وَهَذَا ضَلَالٌ فِي الشَّرْعِ وَكَذِبٌ وَإِنَّمَا وَضَعُوا لَفْظَ الرَّحْمَةِ وَالْعِلْمِ وَالْإِرَادَةِ لِمَا يَكُونُ مَحَلُّهُ مُضْغَةَ لَحْمٍ وَفُؤَادٍ وَهَذَا كُلُّهُ جَهْلٌ مِنْهُ.
 فَإِنَّ الْعَرَبَ إنَّمَا وَضَعَتْ لِلْإِنْسَانِ مَا أَضَافَتْهُ إلَيْهِ فَإِذَا قَالَتْ:
 سَمْعُ الْعَبْدِ وَبَصَرُهُ وَكَلَامُهُ وَعِلْمُهُ وَإِرَادَتُهُ وَرَحْمَتُهُ فَمَا يَخُصُّ بِهِ يَتَنَاوَلُ ذَلِكَ خَصَائِصَ الْعَبْدِ.
 وَإِذَا قِيلَ:
 سَمْعُ اللَّهِ وَبَصَرُهُ وَكَلَامُهُ وَعِلْمُهُ وَإِرَادَتُهُ وَرَحْمَتُهُ كَانَ هَذَا مُتَنَاوِلًا لِمَا يُخَصُّ بِهِ الرَّبُّ لَا يَدْخُلُ فِي ذَلِكَ شَيْءٌ مِنْ خَصَائِصِ الْمَخْلُوقِينَ فَمَنْ ظَنَّ أَنَّ هَذَا الِاسْتِوَاءَ إذَا كَانَ حَقِيقَةً يَتَنَاوَلُ شَيْئًا مِنْ صِفَاتِ الْمَخْلُوقِينَ مَعَ كَوْنِ النَّصِّ قَدْ خَصَّهُ بِاَللَّهِ كَانَ جَاهِلًا جِدًّا بِدَلَالَاتِ اللُّغَاتِ وَمَعْرِفَةِ الْحَقِيقَةِ وَالْمَجَازِ.
translated_text:
Thus, those realities in the Hereafter are not identical to these realities in this world, although they resemble them in some respects and the terms apply to them literally. It is well known that the Creator is far further removed from resembling created beings. How, then, can anyone suppose that the names and attributes Allah Most High has affirmed for Himself involve any likeness to His creatures, or say that they do not apply literally? Who could be more entitled to these Most Beautiful Names and Most Exalted Attributes than the Lord of the heavens and the earth, when His distinctness from created things is greater than that of any created thing from another?

The ignorant person is misled by the speculative theologians’ claim: “The Arabs established the term istiwā’ (rising above) to denote a person’s settling upon a house or a vessel, or a ship’s coming to rest on Mount Jūdī, and similar instances of istiwā’ among created things.” This is like someone saying, “They established the terms hearing, sight, and speech only for what resides in an eyeball, eyelids, ear canals, an ear, and two lips.” This is religious error and falsehood. Or saying, “They established the terms mercy, knowledge, and will only for what resides in a lump of flesh and a heart.” All this reflects his ignorance.

For the Arabs assigned to a human being only what they expressly attributed to him. When they say, “The servant’s hearing, sight, speech, knowledge, will, and mercy,” these expressions, being qualified as his, denote attributes particular to the servant.

When one says, “Allah’s hearing, sight, speech, knowledge, will, and mercy,” these expressions denote what is particular to the Lord; nothing peculiar to created beings is included in them. Whoever supposes that this rising above, if understood literally, includes any attribute of created beings—even though the revealed text expressly attributes it to Allah—is profoundly ignorant of how language conveys meaning and of the distinction between literal and figurative usage.

original_text:
وَهَؤُلَاءِ الْجُهَّالُ يُمَثِّلُونَ فِي ابْتِدَاءِ فَهْمِهِمْ صِفَاتِ الْخَالِقِ بِصِفَاتِ الْمَخْلُوقِ:
 ثُمَّ يَنْفُونَ ذَلِكَ وَيُعَطِّلُونَهُ فَلَا يَفْهَمُونَ مِنْ ذَلِكَ إلَّا مَا يَخْتَصُّ بِالْمَخْلُوقِ وَيَنْفُونَ مَضْمُونَ ذَلِكَ وَيَكُونُونَ قَدْ جَحَدُوا مَا يَسْتَحِقُّهُ الرَّبُّ مِنْ خَصَائِصِهِ وَصِفَاتِهِ وَأَلْحَدُوا فِي أَسْمَاءِ اللَّهِ وَآيَاتِهِ وَخَرَجُوا عَنْ الْقِيَاسِ الْعَقْلِيِّ وَالنَّصِّ الشَّرْعِيِّ فَلَا يَبْقَى بِأَيْدِيهِمْ لَا مَعْقُولٌ صَرِيحٌ وَلَا مَنْقُولٌ صَحِيحٌ ثُمَّ لَا بُدَّ لَهُمْ مِنْ إثْبَاتِ بَعْضِ مَا يُثْبِتُهُ أَهْلُ الْإِثْبَاتِ مِنْ الْأَسْمَاءِ وَالصِّفَاتِ فَإِذَا أَثْبَتُوا الْبَعْضَ وَنَفَوْا الْبَعْضَ قِيلَ لَهُمْ: مَا الْفَرْقُ بَيْنَ مِمَّا أَثْبَتُّمُوهُ وَنَفَيْتُمُوهُ؟ وَلِمَ كَانَ هَذَا حَقِيقَةً وَلَمْ يَكُنْ هَذَا حَقِيقَةً؟ لَمْ يَكُنْ لَهُمْ جَوَابٌ أَصْلًا وَظَهَرَ بِذَلِكَ جَهْلُهُمْ وَضَلَالُهُمْ شَرْعًا وَقَدْرًا. وَقَدْ تَدَبَّرْت كَلَامَ عَامَّةِ مَنْ يَنْفِي شَيْئًا مِمَّا أَثْبَتَهُ الرُّسُلُ مِنْ الْأَسْمَاءِ وَالصِّفَاتِ فَوَجَدْتهمْ كُلَّهُمْ مُتَنَاقِضِينَ؛ فَإِنَّهُمْ يَحْتَجُّونَ لِمَا نَفَوْهُ بِنَظِيرِ مَا يَحْتَجُّ بِهِ النَّافِي لِمَا أَثْبَتُوهُ؛ فَيَلْزَمُهُمْ إمَّا إثْبَاتُ الْأَمْرَيْنِ وَإِمَّا نَفْيُهُمَا؛ فَإِذَا نَفَوْهُمَا فَلَا بُدَّ لَهُمْ أَنْ يَقُولُوا بِالْوَاجِبِ الْوُجُودِ وَعَدَمِهِ جَمِيعًا وَهَذَا نِهَايَةُ هَؤُلَاءِ الْنُّفَاةِ الْمَلَاحِدَةِ الْغُلَاةِ مِنْ الْقَرَامِطَةِ وَغُلَاةِ الْمُتَفَلْسِفَةِ؛ فَإِنَّهُمْ إذَا أَخَذُوا يَنْفُونَ النَّقِيضَيْنِ جَمِيعًا؛ فَالنَّقِيضَانِ كَمَا أَنَّهُمَا لَا يَجْتَمِعَانِ؛ فَلَا يَرْتَفِعَانِ. وَمِنْ جِهَةِ إنَّ مَا يَسْلُبُونَ عَنْهُ النَّقِيضَيْنِ لَا بُدَّ أَنْ يَتَصَوَّرُوهُ وَأَنْ يُعَبِّرُوا عَنْهُ؛ فَإِنَّ التَّصْدِيقَ مَسْبُوقٌ بِالتَّصَوُّرِ وَمَتَى تَصَوَّرُوهُ وَعَبَّرُوا عَنْهُ كَقَوْلِهِمْ الثَّابِتِ وَالْوَاجِبِ أَوْ أَيُّ شَيْءٍ قَالُوهُ لَزِمَهُمْ فِيهِ مِنْ إثْبَاتِ الْقَدْرِ الْمُشْتَرَكِ نَظِيرُ مَا يَلْزَمُهُمْ فِيمَا نَفَوْهُ
translated_text:
These ignorant people initially understand the Creator’s attributes by likening them to those of created beings. They then deny and nullify what they have thus understood. They understand these attributes only in terms peculiar to created beings and then deny their import. In doing so, they reject the distinctive qualities and attributes that rightfully belong to the Lord, deviate concerning Allah’s names and signs, and depart from rational argument and revealed scripture. They are thus left with neither sound reason nor authentic revelation.

Yet they must inevitably affirm some of the names and attributes affirmed by those who uphold them. When they affirm some and deny others, they are asked: “What distinguishes what you affirm from what you deny? Why should one be understood literally but not the other?” They have no answer whatsoever. Their ignorance and error thus become manifest in terms of both divine revelation and divine decree.

I have carefully considered the statements of the generality of those who deny any of the names and attributes affirmed by the Messengers, and I have found them all inconsistent. The arguments they use to deny certain attributes are analogous to those used by others to deny the attributes they themselves affirm. They must therefore either affirm both or deny both. If they deny both, they must ultimately affirm both the Necessary Existent and His nonexistence. This is the endpoint reached by these extreme, heretical negators among the Qarmatians and the extremists among the adherents of philosophy. For they proceed to deny both sides of a contradiction, yet just as two contradictories cannot both be true, neither can they both be false.

Moreover, they must conceive of, and give expression to, that of which they deny both contradictories, since judgment presupposes conception. Whenever they conceive of it and express it—as when they call it “the Existent,” “the Necessary,” or whatever else they may say—they are bound to affirm a common element of meaning, analogous to what they would be bound to affirm in what they have denied.

original_text:
وَلَا يُمْكِنُ أَنْ يُتَصَوَّرُ شَيْءٌ مِنْ ذَلِكَ مَعَ قَوْلِهِمْ:
 أَسْمَاءُ اللَّهِ مَقُولَةٌ بِالِاشْتِرَاكِ اللَّفْظِيِّ فَقَطْ.
 فَإِنَّ الْمُشْتَرِكِينَ اشْتِرَاكًا لَفْظِيًّا لَا مَعْنَوِيًّا كَلَفْظِ الْمُشْتَرَى الْمَقُولِ عَلَى الْكَوْكَبِ وَالْمُبْتَاعِ وَسُهَيْلٍ الْمَقُولِ عَلَى الْكَوْكَبِ وَعَلَى ابْنِ عَمْرٍو فَإِنَّهُ إذَا سَمِعَ الْمُسْتَمِعُ قَائِلًا يَقُولُ لَهُ:
 جَاءَنِي سُهَيْلُ بْنُ عَمْرٍو وَهَذَا هُوَ الْمُشْتَرِي لِهَذِهِ السِّلْعَةِ لَمْ يَفْهَمْ مِنْ هَذَا اللَّفْظِ كَوْكَبًا أَصْلًا إلَّا أَنْ يَعْرِفَ أَنَّ اللَّفْظَ مَوْضُوعٌ لَهُ فَإِذَا لَمْ تَكُنْ أَسْمَاؤُهُ مُتَوَاطِئَةً لَمْ يَفْهَمْ الْعِبَادُ مِنْ أَسْمَائِهِ شَيْئًا أَصْلًا إلَّا أَنْ يَعْرِفُوا مَا يَخُصُّ ذَاتَهُ وَهُمْ لَمْ يَعْرِفُوا مَا يَخُصُّ ذَاتَهُ فَلَمْ يَعْرِفُوا شَيْئًا.
ثُمَّ إنَّ الْعِلْمَ بِانْقِسَامِ الْوُجُودِ إلَى قَدِيمٍ وَمُحْدَثٍ وَأَمْثَالِ ذَلِكَ عِلْمٌ ضَرُورِيٌّ فَالْقَادِحُ سوفسطائي. وَكَذَلِكَ الْعِلْمُ بِأَنَّ بَيْنَ الِاسْمَيْنِ قَدْرًا مُشْتَرَكًا عِلْمٌ ضَرُورِيٌّ.
 وَإِذَا قِيلَ:
 إنَّ اللَّفْظَ حَقِيقَةٌ فِيهِمَا لَمْ يَحْتَجْ ذَلِكَ إلَى أَنْ يَكُونَ أَهْلُ اللُّغَةِ قَدْ تَكَلَّمُوا بِاللَّفْظِ مُطْلَقًا فَعَبَّرُوا عَنْ الْمَعْنَى الْمُطْلَقِ الْمُشْتَرَكِ؛

translated_text:
And none of this can be conceived while they maintain:

“Allah’s names are shared only in wording, not in meaning.”

For things that share a term but not a meaning are exemplified by mushtarī, which denotes both the planet Jupiter and a buyer, and Suhayl, which denotes both the star Canopus and Ibn ‘Amr. If someone hears another say, “Suhayl ibn ‘Amr came to me, and he is the buyer of this commodity,” he derives no notion of a celestial body from these words at all unless he knows that the term is also used for one. Thus, if Allah’s names did not convey a common meaning across their different applications, His servants would understand nothing whatsoever from His names unless they knew what is peculiar to His essence. Yet they do not know what is peculiar to His essence, so they would know nothing.

Furthermore, the division of existence into the beginningless and the originated, and similar distinctions, is known self-evidently; anyone who challenges this is a sophist. Likewise, it is self-evident that the two names share a common element of meaning.

To say that a term applies literally to both does not require that speakers of the language should have used it without qualification to express the unrestricted, common meaning. For meanings such as life, knowledge, power, and rising over—and indeed a hand and other such things—exist only in relation to something else: either as an attribute subsisting in another or as a body subsisting in another, with no external existence apart from its locus.

However, when rational investigators sought to abstract unrestricted universal meanings, they expressed them through unrestricted universal terms. Speakers of the language, by contrast, begin their discourse by saying, for example, “Zayd came,” and “This is Zayd’s face.” They point to his coming and his face, and the person addressed understands this.

Then, on another occasion, they say: “‘Amr came,” “I saw ‘Amr’s face,” “The horse came,” and “I saw the horse’s face.” The listener understands that these have both a common element and a distinguishing element, and that ‘Amr’s coming and face stand in the same relation to him as Zayd’s coming and face do to Zayd. If it is known that ‘Amr is like Zayd, it is understood that his coming is like Zayd’s coming and his face like Zayd’s face. If, however, it is known that the horse is not like Zayd but resembles him in certain respects, it is understood that its coming and face are not like Zayd’s coming and face, but resemble them in certain respects.

Likewise, when it is said, “The angels came,” and “The prophets saw the angels’ faces,” it is understood that the angels have a coming and faces that stand in the same relation to them as a human being’s coming and face do to him. One’s knowledge of the true nature of these then depends on one’s knowledge of the true nature of the angels. If one knows the angels only in general terms and cannot conceive what they are like, the same applies to their coming and their faces: one knows them only in general terms and cannot conceive what they are like.

The same applies when it is said, “The jinn came.” In all these instances, the words convey their meanings literally. Indeed, if it is said, “The reality and essence of an angel are not like the reality and essence of a jinn,” the terms “reality” and “essence” are used literally of both. They are terms with a common meaning across their applications, even though the things they designate have explicitly been stated not to be alike. If someone were to say, “This created being is not like that created being,” “This animal endowed with speech is not like the animal without speech,” “This color, which is white, is not like black,” or “The existent being who is the Creator is not like the existent being who is created,” and so forth, these terms would be used literally of both things designated, despite the explicit denial that they are alike. Whoever supposes that taking Allah’s names and attributes literally necessarily means that He resembles created beings and that His attributes resemble theirs is among the most ignorant of people. Whoever distinguishes between one attribute and another, although the grounds for literal and figurative usage apply equally to both, contradicts himself and holds an incoherent position, resembling someone who believes in part of the Scripture and disbelieves in another.  كَانَتْ الْمُقَدِّمَةُ الْأَوْلَى مَمْنُوعَةً؛ فَإِنَّ عَاقِلًا لَا يَقُولُ إنَّهُ لَوْ كَانَ فَوْقَ الْعَرْشِ لَكَانَ جَسَدًا؛
 وَلَا يَقُولُ عَاقِلٌ إنَّهُ لَوْ كَانَ لَهُ عِلْمٌ وَقُدْرَةٌ:
 لَكَانَ جَسَدًا وَلَا يَقُولُ عَاقِلٌ: إنَّهُ لَوْ كَانَ يَرَى وَيَتَكَلَّمُ لَكَانَ جَسَدًا وَبَدَنًا. فإن الْمَلَائِكَةَ لَهُمْ عِلْمٌ وَقُدْرَةٌ وَتَرَى وَتَتَكَلَّمُ وَكَذَلِكَ الْجِنُّ وَكَذَلِكَ الْهَوَاءُ يَعْلُو عَلَى غَيْرِهِ وَلَيْسَ بِجَسَدِ. وَإِنْ عَنَى بِالْجِسْمِ مَا يَعْنِيه أَهْلُ الْكَلَامِ؛ مِنْ أَنَّهُ الَّذِي يُشَارُ إلَيْهِ وَجَعَلُوا كُلَّ مَا يُشَارُ إلَيْهِ جِسْمًا وَكُلَّ مَا يُرَى جِسْمًا أَوْ كُلَّ مَا يُمْكِنُ أَنَّهُ يُرَى أَوْ يُوصَفُ بِالصِّفَاتِ فَهُوَ جِسْمٌ أَوْ كُلَّ مَا يَعْلُو عَلَى غَيْرِهِ وَيَكُونُ فَوْقَهُ فَهُوَ جِسْمٌ.
 فَيُقَالُ لَهُ:
 فَالْجَسَدُ وَالْجِسْمُ بِهَذَا التَّفْسِيرِ الْكَلَامِيِّ لَيْسَ هُوَ جَسَدًا فِي لُغَةِ الْعَرَبِ؛ بَلْ هُوَ مُنْقَسِمٌ إلَى غَلِيظٍ وَرَقِيقٍ إلَى مَا هُوَ جَسَدٌ وَإِلَى مَا لَيْسَ بِجَسَدِ.
translated_text:
a jasad—then the reply to you is:

Affirming His rising over the Throne does not entail that He is a jasad, which is what jism means in ordinary language. We know necessarily that air is above the earth, yet it is not a jasad; and jasad is what jism means in ordinary language.

Thus, the assertion, “If He were established over the Throne, He would be a jism; a jism is a jasad; and revelation rules out His being a jasad,” is misleading.

If by jism the speaker means jasad, then the first premise is disputed. No rational person would say that if He were above the Throne, He would be a jasad. Nor would any rational person say that if He possessed knowledge and power, He would be a jasad, or that if He saw and spoke, He would be a jasad and a physical body. The angels possess knowledge and power, and they see and speak; so too do the jinn. Likewise, air is above other things, yet it is not a jasad.

If, however, by jism he means what the speculative theologians mean—something that can be pointed to, classifying everything that can be pointed to as a jism, and everything that can be seen as a jism; or everything that could be seen or described by attributes as a jism; or everything that is above something else and over it as a jism—then the reply to him is:

Jasad and jism, according to this definition used by the speculative theologians, do not mean jasad in Arabic usage. Rather, what they denote is divided into dense and subtle: that which is a jasad and that which is not.

original_text:
وَلِذَا يَقُولُ الْفُقَهَاءُ:
 النَّجَاسَةُ إنْ كَانَتْ مُتَجَسِّدَةً كَالْمَيْتَةِ فَحُكْمُهَا كَذَا وَإِنْ كَانَتْ غَيْرَ مُتَجَسِّدَةٍ كَالْبَوْلِ فَحُكْمُهَا كَذَا. وَإِذَا قُدِّرَ أَنَّ الدَّلِيلَ عَلَى أَنَّهُ لَيْسَ بِجَسَدِ لَمْ يَلْزَمْ أَنْ لَا يَكُونُ جِسْمًا بِهَذَا الِاصْطِلَاحِ؛ لِأَنَّ الْجِسْمَ أَعَمُّ عِنْدَهُمْ مِنْ الْجَسَدِ وَلَا يَلْزَمُ مِنْ نَفْيِ الْخَاصِّ نَفْيُ الْعَامِّ؛ كَمَا إذَا قُلْت لَيْسَ هُوَ بِإِنْسَانِ فَإِنَّهُ لَا يَلْزَمُ أَنَّهُ لَيْسَ بِحَيَوَانِ. فَلَفْظُ الْجِسْمِ فِيهِ اشْتِرَاكٌ بَيْنَ مَعْنَاهُ فِي اللُّغَةِ وَمَعْنَاهُ فِي عُرْفِ أَهْلِ الْكَلَامِ؛ فَإِذَا كَانَ مَعْنَاهُ فِي اللُّغَةِ هُوَ مَعْنَى الْجَسَدِ - وَهَذَا مُنْتَفٍ بِمَا ذَكَرَ مِنْ الدَّلِيلِ - بَطَلَ قَوْلُ مَنْ نَفَى الِاسْتِوَاءَ بِالذَّاتِ؛ أَوْ غَيْرَهُ مِنْ الصِّفَاتِ.
 بِأَنَّهُ لَوْ كَانَ مَوْصُوفًا بِذَلِكَ:
 لَكَانَ جِسْمًا فَإِنَّ التَّلَازُمَ حِينَئِذٍ مُنْتَفٍ فَإِحْدَى الْمُقَدِّمَتَيْنِ بَاطِلَةٌ؛ إمَّا الْأُولَى وَإِمَّا الثَّانِيَةُ.
 وَنَظِيرُ هَذَا أَنْ يَقُولَ:
 لَوْ كَانَ لَهُ عِلْمٌ وَقُدْرَةٌ لَكَانَ مَحَلًّا لِلْأَعْرَاضِ وَمَا كَانَ مَحَلًّا لِلْأَعْرَاضِ فَهُوَ مَحَلُّ الْآفَاتِ وَالْعُيُوبِ فَلَا يَكُونُ قُدُّوسًا وَلَا سَلَامًا لِأَنَّ أَهْلَ اللُّغَةِ قَالُوا: الْعَرَضُ بِالتَّحْرِيكِ مَا يَعْرِضُ لِلْإِنْسَانِ مِنْ مَرَضٍ وَنَحْوِهِ فَلَوْ جَازَ أَنْ تَقُومَ بِهِ هَذِهِ لَكَانَ تَعَالَى وَتَقَدَّسَ مَعِيبًا نَاقِصًا وَهُوَ سُبْحَانَهُ مُقَدَّسٌ عَنْ ذَلِكَ؛ إذْ هُوَ السَّلَامُ الْقُدُّوسُ.
 فَيُقَالُ:
 لَفْظُ الْعَرَضِ مُشْتَرِكٌ بَيْنَ مَا ذَكَرَ مِنْ مَعْنَاهُ فِي اللُّغَةِ وَبَيْنَ مَعْنَاهُ فِي عُرْفِ أَهْلِ الْكَلَامِ فَإِنَّ مَعْنَاهُ - عِنْدَ مَنْ يُسَمِّي الْعِلْمَ وَالْقُدْرَةَ
translated_text:
Hence the jurists say: “If an impure substance has a solid bodily form, such as carrion, its ruling is such-and-such; if it does not, such as urine, its ruling is such-and-such.” Even supposing there is proof that He is not a jasad, it does not follow that He is not a jism according to this terminology. For them, jism is broader than jasad, and negating the narrower category does not entail negating the broader one. If, for example, you say that something is not a human being, it does not follow that it is not an animal.

Thus, the term jism has different meanings in ordinary language and in the terminology of the speculative theologians. If its linguistic meaning is that of jasad—and this is ruled out by the proof he has cited—then the argument of someone who denies His rising over the Throne in His essence, or any other attribute, on the grounds that possessing that attribute would make Him a jism, is invalid. The supposed entailment does not hold in that case. One of the two premises must therefore be false: either the first or the second.

A parallel example would be someone saying:

“If He possessed knowledge and power, He would be a locus of accidents. Whatever is a locus of accidents is a locus of afflictions and defects, and therefore cannot be the All-Holy or the One free from every defect. For the lexicographers say: ‘ʿArad, pronounced with two short a vowels, denotes an illness or similar affliction that befalls a person.’ If such things could inhere in Him, He—exalted and holy is He—would be defective and imperfect. Yet He, glory be to Him, is utterly free of that, for He is the One free from every defect, the All-Holy.”

The reply is:

The term ʿarad has different meanings: the linguistic meaning just mentioned, and its meaning in the terminology of the speculative theologians. For its meaning—according to those who call knowledge and power

مُطْلَقًا عَرَضًا - مَا قَامَ بِغَيْرِهِ كَالْحَيَاةِ وَالْعِلْمِ وَالْقُدْرَةِ وَالْحَرَكَةِ. وَالسُّكُونِ وَنَحْوِ ذَلِكَ.
