translated_text:
This is illustrated by the following: at most, the opponent can say, “If He were outside the world, He would be a body or would be spatially confined. That is ruled out, so He cannot be outside the world.”

The premises of the argument by which they deny this contain obscurities and ambiguities evident to anyone who examines the matter. These very obscurities and ambiguities have led many people to place confidence in those premises. Their confidence rests on uncritically following those who proposed them, not on their own rational certainty. Thus, they forbid ordinary people to follow the messengers in what they have reported about Allah’s attributes, claiming that reason contradicts those reports, despite the certainty that the messengers speak only the truth. Yet they themselves uncritically follow their leaders in opposing those reports through premises they claim to be rational. Their followers have reached no rational certainty concerning these premises; they merely follow their leaders in accepting them.

Hence, when they examine these premises thoroughly, are challenged about them, and are shown the grounds for rejecting them, you find them resorting to sheer ignorance. Either they refer the answer to someone who is dead and gone—who, upon scrutiny, proves even more deeply mired than they in doubt and confusion—or they abandon the proper conduct of debate and disputation and adopt the behavior of the unjust and foolish. Or they imagine that this is disbelief contrary to religion. Yet their own position contradicts the Book and the Messenger, follows a path other than that of the believers, and asserts what none of the Companions, the Successors, or the other leading scholars of the Muslims ever said.

Another point that clarifies this matter is that those who deny the attributes do not have a single argument for which there is agreement among them on

its premises. Rather, each group challenges the other’s argument. The philosophers challenge the Muʿtazilah’s argument for denying the attributes—indeed, for denying corporeality, spatial confinement, and the like. For the Muʿtazilah’s argument rests on the premise that what is eternal cannot be a locus for attributes and motions, and therefore cannot be a body or be spatially confined. Attributes, they maintain, are accidents. They argue that bodies originate in time because their accidents and motions originate in time, no body is ever devoid of them, and whatever is never devoid of temporally originated events must itself originate in time.

Indeed, al-Ashʿarī himself stated in his Epistle to the People of the Frontier that this argument, which they used to establish the temporal origination of the world—namely, inferring the temporal origination of bodies from that of their accidents—is an argument forbidden in the revealed laws of the prophets, which none of the messengers or their followers ever employed. In another work, he explained the Muʿtazilah’s inability to establish a proof that He is not a body.

Abū Hāmid al-Ghazālī and other leading scholars of rational inquiry demonstrated the unsoundness of the philosophers’ method of denying the attributes. They also demonstrated their inability to establish a proof that He is not a body—indeed, their inability to establish a proof of divine oneness—and explained that His being a body could be ruled out only through the first method: that of the Muʿtazilah, concerning which al-Ashʿarī made the remarks just mentioned.

Thus, when the most intelligent and accomplished rational thinkers on each side challenge the premises of the other side’s argument, on which that side claims to base its denial, this is evidence that those premises are not self-evident. For self-evident truths cannot be impugned. If, however, it is said: “These people

have challenged these self-evident premises,” the reply is:

If you allow that the leading proponents of negation may falsely challenge self-evident premises, then it is all the more possible for them to challenge the premises used by those who affirm the attributes. Elsewhere, the arguments of those who deny the attributes and the premises underlying those arguments have been discussed in detail, making it clear to anyone possessed of reason that their proponents have departed from the straight path. They have resorted to sophistry in rational matters and treated revelation in the manner of the Qarmatians. Their denial is supported by neither reason nor revelation, neither sound judgment nor divine law. Rather, they possess specious arguments that those who examine them mistake for clear proofs:

“Like a mirage on a level plain, which a thirsty man mistakes for water, until, when he reaches it, he finds nothing there, but finds Allah there, who settles his account in full. And Allah is swift in reckoning.”

This is why bewilderment, uncertainty, doubt, and confusion prevail among them. Those specious arguments have become accepted premises in their eyes, which they suppose to be rational truths or demonstrative proofs. Yet they are accepted only because of the equivocation and ambiguity they contain. You will find no premise of theirs without ambiguous expressions whose vagueness and obscurity lead people astray. How, then, could a conclusion established through such premises overturn those self-evident propositions?

The more closely an investigator examines what has been pointed out here, together with the discussions of those who deny the attributes, the greater his insight and understanding become. For it is inconceivable that negation could rest on self-evident premises of which reason is as certain as it is of the premises of those who affirm the attributes—premises that conclusively establish

translated_text:
the falsity of their conclusion, namely their claim that He exists neither within the world nor outside it—with a certainty unmatched by reason’s certainty concerning the premises on which this established conclusion rests. It is therefore impossible for that self-evident rational certainty to be displaced by a conclusion drawn from premises that do not command the same certainty. This holds even before examining whether the premises advanced against that certainty are sound or unsound. The point here is simply that it is neither legitimate nor acceptable in debate to challenge this certainty, firmly rooted in human nature, with what the opponent claims to be inferential proofs. This alone suffices to refute him, even without resolving his specious arguments. Likewise, it suffices to refute a sophist by saying: “What you deny consists of self-evident propositions; their denial cannot therefore be accepted on the strength of the specious inferential arguments you present.”

The second, detailed response is to demonstrate the unsoundness of the arguments offered by those who deny the attributes to establish the possibility of what they claim.

Those who affirm the attributes say:

The arguments you have presented to establish the existence of a being neither within the world nor outside it are the arguments of a sophist. As for the humanity shared by human beings and other such “universals,” these cannot be said to exist outside the mind while being neither within the world nor outside it. They are things established in the mind and in conception. If they are said to exist in external reality, they must be either an entity subsisting in its own right or an attribute subsisting in an entity. Undoubtedly, they do not exist in external reality as unrestricted universals, subject to the unrestrictedness with which they are conceived. Rather, they exist in external reality only as particular, individual instances.

As for the assertion, “Examination extracts the intelligible from the sensible”: if this means something intelligible that exists in the mind, then what exists in the mind is not the very thing that exists in external reality. If, however, it means that a sensible object existing in external reality contains something intelligible that is not in the mind, this is false. A particular human being contains only what is particular: this individual’s body, soul, and attributes. All of this is particular, determinate, and individual—not universal or unrestricted.

What he mentions in conjunction with affirming mutually separate beings—intellects and souls—that are neither within the world nor outside it constitutes no proof. Rather, this very argument, along with others, refutes them just as it refutes their counterparts. Indeed, their position is more manifestly unsound and less defensible than the positions of those who deny the attributes and Allah’s being above creation. How, then, can a position be supported by something weaker and further removed from the truth? It is well known that rational people generally, whether adherents of religious traditions or otherwise, reject this claim of theirs.

As for his assertion that, in maintaining this, they were not advancing a position whose falsity is self-evident, that is not the case. Rather, those who affirm the attributes and maintain that two existing beings must either be separate from one another or co-located say that these people’s claims to the contrary are self-evidently false. Indeed, even the leading speculative theologians who deny that Allah is above creation claim to know self-evidently that a contingent being is either a body or something subsisting in a body. These men debated the philosophers more effectively than the former group did. They and others do not concede to the philosophers the possibility of a contingent being that is neither a body nor something subsisting in a body. Indeed, their leading authorities have explicitly declared the invalidity of this “third category” to be self-evident.

Indeed, Abū Muhammad ‘Abd Allāh ibn Sa‘īd ibn Kullāb, the leading authority of those who affirm the divine attributes—such as Abū al-‘Abbās al-Qalānisī, Abū al-Hasan al-Ash‘arī, Abū ‘Abd Allāh ibn Mujāhid, and others—demonstrated that existing things must be either separate from or co-located with another, and that the claim that something exists which is neither separate from nor co-located with another is self-evidently false. His demonstration was comparable to, and even more forceful than, those thinkers’ demonstration that contingent beings are confined to bodies and their accidents.

Some groups of speculative thinkers have maintained that nothing exists except a body or something subsisting in a body—when “body” is understood in its technical rather than its linguistic sense. This is firmly rooted in the innate understanding of ordinary people. It is also the position of many philosophers, or most of them.

Likewise, the great imams, such as Imam Ahmad in his refutation of the Jahmiyyah, ‘Abd al-‘Azīz al-Makkī in his refutation of the Jahmiyyah, and others, explained that the claim made by those who negate the attributes—that there is a third category, neither separate from nor co-located with another—is manifestly false according to sound reason. This is among the evident propositions that rational people recognize through their own reason.

Whoever examines people’s statements on this subject will find that most of those renowned for reason and knowledge explicitly state that affirming the existence of a being neither co-located with nor separate from another, and similar claims, is known by clear reason, with necessary certainty, to be [unsound or false] (*).

As for the third argument, he says:

“Reason divides what is known into that which is separate, that which is co-located, and that which is neither separate nor co-located,” and similarly with other divisions.

The reply is:

The familiar division into the necessary, the contingent, and that which is neither necessary nor contingent; into the eternal, the originated, and that which is neither eternal nor originated; into that which subsists in itself, that which subsists in another, and that which subsists neither in itself nor in another—and similar divisions—are mental suppositions. It is well known that such suppositions do not establish that these things are possible in external reality. Not every category or supposition posited by the mind is possible or actually exists outside it. Rather, the mind divides whatever occurs to it into the necessary, the impossible, and the contingent, and into the existent and the nonexistent. The mind thus entertains whatever occurs to it, and it is well known that this includes impossibilities that cannot exist outside the mind.

As for his statement:

“The division into the separate and the co-located is not known to be false, just as the proposition that one is half of two is not known to be false.”

their constituent concepts be clear to everyone; rather, the requirement is that, once those concepts are grasped, reason should assent to the propositions with certainty. The conception of one as half of two is clear to everyone; hence the assent that follows it is more evident than in other cases. This is also why its clarity to the mind differs from that of the proposition that fifty-five and a quarter and an eighth is half of one hundred and ten and a half and a quarter, although both are self-evident. There are many comparable examples.

The meaning of “separate” and “co-located” is not immediately clear, since these terms are ambiguous, as explained earlier. Yet once their meaning is explained to rational people, they affirm with certainty that there is no “third category.” Likewise, since the meanings of the eternal and the originated, the necessary and the contingent, substance and accident, and similar terms are not clear in themselves to rational people generally, they do not affirm with certainty that whatever exists must fall within one of the two categories. Once the meaning is explained to them, however, they affirm this with certainty.

Thus, if rational people are told, “There are two self-subsisting beings, one of which is neither outside and separate from the other, nor inside it; neither distant, nor near it, nor far from it; neither above it nor below it; neither to its right nor to its left; neither in front of it nor behind it. Nor can one conceive of either pointing to the other, going to it, drawing near to it, becoming distant from it, moving towards it or away from it, turning towards it or turning away from it, veiling itself from it or revealing itself to it, appearing before its eyes or concealing itself from it”—or are presented with similar notions asserted by those who advocate negation—they know with necessary certainty that the existence of two such beings is impossible.

translated_text:
As for the objector’s statement:

“This can only be conceived in the case of a body occupying space. If something is posited that is neither a body nor occupies space, it falls outside these two categories, and the division into them is no longer exhaustive.”

The response is as follows:

First, the terms “body,” “space,” and “direction” are ambiguous and imprecise. They are conventional technical terms that may convey various meanings. Neither the Quran nor the Sunnah affirms or denies these terms, nor has any affirmation or denial of them whatsoever been transmitted from the early generations of this community or its imams. An objection framed in these terms is therefore not an objection based on scriptural evidence—whether from the Quran, the Sunnah, or consensus. Indeed, it is not even based on a report from a Companion, a Successor, or any imam of the Muslims. Rather, the leading imams denounced those who spoke in such terms and counted them among the practitioners of false, innovated speculative theology. They made stern statements about them, well known from the imams, such as the statement of al-Shāfi‘ī, may Allah have mercy on him:

“My judgment concerning the practitioners of speculative theology is that they should be beaten with palm branches and sandals and paraded among the tribes and clans, while it is proclaimed: ‘This is the recompense of whoever abandons the Quran and the Sunnah and turns to speculative theology.’”

In short, it is well known that terms are of two kinds. The first is a term found in the Quran, the Sunnah, or consensus. What such a term entails must be affirmed, whether or not we understand its meaning, because the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, speaks nothing but the truth, and the Muslim community does not unanimously agree upon misguidance.

translated_text:
The second kind is a term for which no scriptural evidence has been given, such as these terms disputed by the practitioners of speculative theology and philosophy. One says, “He occupies space,” while another says, “He does not occupy space.” One says, “He is in a direction,” while another says, “He is not in a direction.” One says, “He is a body or a substance,” while another says, “He is neither a body nor a substance.”

No one is obliged to affirm or deny anything using these terms until the person using them is asked to clarify his meaning. If he makes clear that he is affirming something true, one affirms it; if he affirms something false, one rejects it. If he denies something false, one denies it; if he denies something true, one does not deny it. Many of these people combine truth and falsehood in these terms, both in affirmation and in negation.

If someone says that He is in a direction, meaning that He is contained and confined within some created thing—whatever it may be—this affirmation is not accepted. This is the position of those who uphold divine indwelling. But if he says that He is separate from created things and above them, this affirmation is not disputed. Indeed, it is the opposite of the position of those who uphold divine indwelling.

If someone says that He is not in a direction, meaning that He is neither separate from the world nor above it, this negation is not accepted.

Likewise, the term “occupying space” may mean that something existent surrounds the thing described, as in the words of the Most High:

“Or joining another group.”

It may also mean that something has withdrawn from and become separate from something else. Thus, if someone says that Allah occupies space

translated_text:
in the first sense, his claim is not accepted. But if he means that Allah is separate from created things, the meaning is accepted, even if the expression itself is not used.

Once this is clear, if someone says, “This division is self-evidently known,” and is told, “This is only conceivable of something that occupies space or has a direction,” this does not undermine what is self-evidently known. Rather, he replies: “Either this is a necessary consequence or it is not. If it is not, the objection falls away. If it is, then a necessary consequence of a self-evident truth is itself true.” For when self-evident propositions entail certain consequences, this establishes the truth of those consequences. One cannot argue that those propositions are false by denying their consequences, because that denial rests on inference, and inferential reasoning cannot undermine self-evident knowledge.

As for his statement, “If an existent is posited that neither occupies space nor is in a direction, this division is valid in its case,” the reply is: its validity on this assumption does not entail its validity in reality unless the assumption itself holds true in reality. Yet this division rules out that assumption’s holding true in reality. If the division is self-evidently known, it necessarily follows that this assumption is false. An attempt to establish this assumption through inferential reasoning is therefore unacceptable, because it entails undermining self-evident knowledge through inference. If there is no way to establish this assumption, the division is not undermined by its being invalid on the supposition that the assumption holds true. For this amounts to the division being invalid on the supposition that something holds true which has not been established and cannot be established.

translated_text:
And even if it were assumed that this supposition could be established, this would constitute a counterargument, not a challenge to any of the premises. A counterargument requires a proof of its own, and we shall discuss that later.

If the objector were to say, “I challenge the validity of the division and make this the basis of my challenge,” this would not be valid. The reply is that a challenge must concern a premise for which no proof has been offered. Yet the proponent has shown that the division is self-evidently valid, so it cannot validly be challenged. If, however, the objector establishes the possibility of an existent that is neither within the world nor outside it, he is presenting an argument for the opposite of his opponent’s position. He would then be usurping the proponent’s role, for such usurpation consists in challenging a premise by establishing the opposite of the conclusion to be proved.

In effect, he is saying: “If the proponent’s proof were sound, my position would be invalid. But my position is not invalid, for such-and-such reasons.” This is usurping the proponent’s role and is therefore not accepted.

The same applies here: if he challenges the division by establishing this supposition, that supposition is itself his position. For he claims that there is an existent to which this division does not apply, and this is precisely the point at issue. If he argues for its possibility, he is usurping the proponent’s role, and this is not accepted from him. Thus, it is clear that the proof is complete.

This objection therefore amounts to saying: “If an existent is posited that is neither eternal nor originated, then the division of existents into originated and eternal is invalid. And if an existent is posited that is neither necessary nor contingent, neither subsisting in itself nor subsisting in another, then the division of existents into the necessary, the contingent, that which subsists in itself, and that which subsists in another is invalid.” And it is well known that a division which is known

At this point, people offer four responses:

This is unacceptable and is comparable to the arguments of the sophists. When we know something by necessity and someone challenges it through reasoning and disputation, we are not obliged to give a detailed response resolving the counterargument. It is enough for us to know that it is unsound because it contradicts necessary knowledge, and whatever contradicts necessary knowledge is unsound.” This is how many hadith scholars, jurists, speculative theologians, and others respond to such objections.

This is maintained by some among the Kullābiyyah, Ashʿariyyah, and Karrāmiyyah, and by those who agree with them among the jurists following the four imams, the scholars of hadith, and the Sufis.

His being above the world, this cannot legitimately be denied. Moreover, the revealed texts, together with the innate disposition, indicate this. On this premise, therefore, He must be separate from the world.”

This is a “sound analysis,” to which attention has also been drawn earlier. These negationists treat reason as authoritative when it supports them, but not when it counts against them. They argue against their opponents on the basis of self-evident propositions, yet oppose them concerning propositions that are even more self-evident. Every objection they raise can be turned against their own position. For example, they say, “This is a judgment of imagination and fancy, not of reason.” This very objection can be raised against their argument here. They may be told:

“Your denial of the existence of a being separate from the world, who is neither a body nor occupies space, is a judgment of imagination and fancy, not of reason.”

Let the discerning reader reflect carefully on this point.

(The third response:

The position of someone who accepts that He occupies space, is in a direction, or is a body, and says: “There is no evidence for denying any of these things, and the arguments advanced by those who deny them are unsound.” They agree that the denial of these things is not known self-evidently; rather, they claim to establish it through discursive reasoning. Yet those who deny these things have not agreed upon a single proof. Instead, each challenges the proof of the other.

As for the philosophers who deny these things on the basis of denying the attributes, the negationists among the speculative theologians—together with other rational thinkers and proponents of affirmation—challenge their proofs with the well-known objections that demonstrate their unsoundness. The speculative theologians who deny these things, together with other rational thinkers and proponents of affirmation, also challenge the proofs of the negationist philosophers: namely, the argument based on the temporal origination of whatever has accidents and acts subsisting in it.

The arguments of the proponents of affirmation establishing the unsoundness of the negationists’ proofs, together with the ambiguous statements, subtle discussions, and rational inquiries involved in these matters, are discussed at length elsewhere.

(The fourth response:

The response of those who seek clarification. They say: The terms “occupying space,” “direction,” “substance,” and the like are ambiguous expressions with no basis in the Book of Allah or the Sunnah of His Messenger. Nor did any of the early generations of the Muslim community or its imams use them concerning Allah Most High, whether in denial or affirmation. Thus, unqualified denial or affirmation of these terms is undoubtedly not the way of Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamā‘ah, nor is there any evidence from revelation supporting it. Rather, unqualified statements on either side are innovations introduced by the speculative theologians who delve into these matters. When we engage them in rational inquiry, we therefore ask them to clarify what they mean by these terms.

If someone who affirms them says, “By His occupying space, being a body, and being in a direction, I mean that He is inside created things, that created things contain Him, that He resembles them, that what is possible for them is possible for Him, or something similar,” then this is false. His being separate from the world does not entail His occupying space, being in a direction, or being a body in this sense.

If, on the other hand, someone who denies these things says: “Whatever is above the world is in a direction, occupies space, and is a body, and that is impossible.”

 نَفْيُ أَنَّهُ مُبَايِنٌ لِلْعَالَمِ بَاطِلٌ وَمَلْزُومُ الْبَاطِلِ بَاطِلٌ فَإِذَا كَانَ نَفْيُ مُسَمَّيَاتِ هَذِهِ الْأَلْفَاظِ مَلْزُومًا لِنَفْيِ الْمُبَايَنَةِ كَانَ نَفْيُهَا بَاطِلًا؛ وَالْأَدِلَّةُ الْمَذْكُورَةُ عَلَى نَفْيِ مُسَمَّاهَا بِهَذَا الِاعْتِبَارِ بَاطِلَةٌ. وَيَقُولُ الْمُثْبِتُ نَفْيُ مُبَايَنَتِهِ لِلْعَالَمِ وَعُلُوِّهِ عَلَى خَلْقِهِ بَاطِلٌ؛ بَلْ هَذِهِ الْأُمُورُ مُسْتَلْزِمَةٌ لِتَكْذِيبِ الرَّسُولِ فِيمَا أَثْبَتَهُ لِرَبِّهِ وَأَخْبَرَ بِهِ عَنْهُ وَهُوَ كُفْرٌ أَيْضًا لَكِنْ لَيْسَ كُلُّ مَنْ تَكَلَّمَ بِالْكُفْرِ يَكْفُرُ حَتَّى تَقُومَ عَلَيْهِ الْحُجَّةُ الْمُثْبِتَةُ لِكُفْرِهِ فَإِذَا قَامَتْ عَلَيْهِ الْحُجَّةُ كَفَرَ حِينَئِذٍ؛ بَلْ نَفْيُ هَذِهِ الْأُمُورِ مُسْتَلْزِمٌ لِلتَّكْفِيرِ لِلرَّسُولِ فِيمَا أَثْبَتَهُ لِرَبِّهِ وَأَخْبَرَ بِهِ عَنْهُ؛ بَلْ نَفْيٌ لِلصَّانِعِ وَتَعْطِيلٌ لَهُ فِي الْحَقِيقَةِ. وَإِذَا كَانَ نَفْيُ هَذِهِ الْأَشْيَاءِ مُسْتَلْزِمًا لِلْكُفْرِ بِهَذَا الِاعْتِبَارِ وَقَدْ نَفَاهَا طَوَائِفُ كَثِيرَةٌ مِنْ أَهْلِ الْإِيمَانِ فَلَازِمُ الْمَذْهَبِ لَيْسَ بِمَذْهَبِ؛ إلَّا أَنْ يَسْتَلْزِمَهُ صَاحِبُ الْمَذْهَبِ فَخَلْقٌ كَثِيرٌ مِنْ النَّاسِ يَنْفُونَ أَلْفَاظًا أَوْ يُثْبِتُونَهَا بَلْ يَنْفُونَ مَعَانِيَ أَوْ يُثْبِتُونَهَا وَيَكُونُ ذَلِكَ مُسْتَلْزِمًا لِأُمُورِ هِيَ كُفْرٌ وَهُمْ لَا يَعْلَمُونَ بِالْمُلَازَمَةِ بَلْ يَتَنَاقَضُونَ وَمَا أَكْثَرَ تَنَاقُضِ النَّاسِ لَا سِيَّمَا فِي هَذَا الْبَابِ وَلَيْسَ التَّنَاقُضُ كُفْرًا.
 وَيَقُولُ النَّاظِمُ:
 أَنَا أُخْبِرْت أَنَّ مَنْ قَالَ ذَلِكَ: هُوَ مَفْتُونٌ وَفَاتِنٌ وَهَذَا حَقٌّ؛ لِأَنَّهُ فَتَنَ غَيْرَهُ بِقَوْلِهِ وَفَتَنَهُ غَيْرُهُ؛ وَلَيْسَ كُلُّ مَنْ فَتَنَ يَكُونُ كَافِرًا وَادَّعَيْت أَنَّ مَنْ قَالَ ذَلِكَ كَانَ قَوْلُهُ مُسْتَلْزِمًا لِلتَّعْطِيلِ؛ فَيَكُونُ الْكُفْرُ كَامِنًا
translated_text:
he is told:

Denying that He is separate from the world is false, and whatever entails a falsehood is itself false. Thus, if denying the meanings designated by these expressions entails denying His separateness, then denying those meanings is false. The aforementioned arguments for denying their meanings, understood in this sense, are therefore invalid.

The proponent of affirmation says: Denying His separateness from the world and His being above His creation is false. Indeed, these denials entail rejecting as false what the Messenger affirmed concerning his Lord and reported about Him, which is also disbelief. Yet not everyone who utters disbelief becomes a disbeliever: the proof establishing his disbelief must first be established against him. Once that proof has been established against him, he then becomes a disbeliever. Indeed, denying these matters entails declaring the Messenger a disbeliever on account of what he affirmed concerning his Lord and reported about Him. In reality, it even amounts to denying the Maker and negating Him.

Although denying these things entails disbelief in this respect, many groups among the believers have denied them. An implication of a position is not itself the position of its adherent unless he accepts that implication. Many people deny or affirm certain expressions—indeed, they deny or affirm certain meanings—and this entails things that constitute disbelief, without their knowing that these implications follow. Rather, they contradict themselves. How frequently people contradict themselves, especially in this matter! Contradiction is not disbelief.

The versifier says:

I was told that whoever says this is both misled and misleading. This is true, for he has misled others through his statement and has himself been misled by others. Not everyone who misleads others is a disbeliever. I also maintained that the statement of anyone who says this entails negation; thus, disbelief lies latent

translated_text:
in his statement. What lies latent in something need not be manifest in it. Were disbelief manifest in his statement, its speaker would necessarily have to be declared a disbeliever. But when it is latent and hidden, someone who does not understand the true nature of the disbelief it contains does not thereby become a disbeliever, even though the statement contains and entails disbelief.

As for the term “corporealism,” it is an ambiguous expression with no basis in revelation. Affirming or denying it therefore requires clarification and evidence, as explained previously.

If someone who affirms it says, “What is meant is that He is above the world and separate from it,” he is told, “This meaning is correct.” If someone who denies it says, “What is meant is that created things neither encompass Him nor resemble Him,” he is told, “This meaning is correct.” There is no contradiction between your two statements: He is above the world and separate from it, while created things neither confine nor encompass Him. He has no need of the Throne or anything else, although He is above created things and separate from them. He does not resemble them, nor can what is possible for them be possible for Him. These meanings expressed by those who deny and those who affirm are correct and acceptable; those other meanings expressed by them are rejected. Praise be to Allah, Lord of all worlds.

Furthermore, the answer given by those who affirm to the eternalists—namely, that acts which He wills and has the power to perform subsist in Him, glorified be He, and that through these He creates things separate from Himself—accords with the accounts transmitted from the Messengers, may Allah’s blessings be upon them. Allah has stated that He created the heavens and the earth in six days, then rose over the Throne. And before His rising

translated_text:
over the Throne:

“He turned toward the heaven while it was smoke and said to it and to the earth, ‘Come, willingly or unwillingly.’ They said, ‘We come willingly.’”

This and similar passages concern the beginning of creation. As for its re-creation, He, exalted is He, says:

“They have not esteemed Allah as He deserves. On the Day of Resurrection, the whole earth will be in His grasp, and the heavens will be rolled up in His right hand. Glorified and exalted is He above what they associate with Him!”

It is authentically reported in the Sahīh collection from Abū Hurayrah that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah will grasp the earth and roll up the heaven in His right hand. Then He will say, ‘I am the King! Where are the kings of the earth?’”

In the two Sahīh collections, Ibn ‘Umar reports:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, recited this verse on the pulpit, then said, ‘Allah will roll up the heavens in His right hand and grasp the earth in His other hand. Then He will say: “I am the King; I am the Most Holy; I am the Source of Peace; I am the Giver of Security; I am the Guardian; I am the Almighty; I am the Compeller; I am the Supreme. I am the One who brought the world into being when it was nothing; I am the One who will restore it.”’ The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, began closing and opening his hands. The pulpit was shaking beneath him so much that I found myself saying, ‘Will it collapse beneath the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace?’”

Ibn ‘Abbās said:

“The seven heavens, the seven earths, and everything within them are, in the Hand of the Most Merciful, no more than a mustard seed in the palm of one of you.”

It is also related that he said:

“He tosses them as a child tosses a ball.”

This shows that the celestial spheres are as nothing compared with the power of Allah, exalted is He, even as He, glorified and exalted is He, rolls up the heaven and grasps the earth.

translated_text:
The two Sahīh collections also relate from Ibn Mas‘ūd:

“A Jewish man said to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ‘On the Day of Resurrection, Allah will hold the heaven on one finger, the earth on one finger, the trees and soil on one finger, the mountains on one finger, and all creatures on one finger.’

“He said: The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, laughed in amazement and in affirmation of the rabbi’s statement. Then he recited the verse beginning, ‘They have not esteemed Allah as He deserves.’”

Here is clear evidence from the acts of the Lord, blessed and exalted is He, that refutes the specious arguments of the philosophizers.

.
 (بَيَانُ مَا أَنْكَرَتْ الْجَهْمِيَّة الضُّلَّالُ أَنْ يَكُونَ اللَّهُ عَلَى الْعَرْشِ وَقَدْ قَالَ تَعَالَى:
 
{الرَّحْمَنُ عَلَى الْعَرْشِ اسْتَوَى}
 وَقَالَ: 
{خَلَقَ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضَ فِي سِتَّةِ أَيَّامٍ ثُمَّ اسْتَوَى عَلَى الْعَرْشِ}

{وَهُوَ اللَّهُ فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ وَفِي الْأَرْضِ}
.
 قُلْنَا:
 قَدْ عَرَفَ الْمُسْلِمُونَ أَمَاكِنَ كَثِيرَةً لَيْسَ فِيهَا مِنْ عَظِيمِ الرَّبِّ شَيْءٌ فَقَالُوا: أَيُّ شَيْءٍ؟
 قُلْنَا:
 أَحْشَاؤُكُمْ وَأَجْوَافُكُمْ وَأَجْوَافُ الْخَنَازِيرِ وَالْحُشُوشِ وَالْأَمَاكِنُ الْقَذِرَةُ لَيْسَ فِيهَا مِنْ عَظِيمِ الرَّبِّ شَيْءٌ؛
 وَقَدْ أَخْبَرَنَا أَنَّهُ فِي السَّمَاءِ فَقَالَ:
 
{أَأَمِنْتُمْ مَنْ فِي السَّمَاءِ أَنْ يَخْسِفَ بِكُمُ الْأَرْضَ فَإِذَا هِيَ تَمُورُ}
 وَقَدْ قَالَ جَلَّ ثَنَاؤُهُ: 
{إلَيْهِ يَصْعَدُ الْكَلِمُ الطَّيِّبُ}
 وَقَالَ تَعَالَى: 
{إنِّي مُتَوَفِّيكَ وَرَافِعُكَ إلَيَّ}

Section:

(*) This “division” mentioned by the questioner is well known in the words of the early generations. The imams use it to argue against the Jahmiyyah who deny the divine attributes—for example, concerning His being distinct from His creation and His being above His Throne. Imam Ahmad said in his book Refutation of the Jahmiyyah and the Heretics:

“An explanation of the misguided Jahmiyyah’s denial that Allah is above the Throne, although He, exalted is He, has said:

‘The Most Merciful rose over the Throne.’

And He said:

‘He created the heavens and the earth in six days, then rose over the Throne.’

They said: ‘He is beneath the seventh earth just as He is above the Throne. Thus, He is above the Throne, in the heavens, on earth, and everywhere. No place is devoid of Him, nor is He in one place rather than another.’ They recite verses from the Quran, such as:

‘And He is Allah in the heavens and on earth.’

We said: ‘Muslims know of many places in which there is nothing of the mighty Lord.’ They asked: ‘Which places?’ We said: ‘Your entrails and your abdominal cavities, the abdominal cavities of pigs, latrines, and filthy places—there is nothing of the mighty Lord in them.’

He has told us that He is in heaven, saying:

‘Do you feel secure that He who is in heaven will not cause the earth to swallow you, and suddenly it will sway?’

He, exalted be His praise, has also said:

‘To Him good words ascend.’

And He, exalted is He, said:

‘I will take you and raise you to Myself.’
translated_footnote:
(*) Shaykh Nāsir ibn Hamad al-Fahd stated (pp. 47–50):
Textual corruptions and omissions have occurred in the quotations from the early generations in this section. The following details those I have identified:

1 — P. 310: “Imam Ahmad said in his book, Refutation of the Jahmiyyah and the Heretics: ‘An explanation of the misguided Jahmiyyah’s denial that Allah is above the Throne. [We said to them: Why do you deny that Allah is above the Throne,] when He, exalted is He, has said: “The Most Merciful rose over the Throne”?’”
I say: The bracketed words have been omitted. They appear in Refutation of the Heretics, p. 92, in ‘Aqā’id al-salaf, and in al-Dar’, 1/138.

2 — P. 313: “When the argument had prevailed against the Jahmī concerning his claim that Allah is with His creation[, he said: He is] in everything, without being in contact with anything or separate from it…”
I say: The bracketed words have been omitted here, and likewise in al-Dar’, 1/147. They appear in ‘Aqā’id al-salaf, p. 97. The context requires them: in his preceding discussion, Ahmad—may Allah have mercy on him—refuted the claim that Allah is with His creation. When the argument prevailed against the Jahmī, he adopted another position: “Allah is in everything, without being in contact with anything or separate from it.”

3 — P. 314: This is quoted from ‘Abd al-‘Azīz al-Makkī’s Refutation of the Heretics and the Jahmiyyah. It has been compared with the same quotation in Dar’ al-ta‘ārud, 6/117 ff.:
He said: “Allah has stated that He created the Throne before creating the heavens and the earth [in six days], then rose over His Throne…”
I say: The bracketed words may be an interpolation, since they make no sense in this context; compare al-Dar’, 6/115.

4 — P. 315: “It is then said: Tell me how He rose over the Throne. Is it as one says, ‘So-and-so rose onto the couch,’ such that the couch would have contained so-and-so alone when he was upon it?”
I say: In al-Dar’, 6/117, it reads: “The Jahmī said: Tell me how He rose…” This is the correct reading.

5 — P. 316: “He has told us that He ‘rose over the Throne,’ but has not told us how He rose over it [so believers must believe their Lord concerning His rising over the Throne, and they are forbidden to describe how He rose over it], because He has not told them how that occurred…”
I say: The bracketed passage was omitted because the copyist’s eye skipped from the first occurrence of ‘how He rose over it’ to the second, leaving out the intervening words. See al-Dar’, 6/118.

6 — P. 317: “For if He were a thing falling within analogy and reason, He would be within a thing or outside it. Since, according to you, He is not a thing, it would be impossible for a thing to be within a thing or outside a thing.”
I say: The correct wording, as found in the manuscript of Naqd al-ta’sīs, is: “For if He were a thing, then, by analogy and reason, He could not fail to be either within a thing or outside it…”

7 — P. 318: This is from Ibn Kullāb’s words, compared with the same passage in al-Dar’, 6/120: “They are asked: Is it not the case that what exists in a human being is not described as ‘neither in contact nor separate’?…”
I say: The correct wording is: “They are asked: Is it not the case that what does not exist in a human being is not described as ‘in contact’ or ‘separate’?” This is the reading in al-Dar’, 6/120. It means that al-madmūm in a human being (“what does not exist in him”) is described as neither “in contact” nor “separate.” This is the basis of Ibn Kullāb’s argument, whereas the wording in al-Fatāwā concerns the description of “what exists.” Allah knows best.

is that He is the God of those in the heavens and the God of those on earth. He is Allah, above the Throne, and His knowledge encompasses everything beneath the Throne. No place is devoid of Allah’s knowledge, nor is Allah’s knowledge in one place rather than another. This is expressed in His words:

‘So that you may know that Allah has power over all things, and that Allah encompasses all things in knowledge.’

translated_text:
the man being inside the cup. Allah—to whom belongs the highest description—encompasses all His creation without being in any part of His creation.

Here is another illustration: If a man built a house with all its facilities, then closed its door and left, he would still know how many rooms his house contained and how spacious each room was, without being inside the house. Likewise, Allah, mighty and majestic—to whom belongs the highest description—encompasses everything He has created and knows what it is and how it is, without being in anything He has created.

As for the Jahmiyyah’s interpretation of Allah’s words, mighty and majestic:

“There is no private conversation among three but He is their fourth,”

they said, “Allah, mighty and majestic, is with us and within us.”

We said, “Why have you quoted only part of His statement? Allah says:

‘Do you not see that Allah knows whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on earth? There is no private conversation among three but He is their fourth, nor among five but He is their sixth, nor among fewer or more than that but He is with them’—meaning, through His knowledge of them—‘wherever they may be. Then, on the Day of Resurrection, He will inform them of what they did. Indeed, Allah knows all things.’”

Thus, He began the statement with His knowledge and ended it with His knowledge.

The Jahmī is also asked, “If Allah is with us in the majesty of His very Self, does Allah forgive you concerning what is between Him and His creation?” If he says yes, he has thereby maintained that Allah, exalted is He, is distinct from His creation and that His creation is beneath Him. If he says no, he has disbelieved.

He said: “If you wish to know that the Jahmī is lying about Allah when he claims that He is everywhere and is not in one place rather than another, say to him, ‘Did Allah not exist when nothing else existed?’”

First, if he claims that Allah created creation within Himself, he has disbelieved by claiming that He created the jinn, human beings and devils within Himself.

If he says, “He created them outside Himself, then entered into them,” this too is disbelief, since he claims that He entered a filthy, unclean and foul place.

If he says, “He created them outside Himself and did not then enter into them,” he has abandoned his position entirely. This is the position of the people of the Sunnah.

Imam Ahmad has thus explained what is known through sound reason and the self-evident dictates of the natural disposition: He must have created creation either within Himself or outside Himself.  قَدْ بَيَّنَ أَنَّ الْقِيَاسَ وَالْمَعْقُولَ يُوجِبُ أَنَّ مَا لَا يَكُونُ دَاخِلًا فِي الشَّيْءِ وَلَا خَارِجًا مِنْهُ فَإِنَّهُ لَا يَكُونُ شَيْئًا وَأَنَّ ذَلِكَ صِفَةُ الْمَعْدُومِ الَّذِي لَا وُجُودَ لَهُ فَالْقِيَاسُ هُوَ الْأَدِلَّةُ الْعَقْلِيَّةُ وَالْمَعْقُولُ الْعُلُومُ الضَّرُورِيَّةُ.
 وَكَذَلِكَ قَالَ:
 
" أَبُو مُحَمَّدٍ عَبْدُ اللَّهِ بْنُ سَعِيدِ بْنِ كُلَّابٍ "
 إمَامُ الْمُتَكَلِّمَةِ الصفاتية: كالقلانسي وَالْأَشْعَرِيِّ وَأَتْبَاعِهِ فِيمَا جَمَعَهُ أَبُو بَكْرِ بْنُ فورك مِنْ كَلَامِ الْأَشْعَرِيِّ أَيْضًا فَذَكَرَ ابْنُ فورك كَلَامَ ابْنِ كُلَّابٍ أَنَّهُ قَالَ: وَأَخْرَجَ مِنْ النَّظَرِ وَالْخَبَرِ قَوْلَ مَنْ قَالَ: لَا هُوَ فِي الْعَالَمِ وَلَا خَارِجٌ مِنْهُ فَنَفَاهُ نَفْيًا مُسْتَوِيًا؛
 لِأَنَّهُ لَوْ قِيلَ لَهُ:
 صِفْهُ بِالْعَدَمِ مَا قَدَرَ أَنْ يَقُولَ فِيهِ أَكْثَرَ مِنْ هَذَا وَرَدَّ أَخْبَارَ اللَّهِ نَصًّا وَقَالَ فِي ذَلِكَ مَا لَا يَجُوزُ فِي نَصٍّ وَلَا مَعْقُولٍ وَزَعَمَ أَنَّ هَذَا هُوَ التَّوْحِيدُ الْخَالِصُ وَالنَّفْيُ الْخَالِصُ عِنْدَهُمْ هُوَ الْإِثْبَاتُ الْخَالِصُ وَهُمْ عِنْدَ أَنْفُسِهِمْ قَيَّاسُونَ.
translated_text:
in a thing, nor as a thing upon a thing, nor as a thing outside a thing, nor separate from a thing.”

He said:

He should be told: “Your position rests on inference and rational understanding, yet by inference and rational understanding you have demonstrated that you worship nothing. For if He were something to which inference and rational understanding applied, He would have to be either within a thing or outside it. Since, according to you, He is not a thing, it is impossible for that thing to be within another thing or outside it. By my life, you have described something obscure that has no existence. This is your religion, and negation is the foundation of your doctrine.”

Thus, ‘Abd al-‘Azīz al-Makkī has explained that inference and rational understanding necessarily establish that whatever is neither within a thing nor outside it is nothing, and that this is the description of something nonexistent, having no existence. Here, inference means rational proofs, while rational understanding means self-evident knowledge.

Likewise, Abū Muhammad ‘Abd Allāh ibn Sa‘īd ibn Kullāb—the leading authority of the theologians who affirm the divine attributes, such as al-Qalānisī, al-Ash‘arī, and his followers—made a similar statement, recorded by Abū Bakr ibn Fūrak in his compilation of al-Ash‘arī’s statements. Ibn Fūrak cited Ibn Kullāb as saying:

“The assertion of someone who says, ‘He is neither within the world nor outside it,’ falls outside the bounds of rational inquiry and revelation. He has thereby negated Him completely. For if he were told, ‘Describe Him as nonexistent,’ he could say no more than this. He has rejected what Allah has explicitly stated and made a claim in this matter that neither revealed texts nor reason allow. He claims that this is pure monotheism. In their view, pure negation is pure affirmation, and they consider themselves exponents of rational inference.”

 فَإِنْ قَالُوا: هَذَا إفْصَاحٌ بِخُلُوِّ الْأَمَاكِنِ مِنْهُ وَانْفِرَادِ الْعَرْشِ بِهِ قِيلَ: إنْ كُنْتُمْ تَعْنُونَ بِخُلُوِّ الْأَمَاكِنِ مِنْ تَدْبِيرِهِ وَأَنَّهُ عَالِمٌ فَلَا.

 وَقَالَ ابْنُ كُلَّابٍ أَيْضًا:

 فَإِذَا قَالُوا نَعَمْ قِيلَ لَهُمْ:
 فَهُوَ بِصِفَةِ الْمُحَالِ الَّذِي لَا يَكُونُ وَلَا يَثْبُتُ فِي الْوَهْمِ؟
 فَإِذَا قَالُوا:
 نَعَمْ قِيلَ: فَيَنْبَغِي أَنْ يَكُونَ بِصِفَةِ الْمُحَالِ مِنْ كُلِّ جِهَةٍ كَمَا كَانَ بِصِفَةِ الْمُحَالِ مِنْ هَذِهِ الْجِهَةِ.
 وَقِيلَ لَهُمْ:
 أَلَيْسَ لَا يُقَالُ لِمَا هُوَ ثَابِتٌ فِي الْإِنْسَانِ لَا مُمَاسَّ وَلَا مُبَايِنَ؟
translated_text:
He said:

“If they say, ‘This explicitly declares that all places are devoid of Him and that the Throne alone is singled out for Him,’ they should be told: ‘If you mean that places lie beyond His governance and His knowledge, then no. But if you mean that He has not risen over them as He has risen over the Throne, we have no hesitation in saying, “Allah rose over the Throne,” whereas we hesitate to say, “He rose over the earth,” “He rose over the wall,” or “in the foremost part of the house.”’”

Abū Muhammad ibn Kullāb also said:

“They should be asked: ‘Is He above what He created?’ If they say, ‘Yes,’ they should be asked: ‘What do you mean when you say that He is above what He created?’ If they say, ‘In power and might,’ they should be told: ‘That is not what we are asking.’ If they say, ‘The question is wrongly framed,’ they should be asked: ‘Then He is not above?’ If they say, ‘Yes, He is not above,’ they should be asked: ‘And He is not below?’ If they say, ‘Nor below,’ they have negated His existence, for whatever is neither below nor above is nonexistent. If they say, ‘He is below and He is above,’ they should be told: ‘Then above is below, and below is above.’”

Ibn Kullāb also said:

“They should be asked: ‘If we say that a human being is neither in contact with nor separate from a place, is this not impossible?’ They must answer, ‘Yes.’ They should then be asked: ‘So He is neither separate nor in contact?’ If they say, ‘Yes,’ they should be asked: ‘Then He has the description of something impossible, which cannot exist or even be conceived?’ If they say, ‘Yes,’ they should be told: ‘Then He must have the description of something impossible in every respect, just as He has that description in this respect.’

“They should also be asked: ‘Is it not the case that something established in a human being cannot be described as neither in contact nor separate?’

translated_text:
If they say, ‘Yes,’ they should be asked: ‘Then tell us about the One you worship: is He in contact or separate?’ If they say, ‘He is described by neither,’ they should be told: ‘Then the description by which you affirm the Creator’s existence is the same as that of a created being’s nonexistence. Why, then, do they not call Him nonexistent, just as they call a human being nonexistent, when you have described Him in terms of nonexistence?’

“They should also be told: ‘If what amounts to nonexistence for a created being amounts to existence for Him, then what amounts to ignorance for a created being amounts to knowledge for Him. For you have made what constitutes nonexistence for a created being constitute existence for Him. If nonexistence is existence, then ignorance is knowledge and inability is power.’”

Ibn Kullāb also said:

“Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace—the one Allah selected from His creation, His chosen servant, and the most knowledgeable of them all—permits the question ‘Where?’ and asks it himself. He approves of someone saying, ‘He is in heaven,’ and testifies to that person’s faith upon hearing it. Yet Jahm ibn Safwān and his followers do not permit the question ‘Where?’ and forbid asking it.”

He said:

“Had this been wrong, Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would have been the foremost to object. He should then have said to her: ‘Do not say that and imagine that He, mighty and majestic, is bounded and is in one place rather than another. Instead, say that He is everywhere, for that is correct, not what you have said.’ But no! Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, approved it, knowing what it entailed and that it was the soundest expression of faith—indeed, a statement on account of which its speaker must be acknowledged as a believer. It was precisely because of this that he testified to her faith when she said it. How could the truth be otherwise, when the Book expressly declares it and bears witness to it?”

He said:

“Even if the only evidence for the soundness of the Muslim community’s position on this particular subject were what we have mentioned

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of all worlds. The first speaker, who quoted the Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was correct in what he said. His statement has been widely transmitted in the Sunnah from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. The early generations of the Muslim community, its leading scholars, and those versed in the Sunnah and hadith have unanimously affirmed its truth and received it with acceptance.

Whoever says what the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said speaks truthfully and correctly, even if he does not know the full reality of the meanings it contains. This is like someone who recites the Quran without understanding its meanings. Indeed, the truest speech is Allah’s speech, and the best guidance is the guidance of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, spoke these words and others like them openly and conveyed them to the entire community. He did not reserve them for some people rather than others, nor did he conceal them from anyone. The Companions and the Successors would mention them, relate them, and convey them

and narrate them in private and public gatherings. They are also contained in the Islamic books read in private and public gatherings, such as the Sahīhs of al-Bukhārī and Muslim, Mālik’s Muwatta’, Imām Ahmad’s Musnad, the Sunan of Abū Dāwūd, al-Tirmidhī, and al-Nasā’ī, and other such books of the Muslims.

However, whoever understands this hadith and others like it to imply something from which Allah must be declared free—such as likening Him to the attributes of created beings or attributing to Him an imperfection incompatible with the perfection that rightfully belongs to Him—has erred. If he expresses this understanding openly, he must be prevented from doing so. If he claims that the hadith indicates and entails such a meaning, he has likewise erred.

For describing Him, glorified and exalted is He, in this hadith as descending is like describing Him with His other attributes: His rising toward heaven while it was smoke; His having created the heavens and the earth in six days, then risen over the Throne; and His coming, as in His words, exalted is He:

“Do they await anything but that Allah should come to them in canopies of clouds, together with the angels?”

And His words:

“Do they await anything but that the angels should come to them, or your Lord should come, or some of your Lord’s signs should come?”

And His words:

“And your Lord comes, and the angels, rank upon rank.”

Likewise, His words, exalted is He:

“He created the heavens and the earth and all that is between them in six days, then rose over the Throne.”

And His words:

“And the heaven We built with might.”

And His words:

“Allah is the One who created you, then provided for you, then will cause you to die, then will bring you to life. Is there any among those you associate with Him who does any of these things?”

And His words:

“He directs the affairs from heaven to earth; then they ascend to Him.”

And other such actions by which

Allah, exalted is He, has described Himself, whether grammarians call them transitive verbs—which constitute most of those mentioned in the Quran—or intransitive verbs, because they do not take a direct object but connect to an object only through a preposition. Examples include His rising toward heaven, His rising over the Throne, His descending to the lowest heaven, and similar actions. Allah has indeed described Himself with these actions.

He has also described Himself as speaking, using both intransitive and transitive verbs, as in His words:

“And when your Lord said to the angels.”

And His words:

“And Allah spoke to Moses directly.”

And His words, exalted is He:

“And their Lord called out to them.”

And His words:

“And on the Day He will call to them and say, ‘How did you respond to the messengers?’”

And His words:

“Allah speaks the truth, and He guides to the way.”

And His words:

“Allah—there is no deity except Him. He will surely gather you on the Day of Resurrection, about which there is no doubt. And who is more truthful than Allah in speech?”

And His words:

“Allah has sent down the best of speech.”

And His words:

“And your Lord’s gracious word to the Children of Israel was fulfilled because of their patience.”

And His words:

“And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice.”

And His words:

“And Allah certainly fulfilled His promise to you.”

Likewise, He has described Himself as possessing knowledge, strength, mercy, and other such attributes, as in His words:

“And they encompass nothing of His knowledge except what He wills.”

And His words:

“Indeed, Allah is the Provider, the Possessor of Strength, the Firm.”

And His words:

“Our Lord, You encompass all things in mercy and knowledge.”

And His words:

“And My mercy encompasses all things.”

The same applies to the other descriptions He has given of Himself in His Book and those authentically reported from His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. For the same principle applies to all of this.

The position of the early generations of this Ummah and its leading scholars is to describe Him as He has described Himself and as His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, has described Him, in both negation and affirmation.

Allah, glorified and exalted is He, has denied that He is like created beings. He, exalted is He, says:

“Say, ‘He is Allah, the One.’”

“Allah, the Eternal Refuge.”

“He neither begets nor is born.”

“Nor is there any equivalent to Him.”

Thus, He has made clear that none is His equal. He, exalted is He, also says:

“Do you know of any equal to Him?”

He thereby denies that He has any equal. He, exalted is He, says:

“So do not set up rivals to Allah.”

And He, exalted is He, says:

“So do not draw comparisons with Allah.”

And He, exalted is He, says:

“There is nothing like Him.”

What He has declared about Himself—that He is above having any equal, peer, likeness or rival, or having comparisons drawn with Him—makes clear that nothing is like Him in His attributes or His actions. For sameness in attributes and actions entails sameness in essence. Two different essences cannot have identical attributes and actions, since identical attributes and actions necessarily entail identical essences. An attribute depends upon that which possesses it, and an action likewise depends upon its agent; indeed, an action is itself something by which the agent is described.

Thus, if two attributes are identical, the two beings possessing them are identical. Indeed, the degree of similarity and difference between attributes corresponds to that between the beings possessing them. Take two human beings, for example: although they belong to a single species, their sizes and attributes differ according to the differences between their individual essences, and resemble one another according to the resemblance between those essences.

Likewise, if it is said that a human being and a horse resemble one another in that the former is an animal and the latter

This is because an essence stripped of attributes exists only in the mind. The mind conceives of an essence stripped of attributes and of an absolute existence that is not individuated. As for things that actually exist, there can be neither an essence stripped of every attribute nor an absolute existence that is neither individuated nor particularized.

When someone who affirms the divine attributes says, “I affirm Allah’s attributes as additional to His essence,” what this really means is that we affirm them as additional to what the deniers have affirmed of the essence. For the deniers believed in the existence of an essence stripped of attributes, so those who affirm the attributes said: “We affirm attributes in addition to what these people have affirmed.” As for the actually existing essence itself, it is inconceivable that it could exist without any attributes whatsoever.

Rather, this is like someone saying: “I affirm a human being who is neither an animal nor rational, who neither subsists in himself nor in anything else, and who has neither power nor life, neither motion nor rest,” or something similar. Or it is like saying: “I affirm a palm tree that has neither stem nor trunk nor fibre nor anything else of that kind.” Such a person affirms something that has no reality outside the mind and cannot be rationally conceived.

For this reason, the early generations and leading scholars called those who deny the attributes “negators,” because the true import of their position is to negate the very essence of Allah, exalted is He—even though they themselves may not realize that their position necessarily entails such negation.
