 مَوْجُودٌ لَيْسَ بِمَوْجُودِ حَقٌّ لَيْسَ بِحَقِّ خَالِقٌ لَيْسَ بِخَالِقِ فَيَنْفُونَ عَنْهُ النَّقِيضَيْنِ: إمَّا تَصْرِيحًا بِنَفْيِهِمَا وَإِمَّا إمْسَاكًا عَنْ الْإِخْبَارِ بِوَاحِدِ مِنْهُمَا. وَلِهَذَا كَانَ مُحَقِّقُوهُمْ 
" وَهُمْ الْقَرَامِطَةُ "
 يَنْفُونَ عَنْهُ النَّقِيضَيْنِ فَلَا يَقُولُونَ: مَوْجُودٌ وَلَا لَا مَوْجُودٌ وَلَا حَيٌّ وَلَا لَا حَيٌّ وَلَا عَالِمٌ وَلَا لَا عَالِمٌ.
 قَالُوا:
 لِأَنَّ وَصْفَهُ بِالْإِثْبَاتِ تَشْبِيهٌ لَهُ بِالْمَوْجُودَاتِ وَوَصْفَهُ بِالنَّفْيِ فِيهِ تَشْبِيهٌ لَهُ بِالْمَعْدُومَاتِ. فَآلَ بِهِمْ إغْرَاقُهُمْ فِي نَفْيِ التَّشْبِيهِ إلَى أَنْ وَصَفُوهُ بِغَايَةِ التَّعْطِيلِ. ثُمَّ إنَّهُمْ لَمْ يَخْلُصُوا مِمَّا فَرُّوا مِنْهُ بَلْ يَلْزَمُهُمْ عَلَى قِيَاسِ قَوْلِهِمْ أَنْ يَكُونُوا قَدْ شَبَّهُوهُ بِالْمُمْتَنِعِ الَّذِي هُوَ أَخَسُّ مِنْ الْمَوْجُودِ وَالْمَعْدُومِ الْمُمْكِنِ. فَفَرُّوا فِي زَعْمِهِمْ مِنْ تَشْبِيهِهِ بِالْمَوْجُودَاتِ وَالْمَعْدُومَاتِ وَوَصَفُوهُ بِصِفَاتِ الْمُمْتَنِعَاتِ الَّتِي لَا تَقْبَلُ الْوُجُودَ بِخِلَافِ الْمَعْدُومَاتِ الْمُمْكِنَاتِ. وَتَشْبِيهُهُ بِالْمُمْتَنِعَاتِ شَرٌّ مِنْ تَشْبِيهِهِ بِالْمَوْجُودَاتِ وَالْمَعْدُومَاتِ الْمُمْكِنَاتِ. وَمَا فَرَّ مِنْهُ هَؤُلَاءِ الْمَلَاحِدَةُ لَيْسَ بِمَحْذُورِ. فَإِنَّهُ إذَا سُمِّيَ حَقًّا مَوْجُودًا قَائِمًا بِنَفْسِهِ حَيًّا عَلِيمًا رَءُوفًا رَحِيمًا وَسُمِّيَ الْمَخْلُوقُ بِذَلِكَ؛ لَمْ يَلْزَمْ مِنْ ذَلِكَ أَنْ يَكُونَ مُمَاثِلًا لِلْمَخْلُوقِ أَصْلًا. وَلَوْ كَانَ هَذَا حَقًّا لَكَانَ كُلُّ مَوْجُودٍ مُمَاثِلًا لِكُلِّ مَوْجُودٍ؛ وَلَكَانَ كُلُّ مَعْدُومٍ مُمَاثِلًا لِكُلِّ مَعْدُومٍ. وَلَكَانَ كُلُّ مَا يُنْفَى عَنْهُ شَيْءٌ مِنْ الصِّفَاتِ مُمَاثِلًا لِكُلِّ مَا يُنْفَى عَنْهُ ذَلِكَ الْوَصْفُ.
translated_text:
the necessary implications of His existence. Their position thus amounts to saying: “He exists but does not exist; He is real but not real; He is a creator but not a creator.” They deny both sides of a contradiction concerning Him, either explicitly denying both or refraining from affirming either. For this reason, their most thoroughgoing exponents—the Qarmatians—deny both sides of a contradiction concerning Him. They do not say that He exists or does not exist, that He is living or not living, or that He is knowing or not knowing.

They say: “Describing Him in affirmative terms likens Him to existing things, while describing Him in negative terms likens Him to nonexistent things.” Their excessive rejection of any likeness thus led them to describe Him in terms of utter negation. Yet they did not escape what they sought to avoid. Rather, by the logic of their own position, they must have likened Him to that which is impossible, which is baser than what exists and what does not exist but could. Thus, while claiming to avoid likening Him to existing and nonexistent things, they described Him with the attributes of impossible things, which cannot exist—unlike nonexistent things whose existence is possible. Likening Him to impossible things is worse than likening Him to existing things and nonexistent things whose existence is possible.

What these heretics sought to avoid is not, in fact, objectionable. For if He is called real, existent, self-subsisting, living, knowing, compassionate, and merciful, and a created being is described by these same terms, it does not follow at all that He is like that created being. Were that true, every existing thing would be like every other existing thing, and every nonexistent thing would be like every other nonexistent thing. Likewise, everything of which an attribute is denied would be like everything else of which that same attribute is denied.

original_text:
فَإِذَا قِيلَ:
 السَّوَادُ مَوْجُودٌ كَانَ عَلَى قَوْلِ هَؤُلَاءِ قَدْ جَعَلْنَا كُلَّ مَوْجُودٍ مُمَاثِلًا لِلسَّوَادِ.
 وَإِذَا قُلْنَا:
 الْبَيَاضُ مَعْدُومٌ كُنَّا قَدْ جَعَلْنَا كُلَّ مَعْدُومٍ مُمَاثِلًا لِلْبَيَاضِ. وَمَعْلُومٌ أَنَّ هَذَا فِي غَايَةِ الْفَسَادِ وَيَكْفِي هَذَا خِزْيًا لِحِزْبِ الْإِلْحَادِ. وَإِذَا لَمْ يَلْزَمْ مِثْلُ ذَلِكَ فِي السَّوَادِ الَّذِي لَهُ أَمْثَالٌ بِلَا رَيْبٍ؛ فَإِذَا قِيلَ فِي خَالِقِ الْعَالَمِ إنَّهُ مَوْجُودٌ لَا مَعْدُومٌ حَيٌّ لَا يَمُوتُ قَيُّومٌ لَا تَأْخُذُهُ سِنَةٌ وَلَا نَوْمٌ فَمِنْ أَيْنَ يَلْزَمُ أَنْ يَكُونَ مُمَاثِلًا لِكُلِّ مَوْجُودٍ وَمَعْدُومٍ وَحَيٍّ وَقَائِمٍ؛ وَلِكُلِّ مَا يُنْفَى عَنْهُ الْعَدَمُ وَمَا يُنْفَى عَنْهُ صِفَةُ الْعَدَمِ وَمَا يُنْفَى عَنْهُ الْمَوْتُ وَالنَّوْمُ كَأَهْلِ الْجَنَّةِ الَّذِينَ لَا يَنَامُونَ وَلَا يَمُوتُونَ وَذَلِكَ أَنَّ هَذِهِ الْأَسْمَاءَ الْعَامَّةَ الْمُتَوَاطِئَةَ الَّتِي تُسَمِّيهَا النُّحَاةُ أَسْمَاءَ الْأَجْنَاسِ سَوَاءٌ اتَّفَقَتْ مَعَانِيهَا فِي مَحَالِّهَا أَوْ تَفَاضَلَتْ كَالسَّوَادِ وَنَحْوِهِ؛
 وَسَوَاءٌ سُمِّيَتْ مُشَكِّكَةً وَقِيلَ:
 إنَّ الْمُشَكِّكَةَ نَوْعٌ مِنْ الْمُتَوَاطِئَةِ - إمَّا أَنْ تُسْتَعْمَلَ 
" مُطْلَقَةً وَعَامَّةً "
 كَمَّا إذَا قِيلَ الْمَوْجُودُ يَنْقَسِمُ إلَى وَاجِبٍ وَمُمْكِنٍ وَقَدِيمٍ وَمُحْدَثٍ وَخَالِقٍ وَمَخْلُوقٍ وَالْعِلْمُ يَنْقَسِمُ إلَى قَدِيمٍ وَمُحْدَثٍ. وَإِمَّا أَنْ تُسْتَعْمَلَ 
" خَاصَّةً مُعَيَّنَةً "
 كَمَا إذَا قِيلَ: وُجُودُ زَيْدٍ وَعَمْرٍو وَعِلْمُ زَيْدٍ وَعَمْرٍو وَذَاتُ زَيْدٍ وَعَمْرٍو. فَإِذَا اُسْتُعْمِلَتْ خَاصَّةً مُعَيَّنَةً دَلَّتْ عَلَى مَا يَخْتَصُّ بِهِ الْمُسَمَّى لَمْ تَدُلَّ عَلَى مَا يُشْرِكُهُ فِيهِ غَيْرُهُ فِي الْخَارِجِ؛ فَإِنَّ مَا يَخْتَصُّ بِهِ الْمُسَمَّى لَا شَرِكَةَ فِيهِ بَيْنَهُ وَبَيْنَ غَيْرِهِ.
translated_text:
Thus, if one says, “Blackness exists,” then, according to their position, we have made everything that exists like blackness. And if we say, “Whiteness does not exist,” we have made everything nonexistent like whiteness. Clearly, this is utterly absurd, and this alone suffices to disgrace the party of heresy.

If no such consequence follows concerning blackness—which undoubtedly has its counterparts—then, when it is said of the Creator of the world that He exists and is not nonexistent, is living and does not die, and is the Self-Subsisting Sustainer whom neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes, how could it follow that He is like every existing, nonexistent, living, and subsisting thing; or like everything of which nonexistence is denied, everything of which the attribute of nonexistence is denied, and everything of which death and sleep are denied, such as the inhabitants of Paradise, who neither sleep nor die?

The reason is that these general, univocal terms—which grammarians call generic nouns—are used in one of two ways. This holds whether their meanings apply equally to their respective subjects or vary in degree, as with blackness and the like; and whether they are called “graded” terms, with graded terms regarded as a kind of univocal term.

They may be used in an “unrestricted and general” sense, as when it is said: “What exists is divided into necessary and contingent, eternal and originated, creator and created; and knowledge is divided into eternal and originated knowledge.” Alternatively, they may be used in a “specific and determinate” sense, as when one speaks of Zayd’s and Amr’s existence, Zayd’s and Amr’s knowledge, or Zayd’s and Amr’s essence.

When used in a specific and determinate sense, they denote what is peculiar to the entity named; they do not denote anything in external reality that it shares with another. For what is peculiar to the entity named is not shared between it and anything else.

original_text:
فَإِذَا قِيلَ:
 عِلْمُ زَيْدٍ وَنُزُولُ زَيْدٍ وَاسْتِوَاءُ زَيْدٍ وَنَحْوُ ذَلِكَ؛ لَمْ يَدُلَّ هَذَا إلَّا عَلَى مَا يَخْتَصُّ بِهِ زَيْدٌ مِنْ عِلْمٍ وَنُزُولٍ وَاسْتِوَاءٍ وَنَحْوِ ذَلِكَ لَمْ يَدُلَّ عَلَى مَا يُشْرِكُهُ فِيهِ غَيْرُهُ. لَكِنْ لَمَّا عَلِمْنَا أَنَّ زَيْدًا نَظِيرُ عَمْرٍو وَعَلِمْنَا أَنَّ عِلْمَهُ نَظِيرُ عِلْمِهِ وَنُزُولَهُ نَظِيرُ نُزُولِهِ وَاسْتِوَاءَهُ نَظِيرُ اسْتِوَائِهِ فَهَذَا عَلِمْنَاهُ مِنْ جِهَةِ الْقِيَاسِ وَالْمَعْقُولِ وَالِاعْتِبَارِ لَا مِنْ جِهَةِ دَلَالَةِ اللَّفْظِ فَإِذَا كَانَ هَذَا فِي صِفَاتِ الْمَخْلُوقِ؛ فَذَلِكَ فِي الْخَالِقِ أَوْلَى.
 فَإِذَا قِيلَ:
 عِلْمُ اللَّهِ وَكَلَامُ اللَّهِ وَنُزُولُهُ وَاسْتِوَاؤُهُ وَوُجُودُهُ وَحَيَاتُهُ وَنَحْوُ ذَلِكَ؛ لَمْ يَدُلَّ ذَلِكَ عَلَى مَا يُشْرِكُهُ فِيهِ أَحَدٌ مِنْ الْمَخْلُوقِينَ بِطَرِيقِ الْأَوْلَى؛ وَلَمْ يَدُلَّ ذَلِكَ عَلَى مُمَاثَلَةِ الْغَيْرِ لَهُ فِي ذَلِكَ كَمَا دَلَّ فِي زَيْدٍ وَعَمْرٍو لِأَنَّا هُنَاكَ عَلِمْنَا التَّمَاثُلَ مِنْ جِهَةِ الِاعْتِبَارِ وَالْقِيَاسِ لِكَوْنِ زَيْدٍ مِثْلَ عَمْرو؛ وَهُنَا نَعْلَمُ أَنَّ اللَّهَ لَا مِثْلَ لَهُ وَلَا كُفُوَ وَلَا نِدَّ؛ فَلَا يَجُوزُ أَنْ نَفْهَمَ مِنْ ذَلِكَ أَنَّ عِلْمَهُ مِثْلُ عِلْمِ غَيْرِهِ وَلَا كَلَامَهُ مِثْلُ كَلَامِ غَيْرِهِ وَلَا اسْتِوَاءَهُ مِثْلُ اسْتِوَاءِ غَيْرِهِ وَلَا نُزُولَهُ مِثْلُ نُزُولِ غَيْرِهِ وَلَا حَيَاتَهُ مِثْلُ حَيَاةِ غَيْرِهِ.
وَلِهَذَا كَانَ مَذْهَبُ السَّلَفِ وَالْأَئِمَّةِ إثْبَاتَ الصِّفَاتِ وَنَفْيَ مُمَاثَلَتِهَا لِصِفَاتِ الْمَخْلُوقَاتِ. فَاَللَّهُ تَعَالَى مَوْصُوفٌ بِصِفَاتِ الْكَمَالِ الَّذِي لَا نَقْصَ فِيهِ مُنَزَّهٌ عَنْ صِفَاتِ النَّقْصِ مُطْلَقًا وَمُنَزَّهٌ عَنْ أَنْ يُمَاثِلَهُ غَيْرُهُ فِي صِفَاتِ كَمَالِهِ.
 فَهَذَانِ الْمَعْنَيَانِ جَمَعَا التَّنْزِيهَ وَقَدْ دَلَّ عَلَيْهِمَا قَوْلُهُ تَعَالَى:
 
{قُلْ هُوَ اللَّهُ أَحَدٌ}
 
{اللَّهُ الصَّمَدُ}
 . فَالِاسْمُ 
" الصَّمَدُ "
 يَتَضَمَّنُ صِفَاتِ الْكَمَالِ وَالِاسْمُ 
" الْأَحَدُ "
 يَتَضَمَّنُ نَفْيَ الْمِثْلِ كَمَا قَدْ بُسِطَ الْكَلَامُ عَلَى ذَلِكَ فِي تَفْسِيرِ هَذِهِ السُّورَةِ.
translated_text:
Thus, when one speaks of Zayd’s knowledge, descent, rising, and the like, these expressions denote only the knowledge, descent, rising, and other attributes peculiar to Zayd; they do not denote anything that another shares with him. Yet we know that Zayd is comparable to Amr, and that his knowledge, descent, and rising are comparable to Amr’s. We know this through analogy, reason, and comparison, not through what the wording itself denotes. If this holds for the attributes of a created being, it holds all the more for the Creator.

Thus, when one speaks of Allah’s knowledge, speech, descent, rising, existence, life, and the like, these expressions, with still greater reason, do not denote anything that any created being shares with Him. Nor do they indicate that another is like Him in these respects, as was established in the case of Zayd and Amr. In that case, we knew their likeness through comparison and analogy, because Zayd is like Amr. Here, however, we know that Allah has no likeness, equal, or rival. We must therefore not understand these expressions to mean that His knowledge is like another’s knowledge, His speech like another’s speech, His rising like another’s rising, His descent like another’s descent, or His life like another’s life.

For this reason, the position of the early generations and the imams was to affirm the attributes while denying that they are like the attributes of created beings. Allah Most High possesses attributes of perfection without any deficiency. He is utterly free of attributes of deficiency, and none is like Him in His attributes of perfection.

These two meanings together encompass His transcendence, and both are indicated by His words, Most High:

“Say: He is Allah, the One.”

“Allah, the Eternal Refuge.”

The name al-Samad (the Eternal Refuge) encompasses the attributes of perfection, while the name al-Ahad (the One) encompasses the denial of any likeness to Him, as has been explained at length in the commentary on this surah.

original_text:
فَالْقَوْلُ فِي صِفَاتِهِ كَالْقَوْلِ فِي ذَاتِهِ وَاَللَّهُ تَعَالَى لَيْسَ كَمِثْلِهِ شَيْءٌ لَا فِي ذَاتِهِ وَلَا فِي صِفَاتِهِ وَلَا فِي أَفْعَالِهِ؛ لَكِنْ يُفْهَمُ مِنْ ذَلِكَ أَنَّ نِسْبَةَ هَذِهِ الصِّفَةِ إلَى مَوْصُوفِهَا كَنِسْبَةِ هَذِهِ الصِّفَةِ إلَى مَوْصُوفِهَا. فَعِلْمُ اللَّهِ وَكَلَامُهُ وَنُزُولُهُ وَاسْتِوَاؤُهُ هُوَ كَمَا يُنَاسِبُ ذَاتَهُ وَيَلِيقُ بِهَا كَمَا أَنَّ صِفَةَ الْعَبْدِ هِيَ كَمَا تُنَاسِبُ ذَاتَه وَتَلِيقُ بِهَا وَنِسْبَةُ صِفَاتِهِ إلَى ذَاتِهِ كَنِسْبَةِ صِفَاتِ الْعَبْدِ إلَى ذَاتِهِ؛
 وَلِهَذَا قَالَ بَعْضُهُمْ:
 إذَا قَالَ لَك السَّائِلُ: كَيْفَ يَنْزِلُ أَوْ كَيْفَ اسْتَوَى أَوْ كَيْفَ يَعْلَمُ أَوْ كَيْفَ يَتَكَلَّمُ وَيُقَدِّرُ وَيَخْلُقُ؟
 فَقُلْ لَهُ:
 كَيْفَ هُوَ فِي نَفْسِهِ؟
 فَإِذَا قَالَ:
 أَنَا لَا أَعْلَمُ كَيْفِيَّةَ ذَاتِهِ؛
 فَقُلْ لَهُ:
 وَأَنَا لَا أَعْلَمُ كَيْفِيَّةَ صِفَاتِهِ فَإِنَّ الْعِلْمَ بِكَيْفِيَّةِ الصِّفَةِ يَتْبَعُ الْعِلْمَ بِكَيْفِيَّةِ الْمَوْصُوفِ. فَهَذَا إذَا اُسْتُعْمِلَتْ هَذِهِ الْأَسْمَاءُ وَالصِّفَاتُ عَلَى وَجْهِ التَّخْصِيصِ وَالتَّعْيِينِ - وَهَذَا هُوَ الْوَارِدُ فِي الْكِتَابِ وَالسُّنَّةِ - وَأَمَّا إذَا قِيلَتْ مُطْلَقَةً وَعَامَّةً -
 كَمَا يُوجَدُ فِي كَلَامِ النُّظَّارِ:
 الْمَوْجُودُ يَنْقَسِمُ إلَى قَدِيمٍ وَمُحْدَثٍ وَالْعِلْمُ يَنْقَسِمُ إلَى قَدِيمٍ وَمُحْدَثٍ وَنَحْوُ ذَلِكَ - فَهَذَا مُسَمَّى اللَّفْظِ الْمُطْلَقِ وَالْعَامِّ وَالْعِلْمُ مَعْنًى مُطْلَقٌ وَعَامٌّ وَالْمَعَانِي لَا تَكُونُ مُطْلَقَةً وَعَامَّةً إلَّا فِي الْأَذْهَانِ لَا فِي الْأَعْيَانِ؛ فَلَا يَكُونُ مَوْجُودٌ وُجُودًا مُطْلَقًا أَوْ عَامًّا إلَّا فِي الذِّهْنِ وَلَا يَكُونُ مُطْلَقٌ أَوْ عَامٌّ إلَّا فِي الذِّهْنِ وَلَا يَكُونُ إنْسَانٌ أَوْ حَيَوَانٌ مُطْلَقٌ وَعَامٌّ إلَّا فِي الذِّهْنِ؛ وَإِلَّا فَلَا تَكُونُ الْمَوْجُودَاتُ فِي أَنْفُسِهَا إلَّا مُعَيَّنَةً مَخْصُوصَةً مُتَمَيِّزَةً عَنْ غَيْرِهَا. فَلْيَتَدَبَّرْ الْعَاقِلُ هَذَا الْمَقَامَ الْفَارِقَ فَإِنَّهُ زَلَّ فِيهِ خَلْقٌ مِنْ أُولِي النَّظَرِ الْخَائِضِينَ
translated_text:
Thus, what is said of His attributes is like what is said of His essence. Nothing is like Allah Most High, whether in His essence, His attributes, or His actions. What is understood, however, is that the relation of an attribute to its possessor is like the relation of the corresponding attribute to its possessor. Allah’s knowledge, speech, descent, and rising are appropriate to His essence and befit it, just as a servant’s attributes are appropriate to his essence and befit it. The relation of His attributes to His essence is like the relation of the servant’s attributes to his essence.

For this reason, some have said:

“If someone asks you, ‘How does He descend? How did He rise? How does He know, speak, decree, and create?’ say to him, ‘What is He like in Himself?’ If he says, ‘I do not know what His essence is like,’ say to him, ‘Nor do I know what His attributes are like, for knowing what an attribute is like depends upon knowing what its possessor is like.’”

This applies when these names and attributes are used with a specific, determinate reference—which is how they occur in the Quran and Sunnah. But when they are used in an unqualified, general sense—as in the statements of speculative thinkers, “What exists is divided into the eternal and the originated,” and “Knowledge is divided into eternal and originated knowledge,” and similar statements—this is what the unqualified, general expression denotes, and knowledge is an unqualified, general concept. Concepts are unqualified and general only in the mind, not in concrete reality. Thus, an existent with unqualified or general existence is found only in the mind; anything unqualified or general is found only in the mind; and an unqualified, general human being or animal is found only in the mind. Existing things themselves, by contrast, are always determinate, particular, and distinct from others.

Let the discerning reader reflect carefully on this crucial distinction, for many speculative thinkers have stumbled here while delving

original_text:
فِي الْحَقَائِقِ حَتَّى ظَنُّوا أَنَّ هَذِهِ الْمَعَانِيَ الْعَامَّةَ الْمُطْلَقَةَ الْكُلِّيَّةَ تَكُونُ مَوْجُودَةً فِي الْخَارِجِ كَذَلِكَ؛
 وَظَنُّوا أَنَّا إذَا قُلْنَا:
 إنَّ اللَّهَ عَزَّ وَجَلَّ مَوْجُودٌ حَيٌّ عَلِيمٌ وَالْعَبْدَ مَوْجُودٌ حَيٌّ عَلِيمٌ؛
 أَنَّهُ يَلْزَمُ وُجُودُ مَوْجُودٍ فِي الْخَارِجِ يَشْتَرِكُ فِيهِ الرَّبُّ وَالْعَبْدُ وَأَنْ يَكُونَ ذَلِكَ الْمَوْجُودُ بِعَيْنِهِ فِي الْعَبْدِ وَالرَّبِّ بَلْ وَفِي كُلِّ مَوْجُودٍ وَلَا بُدَّ أَنْ يَكُونَ لِلرَّبِّ مَا يُمَيِّزُهُ عَنْ الْمَخْلُوقِ فَيَكُونُ فِيهِ جُزْءَانِ:
أَحَدُهُمَا:
 لِكُلِّ مَخْلُوقٍ وَهُوَ الْقَدْرُ الْمُشْتَرَكُ بَيْنَهُ وَبَيْنَ سَائِرِ الْمَوْجُودَاتِ.
وَالثَّانِي:
 يَخْتَصُّ بِهِ وَهُوَ الْمُمَيِّزُ لَهُ عَنْ سَائِرِ الْمَوْجُودَاتِ ثُمَّ لَا يَذْكُرُونَ فِيمَا يَخْتَصُّ بِهِ إلَّا مَا يَلْزَمُ فِيهِ مِثْلُ ذَلِكَ.
فَإِذَا قَالُوا:
 يَمْتَازُ بِذَاتِهِ أَوْ بِحَقِيقَتِهِ أَوْ مَاهِيَّتِهِ أَوْ نَحْوَ ذَلِكَ؛ كَانَ ذَلِكَ بِمَنْزِلَةِ قَوْلِهِمْ يَمْتَازُ بِوُجُودِهِ؛ فَإِنَّ الذَّاتَ وَالْحَقِيقَةَ وَالْمَاهِيَّةَ تُسْتَعْمَلُ مُطْلَقًا وَمُعَيَّنًا كَلَفْظِ الْوُجُودِ سَوَاءً.
 وَهَذَا الْمَقَامُ حَارَ فِيهِ طَوَائِفُ مِنْ أَئِمَّةِ النُّظَّارِ حَتَّى قَالَ طَائِفَةٌ:
 إنَّ لَفْظَ الْوُجُودِ وَغَيْرَهُ مَقُولٌ بِالِاشْتِرَاكِ اللَّفْظِيِّ فَقَطْ وَحَكَوْا ذَلِكَ عَنْ كُلِّ مَنْ قَالَ بِنَفْيِ الْأَحْوَالِ - وَهُمْ عَامَّةُ أَهْلِ الْإِثْبَاتِ - فَصَارَ مَضْمُونُ نَقْلِهِمْ أَنَّ مَذْهَبَ عَامَّةِ أَهْلِ الْإِسْلَامِ وَمُتَكَلِّمَةِ الْإِثْبَاتِ -
 كَابْنِ كُلَّابٍ وَالْأَشْعَرِيِّ وَابْنِ كَرَّامٍ وَغَيْرِهِمْ بَلْ وَمُحَقِّقِي الْمُعْتَزِلَةِ:
 كَأَبِي الْحُسَيْنِ الْبَصْرِيِّ وَغَيْرِهِ - أَنَّ لَفْظَ الْمَوْجُودِ وَغَيْرِهِ - مِمَّا يُسَمَّى اللَّهُ بِهِ وَيُسَمَّى بِهِ الْمَخْلُوقُ -
 إنَّمَا يُقَالُ بِالِاشْتِرَاكِ اللَّفْظِيِّ فَقَطْ مِنْ غَيْرِ أَنْ يَكُونَ بَيْنَ الْمُسَمَّيَيْنِ مَعْنًى عَامٌّ:
 كَلَفْظِ الْمُشْتَرِي إذَا سُمِّيَ بِهِ الْمُبْتَاعُ وَالْكَوْكَبُ وَلَفْظِ سُهَيْلٍ الْمَقُولِ عَلَى الْكَوْكَبِ وَالرَّجُلِ
translated_text:
into the nature of things, until they came to suppose that these general, unqualified, universal concepts exist as such in external reality. They supposed that if we say, “Allah, Mighty and Majestic, exists, lives, and knows, and the servant exists, lives, and knows,” this necessarily entails something existing in external reality that the Lord and the servant share, with that very same thing present in both the servant and the Lord—indeed, in every existing thing. The Lord must also have something distinguishing Him from creation, so He would consist of two parts:

The first belongs to every creature: the common element shared by Him and all other existing things.

The second is exclusive to Him: that which distinguishes Him from all other existing things. Yet whatever they identify as exclusive to Him entails the same difficulty.

Thus, when they say, “He is distinguished by His essence, His reality, His quiddity,” or something similar, this amounts to saying that He is distinguished by His existence. For “essence,” “reality,” and “quiddity” can be used both without qualification and with a determinate reference, exactly like the term “existence.”

This issue has bewildered groups of leading speculative thinkers, to the point that some have said that “existence” and other such terms are used purely equivocally. They attributed this view to everyone who denies states—and these constitute the general body of those who affirm the divine attributes. Their account thus amounts to attributing the following position to the general body of Muslims and to speculative theologians who affirm the divine attributes—such as Ibn Kullāb, al-Ash'arī, Ibn Karrām, and others, and even to such exacting Mu'tazilī scholars as Abū al-Husayn al-Basrī and others: the term “existent,” and other terms applied both to Allah and to created beings, are used purely equivocally, without any general meaning shared by the two referents. This would be like the word mushtarī, used for both a purchaser and the planet Jupiter, or the name Suhayl, applied both to a star and to a man.

original_text:
وَهَذَا النَّقْلُ غَلَطٌ عَظِيمٌ عَمَّنْ نَقَلُوهُ عَنْهُ فَإِنَّ هَؤُلَاءِ مُتَّفِقُونَ عَلَى أَنَّ هَذِهِ الْأَسْمَاءَ عَامَّةٌ مُتَوَاطِئَةٌ - كَالتَّوَاطُؤِ الْعَامِّ الَّذِي يَدْخُلُ فِيهِ الْمُشَكِّكُ -
 تَقْبَلُ التَّقْسِيمَ وَالتَّنْوِيعَ وَذَلِكَ لَا يَكُونُ إلَّا فِي الْأَسْمَاءِ الْمُتَوَاطِئَةِ كَمَا نَقُولُ:
 الْمَوْجُودُ يَنْقَسِمُ إلَى قَدِيمٍ وَمُحْدَثٍ وَوَاجِبٍ وَمُمْكِنٍ.
 بَلْ هَؤُلَاءِ النَّاقِلُونَ بِأَعْيَانِهِمْ:
 كَأَبِي عَبْدِ اللَّهِ الرَّازِي وَأَمْثَالِهِ مِنْ الْمُتَأَخِّرِينَ يَجْمَعُونَ فِي كَلَامِهِمْ بَيْنَ دَعْوَى الِاشْتِرَاكِ اللَّفْظِيِّ فَقَطْ وَبَيْنَ هَذَا التَّقْسِيمِ فِي هَذِهِ الْأَسْمَاءِ؛ مَعَ قَوْلِهِمْ إنَّ التَّقْسِيمَ لَا يَكُونُ إلَّا فِي الْأَلْفَاظِ الْمُتَوَاطِئَةِ الْمُشْتَرَكَةِ لَفْظًا وَمَعْنًى لَا يَكُونُ فِي الْمُشْتَرَكِ اشْتِرَاكًا لَفْظِيًّا. وَمِنْ جُمْلَتِهَا الَّتِي يُسَمُّونَهَا الْمُشَكِّكَةَ لَا يَكُونُ التَّقْسِيمُ فِي الْأَسْمَاءِ الَّتِي لَيْسَ بَيْنَهَا مَعْنًى مُشْتَرَكٌ عَامٌّ. فَهَذَا تَنَاقُضُ هَؤُلَاءِ الَّذِينَ هُمْ مِنْ أَشْهَرِ الْمُتَأَخِّرِينَ - بِالنَّظَرِ وَالتَّحْقِيقِ لِلْفَلْسَفَةِ وَالْكَلَامِ قَدْ ضَلُّوا فِي هَذَا النَّقْلِ - وَهَذَا الْبَحْثُ فِي مِثْلِ هَذَا الْأَصْلِ ضَلَالٌ لَا يَقَعُ فِيهِ أَضْعَفُ الْعَوَامِّ - وَذَلِكَ لِمَا تَلَقَّوْهُ عَنْ بَعْضِ أَهْلِ الْمَنْطِقِ مِنْ الْقَوَاعِدِ الْفَاسِدَةِ الَّتِي هِيَ عَنْ الْهُدَى وَالرُّشْدِ حَائِدَةٌ؛ حَيْثُ ظَنُّوا أَنَّ الْكُلِّيَّاتِ الْمُطْلَقَةَ ثَابِتَةٌ فِي الْخَارِجِ جُزْءًا مِنْ الْمُعَيَّنَاتِ؛ وَأَنَّ ذَلِكَ يَقْتَضِي تَرْكِيبَ الْمُعَيَّنِ مِنْ ذَلِكَ الْكُلِّيِّ الْمُشْتَرَكِ وَمِمَّا يَخْتَصُّ بِهِ؛ فَلَزِمَهُمْ عَلَى هَذَا الْقَوْلِ أَنْ يَكُونَ الرَّبُّ تَعَالَى الْوَاجِبُ الْوُجُودِ مُرَكَّبًا مِنْ الْوُجُودِ الْمُشْتَرَكِ وَمِمَّا يَخْتَصُّ بِهِ مِنْ الْوُجُوبِ أَوْ الْوُجُودِ أَوْ الْمَاهِيَّةِ. مَعَ أَنَّهُ مِنْ الْمَشْهُورِ عِنْدَ أَهْلِ الْمَنْطِقِ أَنَّ الْكُلِّيَّاتِ إنَّمَا تَكُونُ كُلِّيَّاتٍ فِي الْأَذْهَانِ لَا فِي الْأَعْيَانِ.
translated_text:
Yet this attribution gravely misrepresents those to whom they ascribe it. These scholars agree that such terms are general and univocal—taking univocity in its broad sense, which includes graded predication—and admit of division and classification into types. This is possible only with univocal terms, as when we say: “Existents are divided into the eternal and the originated, and into the necessary and the contingent.”

Indeed, the very people who report this view, such as Abū ‘Abd Allāh al-Rāzī and other later thinkers, combine in their writings the claim that these terms are purely equivocal with this division of them. Yet they themselves maintain that division applies only to univocal terms, which share both wording and meaning, not to terms that share wording alone. These include what they call graded terms. Division cannot apply to terms whose referents share no general meaning.

Such is the contradiction of these men, who rank among the later thinkers most renowned for rational inquiry and rigorous investigation in philosophy and speculative theology. In this attribution and their investigation of so fundamental a principle, they have fallen into an error into which even the least discerning ordinary person would not fall. This stems from the unsound principles they received from certain logicians—principles that stray from guidance and sound judgment. They supposed that unqualified universals exist in external reality as parts of particular things, and that this entails each particular being composed of that shared universal and whatever is exclusive to it. On this view, they were thus committed to holding that the Lord Most High, whose existence is necessary, is composed of shared existence and whatever is exclusive to Him, whether necessity, existence, or quiddity. Yet it is well known among logicians that universals are universal only in minds, not in external entities.

original_text:
وَمَنْ هَدَاهُ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى يَعْلَمُ أَنَّ الْمَوْجُودَاتِ لَا تَشْتَرِكُ فِي شَيْءٍ مَوْجُودٍ فِيهَا أَصْلًا؛
 بَلْ كُلُّ مَوْجُودٍ مُتَمَيِّزٌ بِنَفْسِهِ وَبِمَا لَهُ مِنْ الصِّفَاتِ وَالْأَفْعَالِ وَأَنَّا إذَا قُلْنَا:
 إنَّ هَذَا الْإِنْسَانَ حَيٌّ مُتَكَلِّمٌ أَوْ حَيَوَانٌ نَاطِقٌ وَنَحْوَ ذَلِكَ؛ لَمْ يَكُنْ مَا لَهُ مِنْ الْحَيَوَانِيَّةِ أَوْ الناطقية أَوْ النُّطْقِ وَالْحَيَاةِ مُشْتَرَكًا بَيْنَهُ وَبَيْنَ غَيْرِهِ بَلْ لَهُ مَا يَخُصُّهُ وَلِغَيْرِهِ مَا يَخُصُّهُ وَلَكِنْ تَشَابَهَا وَتَمَاثَلَا بِحَسَبِ تَشَابُهِ حيوانيتهما وَنُطْقِيَّتِهِمَا وَغَيْرِ ذَلِكَ مِنْ صِفَاتِهِمَا.
 وَمَنْ قَالَ:
 إنَّ الْإِنْسَانَ مُرَكَّبٌ مِمَّا بِهِ الِاشْتِرَاكُ: وَهُوَ الْحَيَوَانِيَّةُ وَمَا بِهِ مِنْ الِامْتِيَازِ: وَهُوَ النُّطْقُ؛ فَإِنْ أَرَادَ بِذَلِكَ أَنَّ هَذَا تَرْكِيبٌ ذِهْنِيٌّ - فَإِنَّا إذَا تَصَوَّرْنَا فِي أَذْهَانِنَا حَيَوَانًا نَاطِقًا؛ كَانَ الْحَيَوَانُ جُزْءَ هَذَا الْمَعْنَى الذِّهْنِيِّ وَالنُّطْقُ جُزْأَهُ الْآخَرَ وَكَانَ الْحَيَوَانُ جُزْءًا لَهُ أَشْبَاهٌ أَكْثَرُ مِنْ أَشْبَاهِ النَّاطِقِ. وَإِذَا تَصَوَّرْنَا مُسَمَّى حَيَوَانٍ وَمُسَمَّى نَاطِقٍ؛ كَانَ مُسَمَّى الْحَيَوَانِ يَعُمُّ الْإِنْسَانَ وَغَيْرَهُ وَكَانَ مُسَمَّى النَّاطِقِ يَخُصُّهُ - فَدَعْوَى التَّرْكِيبِ فِي هَذِهِ الْمَعَانِي الذِّهْنِيَّةِ صَحِيحٌ لَكِنْ لَيْسَ هَذَا ضَابِطًا. بَلْ هُوَ بِحَسَبِ مَا يَتَصَوَّرُهُ الْإِنْسَانُ سَوَاءٌ كَانَ تَصَوُّرُهُ حَقًّا أَوْ بَاطِلًا. وَمَتَى أُرِيدَ بِجُزْءِ الْمَاهِيَّةِ الدَّاخِلِ فِيهَا مَا يَدْخُلُ فِي هَذَا التَّصَوُّرِ وَبِجُزْئِهَا الْخَارِجِ عَنْهَا اللَّازِمِ لِوُجُودِهَا مَا يَدُلُّ عَلَيْهِ هَذَا اللَّفْظُ بِالتَّضَمُّنِ وَالِالْتِزَامِ وَأَرَادَ بِتَمَامِ الْمَاهِيَّةِ مَا يَدُلُّ عَلَيْهِ هَذَا بِالْمُطَابَقَةِ؛ فَهَذَا صَحِيحٌ لَكِنَّ هَذَا لَا يَقْتَضِي أَنْ
translated_text:
Anyone whom Allah Most High guides knows that existent things share nothing that actually exists within them. Rather, each existent is distinct in itself and in its attributes and actions. When we say, “This human being is alive and speaks,” or “is a rational animal,” or the like, his animality or rationality, or his speech and life, are not shared between him and anyone else. Rather, he has what is particular to him, and another has what is particular to that other. They resemble one another to the extent that their animality, rationality, and other attributes resemble one another.

If someone says that a human being is composed of that by which he shares something with others—animality—and that by which he is distinguished—rationality—then, if he means a mental composition, the claim is correct. For when we conceive a rational animal in our minds, animality is one part of this mental meaning and rationality its other part; and the animal component has more counterparts than the rational component. When we conceive what is designated by “animal” and what is designated by “rational,” the former encompasses human beings and others, whereas the latter is specific to human beings. Thus, the claim of composition in these mental meanings is correct. Yet this provides no fixed criterion. Rather, it depends on what a person conceives, whether that conception is true or false.

If by the part internal to a quiddity one means what enters into this conception; by its part external to it but necessarily accompanying its existence, what this expression signifies by inclusion and necessary implication; and by the whole quiddity, what it signifies by correspondence—then this is correct. But this does not entail that

 الْإِنْسَانُ مُرَكَّبٌ مِنْ هَذَا وَهَذَا إذَا أُرِيدَ بِهِ أَنَّ هُنَا شَيْئًا

realities existing outside the mind are composed of particular and general attributes, nor that some of their inseparable attributes are internal to their reality and essential to it, while others are external to their reality and accidental to it, as the proponents of Greek logic claim. This is one of the matters in which they went astray, and their error led astray those groups of speculative thinkers who followed them in it. They were also blindly followed in this by those who neither understood the true meaning and implications of their position nor conceived it fully.

If by composition they mean that a human being possesses life and rationality—with one attribute having counterparts in other animals and the other being specific to human beings—then this is a sound meaning. But if they mean that his animality is shared between him and others, they are mistaken. The animality of each animal is like the rationality of each rational being: each is particular to the subject in which it inheres.

Likewise, if by composition they mean that there is an existent described as an animal distinct from the existent described as rational or as neighing, and that a human being is composed of this existent and that existent, and a horse is composed of this existent and that existent, then they are mistaken. Rather, nothing exists here except this human being, described as a rational animal, and this horse, described as a neighing animal. The same applies to all other animals and existent things.

Thus, if someone’s statement, “A human being is composed of this and that,” is intended to mean that there is something

The following meaning, however, is correct: a human being is truly described as an animal and as rational, and is an essence that necessarily entails its attributes. The thing described cannot exist without its inseparable attribute. But this is not composition in external reality.

Nor is there in external reality an inseparable essential attribute, another accidental attribute inseparable from the quiddity, and yet another inseparable from its existence. Rather, there is only the particular existent, whose attributes fall into two categories: inseparable and incidental. It cannot exist without any one of its inseparable attributes. Thus, none of these attributes is inseparable from the essence existing in external reality yet not inseparable from that essence, being instead inseparable from the externally existing thing—as some logicians suppose.

Their fundamental error is that they confused what is conceived in the mind with what exists in concrete reality. The mind conceives a triangle before it exists externally, and they supposed that quiddity is distinct from existence. This is correct if quiddity is understood as what the mind conceives.

But to suppose that a triangle in external reality has a quiddity established externally that is distinct from the thing existing externally is a manifest error. Once this is understood concerning the attributes of a created being, the Creator is even further removed from what these people call composition.

translated_text:
Thus, when it is said that Allah, glorified and exalted be He, is living, knowing and powerful, He is being described as the Ever-Living, the All-Knowing, the All-Powerful. When it is said that He exists and is necessary in Himself, He, glorified be He, is being described as possessing existence and necessity. There is therefore no actually existing thing shared between Him and anything else. Nor is He composed of two parts, or of constitutive attributes that form parts of His existence, or anything similar among the alleged forms of composition that are impossible even in a created being—and still more emphatically impossible in the Creator.

However, the term “composition” is ambiguous. These people include within it a thing’s possession of its inseparable attributes, although this is not what is ordinarily understood by “composition.” They have introduced their own technical usage of this term, without precedent among the authorities on the language or any group of scholars. They have made “composition” encompass “five kinds”:

First: composition from existence and quiddity, because they suppose that the external existence of every contingent being is distinct from its quiddity. Whenever the “internal part of quiddity” is understood as what enters into this conception, and its “external concomitant” as what this conception necessarily entails, these are the two meanings signified by the expression.

Second: composition from genus and differentia, as when they say that a human being is composed of animality and rationality. They may also include composition from a general meaning and a specific meaning, calling it composition from a genus and a differentia, or from a specific property and a common accident.

Third: composition from essence and attributes, as in that which is designated as living, knowing and capable

translated_text:
and the composition of a body from its sensible parts, according to those who say that it is composed of indivisible atoms (1), or its composition from two intelligible components, according to those who say that it is composed of matter and form.

As for the “first” and “second” kinds of composition, the majority of rational thinkers dispute their existence in external reality, saying that no composition of this sort exists there. The “fourth” and “fifth” kinds are the subject of a well-known dispute among rational thinkers: some affirm one of these two kinds of composition in a body, while others say that it is composed in neither way.

As for the “fourth,” the great majority of rational thinkers agree with them in affirming it; I know of no one who disputes it in substance (*). However, a group of speculative thinkers, such as ʿAbd al-Rahmān ibn Kaysān al-Asamm and others, are reported to have denied accidents: they did not affirm accidents as something additional to the body, and denied that motion was something additional to the body. Most thinkers disagreed with them on this.

This—and Allah knows best—is a verbal dispute: does the term “body” encompass the body together with its accidents, or are accidents additional to what the term “body” designates? Otherwise, no rational person denies the existence of taste, colour, smell, motion, and other attributes inhering in the things they qualify.

“I draw attention here to two points:

First: The ‘fourth type’ of composition is the composition of a body from its sensible parts, according to those who maintain that it is composed of indivisible atoms.

The ‘fifth type’ is its composition from two intelligible components, according to those who maintain that it is composed of matter and form.

Both were mentioned above, but they were not distinguished from one another. The Shaykh—may Allah have mercy on him—mentioned these types in several places in his books and treatises, including his statement in al-Safadiyya, 1:105: ‘Fourth: composition in quantity, namely, the composition of a body from its constituent parts: either from indivisible atoms, which is sensible composition, or from matter and form, which is intelligible composition. These two types are the fourth and fifth.’

Second: His statement, ‘As for the “fourth,” the great majority of scholars agree with them in affirming it…,’ may contain a copyist’s error. The correct reading is ‘third,’ namely, composition from ‘essence’ and ‘attributes,’ which is the subject of the ensuing discussion.

This occurs again on the following page, p. 338, where he says: ‘As for the fourth type: if someone disputes whether attributes are additional to the essence or not, this is a verbal dispute…’ What is meant is the ‘third type,’ not the ‘fourth.’”

translated_text:
This resembles the dispute over whether attributes are additional to the essence. For whoever means by “essence” the “bare essence,” the attributes are additional to it. But for whoever means the “essence qualified by attributes,” the attributes are not separate from the essence qualified by its inseparable attributes.

These people then claimed that they deny these types of composition. As for the “four types,” whoever holds that they are absent from created beings must hold that they are all the more absent from the Creator. As for the “fourth type,” if the dispute concerns whether attributes are additional to the essence, then it is a verbal dispute. But if someone disputes the actual existence of these attributes, denies that Allah has knowledge, power, and will, and regards one attribute as identical with another, and the attribute as identical with the one it qualifies, then the falsity of his position becomes evident once it is fully understood.

Once it is known that He—glorified be He—is Living, All-Knowing, and All-Powerful, and that what it means for Him to be Living differs from what it means for Him to be All-Knowing, and that what it means for Him to be All-Knowing differs from what it means for Him to be All-Powerful, this is precisely the affirmation of the attributes. If someone says that what it means for Him to be All-Knowing is the same as what it means for Him to possess will, to be All-Powerful, and to be Living, this is a wilful denial of the obvious. The same applies if he claims that these meanings are identical with the meaning of the essence qualified by them.

But if he acknowledges that these qualities belong to Allah and says, “I deny that Allah depends on entities or qualities through which He becomes living, knowing, and powerful,” then his dispute is with those who affirm “states”

translated_text:
such as al-Qādī Abū Bakr, Abū Ya‘lā, and others who say: “He possesses knowledge and the state of being knowing, and His state of being knowing is a meaning additional to His knowledge.” This is the position of some who affirm the attributes, but the majority of them reject it, saying instead: “Knowledge and being knowing have the same meaning.”

There are “three matters” concerning the attributes:

The first is describing Him as Living, All-Knowing, and All-Powerful. There is agreement on affirming this, and it is termed predication.

The second is that these are meanings subsisting in His essence. This, too, is affirmed by those who affirm the attributes: the early generations, the imams, and those affiliated with the Sunnah across the various groups.

The third is states, namely, the states of being knowing and being powerful. There is disagreement concerning these among both those who affirm the attributes and those who deny them. Abū Hāshim and his followers affirm states but not attributes; al-Qādī Abū Bakr and his followers affirm both states and attributes; and most of the Jahmiyyah and Mu‘tazilah deny both states and attributes.

As for the great majority of the “people of the Sunnah,” they affirm the attributes but not states. A fuller discussion of this belongs elsewhere.

 وَقَدْ يَقُولُونَ:
 هُوَ الْمَعْلُومُ - فَيَجْعَلُونَ الصِّفَةَ هِيَ الْمَوْصُوفَ أَوْ هِيَ الْمَخْلُوقَاتِ. وَهَذِهِ أَقْوَالُ رُؤَسَائِهِمْ وَهِيَ فِي غَايَةِ الْفَسَادِ فِي صَرِيحِ الْمَعْقُولِ؛ فَهُمْ مُضْطَرُّونَ إلَى الْإِقْرَارِ بِمَا يُسَمُّونَهُ تَشْبِيهًا وَتَرْكِيبًا وَيَزْعُمُونَ أَنَّهُمْ يَنْفُونَ التَّشْبِيهَ وَالتَّرْكِيبَ وَالتَّقْسِيمَ؛ فَلْيَتَأَمَّلْ اللَّبِيبُ كَذِبَهُمْ وَتَنَاقُضَهُمْ وَحَيْرَتَهُمْ وَضَلَالَهُمْ؛ وَلِهَذَا يَئُولُ بِهِمْ الْأَمْرُ إلَى الْجَمْعِ بَيْنَ النَّقِيضَيْنِ أَوْ الْخُلُوِّ عَنْ النَّقِيضَيْنِ. ثُمَّ إنَّهُمْ يَنْفُونَ عَنْ اللَّهِ مَا وَصَفَ بِهِ نَفْسَهُ وَمَا وَصَفَهُ بِهِ رَسُولُهُ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ لِزَعْمِهِمْ أَنَّ ذَلِكَ تَشْبِيهٌ وَتَرْكِيبٌ. وَيَصِفُونَ أَهْلَ الْإِثْبَاتِ بِهَذِهِ الْأَسْمَاءِ وَهُمْ الَّذِينَ أَلْزَمُوهَا بِمُقْتَضَى أُصُولِهِمْ وَلَا حِيلَةَ لَهُمْ فِي دَفْعِهَا.
 فَهُمْ:
 كَمَا قَالَ الْقَائِلُ: رَمَتْنِي بِدَائِهَا وَانْسَلَّتْ
translated_text:
The purpose here is to discuss composition, both as a term and as a concept, and to show that these people use it in a technical sense at odds with that of most rational people, and that they are compelled to acknowledge the reality of what they deny. Yet they say, “This is commonality, and commonality is resemblance.” They also say, “These are parts, and this is composition from these parts.” Nevertheless, they cannot deny what they have called commonality and resemblance, nor can they deny these things that they have called parts, composition, and division. For they say, “He is the one who apprehends, the object of apprehension, and intellect itself; the object of pleasure, pleasure itself, and the one who takes pleasure; the lover, the beloved, and love itself.”

They may also say, “He is knowing, powerful, and willing,” and then say, “Knowledge is power, and power is will,” thus identifying each attribute with the other. They also say, “Knowledge is the knower”—and may say, “It is the object known”—thus identifying the attribute with the one possessing it, or with created things.

These are the statements of their leading authorities, and they are utterly unsound in the light of plain reason. They are compelled to acknowledge what they call resemblance and composition, while claiming to deny resemblance, composition, and division. Let the discerning reader reflect on their falsehood, inconsistency, bewilderment, and misguidance. This is why they ultimately end up either affirming both of two contradictories or denying both.

Moreover, they deny of Allah what He has affirmed of Himself and what His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, has affirmed of Him, claiming that this entails resemblance and composition. They apply these labels to those who affirm the attributes, yet it is they themselves whom their own principles bind to these things, with no way to escape them.

They are thus as the saying goes:
“She accused me of her own disease, then slipped away.”

original_text:
وَهُمْ لَمْ يَقْصِدُوا هَذَا التَّنَاقُضَ؛ وَلَكِنْ أَوْقَعَتْهُمْ فِيهِ قَوَاعِدُهُمْ الْفَاسِدَةُ الْمَنْطِقِيَّةُ الَّتِي زَعَمُوا فِيهَا تَرْكِيبَ الْمَوْصُوفَاتِ مِنْ صِفَاتِهَا وَوُجُودِ الْكُلِّيَّاتِ الْمُشْتَرَكَةِ فِي أَعْيَانِهَا. فَتِلْكَ الْقَوَاعِدُ الْمَنْطِقِيَّةُ الْفَاسِدَةُ الَّتِي جَعَلُوهَا قَوَانِينَ تَمْنَعُ مُرَاعَاتُهَا الذِّهْنَ أَنْ يَضِلَّ فِي فِكْرِهِ أَوْقَعَتْهُمْ فِي هَذَا الضَّلَالِ وَالتَّنَاقُضِ. ثُمَّ إنَّ هَذِهِ الْقَوَانِينَ فِيهَا مَا هُوَ صَحِيحٌ لَا رَيْبَ فِيهِ؛
 وَذَلِكَ يَدُلُّ عَلَى تَنَاقُضِهِمْ وَجَهْلِهِمْ فَإِنَّهُمْ قَدْ قَرَّرُوا فِي الْقَوَانِينِ الْمَنْطِقِيَّةِ:
 أَنَّ الْكُلِّيَّ هُوَ الَّذِي لَا يَمْنَعُ تَصَوُّرُهُ مِنْ وُقُوعِ الشَّرِكَةِ فِيهِ؛ بِخِلَافِ الْجُزْئِيِّ.
 وَقَرَّرُوا أَيْضًا أَنَّ الْكُلِّيَّاتِ لَا تَكُونُ كُلِّيَّةً إلَّا فِي الْأَذْهَانِ:
 دُونَ الْأَعْيَانِ. وَأَنَّ الْمُطْلَقَ بِشَرْطِ الْإِطْلَاقِ لَا يَكُونُ إلَّا فِي الذِّهْنِ وَهَذِهِ قَوَانِينُ صَحِيحَةٌ. ثُمَّ يَدَّعُونَ مَا ادَّعَاهُ أَفْضَلُ مُتَأَخِّرِيهِمْ أَنَّ الْوَاجِبَ الْوُجُودِ هُوَ الْوُجُودُ الْمُطْلَقُ بِشَرْطِ الْإِطْلَاقِ عَنْ كُلِّ أَمْرٍ ثُبُوتِيٍّ.
 أَوْ كَمَا يَقُولُهُ طَائِفَةٌ مِنْهُمْ:
 إنَّهُ الْوُجُودُ الْمُطْلَقُ بِشَرْطِ الْإِطْلَاقِ عَنْ كُلِّ أَمْرٍ ثُبُوتِيٍّ وَسَلْبِيٍّ؛ كَمَا يَقُولُ ذَلِكَ مَنْ يَقُولُهُ مِنْ الْمَلَاحِدَةِ الْبَاطِنِيَّةِ الْمُنْتَسِبِينَ إلَى التَّشَيُّعِ وَالْمُنْتَسِبِينَ إلَى التَّصَوُّفِ.
 أَوْ يَقُولُهُ طَائِفَةٌ ثَالِثَةٌ:
 إنَّهُ الْوُجُودُ الْمُطْلَقُ لَا بِشَرْطِ كَمَا تَقُولُهُ طَائِفَةٌ مِنْهُمْ. وَهُمْ مُتَّفِقُونَ عَلَى أَنَّ الْمُطْلَقَ بِشَرْطِ الْإِطْلَاقِ عَنْ الْأُمُورِ الْوُجُودِيَّةِ وَالْعَدَمِيَّةِ
translated_text:
They did not intend this contradiction; rather, they were led into it by their unsound rules of logic, in which they claimed that things possessing attributes are composed of their attributes, and that shared universals exist in their concrete instances. Those unsound rules of logic—which they made into laws whose observance supposedly prevents the mind from going astray in its thinking—led them into this very error and contradiction. Yet some of these laws are undoubtedly sound, which further demonstrates their inconsistency and ignorance. For they have established among their logical laws that a universal is that whose conception does not preclude its being shared, unlike a particular.

They have also established that universals are universal only in minds, not in concrete reality, and that the absolute, taken on condition of its absoluteness, exists only in the mind. These are sound laws. Yet they then claim, as the foremost of their later thinkers claimed, that the Necessary Existent is absolute existence, on condition that it be free of every positive determination.

Or, as one group among them says, He is absolute existence, on condition that it be free of every positive and negative determination. This is the position maintained by some of the heretical esotericists who affiliate themselves with Shiism or Sufism.

Or a third group says that He is absolute existence without any condition, as some among them put it. They agree that the absolute, on condition that it be free of all determinations involving existence and nonexistence

لَا يَكُونُ فِي الْخَارِجِ مَوْجُودًا.
فَالْمُطْلَقُ بِشَرْطِ الْإِطْلَاقِ عَنْ كُلِّ أَمْرٍ ثُبُوتِيٍّ؛ أَوْلَى أَنْ لَا يَكُونَ مَوْجُودًا. فَإِنَّ الْمُقَيَّدَ بِسَلْبِ الْوُجُودِ وَالْعَدَمِ نِسْبَتُهُ إلَيْهِمَا سَوَاءٌ وَالْمُقَيَّدَ بِسَلْبِ الْوُجُودِ يَخْتَصُّ بِالْعَدَمِ دُونَ الْوُجُودِ وَالْمُطْلَقَ لَا بِشَرْطِ إنَّمَا يُوجَدُ مُطْلَقًا فِي الْأَذْهَانِ.
 وَإِذَا قِيلَ:
 هُوَ مَوْجُودٌ فِي الْخَارِجِ؛ فَذَلِكَ بِمَعْنَى أَنَّهُ يُوجَدُ فِي الْخَارِجِ مُقَيَّدًا لَا أَنَّهُ يُوجَدُ فِي الْخَارِجِ مُطْلَقًا فَإِنَّ هَذَا بَاطِلٌ؛ وَإِنْ كَانَتْ طَائِفَةٌ تَدَّعِيهِ. فَمَنْ تَصَوَّرَ هَذَا تَصَوُّرًا تَامًّا؛ عَلِمَ بُطْلَانَ قَوْلِهِمْ وَهَذَا حَقٌّ مَعْلُومٌ بِالضَّرُورَةِ. فَهَذَا الْقَانُونُ الصَّحِيحُ لَمْ يَنْتَفِعُوا بِهِ فِي إثْبَاتِ وُجُودِ الرَّبِّ؛ بَلْ جَعَلُوهُ مُطْلَقًا بِشَرْطِ الْإِطْلَاقِ عَنْ النَّقِيضَيْنِ أَوْ عَنْ الْأُمُورِ الْوُجُودِيَّةِ. أَوْ لَا بِشَرْطِ وَذَلِكَ لَا يُتَصَوَّرُ إلَّا فِي الْأَذْهَانِ. وَالْقَوَانِينُ الْفَاسِدَةُ أَوْقَعَتْهُمْ فِي ذَلِكَ التَّنَاقُضِ وَالْهَذَيَانِ وَهُمْ يَفِرُّونَ مِنْ التَّشْبِيهِ بِوَجْهِ مِنْ الْوُجُوهِ؛
 ثُمَّ يَقُولُونَ:
 الْوُجُودُ يَنْقَسِمُ إلَى: وَاجِبٍ وَمُمْكِنٍ فَهُمَا مُشْتَرِكَانِ فِي مُسَمَّى الْوُجُودِ وَكَذَلِكَ لَفْظُ الْمَاهِيَّةِ وَالْحَقِيقَةِ وَالذَّاتِ.
 وَمَهْمَا قِيلَ:
 هُوَ يَنْقَسِمُ إلَى وَاجِبٍ وَمُمْكِنٍ. وَمَوْرِدُ التَّقْسِيمِ مُشْتَرَكٌ بَيْنَ الْأَقْسَامِ فَقَدْ اشْتَرَكَتْ الْأَقْسَامُ فِي الْمَعْنَى الْعَامِّ الْكُلِّيِّ الشَّامِلِ لِمَا تَشَابَهَتْ فِيهِ فَهَذَا تَشْبِيهٌ يَقُولُونَ بِهِ وَهُمْ يَزْعُمُونَ أَنَّهُمْ يَنْفُونَ كُلَّ مَا يُسَمَّى تَشْبِيهًا حَتَّى نَفَوْا الْأَسْمَاءَ فَكَانَ الْغُلَاةُ مِنْ الْجَهْمِيَّة وَالْبَاطِنِيَّةِ لَا يُسَمُّونَهُ شَيْئًا فِرَارًا مِنْ ذَلِكَ.
translated_text:

The absolute, on condition that it be free of every positive determination, is even less capable of existing. For what is conditioned by the negation of both existence and nonexistence stands in the same relation to both, whereas what is conditioned by the negation of existence pertains exclusively to nonexistence, not existence. As for the absolute without any condition, it exists as absolute only in minds.

When it is said, “It exists in concrete reality,” this means that it exists there with determinations, not that it exists there as absolute. The latter is false, even though a group claims it. Whoever fully grasps this will recognize the falsity of their position. This is self-evidently true. Yet this sound principle did not benefit them in establishing the existence of the Lord. Instead, they made Him absolute, either on condition that He be free of both contradictories, or of all positive determinations, or without any condition. Such an absolute can be conceived only in minds. Their unsound principles led them into this contradiction and nonsense.

They seek to avoid affirming any likeness whatsoever, yet they say, “Existence is divided into necessary and contingent.” Thus, the two share in what is denoted by “existence.” The same applies to the terms “quiddity,” “reality,” and “essence.”

Whatever is said to be divided into necessary and contingent, the subject of that division is shared by its divisions. These divisions therefore share a general, universal meaning encompassing that in which they resemble one another. This is a likeness that they themselves affirm, although they claim to deny everything that could be called likeness, to the point of denying the names. Thus, the extremists among the Jahmiyyah and the esotericists would not even call Him a “thing,” seeking to avoid this.

وَأَيُّ شَيْءٍ أَثْبَتُوهُ؛ لَزِمَهُمْ فِيهِ مِثْلُ ذَلِكَ وَإِلَّا لَزِمَ أَنْ لَا يَكُونَ وُجُودُ وَاجِبِ الْوُجُودِ مُمْكِنًا وَقَدِيمًا وَمُحْدَثًا وَأَنَّ الْمُحْدَثَ وَالْمُمْكِنَ لَا بُدَّ لَهُ مِنْ قَدِيمٍ وَمِنْ الْمَعْلُومِ بِالِاضْطِرَارِ أَنَّ الْوُجُودَ فِيهِ مُحْدَثٌ مُمْكِنٌ وَأَنَّ الْمُحْدَثَ الْمُمْكِنَ لَا بُدَّ لَهُ مِنْ قَدِيمٍ وَاجِبٍ بِنَفْسِهِ؛ فَثُبُوتُ النَّوْعَيْنِ ضَرُورِيٌّ لَا بُدَّ مِنْهُ. وَحَقِيقَةُ الْأَمْرِ أَنَّ لَفْظَ الْمُطْلَقِ قَدْ يُعْنَى بِهِ مَا هُوَ كُلِّيٌّ لَا يَمْنَعُ تَصَوُّرُ مَعْنَاهُ مِنْ وُقُوعِ الشَّرِكَةِ فِيهِ. وَيَمْتَنِعُ أَنْ يَكُونَ شَيْءٌ مَوْجُودٌ فِي الْخَارِجِ قَائِمًا بِنَفْسِهِ أَوْ صِفَةً لِغَيْرِهِ بِهَذَا الِاعْتِبَارِ؛ فَضْلًا عَنْ أَنْ يَكُونَ رَبُّ الْعَالَمِينَ الْأَحَدُ الصَّمَدُ كَذَلِكَ.
 وَقَدْ يُرَادُ بِالْمُطْلَقِ:
 الْمُجَرَّدُ عَنْ الصِّفَاتِ الثُّبُوتِيَّةِ أَوْ عَنْ الثُّبُوتِيَّةِ وَالسَّلْبِيَّةِ جَمِيعًا؛ وَالْمُطْلَقُ لَا بِشَرْطِ الْإِطْلَاقِ. وَهَذَا إذَا قُدِّرَ جُعِلَ مُعَيَّنًا خَاصًّا لَا كُلِّيًّا فَإِنَّهُ يَمْتَنِعُ وُجُودُهُ فِي الْخَارِجِ أَعْظَمُ مِنْ امْتِنَاعِ الْكُلِّيَّاتِ الْمُطْلَقَةِ بِشَرْطِ لِكَوْنِهَا كُلِّيَّةً. فَإِنَّ تِلْكَ الْكُلِّيَّاتِ لَهَا جُزْئِيَّاتٌ مَوْجُودَةٌ فِي الْخَارِجِ وَالْكُلِّيَّاتُ مُطَابِقَةٌ لَهَا. وَأَمَّا وُجُودُ شَيْءٍ مُجَرَّدٍ عَنْ أَنْ يُوصَفَ بِصِفَةِ ثُبُوتِيَّةٍ وَسَلْبِيَّةٍ؛ فَهَذَا يَمْتَنِعُ تَحَقُّقُهُ فِي الْخَارِجِ كُلِّيًّا وَجُزْئِيًّا. وَكَذَلِكَ الْمُجَرَّدُ عَنْ أَنْ يُوصَفَ بِصِفَةِ ثُبُوتِيَّةٍ بَلْ هَذَا أَوْلَى بِالِامْتِنَاعِ مِنْهُ. وَإِذَا كَانَ هَذَا قَدْ شَارَكَ سَائِرَ الْمَوْجُودَاتِ فِي مُسَمَّى الْوُجُودِ وَلَمْ يُمَيَّزْ عَنْهَا إلَّا بِالْقُيُودِ السَّلْبِيَّةِ وَهِيَ قَدْ امْتَازَتْ عَنْهُ بِالْقُيُودِ الْوُجُودِيَّةِ؛
translated_text:
Whatever they affirm, the same consequence follows. Otherwise, it would follow that the existence of the Necessary Existent is not contingent, eternal, and originated, and that whatever is originated and contingent must have an eternal cause. It is necessarily known that among existing things are those that are originated and contingent, and that whatever is originated and contingent must have an eternal cause that exists necessarily in itself. The existence of both kinds is therefore a necessary, inescapable fact.

The truth of the matter is that the term “absolute” may mean something universal, the conception of whose meaning does not preclude its being shared by multiple things. Nothing existing in concrete reality, whether self-subsisting or an attribute of something else, can exist in this manner—let alone the Lord of the worlds, the One, the Self-Sufficient.

The term “absolute” may also mean that which is divested of positive attributes, or of both positive and negative attributes; and the absolute without the condition of absoluteness. If this is conceived as something determinate and particular rather than universal, its existence in concrete reality is even more impossible than that of absolute universals conditioned by their universality. For those universals have particulars existing in concrete reality, to which the universals correspond. By contrast, something divested of any positive or negative attribute cannot be realized in concrete reality, whether as a universal or as a particular. The same applies to something divested of positive attributes; indeed, this is even more impossible than the former.

then every contingent existent would be more perfect than this which they claim is the Necessary Existent. For universal existence is shared by it and them; it is distinguished from them only by an absence, whereas they are distinguished from it by something existent. Thus, what distinguishes them from it is more perfect than what distinguishes it from them, since existence is more perfect than nonexistence.

If, however, it is said that it is existence without qualification, then this is universal and natural existence, applicable to every existent. This is universal only in the mind; in external reality, it exists only as something particular.

Some people say that this universal is a part of particular existents. If the first view is correct, it follows either that the Necessary Existent does not exist in external reality, or that the Necessary Existent and the contingent existent are one and the same entity, as some proponents of the oneness of existence maintain. If the second view is correct, it follows that its existence is a part of every existent; the Necessary Existent would thus be a part of the existence of contingent things.

Sound reason plainly recognizes that a part of something cannot be the creator of that thing in its entirety. Indeed, it cannot even create itself, let alone create that of which it is a part, since the whole is greater than the part. If it cannot create the part, its inability to create the whole is all the more evident.

Thus, they have gained no benefit from sound logic in knowing Allah, while false logic has led them into the utmost falsehood and ignorance concerning Allah.

“Whoever Allah does not grant light has no light.”

And “Allah is the Protector of

those who believe. He brings them out of darkness into light. As for those who disbelieve, their protectors are false gods, who bring them out of light into darkness.”

He also says:

“We have certainly sent Our messengers with clear proofs, and sent down with them the Scripture and the balance so that people may uphold justice. And We sent down iron, in which there is great strength and benefits for people, so that Allah may know who supports Him and His messengers unseen. Indeed, Allah is All-Strong, Almighty.”

He also says:

“Mankind was one community. Then Allah sent the prophets as bearers of good tidings and warners, and sent down with them the Scripture in truth to judge between people concerning their differences. When the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, rose to pray at night, he would say, as Muslim reported in his Sahīh:

translated_text:
Section

To complete the discussion of this subject, you should understand that we can know what lies beyond our experience only through knowing what we have experienced. We know things through our outward or inward senses, and this knowledge concerns particular, specific things. Then, through reason, we infer what lies beyond our experience from what we have experienced, leaving general, universal propositions in our minds. Thus, when something beyond our experience is described to us, we understand what we are told only through our knowledge of what we have experienced. Had we not experienced within ourselves hunger and thirst, satiety and the quenching of thirst, love and hatred, pleasure and pain, contentment and displeasure, we would not understand the reality of these things when they are described to us and we are told that others experience them.

Likewise, had we not known life, power, knowledge, and speech in the realm of our experience, we would not understand what we are told when something beyond our experience is described in these terms. Similarly, had we never experienced anything that exists, we would not know of the existence of anything beyond our experience. There must therefore be a shared element between what we have experienced and what lies beyond our experience: this is what a univocal term denotes. Through this agreement, commonality, similarity, and correspondence, we understand what lies beyond our experience and affirm its reality. This is the distinctive function of reason. Without it, we would know only what we perceive through our senses; we would know neither general truths nor things beyond our outward and inward senses. Hence, whoever has never perceived a thing or anything comparable to it cannot know its reality.

Furthermore, Allah Most High has told us of the bliss and punishment He has promised us in the Hereafter, and of its food, drink, spouses, furnishings, and other things. Were we not familiar with things resembling these in this world, we would not understand what He has promised us. Yet we know that those realities are not like these. Indeed, Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him, said: “Nothing of what is in Paradise is found in this world except the names.” According to one view, this explains His words:

“And it is given to them in likeness.”

Thus, the things that exist in this world and those that exist in the Hereafter resemble one another, correspond, and share certain features. Through this, we understand what is meant and come to love and desire it, or to hate it and recoil from it. Yet between them lie differences and disparities in excellence whose extent cannot be measured in this world. This belongs to the ta’wīl—the ultimate reality—that we do not know, but Allah Most High knows.

Hence, the statement, “None but Allah knows the ta’wīl of the ambiguous passages,” is true, as is the statement, “Those firmly grounded in knowledge know their ta’wīl.” Both statements have been transmitted from the early generations: the Companions and those who followed them in righteousness.

Those who said that they know their ta’wīl meant that they know their explanation and meaning. Otherwise, could a Muslim permissibly say that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not know the meaning of the verses and hadiths he uttered and conveyed, but instead spoke words whose meanings he did not know?  نَعْلَمُ تَفْسِيرَهُ وَمَعْنَاهُ وَنَفْهَمُ الْكَلَامَ الَّذِي خُوطِبْنَا بِهِ وَنَعْلَمُ مَعْنَى الْعَسَلِ وَاللَّحْمِ وَاللَّبَنِ وَالْحَرِيرِ وَالذَّهَبِ وَالْفِضَّةِ وَنُفَرِّقُ بَيْنَ مُسَمَّيَاتِ هَذِهِ الْأَسْمَاءِ وَأَمَّا حَقَائِقُهَا عَلَى مَا هِيَ عَلَيْهِ فَلَا يُمْكِنُ أَنْ نَعْلَمَهَا نَحْنُ وَلَا نَعْلَمَ مَتَى تَكُونُ السَّاعَةُ. وَتَفْصِيلُ مَا أَعَدَّ اللَّهُ عَزَّ وَجَلَّ لِعِبَادِهِ لَا يَعْلَمُهُ مَلَكٌ مُقَرَّبٌ وَلَا نَبِيٌّ مُرْسَلٌ. بَلْ هَذَا مِنْ التَّأْوِيلِ الَّذِي لَا يَعْلَمُهُ إلَّا اللَّهُ تَبَارَكَ وَتَعَالَى. فَإِذَا كَانَ هَذَا فِي هَذَيْنِ الْمَخْلُوقَيْنِ فَالْأَمْرُ بَيْنَ الْخَالِقِ وَالْمَخْلُوقِ أَعْظَمُ؛
translated_text:
Allah.

This is why the early generations, including Rabīʿah, Mālik ibn Anas, and others, would say: “Rising over is known, but its manner is unknown.” This was also the position of the rest of the early generations, including Ibn al-Mājishūn, Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and others, and it applies to the other attributes as well. The meaning of rising over is thus known: this is the ta’wīl—the explanation—known to those firmly grounded in knowledge. Its actual manner, however, is the ta’wīl unknown to the children of Adam and all others, which none knows except Allah, glorified and exalted is He.

Likewise, regarding what He has promised in Paradise, His servants understand the meaning of what Allah has told them. As for its actual manner, He Most High has said:

“No soul knows what delights have been hidden for them as a reward for what they used to do.”

And the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in an authentic hadith:

“Allah Most High says: ‘I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has ever conceived.’”

Thus, we know the explanation and meaning of what Allah has told us about the attributes of created things, and we understand the words addressed to us. We know what honey, meat, milk, silk, gold, and silver mean, and we distinguish between the things these names denote. As for their true realities as they actually are, we cannot know them, nor do we know when the Hour will come. No angel brought near to Allah and no prophet sent by Him knows the full details of what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has prepared for His servants. Rather, this belongs to the ta’wīl that none knows except Allah, blessed and exalted is He. If this is the case with these two created realities, then the distinction between the Creator and creation is greater still;

translated_text:
for Allah’s distinction from His creation, His greatness, majesty, and superiority, far exceed any difference between one created thing and another.

If the attributes of that created thing, despite their resemblance to those of this created thing, differ in excellence and nature to an extent that we neither know nor can know in this world—rather, this belongs to the ta’wīl known only to Allah, blessed and exalted is He—then all the more must the attributes of the Creator, Mighty and Majestic, differ from those of creation in nature and excellence to an extent known only to Allah, blessed and exalted is He. This must likewise belong to the ta’wīl that not everyone knows: some of it is known to those firmly grounded in knowledge, some to the prophets and angels, and some to Allah alone.

As it is reported that Ibn ‘Abbās, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

“Quranic explanation is of four kinds: explanation that the Arabs know from their own language; explanation of which no one is excused for being ignorant; explanation known to the scholars; and explanation known only to Allah. Whoever claims knowledge of this last kind is a liar.”

In the speech of the early generations, the term “ta’wīl” means only explanation or the concrete reality to which something ultimately refers, as in His Most High’s words:

“Are they waiting for anything but its fulfilment? On the Day its fulfilment comes…”

And so on in the verse.

translated_text:
some later scholars; none of the early generations ever used the word ta’wīl in this sense.

Then, when this usage became widespread among later scholars, they began to suppose that this was the ta’wīl meant in His Most High’s words:

“No one knows its interpretation except Allah.”

One group then said, “No one knows it except Allah,” while another said, “Rather, those firmly grounded in knowledge know it.” Both groups are mistaken, for this has no reality; rather, it is false, and Allah knows that it is unfounded and that He did not intend it. Such are the interpretations of the Qarmatian esotericists, the Jahmiyyah, and other proponents of heresy and religious innovation. These interpretations are false, and Allah did not intend them by His words. What He did not intend, we cannot say He knows to be His intended meaning, for this would be a lie against Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

Those firmly grounded in knowledge do not speak falsely about Allah, blessed and exalted is He, even though we know from what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has told us about Himself—indeed, also through rational consideration of the fact that to Allah belongs the highest description—that Allah is described by attributes of perfection. He possesses life, knowledge, and power, and these are attributes of perfection. The Creator is more entitled to them than the created being. It is therefore impossible for the created being to possess attributes of perfection that the Creator does not possess.

Were it not that these names and attributes signify a shared, universal meaning, involving sufficient correspondence, agreement, and resemblance for these meanings to be understood and affirmed of Allah, we would have known nothing of Allah, nor would our hearts have contained any faith in Him, knowledge, recognition, or love

translated_text:
or any desire to worship Him, supplicate to Him, ask of Him, love Him, or magnify Him. All these things require knowledge, and knowledge is possible only by affirming “those meanings,” which contain the correspondence and agreement through which we have acquired whatever knowledge we possess of what lies beyond our observation.

Whoever understands these noble truths and these great, beneficial principles will gain knowledge, recognition, sound understanding, affirmation of Allah’s oneness, and faith, while doubts, misguidance, and bewilderment will be dispelled from him. This will make him, in this field, among the finest of those whom Allah has favored—not those who have incurred His anger, nor those who have gone astray—and among the foremost people of knowledge and faith. It will become clear to him that what is said concerning some of the “attributes of Allah” applies equally to the rest, and that what is said concerning His attributes is like what is said concerning “His essence.” Whoever affirms one attribute conveyed by the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, while denying another, even though both share the very feature on which he bases his denial, is inconsistent.

Thus, whoever denies descent and rising above, or pleasure and anger, or knowledge and power, or the name “the All-Knowing” or “the All-Powerful,” or the designation “the Existing One,” seeking, as he claims, to avoid a resemblance involving composition and corporeality, faces an analogous objection regarding what he affirms to the objection he levels against others regarding what he himself denies and they affirm.

Every argument used to deny descent, rising above, pleasure, and anger can be matched by his opponent with an analogous argument denying will, hearing, sight, power, and knowledge.

Every argument he uses to deny power, knowledge, hearing, and sight can be matched by his opponent with an analogous argument denying the All-Knowing, the All-Powerful, the All-Hearing, and the All-Seeing.

And every argument he uses to deny these names can be used by his opponent to deny the Existing One and the Necessary Existent.

translated_text:
It is self-evident that there must be a beginningless being whose existence is necessary in itself and whose nonexistence is impossible. For whatever exists is either contingent and originated, or necessary and beginningless. What is contingent and originated can exist only through a necessary, beginningless being. Thus, if the arguments used to deny the established attributes entail denying the necessary, beginningless being, and denying that being entails denying existence altogether, it follows that whoever denies any established attribute through such an argument advances a position that necessarily entails denying the existence of what we plainly observe.

For example, someone may say: “Descent, rising above, and the like are attributes of bodies, for descent and rising above can only be conceived of in a composite body. Allah, glorified be He, is far above these necessary consequences, so He must also be declared free of that which entails them.” Or he may say: “These occur in time, and temporal occurrences can subsist only in a composite body.” Likewise, he may say: “Pleasure, anger, joy, love, and the like are attributes of bodies.”

He is then told: “The same applies to will, hearing, sight, knowledge, and power: they too are attributes of bodies. For just as we can conceive of nothing that descends, rises above, becomes angry, or is pleased except a body, we can conceive of nothing that hears, sees, wills, knows, or decrees except a body.”

If he says: “His hearing is not like our hearing, His sight is not like our sight, and His will is not like our will; the same applies to His knowledge and power,” he is told: “Likewise, His pleasure is not like our pleasure, His anger is not like our anger, His joy is not like our joy, and His descent and rising above are not like our descent and rising above.”

translated_text:
If he then says: “In the observable world, anger can only be conceived of as the boiling of the heart’s blood in pursuit of revenge, and descent can only be conceived of as movement from one place to another. Such movement requires vacating one space and occupying another. Thus, if He were to descend, no Lord would remain above the Throne.”

The reply is:

Nor, in the observable world, can will be conceived of except as the heart’s inclination to obtain what one needs and benefits from—things for which one depends upon others—and to ward off what harms one. Yet Allah, glorified and exalted be He, has said concerning His holy Self in His divine hadith:

“O My servants, you will never be able to benefit Me, nor will you ever be able to harm Me.”

Thus, He is far above the only kind of will conceivable in the observable world. Likewise, hearing can only be conceived of in the observable world as sound entering the ear canal, which can occur only in something with an internal cavity. Allah, glorified be He, is One and al-Samad, far above anything of that kind. Indeed, the same applies to sight and speech: in the observable world, they can only be conceived of as residing in something with an internal cavity. Allah, glorified be He, is One and al-Samad, far above that.

Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Hasan, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, and many of the early generations said: “Al-Samad is He who has no internal cavity.” Others said: “He is the Master whose mastery is perfect.” Both statements are true, for the Arabic word al-Samad encompasses both meanings. In Arabic, al-samad means “the master”; it also means al-musammad (solid), and al-musammad means al-musmat (without an internal cavity). Both usages are well established in Arabic.

translated_text:
For this reason, Yahyā ibn Abī Kathīr said: “Angels have no internal cavities, whereas human beings do.”

This also provides another proof. For if the angels—who were created from light, as established in Sahīh Muslim on the authority of ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, who reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Angels were created from light, jinn were created from fire, and Adam was created from what has been described to you”—

if, then, they are created from light, neither eat nor drink, and have no internal cavities as human beings do, yet speak, hear, see, ascend and descend, as established by authentic texts, while their attributes and actions nevertheless do not resemble human attributes and actions, then the Creator, exalted is He, differs from His creatures far more than angels differ from human beings. For both angels and human beings are created, and one creature is closer to resembling another creature than to resembling the Creator, glorified and exalted be He.

Likewise, the human soul hears, sees, speaks, descends and ascends, as established by authentic texts and clear rational evidence. Nevertheless, its attributes and actions are not like those of the body.

If, then, one may not say that the soul’s attributes and actions are like the attributes of the body—the physical frame—even though the soul is joined to it and together they constitute the human being, and if the human soul is not like the physical body, how can it be permissible to liken the Lord, blessed and exalted be He, His attributes and His actions to the body, its attributes and its actions?!

If the one who negates these attributes wishes to remain consistent with his own principle and says: “I maintain that He has no speech subsisting in Him; rather,

 فَلَا بُدَّ لَهُ أَنْ يَقُولَ بِقَوْلِ طَائِفَةٍ مِنْهُمْ فَيَقُولَ:
translated_text:
His speech is created,” he should be told: “Then the same implication applies to hearing and sight, for the Basran Mu‘tazilah affirm perception.”

If he says: “I follow the position of the Baghdadi Mu‘tazilah: I do not affirm hearing, sight, or speech subsisting in Him. Rather, I say that His speech is one of His created things, because affirming these attributes amounts to ascribing corporeality to Him and likening Him to creation. Indeed, I do not even affirm will for Him, just as the Baghdadis do not affirm it. Instead, I treat it as a negation or a relation: I say that His being willing means that He is neither overpowered nor compelled, or that it means His being a creator and commander”—he should be told: “Then the same implication applies to His being living, knowing, and powerful, for the Mu‘tazilah unanimously affirm that He is living, knowing, and powerful.” He should also be told: “You know of nothing living, knowing, and powerful except a body. Thus, if you affirm that He is living, knowing, and powerful, your position entails ascribing corporeality to Him and likening Him to creation.”

If he goes further in negating the divine attributes and says: “I do not follow the Mu‘tazilah, but rather the pure Jahmiyyah and the esotericists among the philosophers and the Qarmatians. I therefore negate the names along with the attributes, and I do not call Him living, knowing, powerful, or speaking except figuratively, in the sense of negation and relation: that is, He is neither ignorant nor powerless, and He has made others knowing and powerful”—he should be told: “Then the same implication applies to His being existent, necessarily existent in Himself, without beginning, and an agent. For it has been said that Jahm affirmed His being an agent and powerful, because, according to him, a human being is neither powerful nor an agent; thus, in his view, this involves no likening of Allah to creation.”

Once he reaches this point, he must adopt the position of one of their groups and say:

“I ascribe to Him neither existence nor nonexistence. I call Him neither existent nor nonexistent—or neither existent nor not existent. Rather, I refrain from either of these contradictories, making neither a denial nor an affirmation.”

Or he may say:

“I never describe Him in affirmative terms, but only in negative terms. Thus, I do not say that He is existent; rather, I say that He is not nonexistent.”

Or it may be said:

“Rather, He is nonexistent.”

The division is exhaustive. Either he describes Him in affirmative terms, in which case the same implications of likening Him to creation and ascribing corporeality to Him that he imposed upon others also apply to him; or he says: “I do not describe Him by affirming existence, but by denying nonexistence. Thus, I do not say that He is existent, but that He is not nonexistent.” Or he commits himself to absolute negation and says:

“Nothing exists necessarily.”

If he adopts the first position and says, “I affirm neither of the two contradictories: neither existence nor nonexistence,” he should be told:

“Suppose you say this with your tongue and believe neither alternative in your heart, choosing instead to turn away from knowing Allah, worshipping Him, and remembering Him, so that you never remember Him, worship Him, supplicate to Him, place your hope in Him, or fear Him. Your denial of Him would then be greater than that of Iblīs, who acknowledged Him. Yet your refusal to affirm either of the two contradictories does not entail that neither holds in reality, for it is impossible for neither of two contradictories to hold. Rather, in reality, anything—whatever it may be—must be either existent or nonexistent: it either is or is not. There is absolutely no middle ground between negation and affirmation. A person’s refusal to look at the sun, the moon, the stars, and the sky does not negate their existence, nor does it prevent one of the two contradictories from holding true. Rather, ‘the sun’ must necessarily be either existent or nonexistent. How, then, could your heart and tongue turning away from the remembrance of Allah negate His existence and entail that neither contradictory holds? In reality, He must be either existent or nonexistent.”

Likewise, whoever says, “I do not say that He is existent; rather, I say that He is not nonexistent,” should be told:

“Negating one of two contradictories affirms the other. You have merely changed the wording, since saying that He is not nonexistent necessarily entails that He is existent. If He is not nonexistent, either He is existent or He is neither existent nor nonexistent. This ‘third alternative’ entails that neither contradictory holds, which is self-evidently invalid. Thus, if He is not nonexistent, He must be existent.”

If he says, “Rather, I commit myself to saying that He is nonexistent,” he should be told:

“Observation and reason establish that existing things exist. It is also known that some of them come into being after not having existed. We know, for example, that we ourselves came into being after not existing, and that clouds, rain, plants, and animals come into being. These familiar things that come into being cannot be necessary existents in themselves. For whatever exists necessarily in itself cannot be nonexistent and must have existed without beginning. These things, however, were nonexistent and then came into existence. Their existence after nonexistence therefore demonstrates that both their existence and their nonexistence are possible, since both have actually occurred. Thus, it is self-evidently known that among existing things there is something that has come into being and is contingent.

We then say:

An existing thing that has come into being and is contingent must have a cause that brings it into existence, exists without beginning, and exists necessarily in itself. For something that comes into being cannot bring itself into existence, just as a person cannot create himself. This is among the most evident, self-evident truths. Even after a person has come into existence and attained strength, he cannot add a limb to his body or increase its size: he cannot make a tall person shorter or a short person taller, nor make his own head larger or smaller than it is. Likewise, his parents cannot do any of these things.

It is self-evidently known that whatever comes into being after not existing must have someone who brings it into being. This is a self-evident proposition known through the innate disposition, even to children. If someone strikes a child while he is unaware and cannot see the person, he will ask, ‘Who struck me?’ If he is told, ‘No one struck you,’ his mind will not accept that the blow occurred without someone causing it. Rather, he knows that whatever occurs must have someone who causes it. Then, if he is told, ‘So-and-so struck you,’ he cries until he strikes the person who struck him. Thus, his innate disposition included acknowledgment

“Or were they created by nothing, or are they the creators?”

The two Sahih collections relate from Jubayr ibn Mut‘im that, when he came to ransom the captives of Badr, he said: “I found the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, reciting Sūrat al-Tūr during the Maghrib prayer. This is an exhaustive division of the possibilities, which Allah presents as a rhetorical question rejecting these alternatives, to show that these premises are self-evidently known and cannot be denied. He says:

“Or were they created by nothing?”

That is, without a creator who created them? Or did they create themselves? They know that both alternatives are false. It therefore follows that they have a Creator who created them—glorified and exalted is He.

There are many ways to establish this. For example, one may say: Whatever exists either has no beginning or has come into being, and whatever has come into being must depend on something without beginning. An existent is either necessary or contingent, and whatever is contingent must depend on something necessary. There are other arguments of this kind.

In every case, it necessarily follows that among existing things there is a being that has no beginning and exists necessarily in itself, and a contingent being that came into existence after not existing. Both share in what is denoted by “existence.” Yet he can conceive of no existent in the observable world except a body. He is therefore subject to the same charge he has brought against others: likening Allah to creation and attributing corporeality to Him.

It is thus clear that anyone’s denial of any of Allah’s attributes on the basis of such a method is false
