even if revelation had not affirmed it, nor reason established it. How, then, can such an argument be used to deny what both revelation and reason establish? It therefore becomes clear that anyone who denies any of the attributes—on the grounds that affirming them entails likening Allah to creation and attributing corporeality to Him—is subject to the very charge he levels against others. The rebuttal thus applies equally to both sides. Moreover, if this consequence follows on every possible assumption, then using it to deny that which entails it is clearly invalid, since that which entails it exists and cannot possibly be denied.

For this reason, such reasoning is not found in the words of any of the early generations of this Ummah or its leading scholars. Rather, it was introduced by the Jahmiyyah and the Muʿtazilah, and many people adopted it from them. A person denies of the Lord what must indeed be denied of Him, such as imperfections from which He must be declared free: ignorance, inability, need, and the like. Declaring Him free of these is correct. Yet this person argues that they must be denied because they entail attributing corporeality to Allah and likening Him to creation. He is then challenged with what he himself affirms, and so falls into contradiction.

Through this opening, the heretical esotericists gained influence among Muslims, until they turned vast numbers away from Islam. They began saying to anyone who denied something of the Lord—such as someone who denied some or all of His attributes, or His most beautiful names—“Did you not deny this to avoid likening Allah to creation and attributing corporeality to Him?”

He replies, “Yes.”

They then say, “But this same consequence follows from what you affirm.”

He thus finds himself obliged to agree with them in denying one thing after another, until he reaches the point where he neither knows Allah in his heart, nor remembers Him with his tongue, nor worships Him, nor calls upon Him—even if he does not categorically affirm His nonexistence, but instead divests himself of faith in Him. The inconsistency of these people is already known.

And if he commits himself to negating Him altogether and denying His existence, in agreement with Pharaoh, his inconsistency is greater still. For he may be told:

“If this existing world has no Maker, then it must be eternal, without beginning, and necessarily existent in its own right—yet, as noted earlier, it is known to contain many things that come into being. Thus, existence includes both the eternal and the originated, both the necessary and the contingent. You must therefore acknowledge two existents: one eternal and necessary, the other originated and contingent. You are consequently bound by the very implications you sought to escape: likening Allah to creation and attributing corporeality to Him.

“Indeed, this follows from your own explicit position. The observable world is a body in which motions occur: the celestial sphere is a body, and likewise the sun, moon, and stars are bodies possessing attributes and undergoing motions. You denied the Lord of the worlds to avoid making the Eternal, Necessary Existent a body possessing attributes and undergoing motions. Yet you ultimately made that which is eternal, without beginning, and necessarily existent in its own right into multiple bodies that resemble others in many respects, possess attributes, and undergo motions—despite their dependence and need. For the sun, moon, and stars depend on the places in which they are situated and the locations that bear them and carry them round. Each celestial sphere also depends on something other than itself, besides the other indications of their imperfection and need.”

The point here is this: the person who refused to acknowledge that the Eternal, Necessary Existent exists and possesses attributes of perfection—lest this entail the likeness to creation and corporeality he mentioned, and who took the negation of this supposed consequence as proof for denying what he claimed entailed it—ultimately fell into the very thing he sought to escape: making the Necessary Existent a body resembling other things. Moreover, he ascribed to it attributes of imperfection from which the Lord must be declared free, while also denying the Creator, majestic is His glory. Thus, besides committing disbelief greater than that of polytheists in general—for they acknowledged the Maker despite worshipping others besides Him—he proved to be among the most ignorant of Adam’s descendants, the most unsound in intellect and reasoning, and the most inconsistent.

This is how Allah deals with those who deviate concerning His names and signs while laying claim to rational inquiry, reason, proof, and inference, like Pharaoh and his followers. Allah Most High said:

“And We certainly sent Moses with Our signs and clear authority”

“To Pharaoh, Hāmān, and Qārūn, but they said, ‘A magician, a liar.’”

“Then, when he brought them the truth from Us, they said, ‘Kill the sons of those who have believed with him and keep their women alive.’ But the plotting of the disbelievers is nothing but futile.”

“And Pharaoh said, ‘Let me kill Moses, and let him call upon his Lord. Indeed, I fear that he will change your religion or cause corruption to appear in the land.’”

“And Moses said, ‘Indeed, I seek refuge in my Lord and your Lord from every arrogant person who does not believe in the Day of Reckoning.’”

“And a believing man from Pharaoh’s household, who concealed his faith, said, ‘Would you kill a man merely for saying, “My Lord is Allah,” when he has brought you clear proofs from your Lord? If he is lying, his lie will be to his own detriment; but if he is truthful, some of what he threatens you with will befall you. Indeed, Allah does not guide anyone who is a transgressor and a liar.’”

“ O my people, sovereignty is yours today, and you hold sway

in the land. But who will protect us from Allah’s punishment if it comes upon us?’ Pharaoh said, ‘I show you only what I see, and I guide you only to the right path.’”

“And the man who believed said, ‘O my people, I fear for you a day like that of the confederates—’”

“‘Like what befell the people of Noah, Ād, Thamūd, and those after them. Allah intends no injustice for His servants.’”

“‘O my people, I fear for you the Day of Mutual Calling—’”

“‘The Day you will turn and flee, with no one to protect you from Allah. Whoever Allah leaves astray will have no guide.’”

“‘Joseph had already come to you before with clear proofs, yet you remained in doubt about what he brought you. Then, when he died, you said, “Allah will never send a messenger after him.” Thus does Allah leave astray whoever is a transgressor and a doubter.’”

“Those who dispute Allah’s signs without any authority having come to them are greatly abhorrent to Allah and to those who believe. Thus does Allah seal the heart of every arrogant tyrant.”

“And Pharaoh said, ‘O Hāmān, build me a lofty tower so that I may reach the ways—’”

“‘The ways into the heavens—and look upon the God of Moses, though I certainly think he is a liar.’ Thus Pharaoh’s evil deeds were made appealing to him, and he was barred from the path. Pharaoh’s plotting led only to ruin.”

Allah Most High also said:

“Indeed, We will surely support Our messengers and those who believe, both in the life of this world and on the Day when the witnesses stand forth—”

“The Day when the wrongdoers’ excuses will not benefit them. The curse will be upon them, and theirs will be the worst abode.”

“We certainly gave Moses guidance and caused the Children of Israel to inherit the Scripture—”

“As guidance and a reminder for people of understanding.”

“So be patient; Allah’s promise is certainly true. Ask forgiveness for your sin, and glorify your Lord with praise in the evening and the morning.”

“Indeed, those who dispute Allah’s signs without any authority having come to them have nothing in their hearts but an ambition for greatness which they will never attain. So seek refuge in Allah. Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing.”

 فِيهِ إجْمَالٌ وَاشْتِبَاهٌ كَمَا سَنُبَيِّنُهُ إنْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى؛ فَإِنَّ هَؤُلَاءِ الْنُّفَاةِ لَا يُرِيدُونَ بِالْجِسْمِ الَّذِي نَفَوْهُ مَا هُوَ الْمُرَادُ بِالْجِسْمِ فِي اللُّغَةِ فَإِنَّ الْمَوْصُوفَ بِالصِّفَاتِ لَا يَجِبُ أَنْ يَكُونَ هُوَ الْجِسْمَ الَّذِي فِي اللُّغَةِ كَمَا نَقَلَهُ أَهْلُ اللُّغَةِ بِاتِّفَاقِ الْعُقَلَاءِ وَسَنَأْتِي بِذَلِكَ؛ وَإِنَّمَا يُرِيدُونَ بِالْجِسْمِ مَا اعْتَقَدُوهُ أَنَّهُ مُرَكَّبٌ مِنْ أَجْزَاءٍ وَاعْتَقَدُوا أَنَّ كُلَّ مَا تَقُومُ بِهِ الصِّفَاتُ فَهُوَ مُرَكَّبٌ مِنْ أَجْزَاءٍ وَهَذَا الِاعْتِقَادُ بَاطِلٌ. بَلْ الرَّبُّ مَوْصُوفٌ بِالصِّفَاتِ وَلَيْسَ جِسْمًا مُرَكَّبًا لَا مِنْ الْجَوَاهِرِ الْمُفْرَدَةِ وَلَا مِنْ الْمَادَّةِ وَالصُّورَةِ كَمَا يَدَّعُونَ كَمَا سَنُبَيِّنُهُ إنْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى؛ فَلَا يَلْزَمُ مِنْ ثُبُوتِ الصِّفَاتِ لُزُومُ مَا ادَّعَوْهُ مِنْ الْمُحَالِ بَلْ غَلِطُوا فِي هَذَا التَّلَازُمِ. وَأَمَّا مَا هُوَ لَازِمٌ لَا رَيْبَ فِيهِ؛ فَذَاكَ يَجِبُ إثْبَاتُهُ لَا يَجُوزُ نَفْيُهُ عَنْ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى.
 فَكَانَ غَلَطُهُمْ بِاسْتِعْمَالِ لَفْظٍ مُجْمَلٍ وَإِحْدَى الْمُقَدِّمَتَيْنِ بَاطِلَةٌ:
 إمَّا الْأُولَى وَإِمَّا الثَّانِيَةُ كَمَا سَيَأْتِي إنْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى. وَهَذِهِ قَوَاعِدُ مُخْتَصَرَةٌ جَامِعَةٌ وَهِيَ مَبْسُوطَةٌ فِي مَوَاضِعَ أُخْرَى.
translated_text:
The reason for this is that the terms “body” and “likening Allah to creation” are ambiguous and liable to cause confusion, as we shall explain, if Allah Most High wills. These negationists do not mean by the “body” they deny what the word means in ordinary language. As all rational people agree, something possessing attributes need not be a body in the linguistic sense recorded by the lexicographers. We shall explain this later. Rather, by “body” they mean something they believe to be composed of parts, and they believe that anything in which attributes subsist is composed of parts. This belief is false. Rather, the Lord possesses attributes without being a body composed of indivisible substances or of matter and form, as they claim. We shall explain this, if Allah Most High wills. Thus, the existence of the attributes does not entail the impossibility they allege; rather, they have erred in asserting this necessary connection. Whatever is unquestionably entailed, however, must be affirmed and may not be denied of Allah Most High.

Their error therefore arose from using an ambiguous expression, while one of the two premises is false—either the first or the second—as will be explained, if Allah Most High wills. These are concise, comprehensive principles, which are discussed at length elsewhere.

فَصْلٌ:
إذَا تَبَيَّنَ هَذَا فَقَوْلُ السَّائِلِ:
 كَيْفَ يَنْزِلُ؟
 بِمَنْزِلَةِ قَوْلِهِ:
 كَيْفَ اسْتَوَى؟
 وَقَوْلُهُ:
 كَيْفَ يَسْمَعُ؟ وَكَيْفَ يُبْصِرُ؟
 وَكَيْفَ:
 يَعْلَمُ وَيُقَدِّرُ؟ وَكَيْفَ يَخْلُقُ وَيَرْزُقُ؟
 وَقَدْ تَقَدَّمَ الْجَوَابُ عَنْ مِثْلِ هَذَا السُّؤَالِ مِنْ أَئِمَّةِ الْإِسْلَامِ مِثْلِ:
 مَالِكِ بْنِ أَنَسٍ وَشَيْخِهِ رَبِيعَةَ بْنِ أَبِي عَبْدِ الرَّحْمَنِ؛
 فَإِنَّهُ قَدْ رُوِيَ مِنْ غَيْرِ وَجْهٍ أَنَّ سَائِلًا سَأَلَ مَالِكًا عَنْ قَوْلِهِ:
 
{الرَّحْمَنُ عَلَى الْعَرْشِ اسْتَوَى}
 كَيْفَ اسْتَوَى؟
 فَأَطْرَقَ مَالِكٌ حَتَّى عَلَاهُ الرُّحَضَاءُ ثُمَّ قَالَ:
 الِاسْتِوَاءُ مَعْلُومٌ وَالْكَيْفُ مَجْهُولٌ وَالْإِيمَانُ بِهِ وَاجِبٌ وَالسُّؤَالُ عَنْهُ بِدْعَةٌ وَمَا أُرَاك إلَّا رَجُلُ سَوْءٍ ثُمَّ أَمَرَ بِهِ فَأُخْرِجَ.
 وَمِثْلُ هَذَا الْجَوَابِ ثَابِتٌ عَنْ رَبِيعَةَ شَيْخِ مَالِكٍ وَقَدْ رُوِيَ هَذَا الْجَوَابُ عَنْ أُمِّ سَلَمَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهَا مَوْقُوفًا وَمَرْفُوعًا وَلَكِنْ لَيْسَ إسْنَادُهُ مِمَّا يُعْتَمَدُ عَلَيْهِ وَهَكَذَا سَائِرُ الْأَئِمَّةِ قَوْلُهُمْ يُوَافِقُ قَوْلَ مَالِكٍ:
 فِي أَنَّا لَا نَعْلَمُ كَيْفِيَّةَ اسْتِوَائِهِ كَمَا لَا نَعْلَمُ كَيْفِيَّةَ ذَاتِهِ وَلَكِنْ نَعْلَمُ الْمَعْنَى الَّذِي دَلَّ عَلَيْهِ الْخِطَابُ فَنَعْلَمُ مَعْنَى الِاسْتِوَاءِ وَلَا نَعْلَمُ كَيْفِيَّتَهُ وَكَذَلِكَ نَعْلَمُ مَعْنَى النُّزُولِ وَلَا نَعْلَمُ كَيْفِيَّتَهُ وَنَعْلَمُ مَعْنَى السَّمْعِ وَالْبَصَرِ وَالْعِلْمِ وَالْقُدْرَةِ وَلَا نَعْلَمُ كَيْفِيَّةَ ذَلِكَ وَنَعْلَمُ مَعْنَى الرَّحْمَةِ وَالْغَضَبِ وَالرِّضَا وَالْفَرَحِ وَالضَّحِكِ وَلَا نَعْلَمُ كَيْفِيَّةَ ذَلِكَ.
translated_text:
Section

With this established, the questioner’s words, “How does He descend?” are like asking, “How did He rise over the Throne?” or “How does He hear? How does He see? How does He know and decree? How does He create and provide?”

The answer given by the imams of Islam to such questions has already been mentioned, including that of Mālik ibn Anas and his teacher, Rabī‘ah ibn Abī ‘Abd al-Rahmān. It has been related through several routes that someone asked Mālik about His saying:

“The Most Merciful rose over the Throne.”

“How did He rise over it?” Mālik lowered his head until he was covered in perspiration, then said: “Rising over the Throne is known; its manner is unknown. Belief in it is obligatory, and asking about it is an innovation. I consider you nothing but an evil man.” He then ordered that the man be removed.

A similar answer is reliably established from Rabī‘ah, Mālik’s teacher. This answer has also been narrated from Umm Salamah, may Allah be pleased with her, both as her own statement and as a statement traced back to the Prophet, but its chain of transmission is not reliable.

The statements of all the other imams likewise agree with Mālik’s: we do not know the manner of His rising over the Throne, just as we do not know the manner of His essence. We do, however, know the meaning conveyed by the revealed words. Thus, we know the meaning of rising over the Throne, but not its manner. Likewise, we know the meaning of descent, but not its manner. We know the meanings of hearing, sight, knowledge, and power, but not their manner. We know the meanings of mercy, anger, pleasure, joy, and laughter, but not their manner.

وَأَمَّا سُؤَالُ السَّائِلِ:
 هَلْ يَخْلُو مِنْهُ الْعَرْشُ أَمْ لَا يَخْلُو مِنْهُ؟ - وَإِمْسَاكُ الْمُجِيبِ عَنْ هَذَا لِعَدَمِ عِلْمِهِ بِمَا يُجِيبُ بِهِ فَإِنَّهُ إمْسَاكٌ عَنْ الْجَوَابِ بِمَا لَمْ يَعْلَمْ حَقِيقَتَهُ - وَسُؤَالُ السَّائِلِ لَهُ عَنْ هَذَا إنْ كَانَ نَفْيًا لِمَا أَثْبَتَهُ الرَّسُولُ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ فَخَطَأٌ مِنْهُ وَإِنْ كَانَ اسْتِرْشَادًا فَحَسَنٌ وَإِنْ كَانَ تَجْهِيلًا لِلْمَسْئُولِ؛ فَهَذَا فِيهِ تَفْصِيلٌ. فَإِنَّ الْمُثْبِتَ الَّذِي لَمْ يُثْبِتْ إلَّا مَا أَثْبَتَهُ الرَّسُولُ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَنَفَى عِلْمَهُ بِالْكَيْفِيَّةِ؛ فَقَوْلُهُ سَدِيدٌ لَا يُرَدُّ عَلَيْهِ سُؤَالُهُ وَالْمُعْتَرِضُ الَّذِي يَعْتَرِضُ عَلَيْهِ بِهَذَا السُّؤَالِ؛ اعْتِرَاضُهُ بَاطِلٌ فَإِنَّ ذَلِكَ لَا يَقْدَحُ فِي جَوَابِ الْمُجِيبِ.
وَقَوْلُ الْمَسْئُولِ:
 هَذَا قَوْلٌ مُبْتَدَعٌ وَرَأْيٌ مُخْتَرَعٌ - حَيْدَةٌ مِنْهُ عَنْ الْجَوَابِ - يَدُلُّ عَلَى جَهْلِهِ بِالْجَوَابِ السَّدِيدِ؛ وَلَكِنْ لَا يَدُلُّ هَذَا عَلَى أَنَّ نَفْيَ الْمُعْتَرِضِ لِمَا أَخْبَرَ بِهِ الرَّسُولُ حَقٌّ وَلَا عَلَى أَنَّ تَأْوِيلَهُ بِنُزُولِ أَمْرِهِ وَرَحْمَتِهِ تَأْوِيلٌ صَحِيحٌ.
 وَمِمَّا يُبَيِّنُ ذَلِكَ:
 أَنَّ هَذَا الْمُعْتَرِضَ إمَّا أَنْ يُقِرَّ بِأَنَّ اللَّهَ فَوْقَ الْعَرْشِ وَإِمَّا أَنْ لَا يَكُونَ مُقِرًّا بِذَلِكَ. فَإِنْ لَمْ يَكُنْ مُقِرًّا بِذَلِكَ؛
 كَانَ قَوْلُهُ:
 هَلْ يَخْلُو الْعَرْشُ مِنْهُ أَمْ لَا يَخْلُو؟ كَلَامًا بَاطِلًا؛ لِأَنَّ هَذَا التَّقْسِيمَ فَرْعُ ثُبُوتِ كَوْنِهِ عَلَى الْعَرْشِ.
 وَإِنْ قَالَ الْمُعْتَرِضُ:
 أَنَا ذَكَرْت هَذَا التَّقْسِيمَ لِأَنْفِيَ نُزُولَهُ وَأَنْفِيَ الْعُلُوَّ -
 لِأَنَّهُ إنْ قَالَ:
 يَخْلُو مِنْهُ الْعَرْشُ لَزِمَ أَنْ يَخْلُوَ مِنْ اسْتِوَائِهِ عَلَى الْعَرْشِ وَعُلُوِّهِ عَلَيْهِ وَأَنْ لَا يَكُونَ وَقْتَ النُّزُولِ هُوَ الْعَلِيَّ الْأَعْلَى بَلْ يَكُونُ فِي جَوْفِ الْعَالَمِ وَالْعَالَمُ مُحِيطٌ بِهِ.
 وَإِنْ قَالَ:
 إنَّ الْعَرْشَ لَا يَخْلُو مِنْهُ قِيلَ لَهُ: فَإِذَا لَمْ يَخْلُ الْعَرْشُ مِنْهُ لَمْ يَكُنْ قَدْ نَزَلَ فَإِنَّ نُزُولَهُ بِدُونِ خُلُوِّ الْعَرْشِ مِنْهُ لَا يُعْقَلُ -
 فَيُقَالُ لِهَذَا الْمُعْتَرِضِ:
translated_text:
As for the questioner’s question, “Is the Throne left without Him, or not?”: if the respondent refrains from answering because he does not know what answer to give, he is refraining from answering about something whose reality he does not know. If the questioner asks this to deny what the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, affirmed, he is mistaken. If he seeks guidance, that is commendable. If he seeks to expose the respondent’s ignorance, then a distinction must be made.

Someone who affirms only what the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, affirmed, while disclaiming knowledge of its manner, has spoken soundly; this question cannot refute him. The objection of anyone who challenges him with this question is invalid, for it does not undermine the respondent’s answer.

The respondent’s statement, “This is an innovated statement and a newly devised opinion”—an evasion of the question—indicates that he does not know the sound answer. Yet this does not establish that the objector is right to deny what the Messenger conveyed, nor that his interpretation of the descent as the descent of Allah’s command and mercy is correct.

This is further clarified by the following: either this objector acknowledges that Allah is above the Throne, or he does not. If he does not acknowledge this, then his question, “Is the Throne left without Him, or not?” is invalid, because this division into alternatives presupposes that He is over the Throne.

If the objector says:

“I introduced this division into alternatives to deny His descent and His being above. For if he says, ‘The Throne is left without Him,’ it follows that He would no longer be rising over the Throne or above it, and that, at the time of descent, He would not be the Most High, the Highest. Rather, He would be within the world, with the world surrounding Him. If he says, ‘The Throne is not left without Him,’ he is told: ‘If the Throne is not left without Him, then He has not descended, for His descending without the Throne being left without Him is inconceivable.’”

Then this objector is told:

original_text:
هَذَا الِاعْتِرَاضُ بَاطِلٌ لَا يَنْفَعُك لِأَنَّ الْخَالِقَ سُبْحَانَهُ وَتَعَالَى مَوْجُودٌ بِالضَّرُورَةِ وَالشَّرْعِ وَالْعَقْلِ وَالِاتِّفَاقِ. فَهُوَ إمَّا أَنْ يَكُونَ مُبَايِنًا لِلْعَالَمِ فَوْقَهُ وَإِمَّا أَنْ يَكُونَ مُدَاخِلًا لِلْعَالَمِ محايثا وَإِمَّا أَنْ يَكُونَ لَا هَذَا وَلَا هَذَا.
 فَإِنْ قُلْت:
 إنَّهُ محايث لِلْعَالَمِ بَطَلَ قَوْلُك فَإِنَّك إذَا جَوَّزْت نُزُولَهُ وَهُوَ بِذَاتِهِ فِي كُلِّ مَكَانٍ؛
 لَمْ يَمْتَنِعْ عِنْدَك خُلُوُّ مَا فَوْقَ الْعَرْشِ مِنْهُ بَلْ هُوَ دَائِمًا خَالٍ مِنْهُ لِأَنَّهُ هُنَاكَ لَيْسَ عِنْدَك شَيْءٌ ثُمَّ يُقَالُ لَك:
 وَهَلْ يُعْقَلُ مَعَ هَذَا أَنْ يَكُونَ فِي كُلِّ مَكَانٍ وَأَنَّهُ مَعَ هَذَا يَنْزِلُ إلَى السَّمَاءِ الدُّنْيَا؟
 فَإِنْ قُلْت:
 نَعَمْ؛
 قِيلَ لَك:
 فَإِذَا نَزَلَ هَلْ يَخْلُو مِنْهُ بَعْضُ الْأَمْكِنَةِ أَوْ لَا يَخْلُو؟
 فَإِنْ قُلْت:
 يَخْلُو مِنْهُ بَعْضُ الْأَمْكِنَةِ؛ كَانَ هَذَا نَظِيرَ خُلُوِّ الْعَرْشِ مِنْهُ.
 فَإِنْ قُلْت:
 لَا يَخْلُو مِنْهُ مَكَانٌ؛ كَانَ هَذَا نَظِيرَ كَوْنِ الْعَرْشِ لَا يَخْلُو مِنْهُ. فَإِنْ جَوَّزْت هَذَا؛ كَانَ لِخَصْمِك أَنْ يُجَوِّزَ هَذَا.
 فَقَدْ لَزِمَك عَلَى قَوْلِك مَا يَلْزَمُ مُنَازِعَك بَلْ قَوْلُك أَبْعَدُ عَنْ الْمَعْقُولِ لِأَنَّ نُزُولَ مَنْ هُوَ فَوْقَ الْعَالَمِ أَقْرَبُ إلَى الْمَعْقُولِ مِنْ نُزُولِ مَنْ هُوَ حَالٌّ فِي جَمِيعِ الْعَالَمِ فَإِنَّ نُزُولَ هَذَا لَا يُعْقَلُ بِحَالِ وَمَا فَرَرْت مِنْهُ مِنْ الْحُلُولِ وَقَعْت فِي نَظِيرِهِ بَلْ مُنَازِعُك الَّذِي يُجَوِّزُ أَنْ يَكُونَ فَوْقَ الْعَالَمِ وَهُوَ أَعْظَمُ عِنْدَهُ مِنْ الْعَالَمِ وَيَنْزِلُ إلَى الْعَالَمِ أَشَدُّ تَعْظِيمًا لِلَّهِ مِنْك وَيُقَالُ لَهُ:
 هَلْ يُعْقَلُ مَوْجُودَانِ قَائِمَانِ بِأَنْفُسِهِمَا أَحَدُهُمَا محايث لِلْآخَرِ؟
 فَإِنْ قَالَ:
 لَا؛ بَطَلَ قَوْلُهُ.
 وَإِنْ قَالَ:
 نَعَمْ؛
 قِيلَ لَهُ:
 فَلْيُعْقَلْ أَنَّهُ فَوْقَ الْعَرْشِ وَأَنَّهُ يَنْزِلُ إلَى السَّمَاءِ الدُّنْيَا وَلَا يَخْلُو مِنْهُ الْعَرْشُ فَإِنَّ هَذَا أَقْرَبُ إلَى الْعَقْلِ مِمَّا إذَا قُلْت: إنَّهُ حَالٌّ فِي الْعَالَمِ.
translated_text:
This objection is invalid and does not help your case, for the existence of the Creator—glorified and exalted be He—is established by self-evident knowledge, revelation, reason, and common agreement. Either He is separate from the world and above it, or He is within the world, occupying the same space as it, or He is neither.

If you say that He occupies the same space as the world, your argument fails. For if you allow that He descends while He Himself is in every place, then, in your view, it would not be impossible for what is above the Throne to be without Him. Indeed, it is always without Him, since, according to you, nothing exists there. You are then asked: “Is it conceivable, on this account, that He is in every place and nevertheless descends to the lowest heaven?”

If you say, “Yes,” you are asked: “When He descends, are some places left without Him, or not?”

If you say, “Some places are left without Him,” this is analogous to the Throne being left without Him. If you say, “No place is left without Him,” this is analogous to the Throne not being left without Him. If you allow that no place is left without Him, your opponent may allow that the Throne is not left without Him.

Thus, your own position entails the very consequence entailed by your opponent’s. Indeed, your position is further removed from what is rationally conceivable, for the descent of One who is above the world is more readily conceivable than the descent of one who indwells the entire world. The latter’s descent is wholly inconceivable. You have fallen into the equivalent of the very indwelling you sought to avoid. Indeed, your opponent, who allows that He is above the world, that He is greater than the world, and that He descends to the world, shows greater reverence for Allah than you do.

He is also asked: “Is it conceivable that there are two independently existing entities, one occupying the same space as the other?”

If he says, “No,” his position is invalidated. If he says, “Yes,” he is told: “Then let it be conceivable that He is above the Throne and descends to the lowest heaven without the Throne being left without Him, for this is more rationally conceivable than your saying that He indwells the world.”

translated_text:
If, however, you say that He is neither separate from the world nor within it, you are asked: “Can one conceive of two independently existing entities, neither of which is separate from the other nor occupies the same space as it?” Most rational people maintain that the invalidity of this is self-evident.

If he says, “Yes, that is conceivable,” he is told: If an independently existing entity can exist without being either separate from the world or occupying the same space as it, then it is more rationally conceivable that One who is separate from the world should descend to it without what is above the world being left without Him. For if you affirm the existence only of what you can conceive as having a reality outside the mind, you cannot conceive, in external reality, of two independently existing entities, neither of which is within the other nor occupies the same space as it. If, however, you affirm something whose reality outside the mind you cannot conceive, then the existence of two entities, one separate from the other, is more rationally conceivable. And His descending without what is above the Throne being left without Him is more rationally conceivable than His being neither above the world nor within it. Thus, if you judge by analogy, analogy counts against you, not for you; and if you do not judge by it, you cannot validly use it to argue against your opponent.

As for the questioner’s statement, “This does not answer my question; rather, it evades the answer,” he is told: There are “two kinds” of response: a response to an objector who denies His descent and His being above creation, and a response to someone who affirms His descent and His being above creation. You did not ask as someone seeking guidance, but as an objector intent on denial.

It has already been made clear to you that this objection is invalid and does not help your case. Whether it is said that the Throne is left without Him or that it is not left without Him, neither statement lends validity to your claim that He is neither within the world nor outside it, or to your claim that He Himself is in every place. these two claims are false, the “third” necessarily follows: that He, glorified and exalted, is above His heavens, over His Throne, separate from His creation. If that is so, the objector’s claim is invalid.

This applies if the objector does not acknowledge that He is above the Throne. One of the leading proponents of the denial of Allah’s being above creation was asked about His descent and replied, “His command descends.” The questioner said to him, “Then who descends? In your view, there is nothing above the world, so from whom does the command descend? From sheer nonexistence?” He was left speechless.

If, however, the objector affirms Allah’s being above creation and says that Allah is above the Throne, but does not acknowledge His descent, instead maintaining that an angel descends, or that His command descends—meaning the thing commanded, which is one of His created things—then he makes the descent a newly originated effect that Allah brings into being in heaven. Similar claims are made concerning His rising over the Throne.

He is then told: This same division of possibilities applies to you. If you say, “When He descends, the Throne is left without Him,” the first unacceptable consequence follows. If you say, “The Throne is not left without Him,” you have affirmed a descent without the Throne being left without Him, and this is inconceivable on your own principles.

If he says, “I affirm this only of some of His created things,” he is told: Whatever you affirm while denying a voluntary act subsisting in Him Himself cannot be understood from this statement; it cannot possibly be what is intended by it. Moreover, you have distorted words from their proper meanings. You have thus combined two things: affirming something that cannot be understood from the words of the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and distorting the words of the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

If you say, “The one who descends is an angel,” the reply is: This is false for several reasons:

(The second point is that he said in it:

“Who asks Me, that I may give to him? Who calls upon Me, that I may answer him? Who seeks My forgiveness, that I may forgive him?”

These are not words that an angel may utter on Allah’s behalf. Rather, what an angel says is illustrated by the authentic report from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“When Allah loves a servant, He calls Gabriel: ‘I love so-and-so, so love him.’ Gabriel then loves him and calls out in heaven: ‘Allah loves so-and-so, so love him.’ The inhabitants of heaven then love him, and acceptance is granted to him on earth.”

Something similar was mentioned concerning hatred. Thus, when an angel makes a proclamation on Allah’s behalf, he does not speak in the first person. Rather, he says, “Allah has commanded such-and-such,” or, “He has said such-and-such.”

Likewise, when a ruler commands a herald to make a proclamation, the herald says, “O people! The ruler has commanded such-and-such, forbidden such-and-such, and decreed this.” He does not say, “I have commanded such-and-such and forbidden such-and-such.” Indeed, were he to say that, he would promptly be punished.

This is one of the Jahmiyyah’s longstanding interpretations. They interpreted Allah’s speaking to Moses, peace be upon him, to mean that He commanded an angel to speak to him. The people of the Sunnah replied to them: Had an angel spoken to him, he would not have said:

“Indeed, I am Allah. There is no deity except Me, so worship Me.”

Rather, he would have spoken as the Messiah, peace be upon him, did:

“I told them only what You commanded me: ‘Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord.’”

The angels are Allah’s messengers to the prophets. They speak as Gabriel, peace be upon him, used to speak

to Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“We descend only by the command of your Lord. To Him belongs whatever is before us, whatever is behind us, and whatever lies between.”

He would say, “Allah commands you to do such-and-such, and says such-and-such.” No angel can say:

“Indeed, I am Allah. There is no deity except Me, so worship Me.”

Nor can he say:

“Who calls upon Me, that I may answer him? Who asks Me, that I may give to him? Who seeks My forgiveness, that I may forgive him?”

Nor can he say, “No one but Me asks about My servants,” as reported by al-Nasā’ī, Ibn Mājah, and others. Both al-Nasā’ī and Ibn Mājah transmit it with an authentic chain, stating that He says:

“I do not ask anyone else about My servants.”

This also refutes the argument advanced by someone who cited a version transmitted by al-Nasā’ī through one of the hadith’s chains, stating that He commands a herald to make a proclamation. If this is authentically established from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, then the Lord says those words and commands a herald to proclaim accordingly; it does not mean that the herald says, “Who calls upon Me, that I may answer him?” Whoever reports from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, that the herald says this, we know that he is lying about the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Besides contradicting the widely disseminated, mass-transmitted wording that the Muslim community has passed down from generation to generation, this is rationally untenable. It is therefore known to be one of the falsehoods fabricated by certain proponents of religious innovation—just as some of them narrated it as yunzilu (“He causes to descend”), with an initial u-vowel, and just as some of them recited, “And Allah spoke directly to Moses,” and other such distortions of both wording and meaning.

If someone interprets this as the descent of His mercy, or something else, he is told: The mercy you affirm must be either a self-subsisting entity or an attribute subsisting in something else.

If it is a self-subsisting entity that has descended to the lowest heaven, it cannot say, “Who calls upon Me, that I may answer him?”—just as an angel cannot say this. If it is an attribute, it does not subsist independently; rather, it must subsist in something. Moreover, neither the attribute nor that in which it subsists can speak these words. Furthermore, if mercy descends to the lowest heaven but does not descend to us, what benefit do we derive from that?

If he says:

“Rather, mercy is what He sends down at that hour upon the hearts of those who stand in prayer at night: the sweetness of intimate prayer and worship, the delight of supplication and knowledge, the increase in knowledge of Allah, faith in Him and remembrance of Him that arises in their hearts, and His manifestation to the hearts of His devoted servants. This is something familiar to those who stand in prayer at night.”

He is told: That these things arise in their hearts is true. However, this descends to earth, to the hearts of His servants; it does not descend to the lowest heaven, nor does it ascend after descending. What is found in their hearts remains after dawn. Yet this light, blessing and mercy within their hearts are effects of what He has described concerning Himself: that He Himself descends—glorified and exalted is He.

Likewise, He has described Himself as “descending on the afternoon of the Day of ‘Arafah” in several authentic hadiths. Among them is the report in Sahīh Muslim from ‘Ā’ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

{هَلْ يَنْظُرُونَ إلَّا أَنْ تَأْتِيَهُمُ الْمَلَائِكَةُ أَوْ يَأْتِيَ رَبُّكَ أَوْ يَأْتِيَ بَعْضُ آيَاتِ رَبِّكَ}
 . وَالْأَحَادِيثُ الْمُتَوَاتِرَةُ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ فِي إتْيَانِ الرَّبِّ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ كَثِيرَةٌ وَكَذَلِكَ إتْيَانُهُ لِأَهْلِ الْجَنَّةِ يَوْمَ الْجُمُعَةِ وَهَذَا مِمَّا احْتَجَّ بِهِ السَّلَفُ عَلَى مَنْ يُنْكِرُ الْحَدِيثَ فَبَيَّنُوا لَهُ أَنَّ الْقُرْآنَ يُصَدِّقُ مَعْنَى هَذَا الْحَدِيثِ كَمَا احْتَجَّ بِهِ إسْحَاقُ
translated_text:
, exposed to the sun, from every distant pass.’”

Umm Salamah, may Allah be pleased with her, reported that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah descends to the lowest heaven and boasts of the people of ‘Arafah before the angels, saying, ‘Look at My servants: they have come to Me dishevelled and dusty.’”

Thus, He is described as drawing near to the lowest heaven on the afternoon of ‘Arafah and boasting of the pilgrims before the angels, saying, “Look at My servants: they have come to Me dishevelled and dusty. What do these people seek?” It is well known that faith, mercy, light and blessing descend upon the pilgrims’ hearts on the afternoon of ‘Arafah to an extent beyond expression. Yet what is in their hearts is not what draws near to the lowest heaven and boasts of the pilgrims before the angels.

The Jahmiyyah and others like them who deny the divine attributes affirm only something created without a Creator, an effect without a cause, and something done without a doer. This is well known from their fundamental principles, and this is one of the implications of the Jahmiyyah’s doctrines.

He may also be told: His description of Himself as descending is like His descriptions in the Quran: that He

“created the heavens and the earth in six days, then rose over the Throne”;

that He turned to the heaven while it was smoke; that He called to Moses and spoke privately with him in the blessed spot, from the tree; and that He comes, as He says:

“And your Lord comes, with the angels, rank upon rank.”

He also says:

“Are they waiting for anything but for the angels to come to them, or for your Lord to come, or for some of your Lord’s signs to come?”

There are many mass-transmitted hadiths from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, concerning the Lord’s coming on the Day of Resurrection, and likewise His coming to the people of Paradise on Friday. This is among the evidence the early generations cited against those who denied the hadith: they explained that the Quran confirms the meaning of this hadith, just as it was cited by Ishāq

translated_text:
ibn Rāhawayh against some of the Jahmiyyah in the presence of the emir ‘Abd Allāh ibn Tāhir, the governor of Khurāsān.

Abū ‘Abd Allāh al-Ribātī said:

“One day I attended the gathering of the emir ‘Abd Allāh ibn Tāhir. Ishāq ibn Rāhawayh was also present and was asked whether the hadith concerning the descent was authentic. He replied, ‘Yes.’ One of ‘Abd Allāh’s commanders asked him, ‘Abū Ya‘qūb, do you maintain that Allah descends every night?’ He replied, ‘Yes.’ The man asked, ‘How does He descend?’ Ishāq said, ‘Affirm that He is above, and then I will describe His descent to you.’ The man replied, ‘I affirm that He is above.’ Ishāq then said to him, ‘Allah Most High says: “And your Lord comes, with the angels, rank upon rank.”’

“The emir ‘Abd Allāh ibn Tāhir said, ‘Abū Ya‘qūb, that is on the Day of Resurrection.’ Ishāq replied, ‘May Allah honour the emir! Who can prevent the One who comes on the Day of Resurrection from coming today?’”

Then there is the further question: when He descends, is the Throne left without Him or not? “This is a separate issue.” Those who affirm the divine attributes have discussed it. Some said that the Throne is not left without Him. This position has been transmitted from Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal in his letter to Musaddad, and from Ishāq ibn Rāhawayh, Hammād ibn Zayd, ‘Uthmān ibn Sa‘īd al-Dārimī and others.

Others rejected this and challenged the authenticity of the letter, saying, “The person who transmitted it from Ahmad ibn Hanbal is unknown and unrecognized.” The first position, however, is well known among such imams as Hammād ibn Zayd and Ishāq ibn Rāhawayh

and others. Al-Khallāl said in Kitāb al-Sunnah (The Book of the Sunnah):

Ja‘far ibn Muhammad al-Firyābī narrated to us: Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Muqaddamī narrated to us: Sulaymān ibn Harb narrated to us, saying:

Bishr ibn al-Sarī asked Hammād ibn Zayd, “Abū Ismā‘īl, concerning the reported hadith, ‘Our Lord descends to the lowest heaven’—does He move from one place to another?” Hammād ibn Zayd remained silent, then said, “He is in His place and draws near to His creation however He wills.”

Ibn Battah also transmitted it in his book al-Ibānah (The Elucidation), saying:

Abū al-Qāsim Hafs ibn ‘Umar al-Ardabīlī narrated to me: Abū Hātim al-Rāzī narrated to us: Sulaymān ibn Harb narrated to us, saying:

Ibn Battah also said:

I went in to see ‘Abd Allāh ibn Tāhir, who asked, “What are these hadiths that you narrate?”

I replied, “Which ones, may Allah set the emir’s affairs aright?”

I replied, “Yes. They were transmitted by the trustworthy narrators who transmit hadiths concerning legal rulings.”

He asked, “Does He descend and leave His Throne?”

I replied, “He is able to descend without the Throne being left without Him.”

He said, “Yes.”

I said, “Then why do you raise this question?”

translated_text:
His being above His Throne. ‘Abd Allāh ibn Tāhir—one of the finest men to govern Khurāsān—knew that Allah is above the Throne, but found His descent difficult to understand because he imagined that it required the Throne to be left without Him. Imam Ishāq affirmed his understanding that Allah is above the Throne and asked him, “Can He descend without the Throne being left without Him?”

The emir replied, “Yes.” Ishāq then asked him, “Why, then, do you raise this question?”

His point was that, if Allah is able to do this, His descent does not necessarily leave the Throne without Him. It is therefore impermissible to object to His descent on the grounds that it necessarily leaves the Throne without Him. This objection was less serious than that of someone who says, “There is nothing above the Throne,” thereby denying both His being above it and His descent.

A similar account was narrated by Abū Bakr al-Athram in al-Sunnah (The Sunnah). He said:

Ibrāhīm ibn al-Hārith—meaning al-‘Abbādī—narrated to us: Al-Layth ibn Yahyā narrated to me, saying: I heard Ibrāhīm ibn al-Ash‘ath say: I heard al-Fudayl ibn ‘Iyād say, “If a Jahmī says, ‘I disbelieve in a Lord who moves from His place,’ say, ‘I believe in a Lord who does whatever He wills.’”

Al-Fudayl ibn ‘Iyād, may Allah have mercy on him, intended to oppose the Jahmī who says that no acts performed by choice subsist in Allah, so that no approach, coming, descent, rising, or any other acts performed by choice and subsisting in Him can be conceived of Him.

Al-Fudayl therefore said, “If a Jahmī says to you, ‘I disbelieve in a Lord who moves from His place,’ say, ‘I believe in a Lord who does whatever He wills.’” He thus instructed him to believe in the Lord who performs whatever acts He wills that subsist in His own Being. He did not mean the things He brings into being that are separate from Him. Similar statements are reported from al-Awzā‘ī and others among the early generations: concerning the hadith of descent, they said, “Allah does whatever He wills.”

Ahmad ibn al-Husayn: Ahmad ibn ‘Alī al-Abbār narrated to us, saying: I heard Yahyā ibn Ma‘īn say, “If you hear a Jahmī say, ‘I disbelieve in a Lord who descends,’ say, ‘I believe in a Lord who does whatever He wills.’”

For some who revere these authorities but deny that acts performed by choice subsist in Him—such as al-Qādī Abū Bakr and his followers, Ibn ‘Aqīl, al-Qādī ‘Iyād, and others—construe their words, “He does whatever He wills,” as meaning that He brings into being something separate from Himself, without any act whatsoever subsisting in Him.

This interpretation follows necessarily from two principles they hold:

(The first is that, in their view, the act is identical to what it produces, and creation is identical to the created thing. Thus, they interpret His transitive acts, as in His saying, “He created the heavens and the earth,” and similar statements, to mean that these things came into existence through His power, without any act proceeding from Him and subsisting in His own Being. Rather, His state before creating and after creating is the same. In their view, nothing new has arisen except a relation and a connection, which is something non-existent, not existent.

They say the same concerning His hearing His servants’ voices and seeing their deeds, His having spoken to Moses and others, His having sent down the Quran or abrogated whatever He abrogated of it, and other such matters. In their view, nothing new has arisen except a mere “connection” and “relation” between the Creator and the created, which is something non-existent, not existent.

They likewise say this concerning His rising over the Throne, if they affirm that He is above the Throne. This is the position of Ibn ‘Aqīl and others, and it was the earlier of al-Qādī Abū Ya‘lā’s two positions. Ibn ‘Aqīl calls this “connection” states; perhaps he likens it to the “states” affirmed by those speculative thinkers who affirm them

The “second principle” is their denial that matters connected with His power and will can subsist in Him. They call this “the inherence of temporal events.” Since they denied this, they deemed it impossible for any act performed by choice through His power and will to subsist in Him, whether intransitive or transitive: neither descending, coming, rising over the Throne, approaching, creating, giving life, causing death, nor anything else of this kind.

For this reason, they interpreted the early scholars’ statement concerning the descent—that “He does whatever He wills”—as meaning that a created thing separate from Him comes into being. Yet the early scholars’ words explicitly show that this was not what they meant. Rather, they meant an act performed by choice that subsists in Him.

Al-Fudayl ibn ‘Iyād—may Allah have mercy on him—did not mean that the Throne is left without Him; rather, he intended to oppose the Jahmiyyah. His statement, “He does whatever He wills,” does not entail that He must be beneath the Throne. Rather, his words are of the same kind as those of his peers among the early scholars, such as al-Awzā‘ī, Hammād ibn Zayd, and others.

Some of them rejected what is reported from Ahmad in his letter to Musaddad, saying: “Its transmitter from Ahmad is unknown; no one named Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Barda‘ī is known among Ahmad’s companions.”

The scholars of hadith hold three positions on this matter. Some reject saying either that the Throne is left without Him or that it is not. This is the position of the hadith master ‘Abd al-Ghanī al-Maqdisī and others.

Others say that the Throne is indeed left without Him. Abū al-Qāsim ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn Abī ‘Abd Allāh Muhammad ibn Mandah wrote a work refuting those who say that the Throne is not left without Him. He entitled it “A Refutation of Those Who Claim That Allah Is Everywhere, Those Who Claim That Allah Has No Place, and Those Who Interpret the Descent as Something Other Than Descent.”

He mentioned that he had been asked about a report recorded by Abū Sa‘īd al-Naqqāsh in “Statements of Ahl al-Sunnah,” from Abū al-Hasan Muhammad ibn ‘Alī al-Marwazī, from Muhammad ibn Ibrāhīm al-Dīnawarī, from ‘Alī ibn Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Mūsā, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Barda‘ī al-Tamīmī, who said: “When Musaddad ibn Musarhad became uncertain about the Sunnah and the controversies into which people had fallen concerning ‘predestination’

 أَحْمَد بْنُ مُحَمَّدٍ البردعي مَجْهُولٌ لَا يُعْرَفُ فِي أَصْحَابِ أَحْمَد مَنْ اسْمُهُ 
" أَحْمَد بْنُ مُحَمَّدٍ "
: فِيمَنْ رَوَى عَنْ أَحْمَد بْنِ مُحَمَّدِ بْنِ حَنْبَلٍ كَأَحْمَدَ بْنِ مُحَمَّدِ بْنِ هَانِئٍ وَأَبِي بَكْرٍ الْأَثْرَمِ وَأَحْمَد بْنِ مُحَمَّدِ بْنِ الْحَجَّاجِ وَأَبِي بَكْرٍ المروذي 
(*)
 وَأَحْمَد بْنِ مُحَمَّدِ بْنِ عِيسَى البراني الْقَاضِي وَأَحْمَد بْنِ مُحَمَّدٍ الصَّائِغِ وَأَحْمَد بْنِ مُحَمَّدِ بْنِ غَالِبٍ الْقَاصِّ غُلَامِ خَلِيلٍ وَأَحْمَد بْنِ مُحَمَّدِ بْنِ مَزِيدٍ الْوَرَّاقِ.
 وَزَادَ ابْنُ الْجَوْزِيِّ:
 أَحْمَد بْنَ مُحَمَّدِ بْنِ خَالِدٍ أَبَا بَكْرٍ الْقَاضِيَ وَأَحْمَد بْنَ خَالِدٍ أَبَا الْعَبَّاسِ البراني وَأَحْمَد بْنَ مُحَمَّدِ بْنِ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ صَدَقَةَ وَأَحْمَد بْنَ مُحَمَّدِ بْنِ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ صَالِحٍ الأسدي وَأَحْمَد بْنَ مُحَمَّدِ بْنِ عَبْدِ الْحَمِيدِ الْكُوفِيَّ وَأَحْمَد بْنَ مُحَمَّدِ بْنِ يَحْيَى الْكَحَّالَ وَأَحْمَد بْنَ مُحَمَّدِ بْنِ الْبُخَارِيِّ وَأَحْمَد بْنَ مُحَمَّدِ بْنِ بَطَّةَ

(*) قال الشيخ ناصر بن حمد الفهد (ص ٥٢):
الواو مقحمة بين اسم الأثرم وكنيته، وبين اسم المروّذي وكنيته، وصواب العبارة (كأحمد بن محمد بن هانئ أبي الأثرم وأحمد بن محمد الحجاج أبي بكر المروذي).
translated_text:
and ‘Rāfidism,’ ‘Mu‘tazilism,’ ‘Murji’ism,’ and ‘the Quran,’ he wrote to Ahmad ibn Hanbal: ‘Write to me the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.’ He wrote back: ‘In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful. To proceed.’ Then, among the things he mentioned in the letter was: ‘Allah descends to the lowest heaven, and the Throne is not left without Him.’” He had also been asked about a report narrated from Ishāq ibn Rāhawayh to the same effect.

‘Abd al-Rahmān claimed that this wording is rejected in the reports transmitted from these two and from others, and that the scholars of transmitted reports classify it as a rejected report. He said:

“Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Barda‘ī is unknown. No one named ‘Ahmad ibn Muhammad’ is known among Ahmad’s companions, among those who narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Hanbal, such as Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Hāni’, and Abū Bakr al-Athram, and Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn al-Hajjāj, and Abū Bakr al-Marwadhī (*), and Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn ‘Īsā al-Barānī, the judge; Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Sā’igh; Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Ghālib al-Qāss, known as Ghulām Khalīl; and Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Mazīd al-Warrāq.”

Ibn al-Jawzī added: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khālid, Abū Bakr, the judge; Ahmad ibn Khālid, Abū al-‘Abbās al-Barānī; Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn ‘Abd Allāh ibn Sadaqah; Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn ‘Abd Allāh ibn Sālih al-Asadī; Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn ‘Abd al-Hamīd al-Kūfī; Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Yahyā al-Kahhāl; Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn al-Bukhārī; and Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Battah
translated_footnote:
(*) Shaykh Nāsir ibn Hamad al-Fahd states (p. 52):
The conjunction wāw (“and”) has been inserted between al-Athram’s name and his kunyah (honorific name), and between al-Marwadhī’s name and his kunyah. The correct wording is: “such as Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Hāni’, Abū al-Athram, and Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Hajjāj, Abū Bakr al-Marwadhī.”

original_text:
وَذَكَرَ أَحْمَد بْنُ الْحَسَنِ أَبَا الْحَسَنِ التِّرْمِذِيَّ؛
 وَأَحْمَد بْنَ سَعِيدٍ وَقِيلَ:
 أَبُو الأشعبة التِّرْمِذِيُّ.
 وَذَكَرَ فِي الْمُحَمَّدِينَ:
 مُحَمَّدَ بْنَ إسْمَاعِيلَ التِّرْمِذِيَّ قَالَ: وَلَمْ يُعَدَّ هَذَا فِيمَنْ رَوَى عَنْ مُسَدَّدٍ أَيْضًا.
 قَالَ:
 وَهَذَا الْحَدِيثُ رَوَاهُ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ جَمَاعَةٌ مِنْ الصَّحَابَةِ عَلَى لَفْظٍ وَاحِدٍ مِنْهُمْ: أَبُو بَكْرٍ الصِّدِّيقُ وَعَلِيُّ بْنُ أَبِي طَالِبٍ وَعَبْدُ اللَّهِ بْنُ مَسْعُودٍ وَعَبْدُ اللَّهِ بْنُ عَبَّاسٍ وَعَبْدُ اللَّهِ بْنُ عُمَرَ وَعُثْمَانُ بْنُ أَبِي العاص وَمُعَاذُ بْنُ جَبَلٍ وَأَبُو أمامة وَعُقْبَةُ بْنُ عَامِرٍ وَأَبُو ثَعْلَبَةَ المروذي وَرِفَاعَةُ بْنُ عَرَابَةَ الجهني وعبادة بْنُ الصَّامِتِ وَعُمَرُ بْنُ عبسة وَأَبُو هُرَيْرَةَ وَأَبُو الدَّرْدَاءِ وَأَبُو مُوسَى الْأَشْعَرِيُّ وَجَابِرُ بْنُ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ وَجُبَيْرُ بْنُ مُطْعَمٍ وَأَنَسُ بْنُ مَالِكٍ وَعَائِشَةُ وَأُمُّ سَلَمَةَ وَغَيْرُهُمْ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ أَجْمَعِينَ وَلَمْ يَقُلْ أَحَدٌ مِنْهُمْ هَذَا اللَّفْظَ؛ وَلَا مَنْ رَوَاهُ مِنْ الصَّحَابَةِ وَالتَّابِعِينَ وَالْأَئِمَّةِ بَعْدَهُمْ. ثُمَّ سَاقَ الْأَحَادِيثَ بِأَلْفَاظِهَا؛ وَذَكَرَ أَنَّ أَحَدًا مِنْهُمْ لَمْ يَقُلْ هَذَا اللَّفْظَ.
 قَالَ:
 وَهُوَ لَفْظٌ مُوَافِقٌ لِرَأْيِ مَنْ زَعَمَ أَنَّهُ لَا يَخْلُو مِنْهُ مَكَانٌ وَرَأَى مَنْ زَعَمَ أَنَّهُ لَيْسَ لَهُ مَكَانٌ.
 قَالَ:
 وَتَأْوِيلُ مَنْ تَأَوَّلَ النُّزُولَ عَلَى غَيْرِ النُّزُولِ مُخَالِفٌ لِقَوْلِ مَنْ قَالَ: يَنْزِلُ رَبُّنَا إلَى السَّمَاءِ الدُّنْيَا كُلَّ لَيْلَةٍ وَلِقَوْلِهِ: فَلَا يَزَالُ كَذَلِكَ إلَى الْفَجْرِ.
 قُلْت:
 الْقَائِلُونَ بِذَلِكَ لَمْ يَقُولُوا: إنَّ هَذَا اللَّفْظَ فِي الْحَدِيثِ؛ وَلَيْسَ فِي
translated_text:
and he mentioned Ahmad ibn al-Hasan, Abū al-Hasan al-Tirmidhī, and Ahmad ibn Sa‘īd—also called Abū al-Ash‘abah al-Tirmidhī. Among those named Muhammad, he mentioned Muhammad ibn Ismā‘īl al-Tirmidhī. He said: “Nor was this man listed among those who narrated from Musaddad.”

He said: “A number of the Companions narrated this hadith from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, with the same wording. They include Abū Bakr al-Siddīq, ‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib, ‘Abd Allāh ibn Mas‘ūd, ‘Abd Allāh ibn ‘Abbās, ‘Abd Allāh ibn ‘Umar, ‘Uthmān ibn Abī al-‘Ās, Mu‘ādh ibn Jabal, Abū Umāmah, ‘Uqbah ibn ‘Āmir, Abū Tha‘labah al-Marwadhī, Rifā‘ah ibn ‘Arābah al-Juhanī, ‘Ubādah ibn al-Sāmit, ‘Umar ibn ‘Abasah, Abū Hurayrah, Abū al-Dardā’, Abū Mūsā al-Ash‘arī, Jābir ibn ‘Abd Allāh, Jubayr ibn Mut‘im, Anas ibn Mālik, ‘Ā’ishah, Umm Salamah, and others—may Allah be pleased with them all. None of them used this wording, nor did any of those who narrated it among the Companions, the Successors, or the imams after them.” He then presented the hadiths with their respective wordings and noted that none of them had used this wording.

He said: “This wording accords with the view of those who claim that no place is without Him, and with the view of those who claim that He has no place.”

He said: “Interpreting the descent as something other than descent contradicts the statement, ‘Our Lord descends to the lowest heaven every night,’ and the statement, ‘He remains thus until dawn.’”

I say: Those who hold this view have not claimed that this wording occurs in the hadith; nor is there in

original_text:
الْحَدِيثِ أَيْضًا أَنَّهُ لَا يَخْلُو مِنْهُ الْعَرْشُ أَوْ يَخْلُو مِنْهُ الْعَرْشُ؛ كَمَا يَدَّعِيهِ الْمُدَّعُونَ لِذَلِكَ فَلَيْسَ فِي الْحَدِيثِ لَا لَفْظُ الْمُثْبِتِينَ لِذَلِكَ وَلَا لَفْظُ الْنُّفَاةِ لَهُ.
 وَهَؤُلَاءِ يَقُولُونَ:
 إنَّهُمْ يَتَأَوَّلُونَ النُّزُولَ عَلَى غَيْرِ النُّزُولِ؛ بَلْ قَدْ يَكُونُ مِنْ هَؤُلَاءِ مَنْ يَنْفِي نُزُولًا يَقُومُ بِهِ وَيَجْعَلُ النُّزُولَ مَخْلُوقًا مُنْفَصِلًا عَنْهُ؛ وَعَامَّةُ رَدِّ ابْنِ منده الْمُسْتَقِيمِ إنَّمَا يَتَنَاوَلُ هَؤُلَاءِ؛ لَكِنَّهُ زَادَ زِيَادَاتٍ نُسِبَ لِأَجْلِهَا إلَى الْبِدْعَةِ؛ وَلِهَذَا كَانُوا يُفَضِّلُونَ أَبَاهُ أَبَا عَبْدِ اللَّهِ عَلَيْهِ وَكَانَ إسْمَاعِيلُ بْنُ مُحَمَّدِ بْنِ الْفَضْلِ التَّيْمِيُّ وَغَيْرُهُ يَتَكَلَّمُونَ فِيهِ فِي ذَلِكَ كَمَا هُوَ مَعْرُوفٌ عَنْهُمْ.
 قَالَ عَبْدُ الرَّحْمَنِ:
 قَالَ أَبِي فِي الرَّدِّ عَلَى مَنْ تَأَوَّلَ النُّزُولَ عَلَى غَيْرِ النُّزُولِ وَاحْتَجَّ فِي إبْطَالِ الْأَخْبَارِ الصِّحَاحِ بِأَحَادِيثَ مَوْضُوعَةٍ وَادَّعَى الْمُدْبِرُ أَنَّهُ يَقُولُ بِحَدِيثِ النُّزُولِ فَحَرَّفَهُ عَلَى مَنْ حَضَرَ مَجْلِسَهُ وَأَنْكَرَ فِي خُطْبَتِهِ مَا أَنْزَلَ اللَّهُ فِي كِتَابِهِ مَنْ حُجَّتِهِ وَمَا بَيَّنَ الرَّسُولُ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ مِنْ أَنَّهُ يَنْزِلُ بِذَاتِهِ وَتَأَوَّلَ النُّزُولَ عَلَى مَعْنَى الْأَمْرِ وَالنَّهْيِ؛ لَا حَقِيقَةِ النُّزُولِ. وَزَعَمَ أَنَّ أَئِمَّتَهُمْ الْعَارِفِينَ بِالْأُصُولِ يُنَزِّهُونَ اللَّهَ عَنْ التَّنَقُّلَاتِ فَأَبْطَلَ جَمِيعَ مَا أَخْرَجَ فِي هَذَا الْبَابِ إذْ كَانَ مَذْهَبُهُ غَيْرَ ظَاهِرِ الْحَدِيثِ وَاعْتِمَادُهُ عَلَى التَّأْوِيلِ الْبَاطِلِ وَالْمَعْقُولِ الْفَاسِدِ. وقَوْله تَعَالَى 
{لَيْسَ كَمِثْلِهِ شَيْءٌ}
 نَفَى التَّشْبِيهَ مِنْ جَمِيعِ الْجِهَاتِ وَكُلِّ الْمَعَانِي وَلَكِنَّ الْبَائِسَ الْمِسْكِينَ لَمْ يَجِدْ الطَّرِيقَ إلَى ثَلْبِ الْأَئِمَّةِ إلَّا بِهَذَا الطَّرِيقِ الَّذِي هُوَ
translated_text:
the hadith any statement that the Throne does not become empty of Him, or that it does become empty of Him, as those who advance such claims maintain. The hadith contains neither the wording of those who affirm this nor that of those who deny it.

These people say that they interpret the descent as something other than descent. Indeed, some of them may deny a descent that subsists in Him and regard the descent as something created and separate from Him. The sound arguments in Ibn Mandah’s refutation are, for the most part, directed against these people alone. However, he added statements on account of which he was accused of innovation. For this reason, they preferred his father, Abū ‘Abd Allāh, to him. Ismā‘īl ibn Muhammad ibn al-Fadl al-Taymī and others criticized him on this account, as is well known of them.

‘Abd al-Rahmān said:

My father said, in refutation of someone who interpreted the descent as something other than descent and sought to invalidate authentic reports by citing fabricated hadiths:

“This man who turns away claimed to accept the hadith of descent, yet distorted it for those attending his gathering. In his sermon, he denied the proof Allah revealed in His Book and what the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, explained: that He Himself descends. He interpreted the descent as referring to commands and prohibitions, rather than actual descent. He claimed that their imams, who were versed in the fundamentals, declared Allah far above moving from place to place. He thus invalidated all the reports cited in this chapter, since his position differed from the hadith’s apparent meaning and he relied upon false interpretation and unsound reasoning.

“His saying, exalted is He,

‘There is nothing like Him,’

rules out likening Him to anything in every respect and in every sense. Yet this wretched, pitiable man could find no way to disparage the imams except through this approach, which is

original_text:
بِهِ أَوْلَى ثُمَّ قَصَدَ تَعْلِيلَ حَدِيثِ النُّزُولِ بِمَا لَا يُعَدُّ عِلَّةً وَلَا خِلَافًا مِنْ قَوْلِ الرَّاوِي 
" يَنْزِلُ "

" يَقُولُ إذَا مَضَى نِصْفُ اللَّيْلِ "

" ثُلُثُ اللَّيْلِ وَنِصْفُ اللَّيْلِ "

" إنَّهُ يَأْمُرُ مُنَادِيًا يُنَادِي كُلَّ لَيْلَةٍ "

Ibn Mandah said: ‘This is not a discrepancy; rather, it is ignorance.’ Alongside these, he cited the hadith transmitted by Muhammad ibn Yazīd ibn Sinān, from his father, from Zayd ibn Abī Anīsah, from Tāriq, from Sa‘īd ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ‘Abbās, from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, who said:

‘He commands a caller to call out every night.’

This is a fabricated hadith that accords with his position. Out of uncertainty and ignorance, he claimed that Yahyā ibn Sa‘īd al-Qattān, Ibn Mahdī, al-Bukhārī and Muslim had included in their books the likes of these weak narrators whose reports are rejected.

He repeated the hadith of Abū Hishām al-Rifā‘ī from Hafs. Muhādir and several others narrated it with the wording:

‘Allah descends every night.’

Likewise, the report of Tāriq, which he narrated from ‘Ubayd Allāh ibn ‘Umar, from Zayd ibn Abī Anīsah, from Tāriq, from Sa‘īd ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ‘Abbās, contains the words:

‘Allah descends every night.’

As for the hadith of al-Hasan from ‘Uthmān ibn Abī al-‘Ās, we have already discussed it above. Nothing concerning these hadiths or their narrators is sound.

He said: ‘Had he remained silent about knowledge of hadith, it would have been more becoming and better for him. Allah has deprived him of that knowledge and firmly entrenched in his heart the rejection of authentic reports and reliance upon his own unsound reasoning.’”

Then it was related through his chain of transmission that al-Fudayl ibn ‘Iyād said: “If a Jahmī says, ‘I disbelieve in a Lord who descends and ascends,’ say, ‘I believe in a Lord who does whatever He wills.’”

I say:

It was from Zakariyyā ibn Yahyā al-Sājī that Abū al-Hasan al-Ash‘arī learned what he learned of the foundational principles of the people of the Sunnah and hadith, as well as much of what he transmitted in his book *Maqālāt al-Islāmiyyīn* (The Doctrines of the Muslims) concerning their doctrine. He reported from them what Hammād ibn Zayd had stated: that Allah is above the Throne and draws near to His creation however He wills.

For him and for those who deny that voluntary acts subsist in Allah’s Essence, this means that He creates accidents in some created beings, which are termed “descent.” Likewise, he said that He creates in the Throne a quality termed “rising over.” According to al-Ash‘arī, this consists of bringing the Throne nearer to His Essence without any act subsisting in Him. Rather, he treats His intransitive acts, such as descending and rising over the Throne, like His transitive acts, such as creating and bestowing kindness. In his view, all of these are the effects produced, separate from Him.

Al-Ash‘arī and the leading scholars among his followers, such as al-Qādī Abū Bakr and others, say that Allah is above the Throne in His Essence. Yet they take this position concerning descent and similar acts on the basis of their principle denying that temporal events subsist in Him.

The early scholars who said, “He does whatever He wills” and “He descends however He wills and in whatever manner He wills,” as well as al-Fudayl ibn ‘Iyād, who said, “If a Jahmī says to you, ‘I disbelieve in a Lord who leaves His place,’ say, ‘I believe in a Lord who does whatever He wills,’” intended the opposite of this position. I heard Ishāq ibn Rāhawayh say:

‘One day, the Jahmiyyah gathered before ‘Abd Allāh ibn Tāhir and said to him, “O governor, you give Ishāq precedence, honour him, and hold him in high esteem, yet he is a disbeliever who claims that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, descends to the lowest heaven every night and that the Throne becomes vacant of Him.”’

He continued: ‘ ‘Abd Allāh became angry and sent for me. I entered his presence and greeted him, but in his anger he neither returned my greeting nor invited me to sit. Then he raised his head and said to me, “Woe to you, Ishāq! What are these people saying?”

‘I replied, “I do not know.”

‘He said, “Do you claim that Allah, glorified and exalted be He, descends to the lowest heaven every night and that the Throne becomes vacant of Him?”

‘I replied, “O governor, it was not I who said it; it was the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Abū Bakr ibn ‘Ayyāsh narrated to us, from Ishāq, from al-Agharr ibn Muslim, that he said: ‘I bear witness that Abū Hurayrah and Abū Sa‘īd testified that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

‘“Allah descends to the lowest heaven every night and says: ‘Who will call upon Me, that I may answer him? Who will ask of Me, that I may give him? Who will seek My forgiveness, that I may forgive him?’”’

‘“But order them to debate me.”

‘When I mentioned the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, his anger subsided. He told me to sit, and I sat down.

‘I said, “O governor, order them to debate me.”

‘He said, “Debate him.”

‘I asked them, “Is He able to descend without the Throne becoming vacant of Him, or is He not?”

‘They remained silent and bowed their heads.

‘I said, “O governor, order them to answer.” But they remained silent.

‘He said, “Come now, Ishāq, what did you ask them?”

‘I replied, “O governor, ask them: Is He able to descend without the Throne becoming vacant of Him, or not?”

‘He said, “What does that mean?”

‘Abd al-Rahmān said:

The authentic account of what took place between Ishāq and ‘Abd Allāh ibn Tāhir is what my father related to us: Abū ‘Uthmān ‘Amr ibn ‘Abd Allāh al-Basrī narrated to us: Muhammad ibn Hātim narrated to us: I heard Ishāq ibn Ibrāhīm ibn Makhlad say:

‘ ‘Abd Allāh ibn Tāhir said to me, “O Abū Ya‘qūb, what are these hadiths you narrate concerning the descent”—meaning this and other matters?

‘I replied, “O governor, these hadiths have been transmitted in the same manner as those concerning legal rulings and what is lawful and unlawful. The scholars have transmitted them, so they may not be rejected. They are accepted as they have come, without specifying how.”

‘ ‘Abd Allāh said, “You have spoken the truth. Until now, I did not understand their import.”’

‘Abd al-Rahmān said: ‘The statement, “The place does not become vacant of Him,” specifies a manner that undermines the descent and invalidates the statement of those who say, “They are accepted as they have come, without specifying how.”’

The response is: Rather, Ishāq’s exchange with ‘Abd Allāh ibn Tāhir included more than this account relates, as is established by other reports. In accounts of such exchanges and debates, however, one narrator relates what another does not. This is likewise the case with the reports of the debates of Ahmad ibn Hanbal and others: one narrator relates what another does not, as in the accounts transmitted by Sālih, ‘Abd Allāh, al-Marwadhī and others, all of whom are trustworthy. Ishāq discussed the matter at length with Ibn Tāhir.

He replied: “Rising over the Throne is not unknown; its manner cannot be comprehended. Belief in it is obligatory, and asking about it is an innovation. I consider you nothing but misguided.” He then ordered that the man leave the gathering.

and Ishāq ibn Ibrāhīm, may Allah have mercy on him, was also present. He was asked whether the hadith concerning the descent was authentic.

He answered, “Yes.” One of ‘Abd Allāh’s commanders then asked him, “O Abū Ya‘qūb, do you maintain that Allah descends every night?”

“Yes,” he replied.

The man asked, “How does He descend?”

Ishāq said, “Affirm Him as being above.” The man replied, “Affirm Him as being above.”

Ishāq then said, “Allah, mighty and majestic is He, says:

‘And your Lord comes, and the angels, rank upon rank.’”

The emir ‘Abd Allāh said, “That is on the Day of Resurrection.”

Ishāq replied, “May Allah honour the emir! Who could prevent the One who comes on the Day of Resurrection from coming today?”’”

Abū ‘Uthmān said: “I read in Abū Bakr al-Ismā‘īlī’s epistle to the people of Jīlān:

‘Allah descends to the lowest heaven, as authentically reported from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. Allah, mighty and majestic is He, has said:

“Are they waiting for anything but for Allah to come to them in canopies of clouds?”

And He has said:

“And your Lord comes, and the angels, rank upon rank.”

We believe in all of this as it has been transmitted, without specifying how. Had He, glorified be He, willed to explain how this occurs, He would have done so. We therefore confine ourselves to what He has made clear and refrain from delving into what is ambiguous, as we have been commanded in His words:

“It is He who has sent down to you the Book. In it are verses that are clear and precise—they are the foundation of the Book—and others that are ambiguous. Those whose hearts are inclined to deviation follow what is ambiguous in it, seeking discord and seeking its interpretation. Yet none knows its interpretation except Allah. Those firmly grounded in knowledge say, ‘We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord.’ But none take heed except people of understanding.”’”

‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn Mandah narrated through his chain of transmission from Harb ibn Ismā‘īl, who said:

“I asked Ishāq ibn Ibrāhīm about the Prophet’s hadith, peace and blessings be upon him, ‘Allah descends to the lowest heaven.’

He replied, ‘Yes, Allah descends every night to the lowest heaven as He wills and in whatever manner He wills.’”

translated_text:
from Harb:

“It is not permissible to delve into matters concerning Allah Most High as one may delve into the actions of created beings, for Allah Most High says:

‘He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned.’”

It was also narrated that Harb said:

“This is the position of the leading scholars, the adherents of hadith and transmitted reports, and the people of the Sunnah renowned for their adherence to it. It is the position of Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Ishāq ibn Rāhawayh, al-Humaydī and others. They held that Allah descends every night to the lowest heaven however He wills and as He wills:

‘There is nothing like Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing.’”

It was also narrated from Harb that Ishāq ibn Ibrāhīm said:

“No one may conceive of the Creator, His attributes and His actions in the same way that one may reflect upon and examine matters concerning created beings. For it is possible for Him to be described as descending to the lowest heaven every night, when two-thirds of it have passed, as He wills. One must not ask how He descends, for He is the Creator and acts however He wills.”

He also narrated from Muhammad ibn Salām, who said:

“Fadālah asked ‘Abd Allāh ibn al-Mubārak about the descent on the fifteenth night of Sha‘bān. ‘Abd Allāh replied, ‘O weak one, tajidu khaddāya khūshīrkun: He descends however He wills.’”

It was narrated that Ibn al-Mubārak said:

“If someone says to you, ‘You liken Allah to His creation,’ know that he is a Jahmī.”

‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn Mandah said:

“Beware of being among those who say, ‘I believe in a Lord who does whatever He wills,’ yet then deny what is in the Book and the Sunnah concerning what Allah has willed and has enjoined upon His creation

A hadith traced back to the Prophet was also narrated through Nu‘aym ibn Hammād, from Jarīr, from Layth, from Bishr, from Anas, that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“When Allah wills to descend from His Throne, He descends Himself.”

I say: Abū al-Qāsim Ismā‘īl al-Taymī and other leading hadith scholars judged this wording weak as a report traced back to the Prophet. Ibn al-Jawzī also included it in al-Mawdū‘āt (Fabricated Reports). Abū al-Qāsim al-Taymī said: “The meaning of ‘He descends’ is correct, and I affirm it; however, it has not been established as a statement of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him.” (*)

The meaning may be correct even though the wording itself has not been transmitted. For example, one might say: Allah Himself, in His own essence, created the heavens and the earth; He Himself, in His own essence, spoke directly to Moses; and He Himself, in His own essence, rose over the Throne. The same applies to His other acts, which He Himself performed and of which He Himself was the doer. The meaning is correct, but not every expression used to explain the meaning of the Quran and hadith is itself part of the Quran or a statement traced back to the Prophet.

This summarizes what ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn Mandah mentioned, although he exhaustively presented the chains of transmission of this hadith and cited its various wordings, such as:

“Our Lord descends every night to the lowest heaven when the first third of the night has passed, saying: ‘I am the King. Who will ask Me, so that I may give to him? Who will call upon Me, so that I may answer him? Who will seek My forgiveness, so that I may forgive him?’ And He continues

In another wording: “Until dawn breaks; then He rises.” In another report, He says: “I ask no one else about My servants. Who will ask Me, so that I may give to him?”

In the report of ‘Amr ibn ‘Abasah:

“The Lord descends to the lowest heaven in the depths of the night.”

In another wording: “Until dawn breaks; then He rises.”

He also mentioned His descent on the afternoon of ‘Arafah through several chains of transmission, and likewise on the night of mid-Sha‘bān; His descent on the Day of Resurrection in canopies of cloud; the hadith concerning the Day of Increase—Friday in the Hereafter—with its mention of His descending and rising; and other similar hadiths. He objects to those who say that the Throne is not left without Him, treating this as equivalent to saying that He is everywhere or that He is nowhere.

His words resemble those of a group who suppose that only one of two views is possible: the view that He descends in such a way that the Throne is left without Him; or the view that there is no descent at all, like the statement of those who say that no act subsists in His essence by His own choice.

These two groups recognize no descent other than that attributed to the bodies of created servants, which entails vacating one place and occupying another. Some therefore deny His descent, declaring Him far above anything of that kind. Others affirm for Him a descent of this kind, entailing the vacating of one place and the occupation of another.

In sum, those who say that the Throne is left without Him are a small group among the adherents of hadith. The majority hold that the Throne is not left without Him. This is the position transmitted from the imams known for their adherence to the Sunnah. It has not been transmitted from any of them, through either a sound or a weak chain, that the Throne is left without Him.

As for ‘Abd al-Rahmān’s assessment of that report from Ishāq as weak, we have already cited the other, soundly established report transmitted by Ibn Battah and others. We have also cited the established wording transmitted by Sulaymān ibn Harb from Hammād ibn Zayd, as related by al-Khallāl and others.

As for Ahmad ibn Hanbal’s letter to Musaddad ibn Musarhad, it is well known among the adherents of hadith and the Sunnah, both Ahmad’s followers and others, who have accepted it. Abū ‘Abd Allāh ibn Battah included it in his book al-Ibānah. More than one scholar relied upon it, including al-Qādī Abū Ya‘lā, who copied it in his own hand.

translated_text:
Section

Some who affiliate themselves with “the Sunnah and hadith” have interpreted figuratively the hadith of the descent and similar texts concerning the Lord’s intransitive acts, such as coming, arriving, descending, and the like. They have transmitted statements to this effect from Mālik and Ahmad ibn Hanbal. Indeed, later scholars among Ahmad’s followers, such as Abū al-Hasan ibn al-Zāghūnī and others, reported two positions from Ahmad concerning figurative interpretation in this category, unlike other categories, concerning which no conflicting positions on figurative interpretation were transmitted from him.

Ibn ‘Aqīl extended these two reported positions on figurative interpretation beyond this attribute. At times he deems figurative interpretation obligatory, at times forbidden, and at times permissible. Sometimes he applies it to “all the scripturally reported attributes,” which he calls attributions—not attributes—in agreement with the Mu‘tazilites from whom he learned this, such as Abū ‘Alī ibn al-Walīd and Abū al-Qāsim ibn al-Tabbān, both of whom were followers of Abū al-Husayn al-Basrī. Abū al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzī agrees with Ibn ‘Aqīl on this in some of his books, such as Kaff al-tashbīh bi-kaff al-tanzīh, but disagrees with him in others.

" الْمِحْنَةِ "

 وَالنَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ قَالَ:

translated_text:
Most of Ahmad’s followers, however, did not affirm that differing positions on figurative interpretation had been transmitted from him, whether concerning these attributes or any others.

As for Abū Hāmid al-Ghazālī’s report from an unnamed Hanbalī that Ahmad interpreted figuratively only “three things”:

“The Black Stone is Allah’s right hand on earth”; “The hearts of His servants are between two fingers of the Most Merciful”; and “Indeed, I sense the breath of the Most Merciful coming from the direction of Yemen”—

this report is falsely attributed to Ahmad. No one has transmitted it from him with a chain of transmission, nor does any of his followers know of such a report from him. Moreover, this Hanbalī whom Abū Hāmid quoted is unidentified: neither his knowledge of what he said nor his truthfulness in saying it is known.

There was also disagreement among Ahmad’s followers: did his considered judgment vary regarding the figurative interpretation of coming, arriving, descending, and the like? For Hanbal related from him that, during the “Inquisition,” they argued against him using the Prophet’s words (may Allah bless him and grant him peace):

“Al-Baqarah and Āl ‘Imrān will come as though they were two clouds, or two canopies, or two flocks of birds with wings outspread,”

and similar hadiths mentioning the Quran’s arriving and coming. They said to him, “Only something created can be described as arriving and coming.” Ahmad countered their argument with his response—Ahmad and other imams of the Sunnah explained this hadith as referring to the coming of the reward for al-Baqarah and Āl ‘Imrān, just as similar reports mention deeds coming in the grave and on the Day of Resurrection, meaning the reward for those deeds.

The Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said:

“Recite al-Baqarah and Āl ‘Imrān, for they will come on the Day of Resurrection as though they were two canopies, or two clouds, or two flocks of birds with wings outspread, pleading

translated_text:
on behalf of those who recite them.” This hadith is in the Sahīh.

Since he commanded that they be recited and mentioned their coming to plead on behalf of the reciter, it is understood that he meant the reciter’s recitation of them, which is his deed. He described this deed—his recitation of the two surahs—as coming in the form he mentioned, just as he described other deeds as coming.

This matter is discussed at length elsewhere: does Allah transform a deed into a self-subsisting substance, or can accidents not be transformed into substances? The same question applies to his statement:

“Death will be brought in the form of a black-and-white ram.”

The point here is that when the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) described the Quran as coming in this form, he meant the reciter’s recitation, which is his deed. That is the reward of the Quran’s reciter. He did not mean that Allah’s very speech, which He uttered and which subsists in Him, takes the form of two clouds. Thus, this provided no evidence for the Jahmiyyah’s claim.

Then, during the Inquisition, Imam Ahmad countered them with the words of the Most High:

“Do they await anything but that Allah should come to them in canopies of clouds?”

He said: “It has been said that it is only His command that comes.” This is how Hanbal transmitted it. No one else who related Ahmad’s debate during the Inquisition transmitted this, including ‘Abd Allāh ibn Ahmad, Sālih ibn Ahmad, al-Marwadhī, and others. Ahmad’s followers therefore differed over this.

Some said: “Hanbal was mistaken; Ahmad did not say this.” They said that Hanbal had made known errors and that this was one of them. This was the approach of Abū Ishāq ibn Shāqlā.

translated_text:
Others said: “Rather, Ahmad said this to hold them to the implications of their own argument.” His point was:

“If He has spoken of Himself as coming, and this does not prove that He is created—rather, you have interpreted it to mean that His command comes—then likewise say that the reward of the Quran comes, not that the Quran itself comes. Such an interpretation is even more compelling here, since the purpose here is to speak of the reward of the Quran’s reciter, and his reward is a deed of his. The intention was not to speak of the Quran itself. Thus, if the Lord has spoken of His own coming and you have interpreted this as referring to His command, then when He speaks of the coming of the Quran’s recitation, you have all the more reason to interpret it as the coming of its reward.”

If Ahmad said this to hold them to the implications of their own argument, it does not follow that he agreed with them on it. Nor does he need to commit himself to this interpretation. This hadith has many parallels concerning the coming of people’s deeds. What is meant is the coming of the reciter’s recitation, which is his deed; people’s deeds are created, and their reward is created.

For this reason, Ahmad and other early scholars said that it is the reward of the Quran that comes. Reward pertains only to people’s deeds, not to the Lord’s attributes and acts.

A “third group” of Ahmad’s followers held that Ahmad did say this at that time, and they treated it as an opinion transmitted from him. Those among them who favor figurative interpretation—such as Ibn ‘Aqīl, Ibn al-Jawzī, and others—then make this their principal support. Abū al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzī even cites it in his Quran commentary without mentioning the statements of Ahmad and the early scholars that contradict it.

 مَعْنَى النُّزُولِ وَالِاسْتِوَاءِ وَغَيْرِ ذَلِكَ: أَفْعَالٌ يَفْعَلُهَا الرَّبُّ فِي الْمَخْلُوقَاتِ.
 وَهَذَا هُوَ الْمَنْصُوصُ عَنْ أَبِي الْحَسَنِ الْأَشْعَرِيِّ وَغَيْرِهِ قَالُوا:
 الِاسْتِوَاءُ فِعْلٌ فَعَلَهُ فِي الْعَرْشِ كَانَ بِهِ مُسْتَوِيًا وَهَذَا قَوْلُ أَبِي الْحَسَنِ بْنِ الزَّاغُونِي. وَهَؤُلَاءِ يَدَّعُونَ أَنَّهُمْ وَافَقُوا السَّلَفَ؛ وَلَيْسَ الْأَمْرُ كَذَلِكَ. كَمَا قَدْ بُسِطَ فِي مَوْضِعِهِ. وَكَذَلِكَ ذُكِرَتْ هَذِهِ رِوَايَةً عَنْ مَالِكٍ رُوِيَتْ مِنْ طَرِيقِ كَاتِبِهِ حَبِيبِ بْنِ
translated_text:
There is no doubt that the reports transmitted from Ahmad through numerous independent channels contradict this account and show that he does not say that it is the Lord’s command that comes, arrives, and descends. Rather, he repudiates those who say this.

Those who attribute to Ahmad a figurative interpretation of the descent and similar “acts” hold two views. Some interpret them as referring to intent, just as some interpret His words,

“Then He turned toward the heaven,”

as referring to intent. This is the interpretation mentioned by Ibn al-Zāghūnī. Others interpret them as the coming and descent of His command, as stated in Hanbal’s report.

A group among Ahmad’s followers and others—including Judge Abū Ya‘lā and others who agree with Abū al-Hasan al-Ash‘arī that the “act” is identical with its effect, and that no voluntary act subsists in His essence—say that descent, rising over the Throne, and similar expressions mean acts that the Lord performs in created things. This is explicitly stated by Abū al-Hasan al-Ash‘arī and others. They said: “Rising over the Throne is an act He performed in the Throne, by which He became established over it.” This is also the view of Abū al-Hasan ibn al-Zāghūnī. These people claim to agree with the early scholars, but that is not the case, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

This interpretation has likewise been cited as a report from Mālik, transmitted through his scribe Habīb ibn

original_text:
أَبِي حَبِيبٍ؛ لَكِنَّ هَذَا كَذَّابٌ باتفاق أَهْلِ الْعِلْمِ بِالنَّقْلِ لا يَقْبَلُ أَحَدٌ مِنْهُمْ نَقْلَهُ عَنْ مَالِكٍ. وَرُوِيَتْ مِنْ طَرِيقٍ أُخْرَى ذَكَرَهَا ابْنُ عَبْدِ الْبَرِّ وَفِي إسْنَادِهَا مَنْ لَا نَعْرِفُهُ.
وَاخْتَلَفَ أَصْحَابُ أَحْمَد وَغَيْرُهُمْ مِنْ الْمُنْتَسِبِينَ إلَى السُّنَّةِ وَالْحَدِيثِ:
 فِي النُّزُولِ وَالْإِتْيَانِ وَالْمَجِيءِ وَغَيْرِ ذَلِكَ. هَلْ يُقَالُ إنَّهُ بِحَرَكَةِ وَانْتِقَالٍ؟ أَمْ يُقَالُ بِغَيْرِ حَرَكَةٍ وَانْتِقَالٍ؟ أَمْ يُمْسِكُ عَنْ الْإِثْبَاتِ وَالنَّفْيِ؟ عَلَى 
" ثَلَاثَةِ أَقْوَالٍ "
 ذَكَرَهَا الْقَاضِي أَبُو يَعْلَى فِي كِتَابِ 
" اخْتِلَافِ الرِّوَايَتَيْنِ وَالْوَجْهَيْنِ "
.
فَالْأَوَّلُ قَوْلُ أَبِي عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ حَامِدٍ وَغَيْرِهِ.
وَالثَّانِي:

وَالثَّالِثُ:
 قَوْلُ أَبِي عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ بَطَّةَ وَغَيْرِهِ. ثُمَّ هَؤُلَاءِ فِيهِمْ مَنْ يَقِفُ عَنْ إثْبَاتِ اللَّفْظِ مَعَ الْمُوَافَقَةِ عَلَى الْمَعْنَى وَهُوَ قَوْلُ كَثِيرٍ مِنْهُمْ كَمَا ذَكَرَ ذَلِكَ أَبُو عُمَرَ بْنُ عَبْدِ الرَّحْمَنِ وَغَيْرُهُ 
(*)
. وَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ يُمْسِكُ عَنْ إثْبَاتِ الْمَعْنَى مَعَ اللَّفْظِ وَهُمْ فِي الْمَعْنَى مِنْهُمْ مَنْ يَتَصَوَّرُهُ مُجْمَلًا وَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ يَتَصَوَّرُهُ مُفَصَّلًا؛ إمَّا مَعَ الْإِصَابَةِ وَإِمَّا مَعَ الْخَطَأِ. وَاَلَّذِينَ أَثْبَتُوا هَذِهِ رِوَايَةً عَنْ 
" أَحْمَد "
 هُمْ وَغَيْرُهُمْ - مِمَّنْ يَنْتَسِبُ إلَى السُّنَّةِ وَالْحَدِيثِ -
 لَهُمْ فِي تَأْوِيلِ ذَلِكَ قَوْلَانِ:
original_footnote:
