translated_text:
As for the first premise, namely their statement, “If the act of creation were eternal, the created thing would necessarily be eternal,” this is disputed by those who hold that creation is an eternal act subsisting in the Creator, while the created thing originates in time. This position is held by some among the Kullābiyya, Hanafis, Hanbalis, Shāfiʿīs, Mālikīs, Sufis and scholars of hadith. They say: “You agree with us that His will is eternal and beginningless, although what He wills comes later. Likewise, the act of creation is eternal and beginningless, although the created thing comes later. Whatever you say concerning the will, we will bind you to its counterpart concerning the act of creation.” This is a dialectical rebuttal that binds them to the implications of their own position, and they have no way out of it.

As for the second premise, namely their statement, “If the act of creation originated in time and subsisted in the Lord, this would entail that events originating in time subsist in Him, which is impossible,” this is disputed by the early generations, the leading scholars of hadith, the foremost philosophers and many of their early and later representatives, and many speculative theologians, such as the Hishāmiyya and the Karrāmiyya. They say: “We do not concede that this consequence is impossible.” This will be discussed, Allah Most High willing, under the “Second Principle.”

As for the third premise, namely their statement, “If it did not subsist in Him, that would be impossible,” this is disputed only by certain groups of speculative theologians among the Muʿtazila and others. Some of them say: “Rather, the act of creation subsists in the created thing.” Others say: “Rather, the act of creation is not in any substrate,” just as the Basran Muʿtazila speak of “an act through a will that subsists in no substrate.” This is impossible, and I know of no one among the early generations, scholars of hadith, jurists, Sufis or philosophers who held this view.

translated_text:
As for the fourth premise, namely their statement, “An act of creation that originates in time requires another act of creation,” this is disputed by the great majority of those who affirm an act of creation originating in time among scholars of hadith, speculative theology, philosophy, jurisprudence and Sufism, and others. These include Abū Muʿādh al-Tūmanī, Zuhayr al-Ibarī, the Hishāmiyya, the Karrāmiyya, Dāwūd ibn ʿAlī al-Asbahānī and his followers, and the scholars of hadith and early generations mentioned by al-Bukhārī and others.

They say: “If He creates the heavens and the earth through an act of creation, it does not follow that this act of creation must require another act of creation. Rather, that act of creation comes about through His power and will, even though it originates in time.”

The proof that the consequence they seek to impose is invalid is that either power and will suffice to bring about something that originates in time, or they do not. If they do not suffice, their claim that created things come into existence through power and will alone, without an act of creation, is invalidated. Once their claim is invalidated, it becomes clear that a created thing must have a Creator who created it—which is precisely the point to be established.

If power and will suffice to bring a created thing into existence, then this act of creation, through which He creates created things, may likewise come about through power and will, without requiring another act of creation. Thus, on either supposition, it is not necessary to say, “Created things were created without an act of creation.” Rather, one may say, “They were created through an act of creation”—which is precisely the point to be established.

It also becomes clear that the proponents of negation never advance an argument based on a premise without having contradicted that premise elsewhere. Thus, all the premises of their argument are contradicted.

translated_text:
through an act that inheres in the agent himself. As for the act itself, which inheres in him, it requires no further act, but comes about through his power and will.

For this reason, those who hold this view say that the act of creation originates in time (hādith), but do not say that it is created. They differ, however, over whether it may be called muhdath (newly brought about), holding two views.

Likewise, they say that He speaks by His will and power, and that His speech is discourse (hadīth)—indeed, the finest discourse. They unanimously agree that it is not created, and it is described as both hadīth and hādith. They also hold two views on whether it may be called muhdath.

For those who customarily use the term muhdath only for a created thing separate from Allah—as was the prevalent usage among those who debated the Quran during the ordeal of Imam Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, and who understood muhdath to mean nothing other than a created thing separate from Allah—Ahl al-Sunnah do not permit the Quran to be called muhdath in this sense. Rather, whoever calls it muhdath has thereby called it created.

For this reason, Imam Ahmad objected to “Dāwūd” using this expression when he received a written report that Dāwūd had said it. Those who employed this terminology assumed that this was what Dāwūd meant, so the imams of the Sunnah rejected it. Yet Dāwūd himself did not intend this meaning. Rather, he and the leading scholars among his followers agree that Allah’s speech is uncreated. He intended only that it inheres in Allah Himself. This is the position of more than one imam of the early generations, including al-Bukhārī and others. The disagreement over this among Ahl al-Sunnah is “terminological”: they agree that it is not a created thing separate from Allah, and that Allah’s speech inheres in His essence. The point here is that the claim, “If His act of creating things were not identical with those things, the act of creation would require another act of creation, and would therefore itself be created,” is untenable. Rather, the act of creation comes about through the Lord’s power and will, while the created thing comes about through the act of creation.

translated_text:
the act of creation; its becoming complete is therefore a new occurrence, and every new occurrence must have a cause. For if that act of creation did not require a newly arising cause, this would entail something coming into being without a newly arising cause.

If it is said that the complete cause is eternal, this would entail the effect being delayed beyond its complete cause, which is impossible.

Those who maintain that the act of creation is distinct from the created thing, and that the act of creation comes into being, offer four answers here.

The first is the position of those who say that the act of creation, though it comes into being, requires no newly arising cause—neither another act of creation nor anything else. They say:

“All of you who dispute our position maintain that something can come into being without a newly arising cause. For whoever says that the created thing is distinct from the act of creation holds that all created things come into being without a newly arising cause. And whoever says that the act of creation is eternal must acknowledge that what is eternal is not confined to any particular time. Thus, no newly arising cause has come about for the created thing that comes into being at its appointed time.”

They say:

“Since this consequence follows on every supposition, the burden of answering it does not fall on us alone. Rather, we say that the created thing came into being through the act of creation, and that the act of creation came about through Allah’s power and His eternal will, without requiring any other cause.”

This is the position of many groups among the adherents of hadith and speculative theology, such as the Karrāmiyyah and others.

The second answer is the position of those among the Mu‘tazilah who say that the act of creation, which comes into being, subsists in the created thing, or subsists without a substrate. Similarly, they say that the will comes into being without subsisting in a substrate and without any cause necessitating its coming into being; rather, He brings it into being solely through His power.

translated_text:
The third answer:

This is the answer of Ma‘mar and his followers, who are known as “Ahl al-Ma‘ānī.” They affirm an infinite regress within a single instant. They say that the act of creation itself has an act of creation, that this act of creation has another act of creation, and so on without end, all existing within a single instant. This position is well known to be theirs.

The fourth answer is the position of those who say:

An act of creation that comes into being requires a newly arising cause; that cause likewise requires another, and so on. This entails the perpetual occurrence of things of this kind, which is not impossible. For the position of the early generations is that Allah has never ceased to speak whenever He wills. His words have no end, and every utterance is preceded by another, without any finite limit. He, glorified be He, speaks by His power and His will.

They likewise say that whatever is living must be active, as al-Bukhārī stated and related from Nu‘aym ibn Hammād, ‘Uthmān ibn Sa‘īd, Ibn Khuzaymah, and others. It must likewise be in motion, as ‘Uthmān ibn Sa‘īd al-Dārimī and others stated. Each of the two mentions that this is the position of Ahl al-Sunnah. This is also affirmed by leading philosophers, both earlier and later, whose statements to this effect have been cited elsewhere.

They say that this is an infinite regress of effects, whereas demonstration establishes only the impossibility of an infinite regress of causes. The invalidity of the latter is known through clear reason, and rational thinkers agree that it is impossible, as has been discussed at length elsewhere.

فَأَمَّا كَوْنُهُ سُبْحَانَهُ وَتَعَالَى يَتَكَلَّمُ كَلِمَاتٍ لَا نِهَايَةَ لَهَا وَهُوَ يَتَكَلَّمُ بِمَشِيئَتِهِ وَقُدْرَتِهِ فَهَذَا هُوَ الَّذِي يَدُلُّ عَلَيْهِ صَحِيحُ الْمَنْقُولِ وَصَرِيحُ الْمَعْقُولِ وَهُوَ مَذْهَبُ سَلَفِ الْأُمَّةِ وَأَئِمَّتِهَا وَالْفَلَاسِفَةُ تُوَافِقُ عَلَى دَوَامِ هَذَا النَّوْعِ وَقُدَمَاءُ أَسَاطِينِهِمْ يُوَافِقُونَ عَلَى قِيَامِ ذَلِكَ بِذَاتِ اللَّهِ كَمَا يَقُولُهُ أَئِمَّةُ الْمُسْلِمِينَ وَسَلَفُهُمْ. وَاَلَّذِينَ قَالُوا إنَّ ذَلِكَ مُمْتَنِعٌ هُمْ أَهْلُ الْكَلَامِ الْمُحْدَثِ فِي الْإِسْلَامِ مِنْ الْجَهْمِيَّة وَالْمُعْتَزِلَةِ وَهُمْ الَّذِينَ اسْتَدَلُّوا عَلَى حُدُوثِ كُلِّ مَا تَقُومُ بِهِ الْحَوَادِثُ بِامْتِنَاعِ حَوَادِثَ لَا أَوَّلَ لَهَا. وَمِنْ هُنَا يَظْهَرُ.
الْأَصْلُ الثَّانِي الَّذِي تُبْنَى عَلَيْهِ أَفْعَالُ الرَّبِّ تَعَالَى اللَّازِمَةُ وَالْمُتَعَدِّيَةُ وَهُوَ أَنَّهُ سُبْحَانَهُ هَلْ تَقُومُ بِهِ الْأُمُورُ الِاخْتِيَارِيَّةُ الْمُتَعَلِّقَةُ بِقُدْرَتِهِ وَمَشِيئَتِهِ أَمْ لَا؟ فَمَذْهَبُ السَّلَفِ وَأَئِمَّةِ الْحَدِيثِ وَكَثِيرٍ مِنْ طَوَائِفِ الْكَلَامِ وَالْفَلَاسِفَةِ جَوَازُ ذَلِكَ. وَذَهَبَ نفاة الصِّفَاتِ مِنْ الْجَهْمِيَّة وَالْمُعْتَزِلَةِ وَالْفَلَاسِفَةِ والْكُلَّابِيَة مِنْ مُثْبِتَةِ الصِّفَاتِ إلَى امْتِنَاعِ قِيَامِ ذَلِكَ بِهِ. أَمَّا 
" نفاة الصِّفَاتِ "

" الْكُلَّابِيَة "

translated_text:
As for His speaking words without end, glorified and exalted is He, and His speaking by His will and power, this is what sound transmitted evidence and clear reason establish. It is the position of the early generations of the Muslim community and its leading scholars. The philosophers agree that this kind of activity continues perpetually, and their foremost early authorities agree that it subsists in Allah’s essence, as the leading Muslim scholars and early generations maintain. Those who declare this impossible are the adherents of speculative theology newly introduced into Islam—the Jahmiyyah and the Muʿtazilah. They argue that everything in which temporal occurrences subsist must itself have come into existence, on the grounds that a beginningless succession of occurrences is impossible.

This brings to light the second principle underlying the exalted Lord’s acts, whether pertaining to Himself or affecting others: do matters subject to His choice and connected with His power and will subsist in Him or not? The position of the early generations, the leading scholars of hadith, and many groups among the speculative theologians and philosophers is that this is possible. By contrast, those who deny the attributes among the Jahmiyyah, the Muʿtazilah, and the philosophers, together with the Kullābiyyah among those who affirm the attributes, maintain that such matters cannot subsist in Him.

As for the “deniers of the attributes,” they deny this and other attributes, saying: “All these are accidents. Accidents subsist only in a body, and bodies have come into existence. Thus, if attributes subsisted in Him, He too would have come into existence.”

As for the “Kullābiyyah,” they say: “We affirm that attributes subsist in Him, but we do not call them accidents, for an accident does not endure for two successive moments. In our view, the attributes of the Lord, blessed and exalted is He, endure, unlike the accidents subsisting in created beings; for we hold that accidents do not endure for two successive moments.”

وَأَمَّا جُمْهُورُ الْعُقَلَاءِ فَنَازَعُوهُمْ فِي هَذَا وَقَالُوا:
 بَلْ السَّوَادُ وَالْبَيَاضُ الَّذِي كَانَ مَوْجُودًا مِنْ سَاعَةٍ هُوَ هَذَا السَّوَادُ بِعَيْنِهِ كَمَا قَدْ بُسِطَ فِي غَيْرِ هَذَا الْمَوْضِعِ إذْ الْمَقْصُودُ هُنَا التَّنْبِيهُ عَلَى مَقَالَاتِ الطَّوَائِفِ فِي هَذَا الْأَصْلِ. قَالَتْ 
" الْكُلَّابِيَة "
: وَأَمَّا الْحَوَادِثُ فَلَوْ قَامَتْ بِهِ لَلَزِمَ أَنْ لَا يَخْلُوَ مِنْهَا فَإِنَّ الْقَابِلَ لِلشَّيْءِ لَا يَخْلُو عَنْهُ وَعَنْ ضِدِّهِ. وَإِذَا لَمْ يَخْلُ مِنْهَا لَزِمَ أَنْ يَكُونَ حَادِثًا فَإِنَّ هَذَا هُوَ الدَّلِيلُ عَلَى حُدُوثِ الْأَجْسَامِ. هَذَا عُمْدَتُهُمْ فِي هَذَا الْأَصْلِ؛ وَاَلَّذِينَ خَالَفُوهُمْ قَدْ يَمْنَعُونَ الْمُقَدِّمَتَيْنِ كِلَيْهِمَا وَقَدْ يَمْنَعُونَ وَاحِدَةً مِنْهُمَا.
 وَكَثِيرٌ مِنْ أَهْلِ الْكَلَامِ وَالْحَدِيثِ مَنَعُوا الْأُولَى:
 كالهشامية والكَرَّامِيَة؛ وَأَبِي مُعَاذٍ وَزُهَيْرٍ الْإِبَرِيِّ وَكَذَلِكَ الرَّازِي والآمدي وَغَيْرُهُمَا مِنْ الْأَشْعَرِيَّةِ مَنَعُوا الْمُقَدِّمَةَ الْأُولَى وَبَيَّنُوا فَسَادَهَا؛ وَأَنَّهُ لَا دَلِيلَ لِمَنْ ادَّعَاهَا عَلَى دَعْوَاهُ. بَلْ قَدْ يَكُونُ الشَّيْءُ قَابِلًا لِلشَّيْءِ وَهُوَ خَالٍ مِنْهُ وَمِنْ ضِدِّهِ كَمَا هُوَ الْمَوْجُودُ؛ فَإِنَّ الْقَائِلِينَ بِهَذَا الْأَصْلِ الْتَزَمُوا أَنَّ كُلَّ جِسْمٍ لَهُ طَعْمٌ وَلَوْنٌ وَرِيحٌ؛ وَغَيْرُ ذَلِكَ مِنْ أَجْنَاسِ الْأَعْرَاضِ الَّتِي تَقْبَلُهَا الْأَجْسَامُ.

 هَذَا مُكَابَرَةٌ ظَاهِرَةٌ؛ وَدَعْوَى بِلَا حُجَّةٍ وَإِنَّمَا الْتَزَمَتْهُ الْكُلَّابِيَة لِأَجْلِ هَذَا الْأَصْلِ. وَأَمَّا (الْمُقَدِّمَةُ الثَّانِيَةُ؛ وَهُوَ مَنْعُ دَوَامِ نَوْعِ الْحَادِثِ فَهَذِهِ يَمْنَعُهَا أَئِمَّةُ السُّنَّةِ وَالْحَدِيثِ الْقَائِلُونَ بِأَنَّ اللَّهَ يَتَكَلَّمُ بِمَشِيئَتِهِ وَقُدْرَتِهِ؛ وَأَنَّ كَلِمَاتِهِ لَا نِهَايَةَ لَهَا؛ وَالْقَائِلُونَ بِأَنَّهُ لَمْ يَزَلْ فَعَّالًا؛ كَمَا يَقُولُهُ الْبُخَارِيُّ وَغَيْرُهُ. وَاَلَّذِينَ يَقُولُونَ
translated_text:
The majority of rational thinkers, however, disputed this and said: “Rather, the blackness and whiteness that existed an hour ago are the very same qualities that exist now.” This has been discussed at length elsewhere; the purpose here is simply to draw attention to the different groups’ positions on this principle.

The “Kullābiyyah” said: “As for temporal occurrences, if they subsisted in Him, it would follow that He could never be free of them, since whatever is receptive to something cannot be devoid of both it and its opposite. If He could never be free of them, it would follow that He too had come into existence, for this is the very argument used to establish that bodies have come into existence.”

This is their principal argument concerning this principle. Their opponents may reject both premises or only one of them.

Many speculative theologians and hadith scholars rejected the first premise, including the Hishāmiyyah, the Karrāmiyyah, Abū Mu‘ādh, and Zuhayr al-Ibrī. Likewise, al-Rāzī, al-Āmidī, and other Ash‘arīs rejected the first premise and demonstrated its invalidity, explaining that those who assert it have no evidence for their claim. Something may, in fact, be receptive to a quality while being devoid of both that quality and its opposite, as actually occurs. Those who uphold this principle committed themselves to maintaining that every body has a taste, a colour, a smell, and all the other kinds of accidents that bodies can receive.

The majority of rational thinkers therefore said: “This is a blatant denial of the obvious and an unsupported claim.” The Kullābiyyah committed themselves to it only because of this principle.

As for the second premise—namely, denying the perpetual succession of temporal occurrences—it is rejected by the leading scholars of the Sunnah and hadith who maintain that Allah speaks by His will and power and that His words have no end; by those who maintain that He has always been active, as al-Bukhārī and others state; and by those who say that

movement is inseparable from life, so life cannot exist without any movement at all, as al-Dārimī and others maintain.

Al-Tha‘labī narrated in his Tafsīr, through his chain of transmission, that Ja‘far ibn Muhammad al-Sādiq, may Allah be pleased with him, was asked concerning Allah’s words, “Did you think that We created you in vain?”: “Why did Allah create creation?” He replied:

“Because Allah has always been beneficent, from eternity and for all eternity. Allah therefore willed to bestow His beneficence upon His creation, though He had no need of them. He did not create them to gain any benefit or avert any harm. Rather, He created them, treated them with goodness, and sent messengers to them so that they might distinguish truth from falsehood. Whoever does good, He rewards with Paradise; and whoever disobeys, He recompenses with the Fire.”

Regarding Allah’s words, “And Allah is ever Forgiving, Merciful,” “And Allah is ever All-Knowing, All-Wise,” and similar expressions, Ibn ‘Abbās, may Allah be pleased with him, said: “He was so, has always been so, and will always remain so.”

This premise is also rejected by the majority of philosophers. The Jahmiyyah, Mu‘tazilah, Kullābiyyah, and Karrāmiyyah, however, maintain that the perpetual succession of temporal occurrences is impossible. This is one of the major principles underlying discussion of Allah’s speech and His creation. This position is the foundation of the speculative theology introduced into Islam that the early generations and leading scholars condemned.

For the adherents of this speculative theology among the Jahmiyyah, Mu‘tazilah, and their followers thought that Allah’s being the Creator of everything—as indicated by the Quran and Sunnah and agreed upon by the adherents of religious communities, including Muslims, Jews, Christians, and others—meant that He, glorified and exalted be He, had always been inactive

لَا يَفْعَلُ شَيْئًا وَلَا يَتَكَلَّمُ بِشَيْءِ أَصْلًا بَلْ هُوَ وَحْدَهُ مَوْجُودٌ بِلَا كَلَامٍ يَقُولُهُ وَلَا فِعْلٍ يَفْعَلُهُ. ثُمَّ إنَّهُ أَحْدَثَ مَا أَحْدَثَ مِنْ كَلَامِهِ وَمَفْعُولَاتِهِ الْمُنْفَصِلَةِ عَنْهُ. فَأَحْدَثَ الْعَالَمَ. وَظَنُّوا أَنَّ مَا جَاءَتْ بِهِ الرُّسُلُ وَاتَّفَقَ عَلَيْهِ أَهْلُ الْمِلَلِ - مِنْ أَنَّ كُلَّ مَا سِوَى اللَّهِ مَخْلُوقٌ وَاَللَّهُ خَالِقُ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ - هَذَا مَعْنَاهُ وَأَنَّ ضِدَّ هَذَا قَوْلُ مَنْ قَالَ بِقِدَمِ الْعَالَمِ أَوْ بِقِدَمِ مَادَّتِهِ فَصَارُوا فِي كُتُبِهِمْ الْكَلَامِيَّةِ لَا يَذْكُرُونَ إلَّا قَوْلَيْنِ.
 أَحَدَهُمَا:
 قَوْلُ الْمُسْلِمِينَ وَغَيْرِهِمْ مِنْ أَهْلِ الْمِلَلِ أَنَّ الْعَالَمَ مُحْدَثٌ وَمَعْنَاهُ عِنْدَهُمْ مَا تَقَدَّمَ.
 وَالثَّانِي:
 قَوْلُ الدَّهْرِيَّةِ الَّذِينَ يَقُولُونَ: الْعَالَمُ قَدِيمٌ وَصَارُوا يَحْكُونَ فِي كُتُبِ الْكَلَامِ وَالْمَقَالَاتِ أَنَّ مَذْهَبَ أَهْلِ الْمِلَلِ قَاطِبَةً مِنْ الْمُسْلِمِينَ وَالْيَهُودِ وَالنَّصَارَى وَغَيْرِهِمْ أَنَّ اللَّهَ كَانَ فِيمَا لَمْ يَزَلْ لَا يَفْعَلُ شَيْئًا وَلَا يَتَكَلَّمُ بِشَيْءِ ثُمَّ إنَّهُ أَحْدَثَ الْعَالَمَ؛ وَمَذْهَبُ الدَّهْرِيَّةِ أَنَّ الْعَالَمَ قَدِيمٌ. وَالْمَشْهُورُ عَنْ الْقَائِلِينَ بِقِدَمِ الْعَالَمِ أَنَّهُ لَا صَانِعَ لَهُ؛ فَيُنْكِرُونَ الصَّانِعَ جَلَّ جَلَالُهُ. وَقَدْ ذَكَرَ أَهْلُ الْمَقَالَاتِ أَنَّ أَوَّلَ مَنْ قَالَ مِنْ الْفَلَاسِفَةِ بِقِدَمِ الْعَالَمِ 
" أَرِسْطُو "
 صَاحِبُ التَّعَالِيمِ الْفَلْسَفِيَّةِ: الْمَنْطِقِيِّ وَالطَّبِيعِيِّ وَالْإِلَهِيِّ.
 وَأَرِسْطُو وَأَصْحَابُهُ الْقُدَمَاءُ يُثْبِتُونَ فِي كُتُبِهِمْ الْعِلَّةَ الْأُولَى وَيَقُولُونَ:
 إنَّ الْفَلَكَ يَتَحَرَّكُ لِلتَّشَبُّهِ بِهَا؛ فَهِيَ عِلَّةٌ لَهُ بِهَذَا الِاعْتِبَارِ إذْ لَوْلَا وُجُودُ مَنْ تَشَبَّهَ بِهِ الْفَلَكُ لَمْ يَتَحَرَّكْ وَحَرَكَتُهُ
translated_text:
doing nothing and saying nothing whatsoever. Rather, He alone existed, uttering no speech and performing no act. Then He brought into being His speech and the things He made that are separate from Him, and thus brought the world into being. They supposed that this was the meaning of what the messengers taught and the adherents of the religious communities agreed upon—namely, that everything other than Allah is created and that Allah is the Creator of everything. They also supposed that the opposing position was that of those who held that the world, or its matter, is eternal. Consequently, they mentioned only two positions in their works of speculative theology.

The first is the position of Muslims and other religious communities: that the world came into being—which, as they understood it, meant what was stated above.

The second is the position of the Dahriyyah, who say that the world is eternal. In their works on speculative theology and the doctrines of various schools, they came to report that all religious communities—Muslims, Jews, Christians, and others—held that Allah had, from eternity, neither done anything nor spoken anything, and then brought the world into being; whereas the Dahriyyah held that the world is eternal. The view commonly attributed to those who maintain the eternity of the world is that it has no Maker; thus, they deny the Maker, majestic is His glory. Writers on the doctrines of various schools have mentioned that the first philosopher to maintain the eternity of the world was Aristotle, the author of philosophical teachings on logic, natural philosophy, and metaphysics.

Yet Aristotle and his early followers affirm the First Cause in their books. They say that the celestial sphere moves in imitation of it, and that it is a cause of the sphere in this respect: were the one whom the sphere imitates not to exist, the sphere would not move, and its motion

 وَلَا قَالَ هُوَ مُوجِبٌ بِذَاتِهِ كَمَا يَقُولُهُ مَنْ يَقُولُ مِنْ مُتَأَخِّرِي الْفَلَاسِفَةِ كَابْنِ سِينَا وَأَمْثَالِهِ وَلَا قَالَ:
 إنَّ الْفَلَكَ قَدِيمٌ وَهُوَ مُمْكِنٌ بِذَاتِهِ؛ بَلْ كَانَ عِنْدَهُمْ مَا عِنْدَ سَائِر الْعُقَلَاءِ أَنَّ الْمُمْكِنَ هُوَ الَّذِي يُمْكِنُ وُجُودُهُ وَعَدَمُهُ وَلَا يَكُونُ كَذَلِكَ إلَّا مَا كَانَ مُحْدَثًا وَالْفَلَكُ عِنْدَهُمْ لَيْسَ بِمُمْكِنِ بَلْ هُوَ قَدِيمٌ لَمْ يَزَلْ وَحَقِيقَةُ قَوْلِهِمْ إنَّهُ وَاجِبٌ لَمْ يَزَلْ وَلَا يَزَالُ. فَلِهَذَا لَا يُوجَدُ فِي عَامَّةِ كُتُبِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُتَقَدِّمَةِ الْقَوْلُ بِقِدَمِ الْعَالَمِ إلَّا عَمَّنْ يُنْكِرُ الصَّانِعَ. فَلَمَّا أَظْهَرَ مَنْ أَظْهَرَ مِنْ الْفَلَاسِفَةِ كَابْنِ سِينَا وَأَمْثَالِهِ أَنَّ الْعَالَمَ قَدِيمٌ عَنْ عِلَّةٍ مُوجِبَةٍ بِالذَّاتِ قَدِيمَةٍ صَارَ هَذَا قَوْلًا آخَرَ لِلْقَائِلِينَ بِقِدَمِ الْعَالَمِ أَزَالُوا بِهِ مَا كَانَ يَظْهَرُ مِنْ شَنَاعَةِ قَوْلِهِمْ مِنْ إنْكَارِ صَانِعِ الْعَالَمِ وَصَارُوا أَيْضًا يُطْلِقُونَ أَلْفَاظَ الْمُسْلِمِينَ مِنْ أَنَّهُ مَصْنُوعٌ وَمُحْدَثٌ وَنَحْوُ ذَلِكَ وَلَكِنَّ مُرَادَهُمْ بِذَلِكَ أَنَّهُ مَعْلُولٌ قَدِيمٌ أَزَلِيٌّ لَا يُرِيدُونَ بِذَلِكَ.
 أَنَّ اللَّهَ أَحْدَثَ شَيْئًا بَعْدَ أَنْ لَمْ يَكُنْ وَإِذَا قَالُوا:
 إنَّ اللَّهَ خَالِقُ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ فَهَذَا مَعْنَاهُ عِنْدَهُمْ؛ فَصَارَ الْمُتَأَخِّرُونَ مِنْ الْمُتَكَلِّمِينَ يَذْكُرُونَ هَذَا الْقَوْلَ وَالْقَوْلُ الْمَعْرُوفُ عَنْ أَهْلِ الْكَلَامِ فِي مَعْنَى حُدُوثِ الْعَالَمِ الَّذِي يَحْكُونَهُ عَنْ أَهْلِ الْمِلَلِ كَمَا تَقَدَّمَ كَمَا يَذْكُرُ ذَلِكَ الشِّهْرِسْتَانِيّ وَالرَّازِي والآمدي وَغَيْرُهُمْ. وَهَذَا الْأَصْلُ الَّذِي ابْتَدَعَهُ الْجَهْمِيَّة وَمَنْ اتَّبَعَهُمْ مِنْ أَهْلِ الْكَلَامِ مِنْ امْتِنَاعِ
translated_text:
is inseparable from its existence; hence, were its motion to cease, it would perish.

Aristotle did not say that the First Cause originated the celestial spheres. Nor did he say that it necessitates its effects by its very essence, as some later philosophers, such as Ibn Sīnā and his like, maintain. Nor did he say that the celestial sphere is eternal yet contingent in itself. Rather, these philosophers shared the understanding of all other rational people: something contingent is that which can either exist or not exist, and only something brought into being can be of this kind. In their view, the celestial sphere is not contingent; rather, it is eternal and has always existed. The actual implication of their position is that its existence is necessary, without beginning or end.

For this reason, in most early works of speculative theology, the doctrine of the eternity of the world is attributed only to those who deny the Maker. But when philosophers such as Ibn Sīnā and his like put forward the view that the world is eternal and proceeds from an eternal cause that necessitates its effects by its very essence, this became another position among those who upheld the eternity of the world. Through it, they removed the apparent odiousness of their position arising from their denial of a Maker of the world. They also began using the expressions employed by Muslims, saying that the world is made, brought into being, and so forth. What they mean, however, is that it is an eternal, beginningless effect. They do not mean that Allah brought something into being after it had not existed. When they say that Allah is the Creator of everything, this is what they mean.

Later speculative theologians thus began mentioning this position alongside the well-known position of the speculative theologians concerning what it means for the world to have come into being—the position they attribute to the adherents of the religious communities, as explained above. Al-Shahrastānī, al-Rāzī, al-Āmidī, and others present the matter in this way.

And this principle, which the Jahmiyyah and the speculative theologians who followed them introduced—namely, the impossibility of

دَوَامِ فِعْلِ اللَّهِ وَهُوَ الَّذِي بَنَوْا عَلَيْهِ أُصُولَ دِينِهِمْ وَجَعَلُوا ذَلِكَ أَصْلَ دِينِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ فَقَالُوا:

 لَكِنَّ مَنْ تَفَطَّنَ مِنْهُمْ لِلْفَرْقِ فَإِنَّهُ يَذْكُرُ دَلِيلًا عَلَى ذَلِكَ بِأَنْ يَقُولَ:

 مِنْ بِدَعِ الْأَشْعَرِيِّ فِي الْفِتْنَةِ الَّتِي جَرَتْ بِخُرَاسَانَ لَمَّا أَظْهَرُوا لَعْنَةَ أَهْلِ الْبِدَعِ وَالْقِصَّةُ مَشْهُورَةٌ.
 ثُمَّ إنَّ أَهْلَ الْكَلَامِ وَأَئِمَّتَهُمْ كَالنَّظَّامِ وَالْعَلَّافِ وَغَيْرِهِمَا مِنْ شُيُوخِ الْمُعْتَزِلَةِ وَالْجَهْمِيَّة وَمَنْ اتَّبَعَهُمْ مِنْ سَائِرِ الطَّوَائِفِ يَقُولُونَ:
 إنَّ دِينَ الْإِسْلَامِ إنَّمَا يَقُومُ عَلَى هَذَا الْأَصْلِ وَأَنَّهُ لَا يُعْرَفُ أَنَّ مُحَمَّدًا رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ إلَّا بِهَذَا
translated_text:
Allah’s acting perpetually—is the very principle upon which they built the foundations of their religion, making it the foundation of the Muslims’ religion. They said:

Bodies are never free of temporally originated events, and whatever is never free of such events is itself temporally originated. Alternatively, whatever does not precede temporally originated events is itself temporally originated, because whatever is neither free of them nor precedes them must exist alongside them or after them. Whatever exists alongside temporally originated events or after them is itself temporally originated.

Many of them offer no proof for this, regarding it as self-evident, since they do not distinguish between events as a class and a particular event. Those among them who recognize the distinction, however, offer a proof by saying:

Events cannot be perpetual; rather, it is impossible for there to be events with no beginning.

Some of them also deny the possibility of events with no end, as do the two leading figures of this speculative theology: Jahm ibn Safwān and Abū al-Hudhayl.

Since the real implication of this position is that Allah, glorified be He, was not capable of acting from eternity, but became capable of acting after having been incapable of it, this was among the things for which Muslims condemned these people. Indeed, it was even counted among al-Ash'arī’s innovations during the unrest in Khurāsān, when curses against the people of innovation were publicly pronounced. The account is well known.

Furthermore, the speculative theologians and their leading figures—such as al-Nazzām, al-'Allāf, and other teachers of the Mu'tazilah and the Jahmiyyah, together with their followers from the various other groups—say:

The religion of Islam rests entirely upon this principle, and it cannot be known that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, except through this

الْأَصْلِ؛ فَإِنَّ مَعْرِفَةَ الرَّسُولِ مُتَوَقِّفَةٌ عَلَى مَعْرِفَةِ الْمُرْسَلِ فَلَا بُدَّ مِنْ إثْبَاتِ الْعِلْمِ بِالصَّانِعِ أَوَّلًا وَمَعْرِفَةِ مَا يَجُوزُ عَلَيْهِ وَمَا لَا يَجُوزُ عَلَيْهِ.

 وَيَقُولُ كَثِيرٌ مِنْهُمْ:
 إنَّ هَذِهِ طَرِيقَةُ إبْرَاهِيمَ الْخَلِيلِ عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ الْمَذْكُورَةِ فِي قَوْلِهِ 
{لَا أُحِبُّ الْآفِلِينَ}
 قَالُوا: فَإِنَّ إبْرَاهِيمَ اسْتَدَلَّ بِالْأُفُولِ - وَهُوَ الْحَرَكَةُ وَالِانْتِقَالُ - عَلَى أَنَّ الْمُتَحَرِّكَ لَا يَكُونُ إلَهًا.
 قَالُوا:
 وَلِهَذَا يَجِبُ تَأْوِيلُ مَا وَرَدَ عَنْ الرَّسُولِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ مُخَالِفًا لِذَلِكَ مِنْ وَصْفِ الرَّبِّ بِالْإِتْيَانِ وَالْمَجِيءِ وَالنُّزُولِ وَغَيْرِ ذَلِكَ؛ فَإِنَّ كَوْنَهُ نَبِيًّا لَمْ يُعْرَفْ إلَّا بِهَذَا الدَّلِيلِ الْعَقْلِيِّ فَلَوْ قَدَحَ فِي ذَلِكَ لَزِمَ الْقَدْحُ فِي دَلِيلِ نُبُوَّتِهِ فَلَمْ يُعْرَفْ أَنَّهُ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ وَهَذَا وَنَحْوُهُ هُوَ الدَّلِيلُ الْعَقْلِيُّ الَّذِي يَقُولُونَ إنَّهُ عَارَضَ السَّمْعَ وَالْعَقْلَ. وَنَقُولُ إذَا تَعَارَضَ السَّمْعُ وَالْعَقْلُ امْتَنَعَ تَصْدِيقُهُمَا وَتَكْذِيبُهُمَا وَتَصْدِيقُ السَّمْعِ دُونَ الْعَقْلِ؛ لِأَنَّ الْعَقْلَ هُوَ أَصْلُ السَّمْعِ فَلَوْ جُرِحَ أَصْلُ الشَّرْعِ كَانَ جَرْحًا لَهُ.
 وَلِأَجْلِ هَذِهِ الطَّرِيقِ أَنْكَرَتْ الْجَهْمِيَّة وَالْمُعْتَزِلَةُ الصِّفَاتِ وَالرُّؤْيَةَ وَقَالُوا:
translated_text:
principle; for recognizing the Messenger depends upon knowing the One who sent him. It is therefore necessary first to establish knowledge of the Maker and to know what is and is not possible with respect to Him.

They said:

This can only be known through this method. For, they claim, there is no way to know the Maker except by knowing His creatures, and no way to know that His creatures originated in time except through this method. Most of them say: A person’s first obligation is to know Allah, and He can only be known through this method.

Many of them say:

This is the method of Abraham, the close friend of Allah, peace be upon him, mentioned in his words:

“I do not love those that set.”

They said: Abraham inferred from setting—which is movement and change of place—that whatever moves cannot be a god.

They said:

For this reason, whatever has been transmitted from the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, that conflicts with this—descriptions of the Lord as coming, arriving, descending, and so forth—must be interpreted figuratively. For his prophethood was only known through this rational proof. Were this proof called into question, the proof of his prophethood would necessarily be called into question, and it would no longer be known that he is the Messenger of Allah.

This and similar arguments constitute the rational proof which they say conflicts with revelation and reason. And we say: When revelation and reason conflict, it is impossible to affirm both, to reject both, or to affirm revelation rather than reason, because reason is the foundation of revelation. Thus, to undermine the foundation of the revealed religion would be to undermine that religion itself.

It was because of this method that the Jahmiyyah and the Muʿtazilah denied the divine attributes and the vision of Allah, and said:

translated_text:
“The Quran is created.” It was because of this method that the Jahmiyyah maintained that Paradise and Hell would perish, and that al-ʿAllāf maintained that movement within them would cease. Many practitioners of speculative theology derived further conclusions from it, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

Others responded to them:

As for your claim that this method is the foundation for knowing the religion of Islam and the prophethood of the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, its falsity is among the self-evident truths of Islam. Everyone acquainted with the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, his Companions, and the faith and Quran he brought knows that he never called people through this method. Nor did any of the Companions or those who followed them in righteousness ever speak of it. How, then, can it be the foundation of faith when the one who brought faith and those whose faith was strongest never spoke of it at all, and none of them pursued it?

Those who recognized that this method was an innovation fall into two groups:

One group considered it sound in itself, but held that the early generations turned away from it because its premises were lengthy and obscure, and because those pursuing it risked becoming entangled in doubt and protracted inquiry. This was the position of a number of scholars, including al-Ashʿarī in his Epistle to the Frontier, al-Khattābī, al-Halīmī, al-Qādī Abū Yaʿlā, Ibn ʿAqīl, Abū Bakr al-Bayhaqī, and others.

The second position is that of those who say: Rather, this method is inherently false, and that is why the early generations condemned it and turned away from it. This was the position of the leading scholars of the early generations, such as Ibn al-Mubārak, al-Shāfiʿī, and Ahmad

ibn Hanbal, Ishāq ibn Rāhawayh, Abū Yūsuf, Mālik ibn Anas, Abd al-Azīz ibn al-Mājishūn, and other scholars of the early generations. When Hafs al-Fard debated al-Shāfi‘ī on the question of the Quran—asserting that the Quran was created, whereupon al-Shāfi‘ī declared him an unbeliever—he had employed this method in his argument. Likewise, Abū Īsā Muhammad ibn Īsā Burghūth was among those who used this method when debating Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal on the question of the Quran.

In his refutation of the Jahmiyyah, Imam Ahmad mentioned, among the things for which he censured them, their assertion that Allah neither speaks nor moves.

As for Abd Allāh ibn al-Mubārak, he had to contend with these people in his own land, and his opposition to them was extensive. Likewise, al-Mājishūn refuted them. The early generations spoke at length in refutation of these people. Others said to them:

“This principle, through which you claim to establish the existence of the Maker, and without which you maintain that He cannot be known as the Creator of created things, is the very opposite of what you claim. Rather, this principle is incompatible with the Lord being the Creator of the world. Upholding it makes it impossible either to affirm that the world came into being or to refute the philosophers. Thus, the speculative theologians who devised it and claimed that through it they defended Islam and refuted its enemies, such as the philosophers, neither defended Islam nor vanquished its enemy. Rather, what they devised corrupted the reality of Islam for those who followed them, corrupting both their reason and their religion

translated_text:
and used it to wrong those Muslims who disputed with them, and opened a path for Islam’s enemy to achieve his aim. For their position really amounts to saying that the Lord had not been capable, nor had speech and action been possible for Him, and that He had always remained so for an unlimited duration—or a supposed duration—before He spoke and acted without any cause necessitating this. They identified the effect He produces with His act, and held His act and His will to act to be beginningless and eternal, while the effect came later. They also held that an agent possessing power selects one of two things within his power over the other without any determining factor. All this contradicts both sound reason and the Quran and Sunnah. They denied His attributes and the possibility of seeing Him, and said that His speech is created—all contrary to the religion of Islam.

Those who followed them while affirming the attributes said that He wills everything He wills by a single will, and that all the speech He has spoken or will speak is but one indivisible thing, admitting neither multiplicity nor division. They said that if He is seen, He is seen neither face-to-face nor by direct sight; and that He did not hear or see things until they existed, yet when they came into existence, no existent reality came to subsist in Him. Rather, His state before hearing and seeing was the same as His state thereafter. They made other such assertions that contradict sound reason and authentic transmitted evidence.

Then, when ‘the philosophers’ saw that this was the extent of these people’s knowledge and that this was the Islam they professed, and recognized its invalidity, they openly proclaimed their doctrine of the eternity of the world. They argued that action cannot arise after there had been none; rather, every new occurrence must have a cause that itself comes into being

For when the sun rises, the stars are said to have disappeared and become hidden, even though they remain in the sky: the sun’s light has simply effaced their radiance. This resolves the difficulty raised concerning the verse’s account of the sun rising after the moon had set.

Abraham, peace be upon him, did not say:

“I do not love those that set,”

when he saw the star, the moon, and the sun moving. Rather, he said this only when the celestial body disappeared and became hidden. If Abraham intended, as they claim, to argue from its setting that the setting body could not be the Lord of all worlds, then Abraham’s account would be evidence against them. For he did not take its rising and its movement through the sky until its disappearance as evidence against its being the Lord of all worlds; rather, he took only its disappearance as evidence. Thus, if their claim about his intended argument were correct, it would establish the opposite of what they seek to prove and invalidate the claim that motion is evidence of having come into existence.

The truth, however, is that Abraham did not intend this. Nor, when he said:

“This is my Lord,”

did he mean that it was the Lord of all worlds. No descendant of Adam has ever believed that any star created the heavens and the earth, nor that the sun or moon did so. Neither did the polytheists among Abraham’s people believe this. Rather, they associated partners with Allah, worshipping the stars, invoking them, building temples for them, and worshipping their idols in those temples. This was the religion of the Chaldeans, the Kashdānians, and the polytheistic Sabians—not the Sabians who adhered to pure monotheism. It was according to the religion of those polytheists that the author of The Hidden Secret of Magic and Addressing the Stars composed his book.

This religion was followed by many people in Syria, Upper Mesopotamia, Iraq, and elsewhere. Its adherents were present before the advent of the religion of the Messiah, peace be upon him. The congregational mosques of Damascus and Harrān, among others, occupied the sites of some of their temples: one a temple of Jupiter, another a temple of Venus. They used to pray facing the north pole, and Damascus has ancient prayer niches facing north. The Greek philosophers belonged to this same kind of polytheist: they worshipped celestial bodies and idols and practised sorcery. The same was true of the people of Egypt and others. Most polytheists acknowledged the Lord of all worlds; those who denied Him, such as Pharaoh and others like him, were few.

Abraham’s people acknowledged the Creator. Hence Abraham, the intimate friend of Allah, said to them:

“Have you considered what you have been worshipping—you and your forefathers? They are enemies to me, except the Lord of all worlds.”

Thus he declared his enmity towards everything they worshipped except the Lord of all worlds. Allah Most High said:

“You have an excellent example in Abraham and those with him, when they said to their people, ‘We disavow you and whatever you worship besides Allah. We reject you, and enmity and hatred have arisen between us and you forever, until you believe in Allah alone’—except for Abraham’s words to his father, ‘I will surely seek forgiveness for you, though I have no power to protect you from Allah at all.’”

Abraham, Allah’s intimate friend, peace be upon him, said:

“Do you worship what you carve, when Allah created you and what you do?”

Allah Most High said in Sūrat al-Anʿām:

“When it set, he said, ‘O my people, I am free of whatever you associate with Allah. I have turned my face towards the One who created the heavens and the earth, devoted to pure monotheism, and I am not one of the polytheists.’

How could I fear what you associate with Allah, when you do not fear associating with Him things for which He has sent you no authority? Which of the two groups has more right to security, if you know?’”

“Those who believe and do not taint their faith with wrongdoing—it is they who will have security, and they are rightly guided.”

Allah Most High said:

“That was Our argument which We gave Abraham against his people. We raise in rank whom We will. Surely your Lord is All-Wise, All-Knowing.”

When these people interpreted “setting” as motion and opened the door to distorting words from their proper meanings, the heretics entered through that door. Ibn Sīnā and other heretics like him interpreted setting as the contingency they postulated. They maintained that the celestial spheres are eternal, without beginning, yet contingent, as are the stars and the two luminaries within them.

They said that Abraham’s words, “I do not love those that set,” mean: “I do not love what is contingent and caused, even if it is eternal and without beginning.” But where in the word “setting” is there anything to indicate this meaning? Such, however, is the way of those who distort words from their proper meanings.

After them came others of the same kind who went further in distortion, saying that “the stars, the sun, and the moon” refer to the soul, the active intellect, and the first intellect. Abū Hāmid al-Ghazālī mentioned this in some of his books and attributed it to others in some of them. These people said: “No rational person can fail to recognize that the stars, the sun, and the moon are not the Lord of all worlds, unlike the soul and the intellect.” For the words “star,” “sun,” and “moon” to signify these meanings—even if such things existed—

is among the astonishing distortions of the esotericist heretics. They likewise reinterpret matters of belief as well as religious practices, saying: “The five daily prayers mean knowing our secrets; fasting Ramadan means concealing our secrets; and pilgrimage means visiting our venerated shaykhs.”

The Jahmiyyah and the Rāfidah opened this door for them. Some of them began saying: “The clear record” is ʿAlī ibn Abī Tālib; “the accursed tree in the Quran” is the Umayyads; the cow they were commanded to slaughter is ʿĀ’ishah; and “pearls and coral” are al-Hasan and al-Husayn.

Some Sufis and Quran commentators have shared in distortions of this kind. For example, some say that “By the fig and the olive,” “and Mount Sinai,” and “and this secure city” mean Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthmān, and ʿAlī—may Allah be pleased with them. Likewise, they interpret “like a plant that produces its shoots” as Abū Bakr; “then strengthens it” as ʿUmar; “then grows thick” as ʿUthmān; and “then stands firm upon its stalks” as ʿAlī.

Some Sufis also say that in “Go to Pharaoh, for he has transgressed,” Pharaoh is the heart; and in “Allah commands you to slaughter a cow,” the cow is the soul. There are other distortions of this kind. Some, however, convey a sound meaning, even though it is not the meaning intended by the wording. This is the case with most Sufi allusions. Some of this is not presented as exegesis, but rather as drawing lessons and analogies. This is a sound, scholarly approach, as with the words of Allah Most High:

“None touch it except the purified,”

and the words of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Angels do not enter a house in which there is a dog.”

Thus, if “none touch it except the purified” applies to its pages, then its meanings provide guidance only to hearts

The point is that when those innovators among the speculative theologians opened “the door to flawed analogy in rational matters and corrupt interpretation in matters of revelation,” this became a gateway for unbelieving heretics to something still worse: sophistry in rational matters and Qarmatian interpretation in matters of revelation. Whoever took this any further was led to something worse still. Eventually, the Qarmatians went so far as to abolish all the known religious laws, as their leader in Syria told them:

“We have relieved you of acts of worship: there is no fasting, no prayer, no pilgrimage, and no zakat.”

This is why some of the early generations said:

“Religious innovations pave the way to disbelief, and sins pave the way to hypocrisy.”

When the leading proponents of innovated speculative theology believed that Allah’s being the Creator of everything meant what was stated earlier—namely, that He had never done anything or spoken anything until He brought the world into existence—they were compelled to say that the Quran, or any other speech of Allah, is created, separate and apart from Him. For if He had eternal speech, or uncreated speech, then, according to the principle they had established, the world would necessarily be eternal. Rational people recognize that speech occurs only through the speaker’s power and will. any rational person, nor do we know of anyone who had professed it. Indeed, it had not even occurred to the vast majority of people until Ibn Kullāb introduced this doctrine.

What drove him to this was the following: when those speculative theologians openly proclaimed the necessary consequence of their foundational principle—namely, that the Quran is created—they did so in the early second century AH. When the scholars of the Muslim community heard this, they denounced it. Thereafter, whenever this doctrine appeared, the scholars rejected it. The statements of the early generations and the imams condemning it are well known and transmitted through numerous independent channels.

Eventually, during al-Ma’mūn’s reign, these proponents of innovated speculative theology gained influence. They drew him into their doctrine and presented him with their arguments. They said:

“Either the world is created or it is eternal. The latter is manifest unbelief, whose falsehood is known through both reason and revelation. If the world was created and brought into existence after not existing, then Allah alone is eternal. For if the world were eternal, there would necessarily be another eternal being alongside Allah. Likewise, if speech subsisted in His very being, this would entail a perpetual succession of originated events and their subsistence in the Lord. This would invalidate their widely known proof that the world came into existence. If, on the other hand, it were separate from Him, this would entail the existence of something created from eternity, which amounts to affirming the eternity of the world.”

When people were subjected to this trial and it became widely known, Allah kept certain imams of the Sunnah steadfast. The imam whom Allah kept steadfast and made a leading authority for the Sunnah was Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal. Indeed, after the trial began, the scholars came to test people by their stance toward him: whoever agreed with him was a Sunni; otherwise, he was an innovator. He remained steadfast in affirming that the Quran is the speech of Allah, uncreated.

And when al-Ma’mūn reached the frontier at Tarsus, he wrote to his deputy in Iraq, Ishāq ibn Ibrāhīm, ordering that people be put to the test. Ishāq summoned the scholars, jurists, and judges, but they refused to assent or comply. He reported their response to al-Ma’mūn, who wrote a second letter, saying of the two judges, Bishr ibn al-Walīd and ʿAbd al-Rahmān ibn Ishāq: “If they do not comply, behead them.” Regarding the others, he said: “If they do not comply, put them in chains and send them to me.”

The two judges complied, telling their companions that they were acting under coercion. Most of the others complied before being chained, upon seeing the threatened punishment. Six men refused, so he had them chained. Once they were chained, the remaining men complied except for two: Ahmad ibn Hanbal and Muhammad ibn Nūh al-Naysābūrī. These two were sent to al-Ma’mūn in chains. Muhammad ibn Nūh died on the journey, and al-Ma’mūn died before Ahmad reached him. His brother Abū Ishāq succeeded him, and Ahmad ibn Abī Du’ād assumed the judgeship. Ahmad ibn Hanbal remained imprisoned from the year eighteen until the year twenty.

They then summoned him and debated with him for several days. He refuted their arguments, demonstrated their unsoundness, and showed that they had produced no evidence for their claims from the Quran, the Sunnah, or transmitted reports. He also explained that they had no right to introduce an innovated doctrine, compel people to agree with them, and punish those who opposed them. People may only be bound by what Allah and His Messenger have made binding upon them, and only those who disobey Allah and His Messenger may be punished. For making things obligatory or forbidden, assigning reward and punishment, and declaring someone an unbeliever or a sinner belong to Allah and His Messenger; no one else has authority to rule on these matters. People are only to deem obligatory what Allah and His Messenger have made obligatory, and to deem forbidden

When this became widely known and people came to understand the true nature of their position—that they denied the divine attributes, saying, “Allah cannot be seen and possesses neither knowledge nor power; there is no Lord above the Throne and no God above the heavens; and Muhammad was not taken up to his Lord,” along with other statements made by the Jahmiyyah who denied the attributes—various groups increasingly refuted them, sometimes through the Quran, hadith, and transmitted reports, sometimes through sound argument, and sometimes through falsehood. Among those who undertook to refute them was Abū Muhammad 'Abd Allāh ibn Sa'īd ibn Kullāb, a man of merit, learning, and religious devotion.

Anyone who claims that he introduced his innovations in order to spread Christianity among Muslims—as some relate when recounting his alleged faults, claiming that he instructed his sister to do this—is lying about him. This allegation was fabricated against him by the Mu'tazilah and Jahmiyyah whom he refuted, for they claim that whoever affirms the divine attributes has adopted the Christian position. Imam Ahmad mentioned a similar claim of theirs in his Refutation of the Jahmiyyah.

This allegation then came to be transmitted by people outside the Mu'tazilah, including members of the Sālimiyyah. It is also related by hadith scholars and jurists who are averse to him because of his innovation concerning the Quran. They bolster their case with statements of this kind, which are fabrications made against him by the Jahmiyyah and Mu'tazilah. These people do not realize that those who disparaged him in this way are worse than he is, and that he is better and closer to the Sunnah than they are.

When Abū al-Hasan al-Ash'arī renounced Mu'tazilism, he followed the approach of Abū Muhammad ibn Kullāb. Some who claimed adherence to the Sunnah and hadith, including members of the Sālimiyyah and others such as Abū 'Alī al-Ahwāzī, consequently began recounting alleged faults of Abū al-Hasan that were fabrications made against him by the Mu'tazilah and others. For al-Ash'arī had exposed the contradictions and unsoundness of the Mu'tazilah’s doctrines as no one else had, until he had utterly cornered them.

When Ibn Kullāb refuted the Jahmiyyah, however, he failed to recognize the unsoundness of the foundational principle underlying the speculative theology they had introduced into Islam. Rather, he agreed with them on it. Those who falsely disparage Ibn Kullāb and al-Ash'arī are drawn from the adherents of hadith and the Sālimiyyah, including Hanbalīs, Shāfi'īs, Mālikīs, and others. Many of them agree with Ibn Kullāb and al-Ash'arī on this point, thus agreeing with the Jahmiyyah on the foundational principle of their innovated doctrine.

When discussing the question of the Quran and its being uncreated, they adopt the arguments of Ibn Kullāb and al-Ash'arī to dispute with the Mu'tazilah and Jahmiyyah, then adopt the arguments of the Jahmiyyah and Mu'tazilah to dispute with Ibn Kullāb and al-Ash'arī. They have fashioned a novel position by combining the views of both sides—a position held by none of the early generations. They agree with Ibn Kullāb, al-Ash'arī, and others in saying that the Quran is eternal, and use their arguments to demonstrate the unsoundness of the position of the Mu'tazilah, Jahmiyyah, and others.

The purpose here is to draw attention to the underlying basis of these groups’ doctrines. Ibn Kullāb introduced what he did because the foundational principle of Jahmī speculative theology had taken root in his heart and driven him to it. Yet he had demonstrated the unsoundness of their denial that Allah is above His creation and their denial of His attributes. He wrote many books on the foundations of Allah’s oneness and His attributes, presenting numerous rational proofs of the unsoundness of the Jahmiyyah’s position. In these works, he explained that Allah’s being above His creation and separate from them is known through both innate human nature and rational inference, just as it is established by the Quran and Sunnah.

Al-Hārith al-Muhāsibī likewise presented these proofs in his book *Fahm al-Qur’ān* (Understanding the Quran) and elsewhere. In it, he explained Allah’s being above His creation and His rising over His Throne in a way that demonstrated the unsoundness of the position of those who deny the attributes.

Many speculative thinkers who understood the foundational principle of the theologians’ doctrine, recognized that Allah’s attributes are established, and rejected the claim that His speech is created welcomed this approach adopted by Ibn Kullāb. They included Abū al-‘Abbās al-Qalānisī, Abū al-Hasan al-Ash‘arī, and al-Thaqafī, as well as their followers, such as Abū ‘Abd Allāh ibn Mujāhid and his companions, Judge Abū Bakr, Abū Ishāq al-Isfarāyīnī, Abū Bakr ibn Fūrak, and others. These scholars proceeded to refute those doctrines of the Mu‘tazilah that had been refuted by Ibn Kullāb and al-Qalānisī

Some of them curbed the power of the Mu‘tazilah and Jahmiyyah sufficiently to bring the hallmarks of the Sunnah to prominence: affirming that the Quran is Allah’s uncreated speech, that Allah will be seen in the Hereafter, and affirming the divine attributes, divine decree, and the other foundations of the Sunnah.

However, the “rational principle” upon which Ibn Kullāb based his position concerning Allah’s speech and attributes was precisely the same principle as that of the Jahmiyyah and Mu‘tazilah. When these scholars discussed Allah’s creation of the heavens, the earth, and other created things, they relied entirely upon the principle introduced by the Jahmiyyah and their followers. Thus, they presented the position of the adherents of the religion as those men had reported it, and supported it using those men’s argument.

The “ordeal of Imam Ahmad” took place in 220 AH. In that year, the esotericist Qarmatians began openly proclaiming their doctrine, for the philosophers’ books had been translated into Arabic and people had become familiar with their views. When the philosophers saw that the doctrine attributed to the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his household was this doctrine espoused by the Jahmī speculative theologians and their followers, and saw that this doctrine was rationally unsound, they aspired to alter the religion. Some of them openly denied the Creator and professed outright unbelief. They fought the Muslims and seized the Black Stone, as did the Qarmatians of Bahrain. translated_text:
the “esotericists” and the stripping away of their veils, for some of them belonged to the negationist, esotericist Khurramiyyah. In their discussions and books, they began employing arguments advanced by Aristotle and his philosophical followers: that motion cannot have a beginning, that time cannot have a beginning, and that an agent cannot begin acting after not having acted. Thus, both these philosophers and these speculative theologians used motion to argue for their respective positions.

Aristotle and his followers say:

“Motion as such cannot begin to exist after not having existed, and an agent cannot begin acting after not having acted. For sound reason clearly establishes that if an entity does nothing and then acts after not having acted, some new event must have occurred. Otherwise, if it is assumed to remain in the same state in which it did not act, it still does not act. If it acts now, its activity must therefore have been perpetual.”

They also say:

“‘Before’ and ‘after’ necessarily imply time. Thus, whoever maintains that time began to exist is committed to affirming its beginninglessness by the very assertion that it began to exist.”

They also say:

“Time is the measure of motion. Its beginninglessness therefore entails the beginninglessness of motion, and the beginninglessness of motion entails the beginninglessness of that which moves—namely, a body. This necessarily establishes the existence of a beginningless body.”

They then identify this beginningless body as the celestial sphere. Yet they have no proof for this, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

The speculative theologians among the Jahmiyyah, Muʿtazilah, Kullābiyyah, and Karrāmiyyah began responding to them, claiming that an agent endowed with power and choice can favour one of two equivalent possibilities within his power over the other, which is identical to it, without any cause whatsoever. On this principle they based their account of Allah as the Creator of created things.

 وَاحْتَجَّ أَهْلُ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبْتَدَعِ بِأَنَّهُ يَمْتَنِعُ وُجُودُ حَوَادِثَ لَا أَوَّلَ لَهَا وَيَقُولُونَ:
 لَوْ وُجِدَتْ حَوَادِثُ لَا أَوَّلَ لَهَا؛ لَكُنَّا إذَا قَدَّرْنَا مَا وُجِدَ قَبْلَ الطُّوفَانِ وَمَا وُجِدَ قَبْلَ الْهِجْرَةِ وَقَابَلْنَا بَيْنَهُمَا؛ فَإِمَّا أَنْ يَتَسَاوَيَا - وَهُوَ مُمْتَنِعٌ - لِأَنَّهُ يَكُونُ الزَّائِدُ مِثْلَ النَّاقِصِ وَإِمَّا أَنْ يَتَفَاضَلَا فَيَكُونُ فِيمَا لَا يُتَنَاهَى تَفَاضَلَا وَهُوَ مُمْتَنِعٌ. وَيَذْكُرُونَ حُجَجًا أُخْرَى قَدْ بُسِطَ الْكَلَامُ عَلَيْهَا فِي غَيْرِ هَذَا الْمَوْضِعِ. وَقَدْ تَكَلَّمَ النَّاسُ فِي هَذِهِ 
" الْحُجَّةِ "
 وَنَحْوِهَا وَبَيَّنُوا فَسَادَهَا؛ بِأَنَّ التَّفَاضُلَ إنَّمَا يَقَعُ مِنْ الطَّرَفِ الْمُتَنَاهِي لَا مِنْ الطَّرَف الَّذِي لَا يَتَنَاهَى وَبِأَنَّ هَذَا
translated_text:
Then those who deny the divine attributes say:

“One possibility prevailed over the other through power alone.”

This is also the principle adopted by the Qadariyyah. The Muʿtazilah combined both positions. As for those who affirm the attributes, such as the Kullābiyyah and Karrāmiyyah, they claim that one possibility prevailed through an eternal, beginningless will. Both views are rejected by most rational people. Thus, many who have written on this subject, such as al-Rāzī and earlier leading figures in speculative theology and philosophy—including al-Shahrastānī and those before him from the various theological and philosophical schools—offer nothing beyond the philosophers’ account in terms of a cause, the Muʿtazilite account in terms of power, or the Kullābī account in terms of will. All three are rejected by reason and revelation. Hence, al-Rāzī’s discussions concerning an agent endowed with power and choice are exceedingly weak in supporting the Muslims’ position; they lend clearer support to the eternalists’ position.

The adherents of innovated speculative theology argued that a beginningless succession of events is impossible. They say:

“If there were a beginningless succession of events, and we considered those that occurred before the Flood and those that occurred before the Hijrah and compared the two, they would either be equal—which is impossible, since the greater would then equal the lesser—or differ in number, so that there would be a difference in magnitude between infinities, which is impossible.”

They advance other arguments that have been discussed at length elsewhere. Others have examined this “argument” and similar ones and demonstrated their invalidity: the difference occurs only at the finite end, not at the infinite end, and because this

 إنَّ ذَلِكَ لَا بِدَايَةَ لَهُ. وَلَيْسَ هَذَا تَعَمُّدًا مِنْهُ لِنَصْرِ الْبَاطِلِ؛ بَلْ يَقُولُ بِحَسَبِ مَا تُوَافِقُهُ الْأَدِلَّةُ الْعَقْلِيَّةُ فِي نَظَرِهِ وَبَحْثِهِ. فَإِذَا وُجِدَ فِي الْمَعْقُولِ بِحَسَبِ نَظَرِهِ مَا يَقْدَحُ بِهِ فِي كَلَامِ الْفَلَاسِفَةِ قَدَحَ بِهِ فَإِنَّ مِنْ شَأْنِهِ الْبَحْثَ الْمُطْلَقَ بِحَسَبِ مَا يَظْهَرُ لَهُ فَهُوَ يَقْدَحُ فِي كَلَامِ هَؤُلَاءِ بِمَا يَظْهَرُ لَهُ أَنَّهُ قَادِحٌ فِيهِ مِنْ كَلَامِ هَؤُلَاءِ وَكَذَلِكَ يَصْنَعُ بِالْآخَرِينَ وَمِنْ النَّاسِ مَنْ يُسِيءُ بِهِ الظَّنَّ وَهُوَ أَنَّهُ يَتَعَمَّدُ الْكَلَامَ الْبَاطِلَ؛ وَلَيْسَ
translated_text:
is refuted by future events, since whether an event is past or future is a relative matter. For this reason, the leading proponents of this view—such as Jahm and al-ʿAllāf—denied the possibility of an endless succession of future events. Jahm maintained that Paradise and Hell would cease to exist, while al-ʿAllāf maintained that movements would cease. All this is discussed at length elsewhere.

“Another group,” familiar with the arguments of both sides—such as al-Rāzī, al-Āmidī, and others—came to write works of speculative theology in which they supported what the innovating theologians presented on behalf of the adherents of the religion concerning “the world’s coming into existence.” They did so through this innovated method of the speculative theologians: asserting the impossibility of a beginningless succession of events. Then they would write philosophical works, such as al-Rāzī’s “Eastern Investigations” and similar writings. In these, he sets out the arguments by which the speculative theologians sought to establish that a beginningless succession of events is impossible and that time, motion, and body have a beginning. He then refutes all these arguments, answers them, and substantiates the argument of those who maintain that these things have no beginning.

This is not a deliberate attempt on his part to support falsehood. Rather, he speaks according to what rational evidence appears to support in his own examination and inquiry. Whenever, in the course of his examination, he finds a rational argument that undermines the philosophers’ position, he uses it against them. His habitual approach is unrestricted inquiry according to what becomes apparent to him. Thus, he criticizes the arguments of one group using whatever arguments of the other appear to him to undermine them, and he treats the other group in the same way. Some people think ill of him, believing that he deliberately advances false arguments; but this is not

the case. Rather, in each instance he spoke according to the extent of his knowledge, reflection, and inquiry, expressing what appeared correct to him. He contradicts himself in most of what he says: he establishes something here, then refutes it elsewhere. This is because the rational material he examined—drawn from the practitioners of innovated speculative theology condemned by the early Muslim generations, and from philosophers outside the faith—contains false arguments on both sides. Thus, he supports one group’s position with arguments that establish it, then refutes it elsewhere with arguments that undermine it.

For this reason, he acknowledged toward the end of his life:

“I have reflected upon the methods of speculative theology and the approaches of philosophy, and I have not found them to heal the sick or quench thirst. I have found the most direct path to be the way of the Quran. Concerning affirmation, read:

‘The Most Merciful rose over the Throne.’

‘To Him ascends good speech.’

And concerning negation, read:

‘There is nothing like unto Him.’

‘They do not encompass Him in knowledge.’

Whoever has experienced what I have experienced will know what I have come to know.”

Al-Āmidī, meanwhile, is largely given to perplexity and suspension of judgment concerning most of the major foundational questions. He even raised an objection to his own argument concerning an infinite regress of causes and claimed that he knew no answer to it, while basing his proof of the Creator’s existence on that argument. Thus, in his books he establishes neither the Creator’s existence, nor the world’s coming into existence, nor Allah’s oneness, nor prophethood, nor any of the fundamental principles that one needs to know.

Although al-Rāzī does establish some of these matters, he generally refutes elsewhere what he establishes. Nevertheless, he is more intent on establishing the fundamental principles that one needs to know than

translated_text:
al-Āmidī. Had he brought together what sound reason establishes in the arguments of both groups, he would have found it all consistent with what the Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—brought, and would have found sound reason in accord with authentic transmitted texts. These thinkers, however, did not understand the true nature of what the Messenger brought, and their rational understanding became confused. Their knowledge of both revelation and reason was therefore deficient. If this deficient understanding represents the utmost a person can attain, and he is unable to overcome it, then his inability excuses him: Allah will not punish him if he has exerted every effort. This accords with the position of the early Muslim generations and the leading scholars: whoever fears Allah to the best of his ability will not be punished for failing to know some aspect of the truth that he is unable to grasp.

As for the claim of some Jahmiyyah and others like them that He may punish those who are incapable, and the claim of some Muʿtazilah and other Qadariyyah that everyone who strives must necessarily come to know the truth, and that whoever fails to know it does so through negligence rather than inability—these are two weak positions. Because of them, the various groups among those who face the qiblah have come to declare one another unbelievers and curse one another.

Thus, “Aristotle and his followers,” who affirm unceasing activity and its necessary implications, may be told:

Sound reason does not establish that any particular thing in the world is beginningless, whether a celestial sphere or anything else. It establishes only that the Lord has always been active. Accordingly, if it is supposed that He has always created one thing after another, then everything other than Him would be created, brought into existence, and preceded by nonexistence, and nothing in the world would be beginningless. You have nothing that invalidates this supposition, so why do you reject it? The very measure of action is

translated_text:
what is called time. For if time is said to be the measure of motion, then time in general is the measure of motion in general; this does not require it to be the measure of the motion of the sun or the celestial sphere.

The adherents of the revealed religions agree that Allah created the heavens and the earth in six days, and that He created them from matter that existed before these heavens and this earth: smoke, which is vapour. As the Most High says:

“Then He turned towards the heaven while it was smoke and said to it and to the earth, ‘Come, willingly or unwillingly.’ They said, ‘We come willingly.’”

This smoke was the vapour of water that existed at that time, as related in reports from the Companions and their successors, and as held by the People of the Book. All this has been discussed elsewhere. Those days were not measured by the motion of this sun and this celestial sphere, for these were among the things created during those days. Rather, those days were measured by another motion.

Likewise, when Allah splits these heavens apart, brings about the Resurrection, and admits the people of Paradise into Paradise, the Most High says:

“And they will have their provision therein, morning and evening.”

Reports from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—state that He, blessed and exalted, manifests Himself to His believing servants on Friday, and that those of the highest rank see Allah Most High twice each day. Yet there is neither sun nor moon in Paradise, nor is there any motion of a celestial sphere there. Rather, that time is measured by movements, as the reports state that they recognize the time by lights appearing from the direction of the Throne.

translated_text:
If rational proof entails that there must be a beginningless Being in whom acts occur one after another, this contradicts only the position of those innovators among the adherents of revealed religions who introduced the speculative theology condemned by the early Muslims and the imams. They said that the Lord had always been devoid of action and speech. Thus, what rational thinkers among the various nations—philosophers and others—have established through clear reason supports and vindicates what the Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—brought, against those who introduced into his religion innovations contrary to his teachings.

What is known through revelation, together with clear reason, also refutes the claim of the eternalist philosophers that anything in the world is beginningless alongside Allah. Indeed, the assertion that “the world has no beginning” is one whose falsity the overwhelming majority of rational thinkers agree upon. It is not rejected by Muslims alone, but by all adherents of revealed religions and most others, including the Magians and the various kinds of polytheists: the polytheists of Arabia, India, and other nations. The overwhelming majority of the leading philosophers acknowledge that this world originated and came into existence after not existing. Indeed, most of them acknowledge that Allah is the Creator of everything. All the Arab polytheists acknowledged that Allah is the Creator of everything, that this entire world is created, and that Allah is its Creator and Lord. These matters are discussed at length in their proper place.

Our purpose here is to discuss what is needed to understand the “hadith of the Descent” and similar reports, namely, “the two principles mentioned earlier.” Completing the discussion of the second principle requires considering the term “motion”: is Allah to be described by it, or must it be denied of Him? There is disagreement on this among Muslims and other adherents of revealed religions

translated_text:
and those outside the revealed religions, with three positions held among hadith scholars, speculative theologians, philosophers, and others. All three positions are found among the followers of the four imams, including the followers of Imam Ahmad and others. Al-Qādī Abū Yaʿlā recorded these three positions among Imam Ahmad’s followers in al-Riwāyatayn wa-l-Wajhayn and other works.

Before discussing this, however, it should be understood that “motion,” “movement from one place to another,” “change,” “transformation,” and similar expressions are terms that admit of more than one meaning. Speculative theologians use the term “motion” only for spatial motion: a body’s movement from one place to another, such that the first space is vacated and the second occupied. Examples include the movement of our bodies from one space to another, and the movement of air, water, earth, and clouds from one space to another, with the first being vacated and the second occupied. Most speculative theologians recognize no meaning of motion other than this.

This is why they denied the forms of motion conveyed by the revealed texts: they assumed that all of them indicated only this meaning. The same applies to those who affirmed them but understood them all in this sense—for example, those who understood His descent to the lowest heaven to mean that some of His creatures remain above Him. He would then not be the Ascendant, above whom there is nothing, nor would He be the Exalted, the Most High. Their position would also entail that He is not established above the Throne at all, as explained earlier.

The philosophers, however, apply the term “motion” to everything involving a transition from one state to another. They also say that the essential nature of motion is coming into being, or coming to be and passing from potentiality to actuality, little by little and by degrees. They say that these expressions convey the meaning of motion.

and they sometimes use these expressions to define motion. They hold two views on whether motion of any kind subsists in the Lord, Most High. Aristotle’s followers restricted motion to bodies, yet they describe the soul as having a kind of motion, although they do not regard it as a body; thus they contradict themselves. They recognized “three types” of motion, but Ibn Sīnā added a fourth category, bringing the total to “four.”

They treat motion as a genus comprising several species: motion in quality, motion in quantity, motion in position, and motion in place.

“Motion in quality” is a thing’s transformation from one quality to another: for example, its becoming black, red, green, or yellow; its becoming sweet or sour; or a change in its smell. The same applies to souls: a person’s acquiring knowledge after ignorance, loving after hating, believing after disbelieving, rejoicing after sorrow, or becoming pleased after anger. All these states of the soul constitute motion in quality. This is among the arguments used by those philosophers who considered motion possible with respect to Him, for, according to them, His willing to bring something into being is motion.

“Motion in quantity” includes a thing’s extension: for example, an animal growing larger after being small and longer after being short, or the growth of trees and plants, with their roots extending into the earth and their branches into the air. This is motion in magnitude and quantity, just as the former is motion in attributes and quality.

It does not pass from one region of space to another; rather, it occupies the same region, but its orientation changes. Thus, one of its parts may face upward and then come to face downward, or face right and then come to face left. This is the type they say Ibn Sīnā added.

In their usage, anyone who performs an action has moved. They also describe states of the soul as motion, saying: “Love stirred within him,” “Zeal stirred within him,” and “His anger was stirred.” These states are described in terms of motion and stillness; thus, one says: “His anger subsided.” Allah, Most High, says:

“When Moses’ anger subsided, he took up the Tablets.”

Al-Ashʿarī argued that motion and its various kinds are not confined to bodies, citing people’s use of such expressions for accidents. He said:

“They say: ‘Fever has come,’ ‘Cold has come,’ ‘Health has come,’ ‘Winter has come,’ and ‘Heat has come,’ and similar expressions in which accidents are described as coming or arriving. The coming of these accidents consists in their arising, in change, and in a transition from one state to another.”

If it is said:

These accidents are described in terms of motion and stillness only because the substrate bearing the accident moves. Otherwise, an accident neither subsists independently nor leaves its substrate. Fever, heat and cold inhere in the air that carries heat and cold. Likewise, anger is the boiling of the heart’s blood in pursuit of revenge, and this is the movement of blood. When the boiling of the blood subsides, anger subsides.

The reply is:

That is not so. Rather, such language is used for accidents that arise gradually in a substrate, even when no body moves along with them, as discussed earlier regarding motion in qualities and attributes. When water grows hot, heat arises in it, and it heats the vessel containing it without any hot body passing into that vessel. When heated water is placed somewhere cold, it cools without any cold body passing into it. Likewise, fever is heat or cold inhering in the body without there passing into each part

of the body a hot or cold body. Although some people say that anger is the boiling of the heart’s blood, it is an attribute inhering in the angry person’s soul, distinct from the boiling of the heart’s blood. That boiling is merely its effect, for the heat of anger warms the blood until it boils. Anger originates in the soul: it is the soul that first acquires this attribute, after which it spreads to the body. The same applies to sorrow, joy, and all other states of the soul. Sorrow causes the blood to withdraw inward, which is why a sorrowful person turns pale. Sorrow is a state of the soul, but the sorrowful person feels unable to repel the misfortune that has befallen him and despairs of doing so; hence his blood retreats inward. An angry person, by contrast, feels capable of repelling the harm or exacting punishment, so his blood spreads outward.

The motion, stillness, and tranquillity attributed to the soul are not like those attributed to the body. Allah Most High says:

“Surely, in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest.”

Tranquillity means stillness. Al-Jawharī said: “Itma’anna al-rajul, with the verbal nouns itmi’nān and tuma’nīnah, means that the man became still.” Allah Most High says:

“O tranquil soul, return to your Lord, well pleased and pleasing to Him.”

Likewise, hearts have a serenity suited to them. Allah Most High says:

“It is He who sent down tranquillity into the hearts of the believers so that they would increase in faith along with their existing faith.”

Likewise, rayb (unease) is the soul’s movement arising from doubt. An example of this usage occurs in the hadith:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, passed by a gazelle lying curled up asleep and said, ‘Let no one disturb it.’”

It is also said, “Something about him aroused my misgivings,” and:

“Leave what makes you uneasy for what does not make you uneasy.”

He also said:

“Lying brings unease, whereas truthfulness brings tranquillity.”
